<meta>This page begins the formal dedication of Galileo's *Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems* to his patron, Ferdinando II de' Medici, the Grand Duke of Tuscany. Following the bureaucratic licenses of the previous page, this is Galileo’s personal introduction, setting the philosophical stage for the work by praising the study of the "Book of Nature."</meta>

## TO THE MOST SERENE
# GRAND DUKE.

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal woodcut ornament consisting of a repeating row of sixteen fleur-de-lis or stylized floral motifs.</image-desc>

THE difference that exists between humans and other animals, however great it may be, if one were to say that a similar degree of difference can exist among humans themselves, they might not be speaking without reason. What proportion is there between one and a thousand? And yet, it is a common proverb that a single man may be worth a thousand, where a thousand are not worth a single one. Such a difference depends on the diverse abilities of intellects, which I attribute to being, or not being, a philosopher. For philosophy—as the proper nourishment of those who can feed upon it—effectively separates them from the common state of the masses, to a greater or lesser degree of worthiness, depending on the variety of such nourishment. 

He who gazes higher, distinguishes himself more highly; and turning toward the great book of Nature—which is the proper object of philosophy—is the way to raise one’s eyes. In that book, although everything one reads is perfectly proportioned (as it is the work of the Almighty Artificer <note>original: "Artefice Onnipotente"; a common 17th-century reference to God as the divine craftsman or architect of the cosmos.</note>), those parts are nonetheless clearer and more worthy where the labor and artistry appear greatest to our sight. The Constitution of the Universe <note>This refers to the physical structure and arrangement of the heavens and the earth.</note>, among things in nature that can be understood, may in my belief be placed in the first rank. For if the universe, as the container of everything, exceeds all others in size, then as the rule and support—

->mantenimento<- 
<note>This is a catchword, a common printing practice where the first syllable of the next page is printed at the bottom right to help the binder assemble the pages in the correct order. The full word on the next page is "mantenimento," meaning maintenance or support.</note>

<summary>This page opens the formal dedication to the Grand Duke of Tuscany, where Galileo argues that the study of the "Book of Nature" (the universe) is the highest form of philosophy and the greatest distinction of the human intellect.</summary>
<keywords>Grand Duke of Tuscany, Ferdinando II de' Medici, Book of Nature, philosophy, intellect, Constitution of the Universe, Almighty Artificer</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Ferdinando II de' Medici, concluding the opening argument about intellectual superiority and the role of the patron in fostering scientific discovery.</meta>

is the foundation of everything, must also surpass them in nobility. Thus, if it ever befell anyone to distinguish himself in intellect far above other men, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer who established the geocentric (earth-centered) model that dominated Western thought for over a millennium.</note> and Copernicus <note>Nicolaus Copernicus, the Renaissance astronomer who formulated the heliocentric model, placing the Sun at the center of the universe.</note> were those who so loftily read, fixed their gaze upon, and philosophized about the Worldly Constitution <term>Worldly Constitution: The physical structure, arrangement, and laws governing the universe.</term>. Since my Dialogues revolve principally around their works, it did not seem right to dedicate them to anyone other than Your Highness. For, as their doctrine rests upon these two—whom I consider the greatest intellects to have left us their works on such speculations—to avoid any loss of prestige, it was fitting to lean them upon the favor of him who is, to me, the Greatest, so that they may receive both glory and patronage. 

And if those two have given so much light to my understanding that this work of mine can be said to be largely theirs, it may well also be called yours, Your Highness; for through your liberal Magnificence <note>Galileo refers to the financial and political support of the Medici family.</note>, I have not only been granted the leisure and quiet <note>original: "ozio, e quiete"; in the 17th century, "ozio" (leisure) was a positive term referring to the freedom from daily toil required for scholarly study.</note> necessary to write, but through your effective help—never tiring of honoring me—it has finally been brought to light. May Your Highness, therefore, accept it with your usual kindness; and if anything should be found therein from which lovers of truth may draw fruit in the form of greater knowledge and benefit, let it be recognized as your own. You are so accustomed to being of help that, within your happy Dominion, no one feels any of those universal hardships present in the world that might disturb them. With this, praying for your prosperity, so that you may ever grow in this pious and magnanimous custom, I offer my most humble reverence.

->Of Your Most Serene Highness<-
->*The most humble and devoted servant and vassal,*<-
->Galileo Galilei.<-

<summary>In this concluding section of the dedication, Galileo identifies Ptolemy and Copernicus as the two greatest minds in astronomy and explicitly links his work to the patronage of Ferdinando II de' Medici. He credits the Grand Duke's support for providing the necessary environment to complete and publish the "Dialogues."</summary>
<keywords>Ptolemy, Copernicus, Worldly Constitution, patronage, Ferdinando II de' Medici, leisure, Galileo Galilei, dedication</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page follows the formal dedication to Grand Duke Ferdinando II de' Medici. It begins the "Preface to the Reader," where Galileo frames the purpose of his work within the context of the Roman Inquisition's 1616 decree against Copernicanism.</meta>

# TO THE DISCREET
## READER.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut headpiece consisting of a horizontal band of symmetrical floral and foliate scrolls centered around a central blossom.</image-desc>

Years ago, a salutary Edict <note>The 1616 Decree of the Index, which prohibited the teaching of the Copernican system as a physical fact to prevent it from contradicting Scripture.</note> was promulgated in Rome which, in order to prevent the dangerous scandals of the present age, imposed a timely silence upon the **Pythagorean opinion** <note>The ancient Greek belief that the Earth moves, a concept Galileo uses here to refer to the Copernican heliocentric model.</note> of the **mobility of the Earth**. There were those who rashly asserted that this decree was the result not of judicious examination, but of poorly informed passion; and complaints were heard that Advisors, totally inexperienced in astronomical observations, should not have clipped the wings of speculative intellects with a sudden prohibition. My zeal could not remain silent upon hearing the audacity of such complaints. Being fully informed of that most prudent determination, I decided to appear publicly on the **Theater of the World** <note>A common Baroque metaphor for the public stage of human history and intellectual debate.</note> as a witness to the sincere truth. I was present in Rome at that time; I received not only audiences, but even applause from the most eminent Prelates of that Court; nor did the publication of that Decree follow without some prior information from me. Therefore, it is my intention in the present work to show to foreign nations that as much is known of this matter in Italy, and particularly in Rome, as **Ultramontane** <note>Literally "beyond the mountains," referring to scholars in Northern Europe, particularly Protestant regions, where the Copernican theory was more openly discussed.</note> diligence could ever have imagined. By gathering together all the specific speculations concerning the **Copernican System**, I wish to make it known that the knowledge of all of them preceded the **Roman censure**; and that from this climate there emerge not only Dogmas for the salvation of the soul, but also ingenious discoveries for the delight of the intellect.

For this purpose, I have taken the Copernican side in the discourse, proceeding by pure **Mathematical Hypothesis** <term>Mathematical Hypothesis: A method of calculating planetary positions without asserting that the model represents physical reality; this was a common way for scientists to discuss forbidden ideas while remaining obedient to the Church.</term>, seeking by every clever means to represent it as superior—not to the absolute stability of the Earth, but according to how it is defended by some who, **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of the philosophy of Aristotle, who taught that the Earth was the unmoving center of the universe.</note> by profession, retain only...

<summary>In this preface, Galileo introduces his work as a defense of the Roman Edict of 1616, arguing that Italy is not scientifically backwards but chooses to treat the Earth's motion as a mathematical hypothesis rather than a physical truth.</summary>
<keywords>Copernican System, Roman Edict, mobility of the Earth, Mathematical Hypothesis, Peripatetics, Rome, scientific censorship</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Preface to the Reader." In the preceding text, Galileo explained that the Roman decree against Copernicanism was not born of ignorance, but of a desire to protect the faith. He continues here by outlining the three main sections of his work and his reasons for choosing the dialogue format.</meta>

...only the name, content to worship shadows without further exploration, not philosophizing with their own insight, but only with the memory of four poorly understood principles.

Three principal headings will be treated. First, I will seek to show that all experiments capable of being performed upon the Earth are insufficient means to conclude its mobility, but can be adapted indifferently both to a moving Earth and to one at rest; and I hope that in this section, many observations unknown to antiquity will be revealed. Secondly, celestial phenomena will be examined, strengthening the **Copernican Hypothesis** <note original: "Ipotesi Copernicana">The model proposed by Nicolaus Copernicus where the Earth and planets revolve around the Sun.</note> as if it were absolutely to emerge victorious, adding new speculations which serve for the ease of Astronomy, rather than by necessity of nature. In the third place, I will propose an ingenious fantasy. I recall having said many years ago that the unknown problem of the **ebb and flow of the sea** <note original: "flusso del Mare">The tides. Galileo believed that the Earth's motion provided the physical explanation for the tides, though this theory was later proven incorrect.</note> might receive some light if the terrestrial motion were admitted. This saying of mine, flying through the mouths of men, found charitable fathers who adopted it as the offspring of their own intellect. Now, so that no stranger may ever appear who, strengthening himself with our own weapons, might reproach us for a lack of insight into such a principal event, I have judged it fit to reveal those probabilities which would make it persuasive, given the premise that the Earth moves. I hope that from these considerations the world will recognize that if other nations have navigated more, we have speculated no less; and that returning to assert the stability of the Earth, and taking the contrary only as a **mathematical whim** <note original: "capriccio Matematico">A phrase used to appease censors, suggesting heliocentrism is a mere calculating tool rather than a physical claim.</note>, does not arise from a lack of awareness of what others have thought, but if for no other reason, from those arguments provided to us by Piety, Religion, the knowledge of Divine Omnipotence, and a consciousness of the weakness of the human intellect.

I then thought it very appropriate to explain these concepts in the form of a **Dialogue**, which, by not being restricted to the rigorous observance of mathematical laws, provides a field for digressions that are sometimes no less curious than the principal argument.

Many years ago, I found myself several times in the wonderful city of **Venice** in conversation with Signor **Giovan Francesco Sagredo**, a man of most illustrious birth and sharpest intellect.

<summary>Galileo outlines the three-part structure of his book—covering terrestrial experiments, celestial observations, and his theory of tides—while explaining that he chose the dialogue format to allow for engaging digressions.</summary>
<keywords>Copernican Hypothesis, mobility of the Earth, tides, mathematical whim, Dialogue, Giovan Francesco Sagredo, Venice, Inquisition decree</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the general plan of the book to the introduction of the specific characters who will conduct the dialogue: Salviati (representing the Copernican view), Sagredo (the intelligent, neutral host), and Simplicio (the traditional Aristotelian).</meta>

Lord Filippo Salviati came there from Florence; in him, the least of his splendors were his noble blood and the magnificence of his riches. He possessed a sublime intellect, which fed upon no delight more greedily than upon exquisite speculations. With these two, I often found myself discussing these matters, alongside a **Peripatetic Philosopher** <note original: "Filosofo Peripatetico">A follower of Aristotle's school of philosophy, so named for the *peripatos* or covered walkways in Athens where the philosopher and his students walked while teaching.</note> who believed that nothing hindered the understanding of truth more than the fame one acquired through traditional **Aristotelian interpretations** <note original: "interpretazioni Aristoteliche">The standard academic readings of the works of the Greek philosopher Aristotle, which dominated the universities of the time.</note>.

Now, since a most bitter death has—in the brightest prime of their lives—deprived Venice and Florence of those two great lights, I have resolved to extend their fame through these writings of mine, as far as my weak powers allow, by introducing them as the speakers in this present controversy. Nor shall the good Peripatetic lack his place; because of his excessive affection for the commentaries of **Simplicius** <note original: "Simplicio">A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle. Galileo uses this name for his fictional Aristotelian character, likely as a pun on the Italian word for "simpleton" (*semplice*).</note>, it seemed appropriate to allow him the name of that revered author, while keeping his own name hidden. May those two great souls, forever venerable to my heart, accept this public monument of my undying love; and through the memory of their eloquence, may they help me explain these promised speculations to posterity.

As often happens, various fragmented discussions had occurred by chance between these gentlemen, which had served more to ignite than to satisfy the thirst for learning in their minds. Therefore, they made the wise resolution to meet for several days to come, during which, setting aside all other business, they would devote themselves to contemplating—through more orderly inquiry—the **wonders of God in the Heavens and on the Earth**. The gathering took place at the Palace of the **Most Illustrious Sagredo** <note original: "Illustrissimo Sagredo">Giovanni Francesco Sagredo (1571–1620), a Venetian nobleman and close friend of Galileo, who acts as the host and the open-minded listener in the book.</note>; after the required, but brief, pleasantries, Lord Salviati began in this manner.

<summary>Galileo introduces the three interlocutors of his dialogue—Salviati, Sagredo, and the Aristotelian Simplicio—and explains that he wrote the work to memorialize his deceased friends and their intellectual pursuits.</summary>
<keywords>Filippo Salviati, Giovanni Francesco Sagredo, Simplicio, Aristotle, Peripatetic, Florence, Venice, dialogue characters, memorial</keywords>

<meta>The previous page fragment appears to be from a completely different, unrelated document concerning a nobleman named Filippo. This page begins the famous scientific dialogue by Galileo Galilei, setting the stage for a debate between different world systems.</meta>

# FIRST DAY.
## Interlocutors,
### SALVIATI, SAGREDO, AND SIMPLICIO.

<image-desc>A small horizontal woodcut ornament with scrolling motifs.</image-desc>

SALV. It was the conclusion and the appointment made yesterday that on this day we should discuss, as distinctly and particularly as we are able, the natural reasons and their effectiveness which have been produced thus far by both sides—by the supporters of the Aristotelian <term>Aristotelian: Referring to the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle, whose views dominated science for centuries.</term> and Ptolemaic <term>Ptolemaic: Referring to Claudius Ptolemy, who proposed the Earth-centered model of the universe.</term> position, and by the followers of the Copernican System. <margin>Copernicus considers the Earth to be a globe similar to a planet.</margin> And because Copernicus, by placing the Earth among the moving bodies of the Heavens, makes it also a globe similar to a planet, it will be well for the beginning of our considerations to be the examination of the force and energy in the Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: A name for the followers of Aristotle, derived from his habit of walking about while teaching.</term> arguments when they demonstrate how such an assumption is entirely impossible. <margin>Celestial substances are unchangeable, and elementary ones are changeable, as is necessary in nature according to the mind of Aristotle.</margin> This is because they find it necessary to introduce into nature substances that are different from one another: namely, the Celestial and the Elementary. The former is impassive <note>original: "impassibile"—meaning it cannot be changed or affected by external forces</note> and immortal, while the latter is changeable and decaying. He treats this argument in his books *On the Heavens* <note>Aristotle's treatise *De Caelo*</note>, introducing it first through discourses depending on certain general assumptions, and later confirming it with experiences and demonstrations.

<summary>This page marks the beginning of the 'First Day' of the dialogue, where the character Salviati proposes examining the Aristotelian belief that the Heavens are unchangeable while the Earth is subject to decay.</summary>
<keywords>Galileo Galilei, Copernican system, Aristotle, Ptolemy, cosmology, celestial substances, Peripatetic philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the opening dialogue of the First Day. Salviati is transitioning from his introductory remarks about the nature of the universe to a specific critique of Aristotle's definition of the "perfect" world. He invites Simplicio, the defender of traditional Aristotelian thought, to engage in the debate. The catchword "tra-" suggests the previous page ended with "dimo-" (forming "dimostrazioni" or "demonstrations").</meta>

# First Dialogue

<header>First Dialogue</header>

<margin>Aristotle makes the world perfect because it has the triple dimension.</margin>

*...particular demonstrations. Following this same order, I will propose and then freely state my opinion, exposing myself to the criticism of you both, and specifically of Signor Simplicio, who is such a strenuous champion and maintainer of the Aristotelian doctrine <term>Aristotelian doctrine: The system of philosophy and science based on the works of Aristotle, which was the standard academic authority in Galileo's time.</term>. The first step of the Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: A name for the followers of Aristotle, who often taught while walking about.</term> progress is that passage where Aristotle proves the integrity and perfection of the World by pointing out to us how it is not a simple line, nor a pure surface, but a body adorned with length, width, and depth. Because dimensions do not exceed these three, and because the world has all three, it has them all; and having all, it is perfect. He argues that from simple length is constituted that magnitude called a line; when width is added, a surface is constituted; and when height or depth is added, a body results. After these three dimensions, there is no passage to any other, so that in these three alone, integrity—and, so to speak, totality—is terminated. I would have dearly wished that Aristotle had demonstrated this to me with necessity <note>original: "con necessità" — meaning a logical proof that cannot be otherwise</note>, especially since it could be performed quite clearly and quickly.*

<margin>Aristotle's demonstrations to prove the dimensions are three, and no more. The number three was famous among the Pythagoreans.</margin>

SIMP. *There is no lack of most beautiful demonstrations in the second, third, and fourth texts, following the definition of the Continuous <term>Continuous: In geometry, a magnitude where the parts are joined at a common boundary.</term>. Do you not have, first of all, the proof that beyond the three dimensions there is no other, because "three" is everything, and "three" is in every direction? And is this not confirmed by the authority and doctrine of the Pythagoreans <term>Pythagoreans: Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe.</term>, who say that all things are determined by three: beginning, middle, and end, which is the number of the "whole"? And where do you leave the other reason—namely, that almost by natural law this number is used in the sacrifices of the Gods? And that, nature itself dictating thus, we attribute the title of "all" to things that are three, and not fewer? For of two things we say "both," and we do not say "all," but of three we certainly do. You have all this doctrine in Text 2. In Text 3, then, <note>original Latin: "ad pleniorem scientiam"</note> for a fuller understanding, one reads that "everything," "the whole," and "the perfect" are formally the same; and that therefore only the body, among magnitudes, is perfect, because it alone is determined by three, which is the "whole." Being divisible in three ways, it is divisible in all directions. But of the others, some are divisible in one way, and some in two, because they possess division and continuity according to the number that has fallen to them; thus one is continuous in one direction, another in two, but the last—that is, the Body—is continuous in all. Furthermore, in Text 4, after some other doctrines, does he not prove the same with another demonstration—namely, that no passage is made...*

**SALV.** *To tell the truth, in all these discourses I have not felt myself compelled to grant anything else except that what has a beginning, a middle, and an end can, and must, be called perfect. <margin>
The human intellect participates in divinity because it understands numbers; the opinion of Plato.
The mysteries of Pythagorean numbers are fables.

**SALV.** *That the Pythagoreans held the science of numbers in the highest esteem, and that Plato himself admired the human intellect and judged it a participant in Divinity solely because it understands the nature of numbers, I know very well, nor would I be far from making the same judgment. But that the mysteries for which Pythagoras and his sect held the science of numbers in such veneration are the nonsense that passes through the mouths and the papers of the common folk, I do not believe in any way. On the contrary, because I know that they—so that marvelous things would not be exposed to the insults and contempt of the masses—condemned as sacrilege the publication of the more hidden properties of numbers and of the incommensurable <term>Incommensurable: Quantities that cannot be measured by the same unit, such as the relationship between the side and the diagonal of a square; this led to the discovery of irrational numbers.</term> and irrational quantities they investigated, and preached that whoever had revealed them would be tormented in the other world; I think that one of them, to give the common people something to chew on and free himself from their questions, told them that their numerical mysteries were those trivialities that then spread...*

**SALV.** *Your choice and the reason you give for it seem most perfect to me; so that thus far we have established that the first dimension is determined by a straight line; the second, that is, the width, by another straight line—and not only straight, but furthermore at right angles to the other which determined the length. Thus we have defined the two dimensions of a surface, namely length and width. **SAGR.** *I would attach a string to the ceiling, and with a small lead weight <term>lead weight: original "piombino," a plumb bob used by builders to find a true vertical line.</term> hanging from it, I would let it hang freely until it reached near the floor; and the length of such a string being the straightest and shortest of all lines that could be drawn from that same point to the floor, I would say that it was the true height of this room.*

**SALV.** *Very well. And when, from the point marked on the floor by this hanging string (assuming the floor is level and not inclined), you were to draw two other straight lines, one for the length and the other for the width of the surface of that floor, what angles would they form with that string?*

**SAGR.** *They would surely form right angles, since the string falls plumb <note>original: "a piombo"—perfectly vertical.</note> and the floor is quite flat and well-leveled.*

**SALV.** *Therefore, if you establish any point as the head and termi—*

# First Dialogue

*...of the measures, and from it you will make a straight line depart, as the determinant of the first measure, that is, the length; it will be necessary by necessity that the one which must define the width departs at a right angle upon the first, and that the one which has to mark the height—which is the third dimension—departing from the same point, also forms with the other two angles that are not oblique, but right. And thus from the three perpendiculars you will have, as from three unique, certain, and shortest lines, the three dimensions determined: A.B. length, A.C. width, A.D. height. And because it is a clear thing that at the same point no other line can meet that makes right angles with those, and the dimensions must be determined by the only straight lines that among themselves make right angles, therefore the dimensions are no more than three; and he who has the three has them all, and he who has them all is divisible in all directions, and he who is such is perfect, etc.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing three lines meeting at a central point 'A'. Line 'AB' extends horizontally to the right. Line 'AD' extends vertically upwards. **SIMP.** *And who says that other lines cannot be drawn? And why can I not make another line come from below up to point A that is square <note>original: "a squadra"—meaning perpendicular or forming a 90-degree angle.</note> with the others?*

**SALV.** *You certainly cannot, at one and the same point, make anything else meet except three straight lines alone which constitute right angles among themselves.*

**SAGR.** *Yes, because the one that Mr. Simplicio mentions seems to me would be the same D.A. prolonged downwards; and in this way one could draw another two, but they would be the same first three, differing in nothing except that where they now only touch, they would then intersect; but they would not bring new dimensions.*

<margin>In natural proofs, one must not seek geometric exactness.</margin>
**SIMP.** *I will not say that this reason of yours cannot be conclusive, but I will say indeed with Aristotle <note>original: "Aristotile"</note> that in natural things <term>natural things: refers to the study of the physical world or physics, as opposed to the abstract world of mathematics.</term> one must not always seek the necessity of a mathematical demonstration.*

**SAGR.** *Yes, perhaps where it cannot be had; but if it is available here, why do you not want to use it? But it will be well not to spend any more words on this particular, because I believe that Mr. Salviati would have granted to Aristotle and to you, without other demonstrations, that the World is a body, and is perfect, and most perfect, as the greatest work of God.*

### [Of Galileo.]

<margin>
The two parts of the world, according to Aristotle: Celestial and Elementary, which are contrary to one another.

<margin>
Local motions are of three kinds: straight, circular, and mixed.

§ **SALV.** That is truly how it is. However, leaving behind the general contemplation of the whole, let us look at the consideration of the parts. Aristotle, in his first division, makes these two, and they are extremely diverse from one another, and in a certain way contrary; I mean the Celestial and the Elementary. The former is ungenerable, incorruptible, unalterable, impassible <note>original: "ingenerabile, incorruttibile, inalterabile, impassibile"—these terms describe a heaven that is eternal and cannot be changed or affected by physical forces.</note>, etc. And the latter is exposed to a continuous alteration, mutation, etc. This difference he derives, as if from its original principle, from the diversity of local motions <term>local motion: the movement of a body from one place to another</term>; and he proceeds with this progression.

<margin>
Straight and circular motions are simple because they are made along simple lines.
</margin>
Stepping out, so to speak, from the Sensible World <note>the physical world we perceive through our senses</note> and retreating to the Ideal World, he begins architecturally to consider that, since nature is the principle of motion, it is fitting that natural bodies should be capable of local motion. He then declares local movements to be of three kinds: namely, circular, straight, and a mixture of the straight and the circular. The first two he calls "simple," because, of all lines, only the circular and the straight are simple. From here, narrowing his focus somewhat, he defines simple movements again: one is circular—that which is made around the center <note>original: "mezzo"—referring to the center of the universe, which in the Aristotelian view is the center of the Earth.</note>—and the others are straight, being upward and downward. Upward is that which moves away from the center; downward is that which goes toward the center. From this he infers, as is necessarily fitting, that all simple movements are restricted to these three species: namely, toward the center, away from the center, and around the center. This corresponds, he says, with a certain beautiful proportion to what was said above regarding the body: that it is perfected in three things, and so is its motion. Having established these movements, he continues by saying that since some natural bodies are simple and others are composed of them (and he calls simple bodies those that have a natural principle of motion, such as fire and Earth), it is fitting that simple movements belong to simple bodies, and mixed movements to compound bodies—in such a way, however, that the compound bodies follow the motion of the part that predominates in the composition.

§ **SAGR.** Please, Mr. Salviati, stop for a moment, because I feel so many doubts sprouting up from so many sides in this progression that I will be forced to either speak them if I want to listen attentively to the things you will add, or else withdraw my attention from what you are about to say if I want to keep the memory of these doubts.

§ **SALV.** I will very gladly stop, because I am running a similar risk myself, and I am on the verge of getting lost from one moment to the next while I must sail between rocks and such broken waves that they make me—

**SAGR.** You, along with Aristotle, at the beginning separated me somewhat from the Sensible World <note>the physical world perceived by the senses</note> to point out the architecture with which it was to be built; and to my delight, you began by telling me that a natural body is by nature mobile, since nature has been defined elsewhere as the principle of motion. </margin>

For if natural bodies all possess a principle of movement, then either it was not necessary to include "rest" in the definition of nature, or it was not necessary to introduce such a definition in this place. <margin>
A helix around a cylinder could be called a simple line.
</margin>

<margin>

</margin>

Furthermore, he posits, as has been said, simple motions and mixed motion, calling circular and straight simple, and mixed the compound of these; of natural bodies he calls some simple (that is, those which have a natural principle for simple motion) and others compound; and he attributes simple motions to simple bodies, and compound to compound ones: But by compound motion he no longer means the mixture of straight and circular, which can exist in the World; but introduces a mixed motion as impossible as it is impossible to mix opposite movements made in the same straight line, so that from them a motion arises that is part upward and part downward; and, to moderate such an incongruity and impossibility, he reduces himself to saying that such mixed bodies move according to the predominant simple part: which finally necessitates others to say that even motion made along the same straight line is sometimes simple, and at other times also compound: so that the simplicity of motion is no longer expected from the simplicity of the line alone.

# First Dialogue

**SAGR.** *Very well indeed; and what do you say, Mr. Simplicio? A moment ago, you wanted simple and mixed motion to teach me which bodies are simple and which are mixed, and now you want me to come to a knowledge of what simple and mixed motion is from the simple and mixed bodies; an excellent rule for never being able to recognize either the motions or the bodies. Furthermore, you have now declared that greater speed is no longer enough for you, but you require a third condition to define simple movement, for which Aristotle was satisfied with only one: namely, the simplicity of the path <note>Original: "spazio" (space), here referring to the geometric line or trajectory.</note>; But now, according to you, simple motion will be that which is made upon a simple line, with a certain determined speed, by a simple moving body. Let it be as you please, and let us return to Aristotle, who defined mixed motion for me as that which is composed of the straight and the circular; but then he did not find any body for me that was naturally moveable by such a motion.*

<margin>
The circular line is perfect according to Aristotle, and the straight line is imperfect, and why.
</margin>

**SALV.** *I return then to Aristotle, who, having begun his discourse very well and methodically, but having more of an eye toward ending up and hitting a target already established in his mind than toward where the progress of the argument was directly leading him, interrupts the thread and steps out sideways to state—as if it were a known and manifest thing—that as for straight motions upward and downward, these naturally belong to Fire and Earth; and that it is therefore necessary that, besides these bodies which are near us, there be another in nature to which circular movement belongs. This body would be as much more excellent as circular motion is more perfect than straight motion. As for how much more perfect the former is than the latter, he determines this from the perfection of the circular line over the straight, calling the circular perfect and the straight imperfect; <note>Aristotle's physics held that the heavens were made of a "fifth element" (aether) because circular motion has no beginning or end, unlike earthly motion which starts and stops.</note> imperfect because if it is infinite, it lacks an end and a limit; if it is finite, there is something outside of it where it can be extended. This is the first stone, the base, and the foundation of the entire fabric of the Aristotelian World, upon which are supported all the other properties of being neither heavy nor light, of being ungenerable, <note>Term: ungenerable - something that cannot be created or born, but has always existed.</note> incorruptible, and exempt from every change except for change of location, etc. And all these qualities <note>Original: "passioni" (passions/attributes).</note> he affirms to be proper to the simple body that moves with circular motion; and the contrary conditions of gravity, lightness, corruptibility, etc., he assigns to the bodies that naturally move with straight motions. Whence, whenever in—*

# Of Galileo.

*...if the foundation established so far is found to be flawed, one may reasonably doubt all the rest that is built upon it. I do not deny that what Aristotle has introduced so far—with a general discourse depending on universal and primary principles—is later reconfirmed in the course of his work with specific reasons and experiments. All of these must be distinctly considered and weighed. However, since many and not insignificant difficulties present themselves in what has been said so far (and it is truly necessary that first principles and foundations be secure, firm, and stable, so that one may build upon them with greater resolution), it might perhaps be well, before the heap of doubts increases, to see if by chance (as I suspect) we might direct ourselves toward a straighter and more secure path by walking another way, and whether we might establish the first foundations with better-considered architectural rules.* <note>Salviati uses the metaphor of "architecture" to describe the logical structure of the universe.</note> *Therefore, suspending for now the progress of Aristotle—which we shall take up again in due time and examine piece by piece—I say that regarding the things he has said so far, I agree with him and admit that the World is a body endowed with all dimensions, and therefore most perfect.* 
<margin>The World is assumed by the author to be perfectly ordered.</margin>
*And I add that, as such, it is necessarily most ordered; that is, composed of parts arranged among themselves with the highest and most perfect order. This assumption, I believe, will not be denied by you or by anyone else.*

**SIMP.** *And who would you have deny it? In the first place, it is a concept from Aristotle himself; and furthermore, its very name <note>Original: "denominazione." In Greek, the world is called "Kosmos," which means "order."</note> does not seem to be taken from anything other than the order which it perfectly contains.*

**SALV.** *This principle being established, then, one can immediately conclude that if the* <term>integral bodies<note>The major, constituent parts of the universe, such as the Earth, the Sun, and the planets.</note></term> *of the World are to be by their nature mobile, it is impossible for their movements to be straight, or anything other than circular. <margin>Straight motion is impossible in a well-ordered World.</margin>
*for that which moves with straight motion changes place, and by continuing to move, it goes further and further away from the point from which it departed, and from all the places through which it successively passes. And if such motion were naturally suited to it, then from the beginning it was not in its natural place; and therefore the parts of the World were not arranged with perfect order. But we suppose them to be perfectly ordered; therefore, as such, it is impossible that they have from nature the impulse to change place, and consequently to move with straight motion. Furthermore, straight motion being by its nature*
<margin>Straight motion is by its nature infinite.</margin>

### Dialogue One

<margin>
Straight motion is impossible by nature.
</margin>
*...infinite, because the straight line is infinite and indeterminate, it is impossible for any moving thing to have from nature a principle of moving in a straight line—that is, toward a place where it is impossible to arrive, there being no predefined boundary;* <margin>
Nature does not undertake to do that which is impossible to be done.
</margin> *and nature, as Aristotle himself well says, does not undertake to do what cannot be done, nor does it undertake to move toward where it is impossible to reach. And even if someone should say that, although the straight line (and consequently motion along it) is producible to infinity—that is, unbounded—nevertheless nature has, so to speak, arbitrarily assigned it certain boundaries and given natural instincts to its natural bodies to move toward them, I will respond that this* <margin>
Straight motion perhaps existed in the first Chaos.
</margin> *could perhaps be told as a fable of what happened in the first Chaos <note>In ancient cosmology, Chaos refers to the formless state of the universe before it was ordered into the cosmos.</note>, where indistinct matters wandered confusedly and inordinately. To order these, nature might have very conveniently made use of straight motions; for just as these motions throw well-constituted bodies into disorder, so* <margin>
Straight motion is suited to ordering ill-ordered bodies.
</margin> *are they suited to properly ordering those that are ill-disposed. But after the optimal distribution and placement, it is impossible that there should remain in them a natural inclination to move further in straight motion, from which now only a removal from their proper and natural place would follow—that is, a falling into disorder. We can therefore say that straight motion serves to bring the materials together to build the work; but once it is built, it must either remain immobile or, if moving, move only circularly.* <margin>
Worldly bodies moved by a principle of straight motion and then circularly according to Plato.
</margin> *Unless we wish to say with Plato that even worldly bodies, after having been built and completely established, were for some time set in straight motion by their Maker; but after having reached certain and determined places, they were revolved one by one in a circle, passing from straight motion to circular, where they have since maintained themselves and still continue. A most lofty thought, and well worthy of Plato: concerning which I happen to have heard our mutual friend, the Lincean Academician <note>original: "Accademico Linceo." Galileo is referring to himself; he was a member of the Academy of the Lincei, or the "Lynx-Eyed," a pioneering scientific society.</note>, discourse; and if I remember correctly, the discourse was as follows:* <margin>
A moving body placed at rest will not move if it has no inclination toward any particular place.
</margin> *Any body established by whatever cause in a state of rest, but which by its nature is movable, when set at liberty will move, provided however that it has by nature an inclination toward some particular place; for if it were indifferent to all, it would remain in its rest, having no more reason to move to this place than to that. From having this inclination, it necessarily follows that in its motion it will go on continually accelerating; and beginning*

<meta>This page continues the First Dialogue. Salviati has been discussing the nature of straight versus circular motion. # Of Galileo.

<margin>A moving body accelerates its motion as it goes toward the place where it has a natural inclination.</margin>
<margin>A moving body, starting from rest, passes through all degrees of slowness. This is the degree of infinite slowness.</margin>
<margin>A moving body does not accelerate except when it gains proximity to its goal.</margin>
<margin>To induce degrees of velocity in a moving body, nature makes it move in a straight line.</margin>
<margin>Uniform velocity is suited to straight motion. <note>The marginal note here mentions "straight motion," though Salviati's argument in the text will conclude that uniform velocity is the natural state of circular motion.</note></margin>
...starting with a very slow motion, it will not acquire any degree of velocity without first having passed through all the lesser degrees of velocity—or, we might say, the greater degrees of slowness. Because, starting from a state of rest (which is the degree of infinite slowness of motion <note>Galileo defines "rest" as "infinite slowness" to show that speed and slowness exist on a continuous scale.</note>), there is no reason why it should enter into a specific, determined degree of velocity before entering a lesser one, and another even lesser before that. Indeed, it seems very reasonable to pass first through the degrees closest to the point of departure, and from those to the more remote. But the degree from which the moving body begins its journey is that of supreme slowness: that is, rest. Now, this acceleration of motion will not happen except when the moving body gains something; and this "gain" is nothing other than its approach to the desired place—that is, where its natural inclination pulls it. It will be led there by the shortest path, which is a straight line. We can therefore reasonably say that nature, to confer a specific velocity upon a moving body previously at rest, makes use of moving it for some time and through some space in a straight line.

Given this discourse, let us imagine that God created a body—for example, Jupiter—to which He determined to grant a specific velocity which it should thereafter preserve perpetually and uniformly. We might say, alongside Plato <note>This refers to the "Platonic Cosmogony," a theory Galileo favored where planets were dropped from a distance and then turned into their orbits once they reached the correct speed.</note>, that He gave it a straight and accelerated motion from the beginning, and then, once it reached that specific degree of velocity, He converted its straight motion into a circular one, for which the velocity is naturally suited to be uniform.

<margin>Between rest and any intermediate degree of velocity, there are infinite lesser degrees of velocity.</margin>
SAGREDO. *I hear this discourse with great pleasure, and I believe my pleasure will be even greater after you have removed a difficulty for me. I do not quite understand why it is a necessity that a moving body, departing from rest and entering into a motion for which it has a natural inclination, must pass through all the preceding degrees of slowness that exist between any marked degree of velocity and the state of rest. Since these degrees are infinite, why could nature not have contributed to the body of Jupiter, immediately upon its creation, its circular motion with such-and-such a velocity?*

<margin>Nature does not immediately confer a determined degree of velocity, even though it could.</margin>
SALVIATI. *I have not said, nor would I dare to say, that it would be impossible for nature and for God to confer that velocity you speak of immediately. But I will say indeed that, in fact <note>original: "de facto"</note>, nature does not do so; so that doing so would be an operation outside the natural course, and therefore a miracle.*

# First Dialogue

**SAGR.** *So you believe that a stone, departing from rest and entering into its natural motion toward the center of the Earth, passes through all the degrees of slowness inferior to any given degree of speed?*

**SALV.** *I believe it; indeed, I am certain of it, and certain with such confidence that I can make you certain of it as well.*

**SAGR.** *If in all of today’s conversation I gained nothing else but such knowledge, I would consider it a great treasure <note>Original: "capitale," implying a significant investment or asset of knowledge.</note>.*

<margin>The moving body, departing from rest, passes through all degrees of speed without lingering in any.</margin>

**SALV.** *As far as I can understand from your reasoning, a large part of your difficulty consists in the requirement of passing, in a time—and even a very brief one—through those infinite degrees of slowness preceding whatever speed is acquired by the moving body in that time. Therefore, before moving on to anything else, I will try to remove this doubt from you. This should be an easy thing to do when I remind you that the moving body passes through the said degrees, but the passage is made without lingering in any one of them. Thus, since the passage requires no more than a single instant of time, and since any small amount of time contains infinite instants, we will not lack enough of them to assign one to each of the infinite degrees of slowness, however brief the time may be.*

**SAGR.** *Up to this point, I follow you; nevertheless, it seems a great thing to me that a cannonball (for such I imagine the falling body to be) which is seen to descend with such precipitous haste that in fewer than ten pulse beats <note>Galileo frequently used the human pulse as a reliable, portable timer for his experiments before the invention of the pendulum clock.</note> it will cover more than two hundred cubits <note>Original: *braccia*. **SALV.** *You might as well say in an entire year, nor in ten, nor in a thousand; just as I shall strive to persuade you, perhaps even without your contradiction, by asking you a few very simple questions. **SAGR.** *Of this, I am most certain.*

### First Dialogue

<margin>
The impetus <note>Galileo uses "impeto" to describe what we might now call momentum or final velocity acquired during a fall.</note> of moving bodies is equal if they have approached the center of the Earth by an equal distance. On a horizontal plane, a moving body will remain still.
</margin>

**SAGREDO:** I resolutely believe so; because, in effect, both have approached the center equally, and based on what I have just now conceded, their acquired impetus would be equally sufficient to restore them to the same height.

**SALVIATI:** Now tell me what you believe that same ball would do if placed on the horizontal plane A-B.

**SAGREDO:** It would stay still, as that plane has no inclination whatsoever.

**SALVIATI:** But on the inclined plane C-A, it would descend, though with a slower motion than along the perpendicular C-B.

**SAGREDO:** I was about to answer resolutely "yes," as it seems to me necessary that the motion along the perpendicular C-B must be faster than along the incline C-A. However, if this is so, how can the body falling along the incline, upon reaching point A, have as much impetus—that is, the same degree of velocity—as the body falling along the perpendicular will have at point B? These two propositions seem to contradict each other.

<margin>
The velocity along the inclined plane is equal to the velocity along the perpendicular, yet the motion along the perpendicular is faster than along the incline.
</margin>

**SALVIATI:** Therefore, it will seem even more false to you if I say that, absolutely, the velocities of bodies falling along the perpendicular and along the incline are equal. And yet, this is a very true proposition, just as this other one is also true: that the falling body moves more quickly along the perpendicular than along the incline.

<note>This is the "Galilean Paradox." While the *final* speed at the bottom of both paths is the same because they started from the same height, the *time* it takes to reach the bottom is much longer on the incline. Therefore, it is "slower" in terms of time, but "equally fast" in terms of final intensity of motion.</note>

**SAGREDO:** To my ears, these sound like contradictory propositions; what do you think, Mr. Simplicio?

**SIMPLICIO:** They seem the same to me.

**SALVIATI:** I believe you are mocking me, pretending not to understand what you actually understand better than I do. So tell me, Mr. Simplicio: when you imagine one moving body to be faster than another, what concept do you form in your mind?

**SIMPLICIO:** I imagine the one passing through a greater space in the same amount of time than the other; or else, passing through an equal space, but in less time.

**SALVIATI:** Very good; and for bodies that are equally fast, what concept do you imagine?

**SIMPLICIO:** I imagine that they pass through equal spaces in equal times.

Thus, there is no doubt that one can mark out planes so little elevated above the **horizon** <term>orizonte: the horizontal line A.B., representing the ground level</term> A.B. that the moving body—that is, the same ball—would take a very long time indeed to reach point A; since to reach it via the plane B.A.,

### First Dialogue

<margin>
The sizes of the orbits and the speeds of the planetary motions correspond proportionately to their having descended from the same place.

*To this I wish to add another particular observation, also by our **Academician** <note>Galileo refers to himself as "the Academician" throughout the dialogue, as he was a member of the Accademia dei Lincei.</note>, which is quite marvelous. Let us imagine that among the decrees of the **Divine Architect** <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for God as a geometer or builder of the universe.</note>, there was the intention to create in the World these globes that we see continually moving in circles, and to have established the center of their **revolutions** <term>revolutions: the complete orbital paths of the planets around a central point</term>, and in it placed the immobile Sun. Then, imagine that He constructed all the said globes in the same place, and from there gave them the inclination to move, descending toward the center until they acquired those degrees of speed that seemed right to that same Divine Mind. Once these speeds were acquired, they were turned into orbits, each in its own circle, maintaining the speed already conceived. We seek to find at what height and distance from the Sun was the place where these globes were first created, and whether it is possible that the creation of all of them occurred in the same place.* 

*To perform this investigation, it is necessary to take from the most expert astronomers the sizes of the circles in which the planets revolve, and likewise the times of their revolutions. From these two pieces of knowledge, one gathers, for example, how much faster the motion of Jupiter is than the motion of Saturn. Having found (as indeed is the case) that Jupiter moves more quickly, it follows that, having departed from the same height, Jupiter has descended further than Saturn, just as we also know to be true, since its orbit is lower than that of Saturn. But moving further, from the proportion between the two speeds of Jupiter and Saturn, and from the distance between their orbits, and from the proportion of the **acceleration of natural motion** <term>natural motion: the spontaneous downward movement of a heavy body toward its center, which Galileo identifies as accelerating</term>, one can find at what height and distance from the center of their revolutions was the place from which they departed. Having found and established this, we search to see if Mars, descending from there to its orbit, matches the size of the orbit and the speed of motion given to us by the calculation; and the same is done for the Earth, Venus, and Mercury, whose circle sizes and motion speeds approach so closely to what the computations give us that it is a marvelous thing.*

**SAGR.** *I have heard this thought with extreme pleasure; and were it not that I believe performing those calculations precisely would be a long and laborious undertaking, and perhaps too difficult for me to understand, I would request them of you.*

**SALV.** *The operation is indeed long and difficult, and I would not even be certain of performing it so readily; therefore, we shall reserve it...*

### Of Galileo

...for another time; and for now we will return to our first proposal, picking up where we digressed, which, if I remember correctly, was in determining how motion along a straight line can be of no use in the well-ordered parts of the World; and we went on to say that it is not so with circular movements; of which that which is performed by the moving body within itself already keeps it always in the same place, and that which carries the moving body along the circumference of a circle around its stable and fixed center does not put in disorder either itself or the neighboring parts; 

<margin>Finite and bounded circular motions do not disrupt the parts of the World.</margin>
because such motion is primarily finite and bounded; or rather, not merely finite and bounded, but there is no point on the circumference that is not both the first and the last boundary of the circulation; and continuing within its assigned circumference, it leaves all the rest, inside and outside of it, free for the needs of others, without ever hindering or disordering them. 

<margin>In circular motion, every point on the circumference is both beginning and end.</margin>
This being a movement that ensures the moving body is always departing and always arriving at its goal, it can, first of all, be the only one 
<margin>Only circular motion is uniform.</margin>
that is uniform. This is because the acceleration of motion occurs in the moving body when it goes toward the goal where it has an inclination <note>Galileo uses "inclination" to describe what we might now call gravitational pull or natural tendency.</note>, and the retardation happens because of the resistance it has to departing and moving away from that same goal; and because in circular motion the moving body is always departing from its natural boundary and always moving toward the same, therefore in it the resistance and the inclination are always of equal force. From this equality results a velocity that is neither retarded nor accelerated—that is, the uniformity of motion. 

<margin>Circular motion can continue perpetually.</margin>
From this uniformity, and from being bounded, it follows that perpetual continuation can occur by always repeating the circulations, which in an unbounded line and in a continuously retarded or accelerated motion cannot naturally be found. And I say naturally, 
<margin>Straight motion cannot naturally be perpetual.</margin>
because straight motion that slows down is "violent" <note>In the physics of this era, "violent motion" referred to motion caused by an external force that pushed an object against its natural tendency.</note>, which cannot be perpetual, and accelerated motion necessarily reaches its goal, if there is one; and if there is not, there can be no motion at all, because nature does not move where it is impossible to arrive.

<margin>Straight motion is assigned to natural bodies to return them to perfect order when they have been removed from it.</margin>
I conclude, therefore, that only circular motion can naturally suit the natural bodies that integrate the universe and are constituted in the best arrangement; and straight motion, at most, can be said to be assigned by nature to its bodies and their parts whenever they find themselves outside of their established places, in a disordered state, and therefore needing to return by the most

<summary>Galileo argues that circular motion is the only "natural" motion for celestial bodies because it is uniform, perpetual, and does not disrupt the order of the universe, whereas straight-line motion is merely a corrective measure for displaced objects.</summary>

# First Dialogue

<margin>Rest alone and circular motion are suited for the preservation of order.</margin>

*...briefly to the natural state. From here it seems to me that it can be quite reasonably concluded that, for the maintenance of perfect order among the parts of the World, it must be said that the mobile ones are mobile only circularly; and if there are some that do not move circularly, these of necessity are immobile. There is nothing else, besides rest and circular motion, that is suited for the preservation of order. And I wonder not a little that Aristotle—who also believed that the terrestrial globe was placed in the center of the world and remained there immovably—did not say that among natural bodies, some were by nature mobile and others immobile; especially since he had already defined nature as the principle of motion and of rest.*

<margin>Sensory experiences must be prioritized over human reasoning.</margin>
<margin>Whoever denies the senses deserves to be deprived of them.</margin>
<margin>The senses show heavy things moving toward the center and light things toward the concavity.</margin>

**SIMP.** *Aristotle, as one who did not promise more from his own genius (however sharp it might be) than was fitting, believed in his philosophizing that sensory experiences should be prioritized over any discourse fabricated by human genius. He said that those who would deny the senses deserved to be punished by being deprived of that very sense. Now, who is so blind that they do not see the parts of Earth and Water moving, as heavy things, naturally downward—that is, toward the center of the universe, assigned by nature herself as the end and boundary of straight downward motion <note>original: "deorsum"</note>? And who does not see Fire and Air move straight upward toward the concavity of the lunar Orb <note>In the Aristotelian system, the "concavity of the lunar orb" refers to the inner edge of the Moon's sphere, which was thought to be the natural destination for the "light" elements like fire.</note>, as the natural boundary of upward motion <note>original: "sursum"</note>? Since this is seen so manifesty, and since we are certain that the same logic applies to the whole and its parts <note>original: "eadem est ratio totius, & partium"</note>, how can it not be said that it is a true and manifest proposition that the natural movement of the Earth is straight toward the center, and of Fire straight away from the center?*

<margin>It is doubtful whether heavy falling objects move in a straight line.</margin>

**SALV.** *By virtue of this discourse of yours, the most you could claim to be granted is that, just as parts of the Earth removed from their whole—that is, from the place where they naturally reside, and thus reduced to a depraved and disordered state—return to their place spontaneously and therefore naturally with straight motion; so (granting that the same logic applies to the whole and its parts <note>original: "eadem sit ratio totius, & partium"</note>) one could infer that if the terrestrial globe were removed by violence from the place assigned to it by nature, it would return there by a straight line. ### Of Galileo. 23

<margin>The Earth is spherical due to the joining together of its parts at its center.</margin>
<margin>The Sun is more likely at the center of the universe than the Earth.</margin>

Add to this that neither Aristotle nor you will ever prove that the Earth is <term>de facto</term> <note>Latin for "in fact" or "actually."</note> in the center of the universe; rather, if any center can be assigned to the universe, we will find the Sun to be placed there instead, as you will understand in the course of our progress.*

<margin>Natural inclination of the parts of all worldly bodies to go to their own centers.</margin>
*Now, just as the harmonious joining of all the parts of the Earth to form its whole results in them converging from all sides with equal inclination—and, in order to unite as much as possible, they adapt themselves into a spherical shape—why should we not believe that the Moon, the Sun, and the other worldly bodies are also round in shape for no other reason than a harmonious instinct and natural convergence of all their component parts? If one of these parts were ever separated from its whole by some violence, is it not reasonable to believe that it would return there spontaneously and by natural instinct? And in this way, can we not conclude that straight motion <note>Galileo is arguing that gravity—the falling of objects—is not a "downward" motion to the center of the universe, but a local return of matter to its parent planet.</note> belongs equally to all worldly bodies?*

<meta>This page continues the speech by Salviati, who is critiquing Aristotle's logic regarding the movement of elements. ### First Dialogue

<margin>
The Paralogism <note>original: "Paralogismo"; a logical fallacy or piece of circular reasoning where the conclusion is hidden in the premises.</note> of *Aristotle* is uncovered from another perspective.
</margin>

...without any doubt it will go toward the circumference, and continuing the motion it will arrive there as well; so that it will be most true to say that it moves toward the circumference. But it will not be true that that which moved by the same lines with contrary motion would go toward the center, unless the point taken were the center itself, or the motion were made along that single line which, produced from the assigned point, passes through the center. So that saying: *Fire*, moving straight, goes toward the circumference of the *World* <note>In this context, Galileo uses "World" (Mondo) to mean the entire Cosmos.</note>, therefore the parts of the *Earth*, which move with contrary motion along the same lines, go toward the center of the *World*, concludes nothing unless it is first supposed that the lines of *Fire*, extended, pass through the center of the *World*; and because we know for certain that they pass through the center of the terrestrial globe (being perpendicular to its surface, and not inclined), therefore to reach the conclusion one must suppose that the center of the *Earth* is the same as the center of the *World*, or at least that the parts of *Fire* and *Earth* do not ascend and descend except along a single line that passes through the center of the *World*; which is then false and repugnant to experience, which shows us that the parts of *Fire* ascend not along a single line, but along infinite lines produced from the center of the *Earth* toward all parts of the *World*, always along lines perpendicular to the surface of the terrestrial globe.

<margin>
It is proven more reasonably that heavy objects tend toward the center of the Earth than toward that of the universe.
</margin>

SALV. *You, Signor* Sagredo <note>A character in the dialogue representing the clever, open-minded Venetian scholar.</note>, *very ingeniously lead* Aristotle *to the same inconvenience, showing the manifest equivocation; but you add another absurdity. <summary>Salviati argues that heavy objects fall toward the center of the Earth because it is their natural "mother" globe, rather than an abstract, potentially non-existent "center of the universe." He exposes Aristotle's circular reasoning, which assumes the Earth is at the center of the cosmos to prove that things fall toward the center of the cosmos.</summary>

### Of Galileo. 29

...manifest by Aristotle's demonstrations that the celestial bodies are impassible <note>original: "impassibili"; meaning incapable of being changed or affected by external force.</note>, impenetrable, indivisible, etc. I respond that none of the conditions by which Aristotle distinguishes celestial bodies from elementary ones have any other basis than what he deduces from the diversity of their natural motions. Thus, if it is denied that circular motion belongs only to celestial bodies, and affirmed that it belongs to all movable natural bodies, it must necessarily follow that the attributes of being generable or ungenerable, alterable or unalterable, divisible or indivisible, etc., belong equally and commonly to all bodies in the world—that is, as much to the celestial as to the elementary—or else Aristotle has poorly and erroneously deduced from circular motion those attributes he assigned to the celestial bodies.

<margin>The conditions by which celestial bodies differ from elementary ones depend on the motions assigned to them by Aristotle.</margin>

SIMPLICIO: *This way of philosophizing tends toward the subversion of all natural philosophy, and to the disordering and throwing into chaos of the Heaven, the Earth, and the whole Universe; but I believe that the foundations of the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, so named because they allegedly walked about while teaching.</note> are so solid that there is no fear that new sciences can be constructed upon their ruin.*

SALVIATI: Do not worry about the Heaven or the Earth, nor fear their subversion, any more than you should fear for philosophy. As for the Heaven, it is in vain for you to fear for that which you yourself consider unalterable and impassible; as for the Earth, we seek to ennoble and perfect it, while we attempt to make it similar to the celestial bodies and, in a certain way, place it almost in Heaven, from where your philosophers have banished it.

<margin>Philosophy can receive growth from the disputes and contradictions of philosophers.</margin>

Philosophy itself cannot but benefit from our disputes; for if our thoughts are true, new discoveries will have been made; if false, by rejecting them, the original doctrines will be more strongly confirmed. Rather, take thought for certain philosophers and see to helping and supporting them; as for science itself, it cannot but advance. And returning to our purpose, bring forth freely whatever occurs to you in support of the supreme difference that Aristotle places between celestial bodies and the elementary part, in making the former ungenerable, incorruptible, and unalterable, and the latter corruptible and alterable.

SIMPLICIO: *I do not yet see that Aristotle is in need of help, as he remains standing, firm and strong; indeed, not having yet been even attacked, let alone knocked down by you.*

### Dialogue the First

<margin>
Aristotle's discourse to prove the incorruptibility of the heavens.
Generation and corruption exist only among contraries, according to Aristotle.
To circular motion, no other motion is contrary.
The heavens as the home of the immortal Gods.
The immutability of the heavens perceived through the senses.
Proof that circular motion has no contrary.

*And what will be your shield in this first assault? Aristotle writes: That which is generated is made from a contrary in some subject, and likewise is corrupted in some subject, from a contrary, into a contrary; so that (note well) corruption and generation occur only among contraries; but among contraries, the movements are contrary; if, therefore, no contrary can be assigned to the celestial body, because no other movement is contrary to circular motion, then nature has done very well to make exempt from contraries that which was to be ungenerable <note>Incapable of being created or coming into existence from something else.</note> and incorruptible. Having established this first foundation, it is quickly drawn as a consequence that it is incapable of growth, unalterable, impassible <note>Incapable of being changed or affected by external force.</note>, and finally eternal, and a dwelling place proportioned to the immortal Gods, in accordance with the opinion of all men who have a concept of the Gods. He then confirms the same even through the senses; for in all time past, according to traditions and memories, nothing is seen to have changed, neither in the whole of the highest Heaven, nor in any of its own parts. That no other motion is contrary to circular motion, Aristotle proves in many ways; but without repeating them all, it remains quite clearly demonstrated since simple motions are no more than three: toward the center, away from the center, and around the center. Of these, the two straight motions, upwards and downwards <note>original: "sursum, & deorsum"</note>, are manifestly contrary; and because one thing has only one contrary, it follows that no other movement remains that can be contrary to the circular. Behold the most subtle and most conclusive discourse of Aristotle, by which the incorruptibility of the Heaven is proven.*

SALVIATI. *This is nothing more than the pure progression of Aristotle, already mentioned by me, in which, so long as I deny to you that the motion you attribute to celestial bodies does not also belong to the Earth, his conclusion remains void. I tell you, therefore, that the circular motion you assign to celestial bodies also belongs to the Earth: from which, assuming that the rest of your discourse is conclusive, one of these three things will follow (as was said a little while ago, and now I repeat to you): either that the Earth is itself also ungenerable and incorruptible, like the celestial bodies; or that the celestial bodies are, like the elementary ones, generable, alterable, etc.; or that this difference of motions has nothing to do with generation and corruption. The discourse of Aristotle, and yours, contains many propositions not to be*

# Of Galileo.

*...be easily admitted, and to better examine it, it will be good to strip it down to the clearest and most distinct form possible; and may Mr. Sagredo excuse me if perhaps he feels some boredom hearing the same things repeated multiple times, and let him imagine he is hearing the arguments taken up again in the public circles of the disputants <note>Scholarly debating societies common in universities during the Renaissance.</note>. You say that generation <note>The process of coming into being or being born.</note> and corruption <note>The process of decaying or ceasing to be.</note> do not occur except where there are contraries; contraries do not exist except among simple natural bodies that move with contrary movements; contrary movements are only those that occur in straight lines between contrary points, and these are only two, namely away from the center and toward the center; and such movements belong to no other natural bodies than the Earth, Fire, and the other two Elements <note>Water and Air.</note>; therefore, generation and corruption exist only among the Elements. And because the third simple movement, namely the circular one around the center, has no contrary (because the other two are contraries of each other, and one thing has only one contrary), therefore that natural body which possesses such motion lacks a contrary; and having no contrary, it remains ingenerable and incorruptible, etc., because where there is no contrariety, there is no generation nor corruption, etc. But such motion belongs only to the celestial bodies; therefore, these alone are ingenerable, incorruptible, etc.*

<margin>
It is easier to perceive if the Earth moves than if corruption is caused by contraries.
</margin>
*And first, it appears to me a much easier thing to be able to assure oneself whether the Earth—a vast body and, by its proximity to us, most manageable—moves with a very great motion, such as it would be to revolve upon itself in twenty-four hours, than it is to understand and be sure whether generation and corruption are caused by contraries; or even whether corruption, generation, and contraries exist in nature at all. And if you, Mr. Simplicio, could show me what nature's way of operating is in generating, in a very short time, a hundred thousand gnats <note>Original: *moscioni*, small flies or gnats often found around fermenting fruit.</note> from a bit of grape must <note>The freshly crushed juice of grapes that contains the skins, seeds, and stems.</note>, showing me which are the contraries there, what thing is corrupted, and how, I would respect you even more than I do; because I understand none of these things. Furthermore, I would very much like to understand how and why these corruptive contraries are so kind toward crows and so fierce toward pigeons, so tolerant toward deer and impatient against horses, so that they grant many years of life—that is, of incorruptibility—to the former, while granting only weeks to the latter. Peach trees and Olive trees have their roots in the same soils, are exposed to the same cold, the same heat, the same rains and winds, and*

**SAGR.** Actually, we do see all these things, and therefore we are willing to grant you Aristotle’s discourse on this point: that generation and corruption are caused by the interaction of opposites. What would you say then?

**SIMP.** I would say that you have done that which is impossible to do.

**SAGR.** Tell me, Mr. Simplicio, are these qualities <note>original: "affezioni"</note> not contrary to one another?

**SIMP.** Which ones?

**SAGR.** These: Alterable and unalterable; <term>passible</term> <note>Able to be changed or acted upon by an external force.</note> and impassible; generable and ungenerable; corruptible and incorruptible?

**SIMP.** They are most contrary.

**SAGR.** Since this is so, and if it is also true that the celestial bodies are ungenerable and incorruptible, I shall prove to you that of necessity the celestial bodies must be generable and corruptible.

**SIMP.** This can be nothing other than a <term>sophism</term> <note>A clever but false argument used to deceive.</note>.

<margin>Celestial bodies are generable and corruptible because they are ungenerable and incorruptible.</margin>
**SAGR.** Hear the argument, then name it and solve it. Celestial bodies, because they are ungenerable and incorruptible, have as their opposites in nature the bodies that are generable and corruptible; but wherever there is contrariety, there is generation and corruption; therefore, celestial bodies are generable and corruptible.

<margin>A horned argument, otherwise called a Sorites.</margin>
**SIMP.** Did I not tell you it could be nothing but a sophism? This is one of those <term>horned arguments</term> <note>A dilemma where both "horns" or choices lead to a problematic conclusion.</note> called a <term>Sorites</term> <note>A chain of logic where the conclusion of one statement forms the start of the next; here, Simplicio uses it to describe a paradox.</note>: like that of the Cretan <note>original: "Candiotto"</note>, who said that all Cretans were liars. Since he was a Cretan himself, he was telling a lie when he said that Cretans were liars; it followed then that Cretans must be truthful, and consequently he, as a Cretan, was being truthful; and yet, in saying that Cretans were liars, he was telling the truth, and including himself as a Cretan, he had to be a liar. And so, in this sort of sophism, one would continue forever turning in circles without ever concluding anything.

<summary>Sagredo uses a logical trap to argue that if celestial bodies are "un-decaying," they must have a "decaying" opposite, and since Aristotle links opposites to change, the heavens must be subject to change. Simplicio dismisses this as a "horned argument" or a paradox similar to the famous Liar Paradox.</summary>
