### First Dialogue ###

<margin>The <term>Peripatetics<note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, so named because Aristotle often taught while walking (peripatos) in the Lyceum.</note></term> assign, with little reason, those motions to the Elements as natural by which they never move, and as preternatural those by which they move constantly.</margin>
straight, let such movements be left to the parts, which alone are altered and corrupted; and to the entire globe and sphere of the Elements, let there be attributed either circular motion or a perpetual stability in its own place: qualities which alone are capable of perpetuation and the maintenance of perfect order. This, which is said of the Earth, can be said with similar reason of Fire and the majority of the Air; to which Elements the Peripatetics have been forced to assign, as their intrinsic and natural motion, one by which they have never moved, nor are ever to move, and to call "outside of their nature" that motion by which they move, have moved, and are to move perpetually. I say this because they assign to Air and Fire upward motion, by which none of the said Elements as a whole has ever moved, but only some of their particles—and this for no other reason than to return to a perfect state while found outside their natural place. Conversely, they call the circular motion by which these elements move incessantly "preternatural," having forgotten, in a sense, what Aristotle said many times: that nothing violent can last for a long time.

<note>original: "Del Galileo ."</note> convinced the Earth to be different from the celestial bodies, immobile, located in the center of the World, and whatever else there is that excludes it from being mobile as well, like a planet, like Jupiter, or the Moon, etc. And Mr. Salviati, by his courtesy, will be content to respond piece by piece.

See if this is being the same thing. bodies are splendid and full of light; therefore, etc. Let these be answered so as not to pile up too much, and then I will bring others.

**SALV.** *And why haven't you observed and seen this for yourself with your own eyes, without reducing yourself to having to believe the reports of others?*

**SIMP.** *Because those countries, besides not being exposed to our eyes, are so remote that our sight could not manage to perceive such mutations in them.*

**SALV.** *Now see how you have accidentally discovered for yourself the fallacy of your argument; for if you say that the alterations seen on Earth near us could not be perceived in America due to the excessive distance, much less could you see them on the Moon, which is many hundreds of times farther away. Therefore, from your failure to see alterations in Heaven—where, if they existed, you could not see them due to the great distance—and from having no reports of them (since reports cannot be had), you cannot argue that they do not exist; just as from seeing and hearing of them on Earth, you rightly argue that they do exist here.*

# Of Galileo. 45

*...come to cloud the Heavens, and even more the Peripatetic philosophy?* <note>original: "peripatetica filosofia" — This refers to the philosophy of Aristotle and his followers, who were known as "Peripatetics" because Aristotle often taught while walking (peripatētikos in Greek).</note> *It is inevitable that, as an intrepid defender of that school, you have found some remedy and solution, of which you must not deprive us.*

<margin>Different opinions concerning sunspots.</margin>
**SIMP.** *I have heard various opinions regarding this particular matter.*
,, *Some say they are Stars that revolve around the Sun in their own orbits, in the manner of*
,, *Venus and Mercury, and when passing beneath it, they appear dark to us; and because they are*
,, *very numerous, it often happens that some of them gather together, and then separate.*
,, *Others believe them to be atmospheric impressions; others, illusions of the lenses;* <note>original: "cristalli" — Referring to the glass lenses of the telescope, which some skeptics claimed created the spots as optical artifacts.</note> *and others, other things. But I am much inclined to believe—indeed, I hold it for certain—that they are a collection of many and various opaque bodies, coinciding with one another almost by chance. Thus, we often see that in one spot, ten or more such minute bodies can be counted, which are of irregular shapes and appear to us like flakes of snow, or wool, or flying flies. They change their position relative to one another; sometimes they disperse and sometimes they gather together, especially beneath the Sun, around which they move as around their center. But it is not, therefore, necessary to say that they are generated and then decay; rather, sometimes they are hidden behind the body of the Sun, and at other times, although distant from it, they are not seen because of the proximity of the Sun’s immeasurable light. For within the eccentric Orb* <term>Eccentric Orb: In ancient astronomy, a circular path whose center is offset from the Earth, used to account for the observed movements of celestial bodies.</term> *of the Sun, there is established something like an onion composed of many layers, one inside the other, each of which moves while being studded with some small spots. And although their movement at first seemed inconstant and irregular, it is nevertheless said to have been recently observed that, after determined periods of time, the very same spots return exactly. This seems to me the most suitable remedy that has been found so far to account for such appearances, and at the same time to maintain the incorruptibility and ungenerability of the Heaven;* <note>The Peripatetic doctrine held that the heavens were "incorruptible" (cannot change or decay) and "ingenerable" (cannot have new things created within them).</note> *and if this were not enough, there will be no lack of more elevated minds who will find even better ones.*

<margin>In the natural sciences, the art of oratory is ineffective.</margin>
**SALV.** *If this matter under dispute were some point of law, or other human studies in which there is neither truth nor falsehood, one could rely heavily on the subtlety of wit, on readiness of speech, and on greater experience among writers, and hope that whoever excelled in these things would make his reasoning appear superior. <meta>This page continues Salviati’s refutation of the idea that sunspots are solid, permanent stars orbiting the Sun. # Concerning Galileo

<margin>Sunspots are not spherical in shape, but flat, like thin flakes.</margin>
...sunspots in the letters to <term>Mr. Mark Welser</term><note>Philipp Eduard Fugger’s business partner and a prominent patron of science; Galileo wrote three famous letters to him in 1612 regarding sunspots.</note>. It is gathered from this same change in shape that none of them is a star, or any other body of spherical shape. This is because among all shapes, only the sphere is never seen <term>foreshortened</term><note>In perspective, "foreshortening" is the visual distortion that makes an object appear shorter or narrower than it actually is when viewed at an angle.</note>, nor can it ever appear as anything but perfectly round. Thus, if any of these particular spots were a round body, as all stars are judged to be, it would show the same roundness both in the middle of the solar disk and toward the edges. However, the fact that they foreshorten so much, appearing so thin toward the edge while, by contrast, appearing spacious and wide toward the middle, makes us certain that they are flakes of little depth or thickness compared to their length and width. Furthermore, as for the recent observation that the spots return exactly the same after their determined periods, do not believe it, **Signor Simplicio**. Whoever told you this wishes to deceive you. To see that this is so, consider that he has remained silent about those spots that are generated and those that dissolve on the face of the Sun far from the circumference; nor has he said a word about that foreshortening, which is a necessary argument for their being contiguous to the Sun. The truth regarding the return of the same spots is nothing other than what one reads in the aforementioned letters: that it may sometimes happen that some spots are of such long duration that they do not break up during a single revolution around the Sun, which is completed in less than a month.

**SIMPLICIO:** To tell the truth, I have not made observations long or diligent enough for them to be sufficient for me to master the <term>quod est</term><note>Latin: "the what it is," meaning the factual nature or the basic reality of a phenomenon.</note> of this matter. But I want to make them anyway, and then try for myself to see if I might succeed in reconciling what experience offers us with what <term>Aristotle</term><note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose theories of an unchanging, perfect heaven formed the basis of medieval science.</note> demonstrates to us; for it is a clear thing that two truths cannot contradict one another.

<margin>According to Aristotle, one cannot speak resolutely of the heavens because of their great distance.</margin>
**SALVIATI:** Whenever you wish to harmonize what your senses show you with the most solid doctrines of *Aristotle*, you will not have any trouble in the world. And to show that this is true, does not *Aristotle* himself say that regarding the things of the Heavens, because of their great distance, one cannot treat them very resolutely?

**SIMPLICIO:** He says it openly.

<margin>According to Aristotle, the senses prevail over discourse.</margin>
**SALVIATI:** Does he not also affirm that what experience and the senses demonstrate to us must be preferred over any discourse, even if it appears quite well-founded? And does he not say this resolutely and without the slightest hesitation?

# Of Galileo.

<margin>Earth is more noble than gold and jewels.</margin>

<margin>Incorruptibility is celebrated by the masses out of fear of death.</margin>

# First Dialogue

<margin>Celestial bodies lack reciprocal interaction among themselves.</margin>
*...most [exalted], most perfect, and most noble celestial bodies—incapable of change, immortal, and divine—serving no other purpose than the service of an Earth that is susceptible to change, fleeting, and mortal? At the service of that which you call the dregs of the world, the sink of all filth? <note>original: "sentina di tutte le immondizie." The "sink" or "sewer" was a common Aristotelian metaphor for Earth being the bottom-most, dirtiest part of the universe.</note> And for what purpose make the celestial bodies immortal, and so on, to serve one that is fleeting, and so on? Once this use of serving the Earth is taken away, the countless host of all the celestial bodies remains entirely useless and superfluous, since they do not have, nor can they have, any reciprocal action among themselves, because they are all unalterable, immutable, and incapable of being acted upon. For if, for instance <note>original: "v. g." stands for "verbi gratia," meaning "for example."</note>, the Moon is incapable of change, what do you expect the Sun or another star to do to it? It would undoubtedly be an action far less effective than that of someone who, with their sight or their thought, wished to melt a large mass of gold. Furthermore, it seems to me that while the celestial bodies contribute to the generations and alterations on Earth, it must follow that they themselves are also alterable; otherwise, I do not see how the application of the Moon or the Sun to the Earth to create life would be anything other than placing a marble statue next to a bride and expecting offspring from such a union.*

<margin>Alterability is not in the entire terrestrial globe, but in some parts.</margin>
**SIMPLICIO:** *Corruptibility, alteration, mutation, and so on, are not in the entire terrestrial globe, which, regarding its integrity, is no less eternal than the Sun or the Moon; but it is subject to generation and decay <term>generation and decay: "generazione e corruzione" in the Aristotelian sense, meaning the coming-into-being and passing-away of physical things</term> regarding its external parts. Yet it is quite true that within these parts, generation and decay are perpetual, and as such they require the eternal celestial operations; and therefore it is necessary that the celestial bodies be eternal.*

**SAGREDO:** *Everything proceeds well; but if the corruptibility of the surface parts is not at all prejudicial to the eternity of the entire terrestrial globe—
<margin>Celestial bodies are alterable in their external parts.</margin>
on the contrary, if this quality of being generable, corruptible, and alterable, etc., brings it great ornament and perfection—why can you not, and should you not, likewise admit alterations, generations, and so on, in the external parts of the celestial bodies? This would add ornament to them without diminishing their perfection or taking away their actions; in fact, it would increase them, by making it so that they all act not only upon the Earth, but reciprocally among themselves, and the Earth also toward them.*

**SIMPLICIO:** *This cannot be, because the generations, mutations, and so on, that might occur, for example, on the Moon, would be useless and in vain, and Nature does nothing in vain. <note>original: "natura nihil frustrà facit." A fundamental axiom of Aristotelian philosophy.</note>*

**SAGREDO:** *And why would they be useless and in vain?*

<margin>

**SIMPLICIO.** *Because we clearly see, and touch with our hands, that all the generations <note>In this context, "generations" refers to the process of coming into being or the birth of living things, while "mutations" refers to changes in state.</note> and changes, etc., that occur on Earth are all, either mediatly or immediately, directed toward the use, the comfort, and the benefit of man. In short, if we were to diligently examine and resolve all these things, we would find that the end toward which they are all directed is the need, the utility, the comfort, and the delight of men. Now, of what use could generations ever be to the human race if they occurred on the Moon or another planet? Unless, of course, you wanted to say that there were men on the Moon as well who might enjoy its fruits; a thought that is either fabulous <note>Meaning "like a fairy tale" or mythological.</note> or impious <note>Simplicio labels this "impious" because the idea of other inhabited worlds challenged the unique status of humanity and the biblical account of creation.</note>.*

</margin>
<margin>

</margin>
<margin>

</margin>

**SAGREDO.** *Whether on the Moon or another planet there are generated herbs, or plants, or animals similar to ours, or whether there occur rains, winds, and thunder as there are around the Earth, I do not know and I do not believe it; and much less do I believe it to be inhabited by men. But I do not understand how, simply because nothing is generated there similar to our things, one must of necessity conclude that no alteration occurs there, nor that there can be other things that change, are generated, and dissolve—things not only different from ours, but furthest from our imagination, and in short, entirely unthinkable to us. Just as I am certain that for someone born and raised in an immense forest among wild beasts and birds, who had no knowledge whatever of the Element of Water, it could never enter his imagination that there existed in nature another world different from the Earth, full of animals which, without legs and without wings, move swiftly—and not only upon the surface like beasts on the Earth, but throughout its entire depth. If, for example, the Moon followed the Sun’s motion exactly and always stayed directly between the Sun and the Earth in that position we call <term>conjunction: The "New Moon" phase, when the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun</term>, it would always see the same hemisphere of the Earth that the Sun sees, and thus would see it perpetually full of light. Thus, only at the quadratures do these observers see a luminous half-circle of the Moon, and those on the Moon see the same of the Earth. *If the Moon had a natural correspondence and sympathy with the Earth, toward which it directed a specific part of itself, it would be necessary for the straight line connecting their centers to always pass through the same point on the surface of the Moon. And because the part of the Moon's circumference that is "upper" when rising is "lower" when setting, a very notable difference must occur in the appearance of these upper and lower parts, as spots or other notable things in those areas are now revealed and now hidden. A similar variation should also be discerned toward the northern and southern extremities of the same disk, depending on whether the Moon finds itself in one or the other "belly" of its <term>Dragon: a term for the Moon's orbital path; the "belly" refers to its maximum distance north or south of the ecliptic</term>; for when it is to the north, some of its northern parts are hidden and the southern ones are revealed, and vice versa. <meta>This page continues the discussion where Simplicio, the defender of Aristotelian physics, responds to the arguments of Salviati (Galileo's spokesperson) and Sagredo regarding the physical composition of the Moon and Earth.</meta>

# First Dialogue

*...while celestial matter <note>Original: "materia celeste." In the Aristotelian view, the heavens were made of a "fifth element" or quintessence, unlike the four earthly elements.</note> cannot be touched because it lacks tangible qualities, it can certainly touch elemental bodies; and for it to strike us is just as harmful—and perhaps even worse—than if we were to strike it.* But let us leave aside these palaces, or rather, castles in the air, so as not to hinder Mr. Simplicio.

<margin>
The surface of the Moon is smoother than any mirror.
</margin>
SIMPLICIO: *The question you have raised so incidentally is one of the most difficult treated in philosophy, and I have some very fine thoughts on it from a great professor in Padua <note>This likely refers to Cesare Cremonini, a famous Aristotelian philosopher at the University of Padua who famously refused to look through Galileo's telescope.</note>; however, this is not the time to enter into that. Returning to our purpose, I repeat that I consider the Moon to be more solid than the Earth. I do not argue this from the roughness and unevenness of its surface, as you do, but rather from the opposite: that is, from its being suited to receive (as we see among us in the hardest gemstones) a polish and luster superior to any mirror, however smooth. It is necessary for its surface to be such to be able to make such a vivid reflection of the Sun's rays. Those appearances you mentioned—of mountains, rocks, ridges, valleys, etc.—are all illusions. I myself have been present at public disputes and heard it vigorously maintained against these "introducers of novelties" <note>Simplicio's derogatory term for Galileo and other modern scientists who challenged ancient authority.</note> that such appearances arise from nothing other than parts that are unequally opaque and transparent <term>perspicue: clear or transparent</term>, of which the Moon is composed both internally and externally. We often see this happen in crystal, in amber, and in many perfectly polished precious stones; where, due to the opacity of some parts and the transparency of others, various*

Heights and hollows on the Moon are illusions of opacity and transparency.

**SALV.** *Do not attribute more to my demonstration, Mr. Sagredo, than is its due. I want to raise an objection against you which I do not know will be easily resolved. But I tell you that that mirror sends the reflection to a single place because its surface is flat, and since the reflected rays must depart at angles equal to those of the incident rays <note>This refers to the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.</note>, it is necessary that from a flat surface they depart together toward the same place. But since the surface of the Moon is not flat, but spherical, the incident rays upon such a surface find themselves reflected at angles equal to those of incidence toward all parts, because of the infinity of inclinations that compose the spherical surface. Therefore, the Moon can send the reflection everywhere, and is not forced to send it to a single place like that mirror which is flat.*

**SIMP.** *This is exactly one of the objections that I wanted to make against him.*

**SAGR.** *If this is one, it is necessary that you have others; therefore tell them, for as for this first one, it seems to me that it will turn out more against you than in your favor.*

</margin>

*SAGR.* And here again I believe that you are greatly mistaken. But I come to the first instance raised by Mr. Salviati. I consider that to make an object appear luminous to us, it is not enough for the rays of the illuminating body to fall upon it; rather, it is necessary that the reflected rays come to our eye. This is clearly seen in the example of a mirror; there is no doubt that the luminous rays of the Sun fall upon it, yet it does not show itself to us as bright and illuminated except when we place our eye in that particular spot where the reflection goes. Let us now consider what would happen if the mirror were of a spherical surface; we would surely find that of the reflection made from the entire illuminated surface, only a very small part reaches the eye of a particular observer. This is because only a very tiny particle of the whole spherical surface is at an inclination that strikes the ray back to the specific location of the eye. Thus, the portion of the spherical surface that appears splendid to the eye must be minimal, while all the rest appears dark.

<margin>
If the Moon were like a spherical mirror, it would be invisible.
</margin>
Therefore, if the Moon were polished like a mirror, a very small part would show itself to the eyes of an individual as illuminated by the Sun, even though an entire hemisphere were exposed to the solar rays; the rest would remain to the eye of the observer as if unlit, and therefore invisible. Finally, the Moon would be entirely invisible, because that tiny particle from which the reflection came would be lost to sight due to its smallness and great distance. And just as it would remain invisible to the eye, so its illumination would remain as nothing; for it is quite impossible for a luminous body to take away our darkness with its splendor without us seeing it.

*SALV.* Wait, if you please, Mr. Sagredo, because I see certain movements in the face and person of Mr. Simplicio, which are signs to me that he remains neither quite convinced nor satisfied with what you have said with such great evidence and absolute truth. And just now it occurred to me that I might remove every doubt from him with another experiment. I have seen a large spherical mirror in a room upstairs; let us have it brought here, and while it is being carried, let Mr. Simplicio return to considering how great is the brightness that comes to the wall here under the lodge from the reflection of the flat mirror.

<meta>This page continues the debate between Salviati and Simplicio regarding the nature of the Moon's surface. <margin>
Reflected light from rough bodies is more universal than that from polished ones; and why.
</margin>
...just as the surface of that wall being rough is the same as being composed of innumerable tiny surfaces, arranged according to innumerable different inclinations. Among these, it necessarily happens that many are arranged to send the rays reflected from them to one place, and many others to another; and in short, there is no place to which very many rays do not arrive, reflected from very many tiny surfaces scattered across the entire surface of the rugged body upon which the light rays fall. From this, it follows by necessity that upon any part of any surface opposite the one receiving the primary incident rays, reflected rays will arrive, and consequently, illumination. It follows also that the same body upon which the illuminating rays fall, when viewed from any place, shows itself to be entirely illuminated and bright. Therefore the Moon, because its surface is rough and not polished, sends the Sun's light back in all directions and appears equally bright to all observers. For if its surface, being spherical, were also smooth like a mirror, it would remain entirely invisible, given that the tiny part from which the Sun's image could be reflected to an individual’s eye would remain invisible due to the great distance, as we have already said.

<margin>
If the Moon were polished and smooth, it would be invisible.
</margin>
**SIMPLICIO.** I understand your discourse well enough; nevertheless, it seems to me that I can resolve it with very little effort, and maintain quite well that the Moon is round and very polished, and that it reflects the Sun's light to us in the manner of a mirror. Nor does the image of the Sun have to be seen in its center, because it is not through the <term>species</term> <note>In older Aristotelian physics, "species" were the "likenesses" or images of objects that were thought to travel through the air to the eye to produce vision.</note> of the Sun itself that the small figure of the Sun can be seen at such a great distance; rather, we perceive the illumination of the entire lunar body by the light produced by the Sun. We can see such a thing in a gilded and well-burnished plate which, when struck by a luminous body, appears entirely shining to anyone looking from a distance; and only from up close can the small image of the luminous body be discerned in its center.

**SALVIATI.** Confessing my own inability frankly, I say that I understand nothing of this discourse of yours except for that gilded plate. <meta>This page continues the argument regarding optical reflection. Salviati (speaking for Galileo) is explaining why a smooth, polished sphere (like a mirror) would not look like the Moon we see in the sky. He is addressing the misconceptions of those who don't understand the geometry of light reflection.</meta>

# Concerning Galileo.

<margin>Some write what they do not understand, and therefore what they write is not understood.</margin>

*...to show themselves, however, to those who—in order to appear intelligent themselves—applaud what they do not understand; they form a higher opinion of people the less they are understood by them. This assumes that the writer himself is not (as many are) one of those who write what they do not understand, and therefore what they write cannot be understood. However, leaving the rest aside, I respond to you regarding the gilded plate: when it is flat and not very large, it can appear entirely resplendent from a distance when struck by a strong light. But it will only be seen as such when the eye is in a specific line—that is, in the line of the reflected rays. <note>Galileo is describing the "Law of Reflection," where the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.</note> It will appear more blazing than if it were, for example, made of silver, because of its color and its suitability, due to the extreme density of the metal, for receiving a perfect polish.*

*And when its surface, being very well polished, is not exactly flat but has various inclinations, then its brilliance would be seen from several places at once—*

<margin>Diamonds are worked with many facets, and why.</margin>

*that is, from as many places as there are different reflections made by the diverse surfaces. This is why diamonds are worked with many facets: so that their delightful brilliance may be perceived from many different vantage points. But if the plate were very large, it would not be seen as entirely resplendent from a distance, even if it were perfectly flat. To explain myself better: imagine a very large, flat, gilded plate exposed to the Sun. To a distant eye, the image of the Sun would appear to occupy only one part of that plate—specifically, the part from which the reflection of the incident solar rays comes. However, it is true that because of the intensity of the light, such an image will appear garlanded with many rays, and will therefore seem to occupy a much larger portion of the plate than it actually does. To prove this is true, if you note the particular spot on the plate where the reflection originates, and similarly visualize how large the resplendent space appears to be, and then cover most of that space, leaving only the middle uncovered, the size of the apparent brilliance will not be diminished at all to the one looking from a distance; rather, the light will be seen widely spread over the cloth or whatever was used to cover it.* <note>Galileo is discussing "irradiation," an optical illusion where a bright object against a dark background appears larger than its physical dimensions.</note> *If, therefore, someone—seeing a small gilded plate appearing entirely resplendent from a distance—imagines that the same must happen even with plates as large as the Moon, he is no less deceived than if he believed the Moon were no larger than the bottom of a tub...*

And that becoming dark proceeds from nothing else than the smoothing of a very fine grain that made the silver's surface rough, and therefore such that it reflected light toward all parts, for which reason it appeared equally illuminated from all directions. When then, by burnishing it, those minute inequalities are exquisitely smoothed so that the reflection of the incident rays <note>The "incident rays" are the rays of light hitting the surface.</note> is all directed to a specific place, then from that place the burnished part shows itself much clearer and more lustrous than the rest, which is only whitened; but from all other places, it is seen as very dark. **SAGR.** I see the effect, but I do not understand the cause.

**SALV.** If you thought about it for a hundredth of an hour you would find it; but in order not to consume time, here is a little demonstration in this figure.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the concentration of light rays on surfaces at different angles. On the left, a vertical line segment is marked with 'A' at the top and 'B' at the bottom. A series of eleven horizontal parallel lines (representing light rays) extend from this left boundary toward the right. A second vertical segment, labeled 'C' at the top and 'D' at the bottom, intercepts all eleven rays at a ninety-degree angle. From point 'D', an inclined line segment labeled 'DO' slants upward and to the right. This inclined segment 'DO' is longer than 'CD' but intercepts only the bottom three rays, demonstrating that an oblique surface of equal or greater size receives fewer rays than a surface perpendicular to the light source.</image-desc>

**SAGR.** The mere sight of the figure has made everything clear to me, so please continue.

**SALV.** Imagine that all the parallel lines you see starting from the points A and B are the rays that come at right angles upon the line C.D. Now incline the same C.D. so that it slants like D.O. Do you not see that a good part of those rays that struck C.D. pass by without touching D.O.? Therefore, if D.O. is illuminated by fewer rays, it is reasonable that the light received by it is weaker. # From Galileo.

**SAGR.** I am satisfied by both the experiment and the reasoning. Now it remains for Mr. Simplicio to answer my other question, declaring to me what reasons move the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, so named because Aristotle often taught while walking about.</note> to insist upon such exact roundness in the celestial bodies.

<margin>Why perfect sphericity is attributed to the celestial bodies by the Peripatetics.</margin>
**SIMP.** The fact that celestial bodies are ungenerable, incorruptible, unalterable, impassible <note>In this context, "impassible" means incapable of being acted upon or suffering change from external forces.</note>, immortal, etc., makes them absolutely perfect; and being absolutely perfect carries the consequence that in them exists every kind of perfection; and therefore, the shape also must be perfect—that is, spherical—and absolutely and perfectly spherical, not rough and irregular.

**SALV.** And this incorruptibility—from where do you derive it?

**SIMP.** From the lack of contraries immediately, and mediately from simple circular motion. <note>Aristotle argued that change only occurs between opposites (contraries). Since he believed celestial bodies moved in "perfect" circles—a motion with no opposite—he concluded they must be changeless and incorruptible.</note>

<margin>Shape is not the cause of incorruptibility, but of longer duration.</margin>
**SALV.** So, from what I gather from your discourse, in establishing the essence of celestial bodies as incorruptible, unalterable, etc., roundness does not enter as a cause or a necessary requirement. If shape itself caused unalterability, we could at our own whim make wood, wax, and other elementary materials incorruptible simply by reducing them to a spherical shape.

**SIMP.** And is it not manifest that a ball of wood will preserve itself better and for a longer time than a spire or another angular shape made of the same amount of that same wood?

<margin>The corruptible receives "more" and "less," but not the incorruptible.</margin>
<margin>Perfection of shape operates in corruptible bodies but not in eternal ones.</margin>
**SALV.** That is most true, but it will not thereby turn from corruptible to incorruptible; rather, it will remain corruptible, though of a much longer duration. However, it should be noted that the corruptible is capable of "more" or "less" of such a quality, so we can say this is less corruptible than that—for example, jasper <note>original: *diaspro*</note> is less corruptible than *pietra serena* <note>A gray sandstone common in Italian architecture, known for being softer and more prone to weathering than jasper.</note>. But the incorruptible does not admit of "more" or "less," so that one could say this is more incorruptible than that other, if both are incorruptible and eternal. The difference of shape, then, can only have an effect on materials that are capable of lasting a longer or shorter time; but in eternal things, which can be nothing other than equally eternal, the influence of shape ceases. Therefore, since celestial matter is not incorruptible because of its shape, but for other reasons, there is no need to be so anxious about this perfect sphericity; for if the matter is incorruptible, let it have whatever shape it wants, it will always remain so.

<meta>This page continues the discussion regarding whether the perfect sphericity of celestial bodies is a requirement for their "incorruptibility" (their status as unchanging and eternal). # First Dialogue

<margin>
If the spherical shape conferred eternity, all bodies would be eternal.
</margin>

**SAGR.** *But I am considering something further; and I say that, granted that the spherical shape had the power to bestow incorruptibility, all bodies of whatever shape would be eternal and incorruptible. For if a round body is incorruptible, then corruptibility would consist of those parts that alter that perfect roundness. For example, inside a cube there is a perfectly round ball, and as such it is incorruptible; it follows then that the corruptible parts are those corners that cover and hide the roundness. Therefore, at most, the only thing that could happen would be that these corners—these "excrescences," so to speak—would decay. But if we consider even more deeply, inside those corner sections there are other smaller balls of the same material, and these too, being round, must be incorruptible. And so, in the residues surrounding these eight smaller spheres, one can imagine others still. Thus, by finally resolving the entire cube into innumerable balls, one would have to confess it to be incorruptible. And this same reasoning and a similar resolution can be applied to all other shapes.*

**SALV.** The argument follows very well. Thus if, for example <note>original: "v.g." (verbi gratia)</note>, a crystal sphere derived the quality of being incorruptible from its shape—that is, the power to resist all internal and external alterations—one cannot see how adding more crystal to it to turn it into, say, a cube, should alter it either inside or out. It would not become less able to resist its new surroundings (made of the same material) than it was when surrounded by a different material. This is especially true if it is true that "corruption is caused by contraries," as Aristotle says <note>Aristotelian physics taught that change or decay only happens when a substance meets its opposite (e.g., heat meeting cold). Since the heavens were thought to have no "contrary," they were deemed changeless.</note>. And what could one surround that crystal ball with that would be less "contrary" to it than the crystal itself? But we are not noticing how the hours are flying by, and we will reach the end of our reasoning very late if we must make such long discourses over every detail. Furthermore, the memory becomes so confused by the multiplicity of things that I can hardly remember the propositions that Mr. Simplicio had originally proposed for our consideration in an orderly fashion.

**SIMP.** I remember them very well. And regarding this detail of the mountainous nature of the Moon, the cause I brought forward for such an appearance still stands; it can be perfectly well saved by saying that it is an illusion proceeding from the parts of the Moon being unequally opaque and transparent <note>original: "perspicue". Simplicio is arguing that the Moon is actually a perfect, smooth sphere, and the "mountains" we see are just dark and light patches inside a translucent solid.</note>.

->First Dialogue<-
80

*...in the dark part [of the Moon], you will see many illuminated peaks detached from the already-lit portion. You will see the shadows of these peaks shrink as the light rises, until they vanish completely when the entire hemisphere is illuminated. On the other hand, as the light moves toward the other lunar hemisphere, you will recognize the same heights you observed before, and you will see their shadows cast in the opposite direction and grow longer. I repeat to you: you cannot represent even one of these things with your theory of varying opacity and transparency <note>The Aristotelian view held that the Moon was a perfect, smooth sphere, and that its "spots" were simply parts of the crystal-like body that were more or less transparent than others.</note>.*

**SAGR.** Indeed, one state *can* be imitated: that of the full moon. When the entire surface is lit, we no longer see shadows or any other variation caused by mountains or craters. But please, Mr. Salviati, do not waste any more time on this point. If someone has the patience to observe one or two lunar cycles <note>original: "lunazioni"; the period of roughly 29.5 days from one new moon to the next.</note> and still cannot grasp this obvious truth, they might as well be declared totally lacking in judgment. Why waste time and words on such people?

**SIMP.** To be honest, I have not made such observations myself. I lacked the curiosity and, more importantly, a suitable instrument <note>A reference to the telescope, which Galileo had recently refined and used to make these discoveries.</note> to do so. However, I certainly intend to make them. In the meantime, let us leave this question pending and move to the next point: the reasons why you believe the Earth can reflect sunlight just as powerfully as the Moon. To me, the Earth seems so dark and dull <note>original: "opaca"</note> that such an effect strikes me as completely impossible.

**SALV.** The reason why you consider the Earth incapable of reflecting light is not actually what you think, Mr. Simplicio. Wouldn't it be something if I understood your own arguments better than you do?

**SIMP.** Whether I reason well or poorly, you might indeed know better than I; but I will never believe that you can understand my own thoughts better than I can.

**SALV.** On the contrary, I shall make you believe it right now. Tell me: when the Moon is nearly full, so that it can be seen by day as well as at midnight, when does it appear more brilliant to you—by day or by night?

### F

**SIMPLICIO.** At night, beyond comparison; and it seems to me that the Moon imitates that pillar of clouds and fire that served as a guide to the children of Israel <note>A reference to Exodus 13:21, where God guided the Israelites with a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night.</note>, which in the presence of the Sun showed itself as a small cloud, but at night was most splendid. Thus have I observed the Moon at times during the day among certain small clouds, appearing no different than one of those white ones; but then at night she shows herself most splendid.

<margin>The Moon appears more resplendent at night than by day. The Moon seen by day is similar to a small cloud.</margin>

**SALVIATI.** So, if you had never happened to see the Moon except during the day, you would not have judged her to be any more splendid than one of those small clouds.

**SIMPLICIO.** I firmly believe so.

**SALVIATI.** Tell me now: do you believe that the Moon is actually more luminous at night than during the day, or rather that she appears so due to some circumstance?

**SIMPLICIO.** I believe that she actually shines in herself as much by day as by night, but that her light appears greater at night because we see her against the dark field of the Sky; whereas during the day, because the whole environment is so bright, she barely exceeds it in light, and thus appears to us much less lucid.

**SALVIATI.** Now tell me: have you ever seen the terrestrial globe illuminated by the Sun at midnight?

**SIMPLICIO.** That seems to me a question not to be asked, except as a joke, or perhaps to someone known to be a complete fool.

**SALVIATI.** No, no; I take you for a most sensible man, and I ask the question in earnest. Therefore, go ahead and answer, and then if it seems to you that I am speaking nonsense, I am content to be the fool; for surely he who asks foolishly is more of a fool than he to whom the question is put.

**SIMPLICIO.** If, then, you do not take me for a total simpleton, consider that I have answered you and said that it is impossible for someone who is on the earth, as we are, to see that part of the Earth where it is day at night—that is, the part that is struck by the Sun.

**SALVIATI.** Therefore, it has never fallen to you to see the Earth illuminated except during the day, but you see the Moon shining in the Sky even in the deepest night. And this, Mr. Simplicio, is the reason that makes you believe the Earth does not shine like the Moon; for if you could see the Earth illuminated while you were in a dark place, like our night, you would see her more splendid than the Moon. Now, if you want...

# First Dialogue
## 82

*...for the comparison to proceed correctly, one must make a parallel between the light of the Earth and that of the Moon as seen by day, and not with the Moon at night: because it is only our lot to see the Earth illuminated during the day. Is it not so?*

**SIMPLICIO.** *That is only right.*

<margin>Clouds are capable of being illuminated by the Sun no less than the Moon.</margin>

**SALVIATI.** *And since you yourself have already admitted to having seen the Moon by day among small, whitening clouds, and appearing very similar in aspect to one of them, you are first and foremost coming to admit that those small clouds—which are, after all, elemental matter <term>elemental matter: substances belonging to the Earth’s sphere (earth, water, air, fire), which traditional philosophers like Simplicio believed were "corruptible" and less perfect than the "quintessence" of the heavens</term>—are as capable of receiving illumination as the Moon. Indeed, they are even more so, if you recall having seen at times certain clouds that are very large and very white, like snow. There can be no doubt that if such a cloud could be kept so luminous in the deepest night, it would illuminate the surrounding areas more than a hundred Moons. If, therefore, we were certain that the Earth is illuminated by the Sun just like one of those small clouds, there would be no doubt that she would be no less shining than the Moon. But all doubt on this point ceases when we see those same clouds, in the absence of the Sun, remain at night as dark as the Earth. What is more, there is not one of us who has not often happened to see such clouds, low and distant, and stood in doubt as to whether they were clouds or mountains—an evident sign that mountains are no less luminous than those clouds.*

<margin>A wall illuminated by the Sun, compared with the Moon, is no less bright than she is.</margin>

**SAGREDO.** *But why more talk? Look up there at the Moon, which is more than half full; look over there at that high wall where the Sun is hitting it; draw back here, so that the Moon is seen next to the wall. Now look: which seems brighter to you? Do you not see that if there is an advantage, the wall has it? The Sun strikes that wall; from there it reverberates onto the walls of the hall, from those it reflects into this chamber, arriving here as a third reflection <term>third reflection: light that has bounced off surfaces three times—from Sun to wall, wall to hall, and hall to chamber—losing intensity with each bounce</term>; and yet, I am sure that there is more light here than if the moonlight were to reach it directly.*

<margin>The third reflection from a wall illuminates more than the first reflection from the Moon.</margin>

**SIMPLICIO.** *Oh, I don't believe that, because the light of the Moon, especially when she is full, provides a great deal of illumination.*

<margin>The light of the Moon is weaker than that of the twilight.</margin>

**SAGREDO.** *It seems great because of the darkness of the surrounding shadowy places; but absolutely speaking, it is not much, and it is less than the light of twilight half an hour after sunset. This is manifest, because not until then will you begin to see the shadows of objects illuminated by the Moon begin to be distinguished on the ground.*

# Of Galileo
## 83

*If then that third reflection in that room illuminates more than the first reflection of the Moon, one could know it by going there, reading a book, and then trying tonight by the light of the Moon to see if one reads more easily or less; I believe, without a doubt, that one will read less.*

**SALVIATI.** Now, Mr. Simplicio (provided you are satisfied), you can understand how you yourself truly knew that the Earth shone no less than the Moon, and that merely remembering some things known by yourself, and not taught by me, has made you certain of it. For I did not teach you that the Moon appears more resplendent at night than by day—you already knew it for yourself; just as you also knew that a small cloud appears as bright as the Moon. You likewise knew that the illumination of the Earth is not seen at night, and in short, you knew everything without knowing that you knew it. From this, it should not reasonably be difficult for you to grant that the reflection from the Earth can illuminate the dark part of the Moon with a light no less than that with which the Moon illustrates the darkness of the night. Indeed, it does so much more, given that the Earth is forty times larger than the Moon.

**SIMPLICIO.** Truly, I believed that that secondary light <note>original: *lume secondario*. This refers to "Earthshine" or the "Ashen Light," where the dark part of a crescent moon is faintly visible because of light reflected from the Earth.</note> was the Moon's own property.

<margin>Illuminated bodies appear brighter in a dark environment.</margin>
**SALVIATI.** And this too you know for yourself, though you do not realize you know it. Tell me, have you not known for yourself that the Moon appears much more luminous at night than by day, relative to the darkness of the surrounding field? And consequently, do you not come to know in general that every bright body appears clearer the darker the environment is?

**SIMPLICIO.** This I know very well.

**SALVIATI.** When the Moon is crescent-shaped, and shows you that secondary light quite clearly, is she not always near the Sun, and consequently in the light of the twilight?

**SIMPLICIO.** She is, and many times I have wished that the air would grow darker so as to see that light more clearly, but she has set before the arrival of the dark night.

**SALVIATI.** You know very well, then, that in the deep of night that light would appear more vivid?

**SIMPLICIO.** Yes, sir; and even more so if one could take away the great light of the horns <note>The bright, sunlit tips of the crescent moon.</note> touched by the Sun, the presence of which greatly obscures the other, lesser light.

### First Dialogue
## 84

**SALVIATI.** *Oh, does it not sometimes happen that you can see the entire disk of the Moon in the deepest night, without any part of it being illuminated by the Sun?*

**SIMPLICIO.** *I do not know if this ever occurs, except during total eclipses of the Moon.*

**SALVIATI.** *Therefore, at that time, its light ought to appear most vivid, being set against a very dark field and not obscured by the brilliance of the luminous horns <note>original: "corna luminose." This refers to the tips of the crescent moon.</note>; but in that state, how bright have you seen it?*

**SIMPLICIO.** *I have seen it sometimes copper-colored, and a bit whitish; but at other times it remained so dark that I lost sight of it entirely.*

**SALVIATI.** *How then can that light be its own—that light which you see so clearly in the dawn of twilight, despite the hindrance of the great and nearby splendor of the horns—and yet in the darkest night, when every other light is removed, it does not appear at all?*

**SIMPLICIO.** *I understand there have been those who believed such light was shared with it by the other stars, and particularly by Venus, its neighbor.*

**SALVIATI.** *And that is likewise an empty notion; because during the time of its total obscuration <note>Referring to a total lunar eclipse.</note> it should surely show itself more brilliant than ever, since it cannot be said that the shadow of the Earth hides the sight of Venus or the other stars from it. But indeed, the Moon is then entirely deprived of it, because the terrestrial hemisphere which at that time looks toward the Moon is the one where it is night—that is, a complete deprivation of the Sun’s light. And if you go on observing diligently, you will see through your senses that just as the Moon, when it is a thin crescent, illuminates the Earth very little, and as the part illuminated by the Sun grows within it, the splendor reflected back to us grows equally; so the Moon, while it is a thin crescent—and because it is between the Sun and the Earth, it reveals a very large part of the illuminated terrestrial hemisphere—shows itself quite bright. Then, as it moves away from the Sun and comes toward quadrature <note>original: "quadratura." This is the "quarter moon" phase, when the Moon is 90 degrees away from the Sun.</note>, one sees that light gradually fading; and beyond quadrature, it is seen as very weak, because it is always losing the view of the luminous part of the Earth. And yet the opposite should happen if such light were its own, or communicated to it by the stars; for then we could see it in the deep night and in a very dark environment.*

<meta>catchword: Simp. Fer-</meta>

<summary>Salviati refutes the idea that the Moon's secondary light is intrinsic or comes from stars, explaining instead that it varies based on how much of the Earth's sunlit side is visible from the Moon.</summary>

-># Of Galileo<-

<margin>Secondary light of the Moon caused by the Sun, according to some</margin>

SIMP. Stop, if you please, for it just now occurs to me that I have read in a modern booklet of confusions <note>original: "libretto moderno di confusioni"; Simplicio likely refers to a contemporary work he finds complex or perhaps Salviati's tone implies it is muddled</note>, full of many novelties, that this secondary light is not caused by the stars, nor is it the Moon's own, and least of all communicated to it by the Earth. Instead, it derives from the illumination of the Sun itself, which—because the substance of the lunar globe is somewhat transparent—penetrates through its entire body. It illuminates the surface of the hemisphere exposed to the Sun's rays most vividly; but the depth, drinking in and, so to speak, soaking itself in such light like a cloud or a crystal, transmits it and becomes visibly bright. And this (if I remember correctly) he proves with authority, with experience, and with reason, citing Cleomedes <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 1st century AD) known for his work on the circular motions of celestial bodies</note>, Vitello <note>original: "Vitellione"; a 13th-century Polish friar and physicist famous for his work on optics</note>, Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial who wrote on Neoplatonism and astronomy</note>, and some other modern author. He adds that it is seen by experience to appear very bright in the days near the conjunction <note>The "New Moon" phase when the Moon is between the Earth and Sun</note>—that is, when it is crescent-shaped—and it shines most greatly around its edge <term>limbo: the outer border or edge of a celestial body</term>. Furthermore, he writes that in solar eclipses, when the Moon is under the disk of the Sun, it is seen to shine through, especially around the outermost circle. As for the reasons, it seems to me he says that since this cannot derive from the Earth, nor from the stars, nor from itself, it necessarily remains that it comes from the Sun. Besides, once this supposition is made, the reasons for all the details that occur are very well accommodated. For the cause of this secondary light appearing more vivid around the extreme edge is the shortness of the space to be penetrated by the Sun's rays; since of the lines that traverse a circle, the greatest is that which passes through the center, and of the others, those furthest from this are always smaller than those closer. From the same principle, he says, it follows that such light diminishes little. And finally, by this path, the cause is assigned for why that brighter circle around the extreme margin of the Moon is perceived in a solar eclipse in that part which is under the disk of the Sun, but not in that which is outside the disk; this happens because the rays of the Sun pass straight through to our eye through the parts of the Moon positioned beneath it, but for the parts that are outside, they fall outside the eye.

SALV. If this philosopher had been the first author of such an opinion, I would not wonder that he was so fond of it that he had received it as true; but receiving it from others...

He cites classical and medieval authorities to argue that this explains why the Moon's edge appears brighter during eclipses and crescents.</summary>

# First Dialogue

<margin>The author of the booklet of conclusions adapts things to suit his purposes, rather than adapting his purposes to the facts.</margin>

...gradually imagining things as he would need them to be to serve his purpose, rather than gradually adapting his purposes to things as they actually are. Look: in order to make it so that the splendor of the Sun can penetrate the substance of the Moon, he makes it partially diaphanous <note>diaphanous: translucent or transparent</note>, such as, for example, the transparency of a cloud or a crystal. But I do not know what he would judge regarding such transparency when the solar rays would have to penetrate a depth of cloud of more than two thousand miles. Yet, let it be admitted that he might boldly answer that this could very well happen in celestial bodies, which are different matters than these impure and drossy <term>Elementary bodies</term> <note>In Aristotelian physics, the "Elementary" region (Earth) was considered corruptible and "drossy" compared to the perfect, unchanging heavens.</note> of ours. Let us then convict him of his error by means of arguments that admit no answer—or to put it better, no subterfuges. If he wishes to maintain that the substance of the Moon is diaphanous, he must say that it is so while the rays of the Sun have to penetrate its entire depth—that is, they must penetrate more than two thousand miles—but that when only one mile, or even less, stands in their way, they will no longer penetrate it any more than they penetrate one of our mountains.

**SAGREDO:** You put me in mind of someone who wanted to sell me a secret: the ability to speak, by means of a certain sympathy of magnetized needles <note>An early conceptual reference to magnetic telegraphy, which Sagredo treats as a scam.</note>, to someone who was two or three thousand miles away. When I told him that I would willingly buy it, but that I wanted to see the experiment performed—and that it would be enough for me to do it with me staying in one of my rooms and him in another—he replied that at such a small distance the operation could not be seen well. Whereupon I dismissed him, saying that I did not feel like going to Cairo or Moscow just then to see such an experiment; but if he wanted to go himself, I would perform the other part by staying in Venice. But let us hear how the author’s logic proceeds, and how it must be that he admits the matter of the Moon to be most permeable by solar rays at a depth of two thousand miles, yet more opaque than one of our mountains at a thickness of only one mile.

<margin>A joke played on one who wanted to sell a certain secret for speaking with someone at a distance of a thousand miles.</margin>

**SALVIATI:** The very mountains of the Moon themselves provide us with testimony. When struck on one side by the Sun, they cast extremely black shadows on the opposite side, which are more defined and sharp than the shadows of our own mountains. If they were diaphanous, we could never have recognized any roughness on the surface of the Moon, nor seen those luminous peaks detached from the...

The other doubt, it seems to me, can be very well understood through what we have observed happening with mirrors: that the reflection of light coming from the sea is much inferior to that which comes from the Earth—meaning, however, the *universal* reflection <note>Galileo distinguishes between "universal" (diffuse) reflection, which scatters in all directions, and "particular" (specular) reflection, which goes in one direction like a mirror.</note>. For as for the *particular* reflection, which the surface of calm water sends to a specific place, there is no doubt that whoever stands in that place will see a most powerful reflection in the water; but from all other places, the surface of the water will appear darker than that of the Earth. To demonstrate this to the senses, let us go here into the Hall and pour a little water on the floor. Tell me now, does this wet brick not appear much darker than the other dry ones? Certainly it does, and it will appear so viewed from any place whatsoever, except for one: and that is the place where the reflection of the light entering through that window arrives. Move yourself toward it very slowly.

**SIMPLICIO:** From here, I see the wet part is more lustrous than the rest of the floor, and I see that this happens because the reflection of the light entering through the window comes toward me.

**SALVIATI:** That wetting has done nothing but fill those small cavities that are in the brick and reduce its surface to an exquisite plane; hence the reflected rays go united toward the same place. But the rest of the dry floor has its roughness—that is, an innumerable variety of inclinations in its tiny particles—whereby the reflections of light go toward all parts, but more weakly than if they all went united together. Therefore, its appearance varies little or nothing when looking at it from different sides; it shows the same from all places, but certainly much less bright than that reflection from the wet part. I conclude, therefore, that the surface of the sea seen from the Moon, just as it would appear most level (excepting the islands and the rocks), so it would appear less bright than that of the mountainous and unequal Earth. ->**SIMPLICIO.** *But do you truly believe that those large spots seen on the face of the Moon are seas, and the brighter remainder is land, or something of that sort?*<-

**SALVIATI.** *What you ask is the beginning of the inconsistencies that I believe exist between the Moon and the Earth, from which it is time we extricate ourselves, for we have stayed too long on this Moon. I say, then, that if in nature there were only one single way to make two surfaces illuminated by the Sun appear one brighter than the other, and that this was by one being land and the other water, it would be necessary to say that the Moon's surface was part earthy and part watery. But because there are several ways known to us that can cause the same effect—and others perhaps may be unknown to us—I would not dare to affirm that it is this rather than that on the Moon.*

*We have already seen above how a plate of whitened silver <note>original: "argento bianchito" - silver treated with acid to create a matte white surface</note>, by touching it with a burnisher, turns from white to dark. The moist part of the Earth appears darker than the dry; on the ridges of mountains, the forested parts appear much gloomier than the bare and sterile ones. This happens because there is a great quantity of shadow among the plants, while the open places are all illuminated by the Sun. This mixture of shadows is so effective that you see in patterned velvets the color of the cut silk appears much darker than that of the uncut, due to the shadows scattered between thread and thread; and plain velvet likewise appears much gloomier than a taffeta <note>original: "ermifino" - a light, plain-weave silk</note> made of the same silk. Thus, if there were things on the Moon that imitated vast forests, their appearance could represent to us the spots that we see. A similar difference would occur if they were seas; and finally, it is not impossible that those spots might actually be of a darker color than the rest, in the same way that snow makes mountains appear brighter.*

*What is clearly seen on the Moon is that the darker parts are all plains with few rocks and ridges within them, though some are present; the remaining brighter part is entirely full of rocks, mountains, circular ridges, and other shapes; and in particular, around the spots, there are very great ranges of mountains.*

# On Galileo

SIMPLICIO. It must then be said either that the Oracle or Socrates himself was a liar, since the former proclaimed him to be the wisest, and the latter claimed to know himself to be the most ignorant.

<margin>Response of the Oracle.</margin>
<margin>Socrates most wise.</margin>
SALVIATI. Neither one nor the other follows, as both pronouncements can be true. The Oracle judges Socrates most wise above other men, whose wisdom is limited; Socrates knows himself to know nothing in relation to absolute wisdom, which is infinite. And because one cannot have science <note>In this context, "science" refers to certain, demonstrative knowledge (Latin: *scientia*).</note> of the infinite, but can only know a tiny fraction of it, which is as good as nothing (because to reach an infinite number, for example, it is the same to accumulate thousands as it is tens or zeros), Socrates therefore well knew his finite wisdom to be nothing compared to the infinite wisdom he lacked. But because some knowledge is indeed found among men, and this is not equally shared by all, Socrates could have had a greater share of it than others, and thus the response of the Oracle is verified.

SAGREDO. I believe I understand this point very well. Among men, Mr. Simplicio, there is the power to act, but it is not equally shared by all; and there is no doubt that the power of an Emperor is much greater than that of a private person; but both this and that are nothing in comparison to divine omnipotence. Among men there are some who understand agriculture better than many others; but what does knowing how to plant a vine cutting in a trench have to do with knowing how to make it take root, draw nourishment, and from that select this good part to make leaves, this other to form tendrils, that for the clusters, that other for the grapes, and another for the skins—which are the works of most wise Nature? This is but a single particular work among the innumerable ones that Nature performs; and in it alone an infinite wisdom is recognized, such that one can conclude divine knowledge to be infinite times infinite.

<margin>Buonarroti <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564), the famous Renaissance artist.</note> of sublime genius.</margin>
SALVIATI. Here is another example. Do we not say that knowing how to discover a most beautiful statue within a block of marble has raised the genius of Buonarroti far, far above the common wits of other men? And yet this work is nothing more than imitating a single posture and the exterior, superficial arrangement of the limbs of an immobile man; therefore, what is this in comparison to a man made by Nature, composed of so many external and internal members, of so many muscles, tendons, nerves, and bones, which serve...

SAGREDO: And what difference do we believe there would be between the mechanical Dove of Archytas <note>Archytas of Taras (4th century BCE) was a Greek philosopher and mathematician reputed to have built a steam-powered wooden bird.</note> and one made by nature?

Among the greatest praises—indeed, as the greatest of all—you attribute to man, as made by nature, this power of understanding; yet a moment ago you said with Socrates that his understanding was nothing. Therefore, one must say that even nature did not understand how to make an intellect that understands.

SALVIATI: You object very sharply; and to respond to the objection, it is necessary to have recourse to a philosophical distinction, saying that "to understand" can be taken in two ways: namely, *intensively* or *extensively*. <note>original: "intensiue, ò vero extensiue"</note> Taken *extensively*—that is, regarding the multitude of 
<margin>Man understands much intensively, but little extensively.</margin>
intelligible things, which are infinite—human understanding is as nothing, even if he understood a thousand propositions; for a thousand, compared to infinity, is like a zero. But taking understanding *intensively*—insofar as that term implies, intensively, the perfect grace of some proposition—I say that the human intellect understands some of them so perfectly, and has such absolute certainty of them, as nature itself possesses. Such are the pure mathematical sciences, namely Geometry and Arithmetic. Of these, the divine intellect indeed knows infinitely more propositions, because it knows them all; but of those few understood by the human intellect, I believe that its knowledge equals the divine in objective certainty, since it succeeds in comprehending their necessity, beyond which it seems there can be no greater security.

SIMPLICIO: This seems to me very resolute and bold talk.

SALVIATI: These are common propositions, far from any shadow of temerity or boldness, and they detract not a bit from the majesty of divine wisdom; just as it in no way diminishes His omnipotence to say that God cannot make what is done to be undone. # First Dialogue

<margin>Human wit: a marvelous sharpness.</margin>
The sharpness of human wit <note>original: "ingegno," referring to innate talent or creative intelligence</note>; and while I discourse upon so many, and such marvelous inventions found by men, both in the arts and in letters, and then reflect upon my own knowledge—so far from being able to promise myself not only the discovery of anything new, but even the learning of what has already been found—confused by wonder and afflicted by despair, I consider myself little less than miserable. If I look upon any excellent statue, I say to myself: when would I ever know how to remove the excess from a block of marble and reveal so beautiful a figure that was hidden within? When could I mix and spread diverse colors upon a canvas or a wall, and with them represent all visible objects, like a Michelangelo, a Raphael, or a Titian? If I look at what men have discovered in partitioning musical intervals, and in establishing precepts and rules to handle them with such admirable delight for the ear, when will I ever cease to wonder? What shall I say of the many and diverse instruments? The reading of excellent poets—with what marvel does it fill anyone who attentively considers the invention of their concepts and the unfolding of them? What shall we say of Architecture? What of the art of Navigation? <margin>The invention of writing: stupendous above all others.</margin> But above all stupendous inventions, what eminence of mind was his, who imagined a way to communicate his most recondite thoughts to any other person, though distant by a very long interval of place and time? To speak with those who are in the Indies; to speak to those who are not yet born, nor will be for a thousand or ten thousand years? And with what ease? With the various arrangements of twenty little characters upon a paper. Let this be the seal of all the admirable human inventions, and the closing of our discussions for this day; and since the hottest hours have passed, I think Mr. Salviati will take pleasure in going to enjoy our cool breezes in a boat, and tomorrow I shall be awaiting you both to continue the discourses we have begun, etc.

# DAY
## SECOND.

->SALVIATI<- The diversions of yesterday, which turned us away from the straight thread of our principal discourse, were so many and of such a kind that I do not know if, without your help, I can get back on track in order to proceed forward.

->SAGREDO<- I am not surprised that you, who have your imagination filled and encumbered as much with the things already said as with those that remain to be said, find yourself in some confusion; but I, who as a simple listener retain nothing but the things I have heard, may perhaps be able to put the reasoning back on its thread by recalling them summarily. According to what has remained in my mind, the sum of yesterday's discourse was the examination, from their foundations, of which of the two opinions is more probable and reasonable: that which holds the substance of the celestial bodies <note>The "heavenly bodies" like stars and planets.</note> to be ungenerable, incorruptible, unalterable, impassive <note>Incapable of being acted upon or changed by external force.</note>, and in short, exempt from every mutation except for that of place, and therefore to be a **fifth essence** <note>term: quintessence; the idea in Aristotelian physics that the heavens were made of a pure, unchanging element different from the four earthly elements.</note> most diverse from that of our elementary bodies—which are generable, corruptible, alterable, etc.—or else the other opinion, which, by removing such deformity <note>Inconsistency or difference in nature.</note> of parts from the World, considers the Earth to enjoy the same perfections as the other integral bodies of the universe: and to be, in short, a mobile and wandering globe, no less than the Moon, Jupiter, Venus, or any other Planet. Finally, many particular parallels were drawn between the Earth and the Moon—more so with the Moon than with any other planet, perhaps because we have greater and more sensory knowledge of it due to its lesser distance. And having finally concluded that this second opinion has more likelihood than the other, it seems to me that our progress should lead us to begin examining whether the Earth should be considered immobile, as has been believed by most until now, or instead mobile, as some ancient philosophers believed and others not long ago have estimated; and if mobile, what its movement might be.

# Second Dialogue

SAGR. I allowed myself to be carried away by my own feeling, *and believing that what I felt in myself must be in others, I made universal that conclusion which should have remained particular; and truly I have erred, especially not knowing the thoughts of Mr. Simplicio here present.*

SIMP. SIMPLICIO: Gentlemen, I want you to know that this dispute over the origin of the nerves is not at all so settled and decided as perhaps some might persuade themselves.

SAGREDO: Nor will it ever be settled as long as there are such opponents; but what you say does not diminish in the least the extravagance of the Peripatetic’s response, who, against such sensory experience, produced no other experiences or reasons from Aristotle, but only his authority and the pure *ipse dixit* <note>Latin: "He himself said it"; an assertion made but not proved.</note>.

SIMPLICIO: Aristotle did not acquire such great authority except by the force of his demonstrations and the depth of his discourses. But one must understand him; and not only understand him, but have such great practice with his books that a most perfect Idea of them is formed, in such a way that every saying of his is always present before the mind. For he did not write for the common people, nor did he feel obliged to string together his syllogisms <note>A form of logical argument</note> with the trivial, ordered method. On the contrary, using a disordered style, he sometimes placed the proof of a proposition among texts that seem to treat of entirely different things. And therefore, one must possess that entire grand Idea, and know how to combine this passage with that one, and couple this text with another very remote from it. There is no doubt that whoever has this practice will know how to draw from his books the demonstrations of everything knowable, because everything is within them.

<margin>Requirements for being able to philosophize well in the Aristotelian way.</margin>

### Fruitful Dialogue

Virgil, or of some other poet? I have a little book much shorter than Aristotle or Ovid, in which all the sciences are contained, and with very little study, one can form a most perfect Idea of them: and this is the alphabet. There is no doubt that he who knows how to properly couple and arrange this or that vowel with those consonants or others, will derive the truest answers to all doubts, and will draw from it the teachings of all sciences and all arts. It is in exactly the same manner that a Painter, from simple diverse colors placed separately upon the palette, goes about mixing a little of this with a little of that or another, depicting men, plants, buildings, birds, fish, and in short, imitating all visible objects—without there being on the palette any eyes, feathers, scales, leaves, or stones. Indeed, it is necessary that none of the things to be imitated, nor any part of them, be actually present among the colors if one wishes to be able to represent all things with them; for if there were, for example, feathers, these would serve for painting nothing but birds or plumes.

SAGREDO: Oh, now this is a doctor who can truly command me! He does not want to let himself be fooled by Aristotle, but rather wants to lead Aristotle by the nose and make him speak in his own way. See how important it is to know how to seize the opportune moment: one must not attempt to negotiate with Hercules while he is enraged and in a fury, but rather when he is telling stories among the Maeonian handmaidens <note>A mythological reference to Hercules serving Queen Omphale of Lydia (Maeonia), during which time he performed feminine tasks and was approachable.</note>. Oh, unheard-of baseness of servile minds! To make oneself spontaneously a <term>Mancipio</term> <note>original: "Mancipio"; a Latin legal term for a formal purchase or a person held as a slave/property.</note>, to accept decrees as inviolable, to oblige oneself to call oneself persuaded and convinced by arguments that are so effective and clearly concluding that the very people using them cannot decide if they were even written for that purpose, or if they serve to prove that specific conclusion. But let us speak of the greater madness: that among themselves they are still in doubt whether the author himself held the affirmative or the negative side. Is this not making an oracle out of a wooden statue, and running to it for responses, fearing it, revering it, and adoring it?

<margin>The small-mindedness of some followers of Aristotle.</margin>
SIMPLICIO: But if we leave Aristotle, who is to be our guide in Philosophy? Name some author.

SALVIATI: There is a need for a guide in unknown and wild lands, but in open and level places, only the blind have need of a leader; and whoever is such, it is well that he stays at home. But he who has eyes in his forehead and in his mind, those he must use as his guide. Nor do I say by this that one should not listen to Aristotle; 

<margin>Too much adherence to Aristotle is blameworthy.</margin>
on the contrary, I praise looking at him and diligently studying him. I only blame giving oneself up as his prey in such a manner that one blindly subscribes to his every word and, without seeking any other reason, must hold it as an inviolable decree. This is an abuse that brings with it another extreme disorder: that people no longer apply themselves to seeking to understand the strength of his demonstrations. And what thing is more shameful than to hear in public disputes, while dealing with demonstrable conclusions, someone come in sideways with a text—and very often one written for an entirely different purpose—and with it shut the mouth of the opponent?
