## Second Dialogue

<margin>It is not fitting that those who never philosophize should usurp the title of philosopher.</margin>
<margin>The sensible world.</margin>
<margin>The sensible world.</margin>
But if you still wish to continue in this method of study, lay aside the name of Philosophers and call yourselves either Historians or Doctors of Memory; for it is not fitting that those who never philosophize should usurp the honored title of Philosopher. But it is well to return to the shore so as not to enter into an infinite ocean from which we would not emerge all day. Therefore, Master Simplicio <note>Simplicio is the character representing the traditional Aristotelian view.</note>, come forward with your reasons and your demonstrations, or those of Aristotle, and not with texts and naked authorities, because our discourses must be concerning the sensible world <note>The physical world as perceived by the senses, rather than the theoretical world of books.</note>, and not upon a world of paper. And because in yesterday's discourse the Earth was drawn out of the darkness and exposed to the open Sky—showing that the desire to number it among those which we call celestial bodies was not a proposition so thoroughly defeated and prostrated that there did not remain some vital spirit in it—it follows that we should go on examining what probability there is in holding it fixed and entirely immobile (referring to its entire globe) and what likelihood there may be in making it mobile with some movement, and of what kind. And because in this question I am undecided, while Master Simplicio is resolved along with Aristotle in favor of immobility, he shall step by step bring forward the motives for their opinion, and I the responses and arguments for the contrary side; and Master Sagredo <note>Sagredo represents the intelligent, open-minded layman.</note> will express the stirrings of his mind and toward which side he feels himself drawn.

SAGREDO. I am very content, provided, however, that I also retain the liberty to produce whatever simple, natural discourse might occasionally dictate to me.

SALVIATI <note>Salviati is the character representing Galileo's own scientific views.</note>. On the contrary, I specifically beg this of you; because regarding the easier and, so to speak, material considerations, I believe few have been left behind by previous writers, such that only some of the more subtle and recondite ones may be desired or missing. And to investigate these, what other subtlety could be more fit than that of the most acute and perspicacious wit of Master Sagredo?

SAGREDO. I am whatever pleases Master Salviati; but please, let us not begin another sort of diversion with ceremonies; for now I am a philosopher, and I am in School, and not at the *Brolo* <note>original: "Broio" (Brolo). # On Galileo
<page-num>107</page-num>

<margin>The motions of the Earth are imperceptible to its inhabitants.</margin>
Since we are participants in that same motion, it remains entirely imperceptible to us, as if it did not exist at all, as long as we look only at terrestrial things. On the other hand, it is equally necessary that this same motion appears to us as common to all other visible bodies and objects which, being separated from the Earth, lack that motion. Thus, the true method for investigating whether any motion can be attributed to the Earth—and if so, what kind it might be—is to consider and observe whether an appearance of motion is perceived in bodies separated from the Earth which belongs equally to all of them. For a motion that is only perceived, for example, in the Moon, and has nothing to do with Venus or Jupiter, nor with other stars, could in no way belong to the Earth, but only to the Moon. 

<margin>The Earth can have no other motions than those which appear to us to be common to the rest of the Universe, excluding the Earth.</margin>
Now, there is a most general and greatest motion of all, which is that by which the Sun, the Moon, the other planets, and the fixed stars—in short, the whole Universe, except for the Earth—appear to us to move together from East to West within the space of twenty-four hours. As far as this first appearance is concerned, there is no reason why this could not belong to the Earth alone just as much as to all the rest of the World, excluding the Earth; for the same appearances would be seen in one position as in the other. 

<margin>The diurnal motion appears common to the whole universe, except for the terrestrial globe.</margin>
Hence it is that Aristotle and Ptolemy <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) and Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE) were the primary historical authorities for the geocentric model, placing the Earth at the center of the universe.</note>, as those who understood this consideration, when wanting to prove the Earth to be immobile, do not argue against any other motion than this diurnal <term>diurnal: the daily rotation occurring every 24 hours</term> one; except that Aristotle says something or other against another motion attributed to it by an ancient <note>Likely a reference to Philolaus or Hicetas, Pythagorean philosophers who proposed the Earth moved.</note>, of which we shall speak in its proper place.

<margin>Aristotle and Ptolemy argue against the diurnal motion being attributed to the Earth.</margin>

**SAGREDO:** I am quite convinced of the necessity with which your discourse concludes; but a doubt arises in me from which I cannot free myself. It is this: since Copernicus attributes to the Earth another motion besides the diurnal one <note>Copernicus proposed that the Earth also orbits the Sun annually.</note>, which, by the rule just now declared, ought to remain imperceptible to us on Earth but visible in all the rest of the World, it seems to me I must necessarily conclude either that he has manifestly erred in assigning to the Earth a motion of which a general correspondence does not appear in the Heavens, or else, if that correspondence is there, Ptolemy was equally deficient in not refuting this one, just as he refuted the other.

->**SALVIATI:** Very<-

# Fruitful Dialogue

SALV. You have doubted quite reasonably; and when we come to treat of the other movement <note>The annual revolution of the Earth around the Sun</note>, you will see by how great an interval **Copernicus** surpassed **Ptolemy** in shrewdness and **perspicacity of wit**, in that he saw what the other did not see—I mean the wonderful correspondence with which such a movement is reflected in all the rest of the celestial bodies. But for now let us suspend this part and return to the first consideration. Regarding this, I shall proceed by proposing, beginning with the most general things, those reasons which seem to favor the mobility of the **Earth**, so as to hear from Mr. **Simplicio** the opposing ones. And first, if we consider only the immense bulk of the **Stellar** sphere in comparison with the smallness of the terrestrial globe (which is contained within the former many millions of times), and further think of the velocity of the motion which must make an entire conversion in one day and one night, I cannot persuade myself that anyone could be found who would hold it more reasonable and credible that the celestial sphere were the one to go around, and the terrestrial globe to remain still.

# On Galileo

<margin>Motion, for things that move equally with it, is as if it did not exist, and it only acts insofar as it has a relation to things that lack it.</margin>...to seek it would be in vain: therefore, take note. Motion is motion only insofar as, and acts as motion only insofar as, it has a relation to things that do not materially participate in it; among those things that participate in it equally, it acts not at all, and is as if it were not. And thus the merchandise with which a ship is loaded moves insofar as it passes from Venice to Corfu, to Crete <note>original: "Candia"</note>, to Cyprus, and goes to Aleppo—which Venice, Corfu, Crete, etc., remain behind and do not move with the ship. But for the bales, coffee, and other packages with which the ship is loaded, and in respect to the ship itself, the motion from Venice to Syria is as nothing, and in no way alters the relationship between them. This is because the motion is common to all, and is shared equally by all. If, of the goods on the ship, a bale were to move away from a chest by a single inch, this alone would be for it a greater movement, in relation to the chest, than the journey of two thousand miles made by them together.

SIMPLICIO: This is good, solid doctrine, and entirely Peripatetic <note>Refers to the followers of Aristotle</note>.

<margin>A proposition taken by Aristotle from the ancients, but altered.</margin>SALVIATI: I consider it to be even more ancient; and I suspect that Aristotle, in taking it from some good school, did not fully penetrate its meaning, and that therefore, having written it in an altered form, he has been the cause of confusion among those who wish to defend his every word. When he wrote that "everything that moves, moves *upon* something immobile," I suspect he equivocated from saying that "everything that moves, moves *in relation to* something immobile." This latter proposition suffers no difficulty at all, whereas the other has many.

SAGREDO: Please, let us not break the thread; continue with the discourse you have begun.

<margin>First discourse to prove the diurnal motion belongs to the Earth.</margin>SALVIATI: It being manifest, then, that motion which is common to many moving bodies is idle and as if null regarding the relationship of those moving bodies to one another (since nothing changes between them), and is operative only in the relationship those moving bodies have with others that lack that motion (among which the relative position changes); and having divided the universe into two parts, one of which is necessarily mobile and the other immobile: for everything that can depend on such movement, it is the same to make the Earth alone move as it is to move all the rest of the world. This is because the operation of such motion exists in nothing other than the relationship between the celestial bodies and the Earth, which is the only relationship that changes. Now, if to achieve the same...

He suggests that the Earth's rotation is more plausible than the movement of the entire universe, as the relative change in position remains the same.</summary>

# Second Dialogue

<margin>Nature does not do with many things what it can do with few.</margin>
...the exact same effect is achieved whether the Earth alone moves, while the rest of the universe remains still, or whether the Earth remains still and the entire universe moves with a single motion. Now, who would believe that Nature (which, by common consent, does not act through the intervention of many things when it can achieve the same result by means of a few) has chosen to move an immense number of vast bodies with an inestimable speed, just to achieve what could be obtained by the moderate movement of a single body around its own center?

**SIMPLICIO**: I do not quite understand how this immense motion is "as nothing" for the Sun, the Moon, the other planets, and the innumerable host of fixed stars. How can you say it is nothing for the Sun to pass from one meridian to another, to rise above this horizon, to sink below that one, and to bring now day, now night? And that the Moon, the other planets, and the fixed stars undergo similar variations?

<margin>No change arises among the celestial bodies from the diurnal motion; they all refer back to the Earth.</margin>
**SALVIATI**: All those variations you recount are nothing except in relation to the Earth. To see that this is true, remove the Earth in your imagination; there would no longer be any rising or setting of the Sun or Moon in the world, nor horizons, nor meridians, nor days, nor nights. In short, through such a movement, no change ever arises between the Moon and the Sun, or any other stars, whether fixed or wandering <note>The "wandering stars" refer to the planets, from the Greek *planētēs*.</note>. All these changes relate to the Earth; they mean nothing more than showing the Sun first to China, then to Persia, then to Egypt, Greece, France, Spain, America, etc., and doing the same for the Moon and the rest of the celestial bodies. This exact same process follows in precisely the same way if, without involving such a vast part of the universe, the terrestrial globe is made to rotate upon itself.

<margin>Second confirmation that the diurnal motion belongs to the Earth.</margin>
But let us double the difficulty with another very great one: if we attribute this great motion to the Heavens, we must of necessity make it contrary to the particular motions of all the planetary spheres. Each of these, without controversy, has its own proper motion from West to East, which is quite pleasant and moderate. We must then have them snatched away in the opposite direction—that is, from East to West—by this extremely rapid diurnal motion. Whereas, by making the Earth move upon itself, the contradiction of motions is removed, and a single movement from West to East accommodates all appearances and satisfies them all completely.

SIMPLICIO. Let us call them contrary.

They are those of two circles that touch from the outside, where the turning of one naturally makes the other move in a different direction; but if one is inside the other, it is impossible that their motions, made in different directions, do not conflict with one another.

# Fruitful Dialogue

<margin>Times of the conjunctions of the Medicean Planets <note>The "Medicean Planets" is the name Galileo gave to the four largest moons of Jupiter (Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto) to honor his patrons, the Medici family.</note>.</margin>
...closest to Jupiter makes its revolution in a very short time, that is, in about forty-four hours; the next in three and a half days; the third in seven days; and the most remote in sixteen. And this very consistent pattern will not be altered at all if we assume that the twenty-four-hour movement belongs to the terrestrial globe itself. However, if one wishes to keep the Earth immobile, it is necessary—after passing from the very short period of the Moon to the others consequently larger, up to that of Mars in two years, and from there to that of the larger sphere of Jupiter in twelve years, and from this to the other larger one of Saturn, whose period is thirty years—it is necessary, I say, to pass to another incomparably larger sphere and make it complete an entire revolution in twenty-four hours. And this is the smallest disorder that could be introduced; because, if one were to pass from Saturn to the starry sphere and make it as much larger than Saturn's as would be proportionally appropriate relative to its very slow movement of many thousands of years <note>Referring to the precession of the equinoxes, a very slow wobble of the Earth's axis that makes the stars appear to shift over millennia.</note>, one would have to, with a much more disproportionate leap, pass from that to another even larger sphere and make it revolve in twenty-four hours. 

But by granting mobility to the Earth, the order of the periods is perfectly observed; from the very sluggish sphere of Saturn, one passes to the Fixed Stars, which are entirely immobile. In this way, one avoids a fourth difficulty which must necessarily be admitted if the starry sphere is made mobile. This is the immense disparity between the motions of these stars, some of which would move extremely fast in vast circles, while others move extremely slowly in tiny circles, depending on whether they are closer to or further from the poles. This is inconvenient, both because we see those bodies whose motion is not doubted all moving in the largest possible circles <note>Meaning their orbits are centered on the primary body, not constrained by a celestial pole.</note>, and also because it seems a poor decision to establish bodies that must move circularly at immense distances from the center, and then make them move in tiny circles. 

<margin>The 24-hour motion attributed to the highest sphere disrupts the period of the lower ones.</margin>

<margin>Great deformity between the movements of individual Fixed Stars while their sphere is mobile.</margin>

<margin>Motions of the Fixed Stars accelerate and slow down at different times when the starry sphere is mobile.</margin>

# On Galileo

It is not impossible that a time may come when one of them, which previously always moved, might—by joining with the pole—be reduced to standing still, and then after a period of rest, begin to move again. Meanwhile, the other stars, which move securely, all describe (as has been said) the greatest circle of their sphere and maintain themselves immutably within it.

It increases the improbability (and let this be the **sixth inconvenience**) to anyone who reasons more solidly, that it is unthinkable what the solidity of that vast sphere must be, in whose depths so many stars are so tenaciously fixed that, without changing their positions relative to one another at all, they are carried around in unison despite such great disparity in their individual motions. Or, if the Heavens are fluid—as is much more reasonable to believe—so that each star wanders through it by itself, what law would regulate their motions, and to what end, to make them appear from Earth as if they were moved by a single sphere? To me, it seems that to achieve this, it is a much easier and more convenient method to establish them as immobile rather than wandering, just as it is easier to keep many stones in formation when they are walled into a pavement than it is to coordinate a troop of children running across it.

And finally, for the **seventh instance**, if we attribute the diurnal <term>diurnal: daily</term> rotation to the highest Heaven, we must make it of such force and power that it carries with it the innumerable multitude of fixed stars—all vast bodies, much larger than the Earth—and furthermore, all the spheres of the Planets. This is required even though both the stars and planets, by their own nature, move in the opposite direction. Beyond this, one must concede that even the element of fire and the greater part of the air are likewise swept along, and that only the small globe of the Earth remains defiant and resistant to such power. This is a thing that seems very difficult to me; I would not know how to understand how the Earth—a body hanging and balanced upon its center, indifferent to motion or rest, placed and surrounded by a liquid environment—should not also yield and be carried around. But we find no such obstacles in making the Earth move, a body minimal and insignificant in comparison to the universe, and therefore unable to do it any violence.

# Second Dialogue

<margin>A simple moving body has only one natural motion; others are by participation.</margin>
**SIMPLICIO:** For a simple moving body, there can be only one motion, and no more, that belongs to it naturally; all others are by accident and by participation. In the same way that for a man walking across a ship, his own proper motion is that of walking, while by participation he possesses the motion that carries him into port—where he would never have arrived by walking alone, had the ship not carried him there with its own motion.

**SAGREDO:** Tell me secondly: that movement which is communicated to a moving body by participation, while it moves by itself with another motion different from the participated one—is it necessary that it resides in some subject by itself, or can it exist in nature without any other support?

**SIMPLICIO:** Aristotle answers all these questions for you, and tells you that just as for one moving body there is one motion, so for one motion there is one moving body; and consequently, without the existence of its subject, no movement can either exist or even be imagined.

<margin>Motion does not exist without a moving subject.</margin>
**SAGREDO:** I would like you to tell me in the third place if you believe that the Moon, and the other Planets and celestial bodies, have their own proper movements, and what they are.

**SIMPLICIO:** They have them, and they are those by which they go running through the Zodiac: the Moon in a month, the Sun in a year, Mars in two, and the starry sphere in those many thousands <note>referring to the Precession of the Equinoxes, then thought to take 36,000 years</note>. **SAGREDO:** But that motion by which I see the fixed Stars, and with them all the Planets, moving together from east to west and returning to the East in twenty-four hours—in what way does that belong to them?

**SIMPLICIO:** They have it by participation.

**SAGREDO:** This, then, does not reside in them; and not residing in them, nor being able to exist without some subject in which it resides, it must necessarily be made the proper and natural motion of some other sphere.

# Concerning Galileo

<page-num>117</page-num>

The point left out is "equally well"; we must therefore examine whether one can satisfy the whole just as well with this assumption as with that one.

<margin>On the Axiom: It is superfluous to do with more what can be done with fewer, etc. <note>original: "Frustra fit per plura, &c." A reference to Ockham's Razor.</note></margin>
SALVIATI: Whether both positions satisfy the requirements equally well will be understood from the particular examinations of the appearances <note>The "appearances" refer to observed celestial phenomena.</note> which must be satisfied; so far we have discussed, and shall continue to discuss, hypothetically, assuming that as far as satisfying the appearances is concerned, both positions are equally suited. As for the phrase you say I left out, I rather suspect it was superfluously added by you. Because to say or add "equally well" is a relationship that necessarily requires at least two terms; a thing cannot have a relationship with itself and be said, for example, "rest is as good as rest." And because, when it is said that it is in vain to do with more means what can be done with fewer, it is understood that what is to be done must be the same thing, and not two different things. Since the same thing cannot be said to be "equally well done" as itself, therefore the addition of the phrase "equally well" is superfluous and a relationship that has only one term.

SAGREDO: If we do not wish to be interrupted as we were yesterday, let us please return to the subject; and let Master Simplicio begin to produce those difficulties which seem to him to contradict this new arrangement of the world.

<margin>Aristotle's reasons for the Earth's rest.</margin>
SIMPLICIO: The arrangement is not new—rather, it is very ancient; and to show that this is true, Aristotle refutes it. His refutations are these:
First: If the Earth moved, either on its own axis while staying at the center, or in a circle while being away from the center, it would necessarily have to move with such motion by force; for such motion is not its natural one. If it were its natural motion, every one of its particles would also possess it; but every one of them moves in a straight line toward the center. Being therefore forced and preternatural, it could not be everlasting; but the order of the world is everlasting; therefore, etc.
Secondly: All other bodies that move with circular motion seem to lag behind and move with more than one motion, except for the "prime mover" <term>Primum Mobile: in Ptolemaic astronomy, the outermost moving sphere that carries all others</term>. For this reason, it would be necessary for the Earth also to move with two motions. And if that were the case, it would necessarily follow that changes would occur in the fixed stars, which is not seen; on the contrary, without any variation, the same stars always rise from the same places.

# Concerning Galileo.

<margin>First argument taken from heavy bodies falling from a height to the base.</margin>
...of heavy bodies, which falling from a height to the base come down along a straight line, perpendicular to the surface of the Earth. This is an argument esteemed as irrefutable proof that the Earth is immobile; because, if it possessed a diurnal rotation, a Tower—from the summit of which a stone was let fall—would be carried by the Earth's whirling motion during the time the stone spends falling. It would sweep many hundreds of <term>braccia<note>An ancient Italian unit of measurement, literally "arms," roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note></term> toward the East, and the stone ought to strike the Earth that same distance away from the foot of the Tower. They confirm this effect with another experiment: by letting a lead ball fall from the top of the mast of a ship that is stationary, noting the mark where it hits, which is near the foot of the mast. But if one lets the same ball fall from the same place when the ship is moving, its strike will be distant from the first mark by as much space as the ship has moved forward during the time of the lead's fall. This occurs for no other reason than that the natural movement of the ball, when set at liberty, is in a straight line toward the center of the Earth. This argument is strengthened
<margin>Confirmed by the example of a falling body from the top of a ship's mast.</margin>
<margin>Second argument taken from a projectile thrown to a great height.</margin>
by the experiment of a projectile shot upward to a very great distance, such as a ball fired from a piece of artillery <note>original: "artiglieria"</note> aimed perpendicularly above the horizon. In its ascent and return, it consumes so much time that, in our latitude <note>original: "parallelo"</note>, the artillery and we together would be carried by the Earth for many miles toward the East <note>original: "Leuante"</note>. Thus, the falling ball could never return near the cannon, but would land as far away toward the West <note>original: "Occidente"</note> as the Earth had moved forward. They add furthermore a third and very effective experiment: if one fires a ball from a <term>Culverin<note>A type of long-range medieval and Renaissance cannon.</note></term> toward the East, and then another with equal charge and at the same elevation toward the West, the shot toward the West would turn out to be extremely much longer than the one toward the East. This is because while the ball goes toward the West and the artillery is carried by the Earth toward the East, the ball would strike the ground at a distance from the cannon equal to the sum of the two journeys: the one made by itself toward the West, and the other by the cannon carried by the Earth toward the East. Conversely, from the journey made by the ball fired toward the East, one would have to subtract the distance the artillery had traveled while following it. Suppose, therefore, for example, that the journey of the ball by itself was five miles, and that the Earth in that latitude, during the time of the ball's flight,

## Second Dialogue

<margin>The argument is confirmed by shots fired toward the south and toward the north.</margin>
...if the Earth moved three miles during a westward shot, the ball would fall to the ground eight miles away from the piece—that is, its own five miles toward the West, and the three miles the cannon moved toward the East. Conversely, the eastward shot would result in a range no longer than two miles, which is what remains from the five miles of the shot after subtracting the three miles of the cannon's motion toward the same direction. But experience shows the shots to be equal; therefore, the artillery remains immobile, and consequently the Earth does as well. But no less than these, shots fired toward the south or toward the north also confirm the stability of the Earth; for one would never hit the mark that had been aimed at. Instead, the shots would always be skewed toward the West, because of the travel of the target, carried by the Earth toward the East while the ball is in the air. And not only shots along the meridian lines <note>Lines running North-South</note>, but not even those made toward the East or toward the West would prove accurate. Rather, the Eastward shots would result high, and the Westward shots low, whenever one fired point-blank <note>original: "di punto in bianco"; a technical term for firing a cannon horizontally without elevation</note>. Because the path of the ball in both shots is made along the tangent—that is, along a line parallel to the horizon—and since in the diurnal motion (if it belonged to the Earth) the horizon is always lowering toward the East and rising from the West (which is why the Eastern stars appear to rise and the Western ones to sink), therefore the Eastern target would go on lowering itself beneath the shot, making the shot result high; and the rising of the Western target would make the shot toward the West result low. Thus, one could never fire accurately toward any direction; and because experience proves the contrary, one is forced to say that the Earth is immobile.
<margin>The same is confirmed for shots toward the east and toward the west.</margin>

SIMPLICIO: Oh, these are certainly reasons to which it is impossible to find a valid answer.

SALVIATI: Are they perhaps new to you?

SIMPLICIO: Truly, yes. And now I see with how many beautiful experiences nature has wished to be courteous to us, to help us come to the knowledge of the truth. Oh, how well one truth accords with another, and all conspire to make themselves impregnable!

SAGREDO: What a pity that artillery did not exist in the time of Aristotle! With it, he would have surely conquered ignorance and spoken without the slightest hesitation about the things of the world.

SAGREDO. It is necessary that on this occasion I tell you of certain events that occurred to me from the time I first began to hear talk of this opinion. Being quite a young man, having barely finished the course of philosophy—which I then set aside to apply myself to other occupations—it happened that a certain foreigner <note>original: "Oltramontano," literally 'one from beyond the mountains' (the Alps)</note> from Rostock, and I believe his name was Christian Wursteisen <note>original: "Cristiano Vorstisio," a mathematician and historian</note>, a follower of the opinion of Copernicus, arrived in these parts. I, however, did not attend, having formed a fixed impression that such an opinion could be nothing other than a solemn madness. Having later questioned some who had been there, I heard everyone making fun of it, except for one, who told me that the business was not entirely ridiculous. Because I considered this man to be quite intelligent and very circumspect, I repented for not having gone. From that time forward, whenever I met someone who held the Copernican opinion, I began to ask him if he had always been of the same mind; and among the many I have questioned, I have not found even one who did not tell me that he had long been of the contrary opinion, but had passed to this one moved by the force of the reasons that persuade him of it. Having then examined them one by one to see how well they possessed the reasons of the other side, I found them all to have them most ready; so that I could not truly say that they had thrown themselves into this opinion out of ignorance, or vanity, or to act, as they say, the "clever wit" <note>original: "bello spirito"</note>. # Second Dialogue

I have sought to understand if any of them had ever held the other opinion, and likewise, I have found no one. Therefore, considering how there is no one who follows the opinion of **Copernicus** who was not first of the contrary opinion, and who is not very well informed of the arguments of **Aristotle** and **Ptolemy**; and that, on the other hand, there is no follower of **Ptolemy** and **Aristotle** who was previously of the opinion of **Copernicus** and left it to adopt that of **Aristotle**—considering, I say, these things, I began to believe that one who leaves an opinion drunk in with their mother's milk <note>original: "imbeuuta col latte" - an idiom meaning an idea held since infancy</note> and followed by infinite numbers, to join another followed by very few and denied by all the schools—and which truly seems a very great paradox—must of necessity be moved, if not forced, by more effective reasons. For this reason, I have become most curious to reach, as they say, the bottom of this business. I count it my great fortune to meet both of you, from whom I can, without any effort, hear all that has been said, and perhaps all that can be said on this matter, certain that by virtue of your reasoning I shall be drawn out of doubt and placed in a state of certainty.

**SIMPLICIO.** Provided that your opinion and hope do not fail you, and that in the end you do not find yourself more confused than before.

**SAGREDO.** It seems to me certain that such a thing cannot happen in any way.

**SIMPLICIO.** And why not? I am a good witness to myself that the further we go, the more confused I become.

**SAGREDO.** That is a sign that those reasons which until now seemed conclusive to you, and kept you sure of the truth of your opinion, are beginning to change appearance in your mind, and are letting you slowly—if not pass over—at least incline toward the contrary. # On Galileo

SAGREDO: ...on the other hand, do the celestial bodies all move, or is it rather that the starry <gloss>original: stellata</gloss> sphere and the Sun remain still in the center, while the Earth is outside it, and those movements which appear to us to belong to the Sun and the fixed stars are actually its own?
SIMPLICIO: These are the conclusions which are being disputed.
SAGREDO: Are these two conclusions not such that, by necessity, one must be true and the other false?
SIMPLICIO: That is so; we are in a dilemma, one part of which must necessarily be true and the other false; because between motion and rest, which are contradictories, there is no third option <note>Simplicio refers to the "Law of the Excluded Middle" in logic: a thing either moves or it does not.</note>, so that one cannot say the Earth neither moves nor stands still, or the Sun and the stars neither move nor stand still.
SAGREDO: What are the Earth, the Sun, and the stars in nature? Are they tiny things, or are they significant?
SIMPLICIO: They are the most principal, most noble, integral bodies of the universe—vast and most significant.
<margin>Motion and rest are the principal accidents in nature.</margin>
SAGREDO: And what kind of "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not change the essence of a thing, such as its location or state of motion.</note> are motion and rest in nature?
SIMPLICIO: So great and principal that nature itself is defined by them.
SAGREDO: So that moving eternally and being entirely immobile are two very significant conditions in nature, indicating a very great diversity; and especially when attributed to the most principal bodies of the universe, only the most dissimilar events can follow as a consequence.
SIMPLICIO: That is certainly so.
SAGREDO: Now answer me another point. Do you believe that in Dialectics, Rhetoric, Physics, Metaphysics, Mathematics, and finally in the entire universe of discourse, there are arguments powerful enough to persuade and demonstrate false conclusions to others no less than true ones?
<margin>Falsehoods cannot be demonstrable like truths. For the proof of true conclusions, arguments can be very conclusive, but for false ones, they cannot.</margin>
SIMPLICIO: No, sir; on the contrary, I hold for certain and am sure that for the proof of a true and necessary conclusion, there exist in nature not just one, but many most powerful demonstrations, and that one can discourse and revolve around it with thousands upon thousands of matches without ever stumbling into any repugnance; and that the more a Sophist <note>A person who uses clever but false arguments.</note> might wish to cloud it, the clearer its certainty would always become. And that, conversely, to make a false proposition appear true and to persuade someone of it, one can produce nothing but fallacies, Sophisms, Paralogisms <note>A piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning.</note>, equivocations, and vain, inconsistent discourses full of repugnance and contradictions.

SAGREDO: Now, if eternal motion and eternal rest are such fundamental properties in nature, and so vastly different that only the most diverse consequences can follow from them—especially when applied to the Sun and the Earth, bodies so vast and significant in the universe—and since it is impossible for one of two contradictory propositions not to be true and the other false; and since nothing but fallacies can be produced to prove the false one, while the true one can be made persuasive through every kind of concluding and demonstrative reason; how can you imagine that whichever of you undertakes to support the true proposition will fail to persuade me? # On Galileo.

...that you should judge me by my speech while we are in the fervor of performing the play; but after I have laid aside the costume, you may perhaps find me different from the one you see on stage. Now let us proceed.
<margin>Argument taken from the clouds and the birds.</margin>
*Ptolemy and his followers produce another experiment similar to that of projectiles, and it concerns things that, being separated from the Earth, remain for a long time in the air, such as clouds and flying birds. Since it cannot be said of these that they are carried by the Earth, not being attached to it, it does not seem possible that they could follow its velocity. On the contrary, it should appear to us that they all move very rapidly toward the West. And if we, carried by the Earth, pass our parallel in twenty-four hours—which is at least sixteen miles <note>Galileo refers here to Italian miles per minute at the equator to illustrate the immense speed of rotation.</note>—how could birds keep up with such a course? Whereas, on the contrary, we see them fly toward the East just as much as toward the West, and toward any part whatever, without any perceptible difference. Besides this, if while we are galloping on horseback we feel the air strike our faces quite strongly, what wind should we perpetually feel from the East, being carried with such a rapid course against the air? And yet no such effect is felt.*
<margin>Argument taken from the wind that seems to strike us while we run on horseback.</margin>
<margin>Argument taken from "vertigo" <term>vertigine: here meaning centrifugal force or circular motion</term>, which has the power to extrude and dissipate.</margin>
Here is another very ingenious reason taken from a certain experience, and it is this: Circular motion has the power to extrude, dissipate, and drive away from its center the parts of the moving body, whenever the motion is not slow enough or the parts are not very firmly attached together. For this reason, if, for example, we were to very rapidly turn one of those great wheels in which one or two men walking move very great weights—such as the mass of great stones for a crane <note>original: "mangano," a type of heavy lifting machine or stone-thrower</note>, or loaded boats being ferried from one water to another by dragging them over land—if the parts of that rapidly turned wheel were not more than firmly woven together, they would all be dissipated. Nor, however tenaciously stones or other heavy materials were attached to its exterior surface, could they resist the impetus that would hurl them with great violence to various places far from the wheel, and consequently from its center. If, then, the Earth moved with so much greater velocity, what gravity, what tenacity of lime or mortar, would hold back the stones, the buildings, and entire cities, so that they were not launched toward the Sky by such a precipitous "vertigo"? # Of Galileo

<margin>Response to the first argument of *Aristotle*?</margin>
I would have preferred that *Aristotle* had explained himself better when he said that the parts [of the Earth] would also move circularly; because this "moving circularly" can be understood in two ways. One is that every particle separated from its whole would move circularly around its own center, describing its own little tiny circles. The other is that, with the whole globe moving around its center in twenty-four hours, the parts would also rotate around the same center in twenty-four hours. The first would be an impertinence no less than if someone said that every part of a circumference of a circle must be a circle; or because the Earth is spherical, every piece of earth must be a ball, because the axiom <note>original: "eadem est ratio totius, & partium"</note> <term>the reasoning for the whole and the parts is the same</term> requires it. But if he meant the other way—that is, that the parts, in imitation of the whole, would move naturally around the center of the entire globe in twenty-four hours—I say that they already do so; and it will be up to you, instead of *Aristotle*, to prove that they do not.

SIMP. This is proven by *Aristotle* in the same passage, where he says that the natural motion of the parts is straight motion toward the center of the universe; therefore, circular motion cannot naturally belong to them.

SALV. But do you not see that in those very words there is also the refutation of this *response*?

SIMP. In what way, and where?

SALV. Does he not say that circular motion for the Earth would be violent <note>In this context, "violent" means forced or contrary to a body's natural inclination</note>? And therefore not eternal? And that this is absurd because the order of the world is eternal?

SIMP. He says so.

<margin>That which is violent cannot be eternal; [therefore] can it not be natural?</margin>
SALV. But if that which is violent cannot be eternal, conversely, that which cannot be eternal cannot be natural. But the downward motion of the Earth cannot be eternally eternal; therefore, it can even less be natural. Nor can any motion be natural to it which is not also eternal to it. But if we make the Earth movable with circular motion, this can be eternal to it and to its parts, and therefore natural.

SIMP. Straight motion is most natural to the parts of the Earth, and it is eternal to them, nor will it ever happen that they do not move with straight motion—understanding, however, that impediments are always removed.

SALV. You are mistaken, Mr. *Simp.*, and I certainly want to see if I can free you from the mistake. Therefore tell me: do you believe that a ship, going from the Strait of Gibraltar toward Palestine, could...

One belongs to those who, placing the Earth in the center, would make it move upon itself around its own center. If the Earth could be that first sphere which, by moving with a single motion <note>original: "lazione sola" - a technical term for local motion or displacement</note>, makes the stars appear to move from East to West, you would not deny it to her. It is necessary then, O Aristotle, if you wish to conclude anything, that you demonstrate that the Earth, placed in the center, cannot move even with a single motion; or else, that not even the first sphere can have a single movement. Otherwise, in your own syllogism, you commit a fallacy and reveal it, by denying and at the same time granting the same thing. I come now to the second position, which belongs to those who, placing the Earth far from the center, make her mobile around it—that is, they make her a planet and a "wandering star" <note>The term "planet" derives from the Greek word for wanderer</note>. Against this position the argument proceeds, and as far as the form is concerned it is conclusive, but it errs in its matter. For even granting that the Earth moves in such a way, and that she moves with two motions, it does not necessarily follow that there must be changes in the rising and setting of the fixed stars, as I shall declare in its proper place. And here I wish to excuse Aristotle's error; indeed, I wish to praise him for having brought forth the most subtle argument against the position of Copernicus that can be brought. And if the objection is acute and in appearance most conclusive, you shall see the solution to be all the more subtle and ingenious, and one not to be found by a wit less sharp than that of Copernicus; and from the difficulty in understanding it, you may judge the much greater difficulty of discovering it.

perpendicular line, which it would describe if the Earth were immobile.

SALVIATI: Therefore, simply by seeing the falling stone graze the Tower, you cannot surely affirm that it describes a straight and perpendicular line, unless it is first assumed that the Earth stands still.

SIMPLICIO: That is so, because if the Earth moved, the motion of the stone would be transverse <note>diagonal or slanted</note> and not perpendicular.

<margin>The fallacy <note>paralogism</note> of Aristotle and Ptolemy in assuming as known that which is under investigation.</margin> SALVIATI: Here then is the fallacy of Aristotle and Ptolemy, evident, clear, and discovered by yourself, in which that which is intended to be demonstrated is assumed as already known.

SIMPLICIO: In what way? To me, it appears to be a syllogism <note>a form of logical argument</note> in good form, and not a "begging of the question" <term>petition of principle: a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premises</term>.

SALVIATI: Here is how. Tell me: in a demonstration, is the conclusion not supposed to be unknown?

SIMPLICIO: Unknown, because otherwise demonstrating it would be superfluous.

SALVIATI: But is it not necessary that the middle term <note>the connecting link in a logical argument</note> be known?

SIMPLICIO: It is necessary, because otherwise it would be an attempt to prove the unknown by the equally unknown <note>original: "ignotum per æque ignotum"</note>.

SALVIATI: Is not our conclusion to be proven, which is unknown, the stability of the Earth?

SIMPLICIO: That is it.

SALVIATI: And is not the middle term, which must be known, the straight and perpendicular fall of the stone?

SIMPLICIO: That is the middle term.

SALVIATI: But was it not concluded just a moment ago that we cannot have knowledge that such a fall is straight and perpendicular, unless it is first known to us that the Earth stands still? Therefore, in your syllogism, the certainty of the middle term is drawn from the uncertainty of the conclusion. You see, then, the nature and extent of the fallacy.

SAGREDO: For the sake of Mr. Simplicio, I would like to defend Aristotle if it were possible, or at least become better able to grasp the force of your inference. You say that seeing the stone graze the Tower is not enough to ensure that the motion of the stone is perpendicular (which is the middle term of the syllogism) unless one supposes that the Earth stands still (which is the conclusion to be proven); because if the Tower moved together with the Earth, and the stone grazed it, the motion of the stone would be transverse and not perpendicular.

But I will respond that if the *Tower* were moving, it would be impossible for the *stone* to fall grazing it; and therefore, from its falling while grazing the tower, the *stability of the Earth* is inferred.
SIMP. That is so, because to require that the *stone* come down grazing the *Tower* when it is being carried by the *Earth*, it would be necessary for the *stone* to have two *natural motions*: namely, the *straight* motion toward the *center*, and the *circular* motion around the *center*, which is then *impossible*.
SALV. The defense of *Aristotle* <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), whose geocentric physics Galileo is challenging here.</note> therefore consists in it *being impossible*, or at least in his having *judged it impossible*, for the *stone* to be able to move with a *mixed motion* of *straight* and *circular*; because if he had not held it as *impossible* for the *stone* to be able to move toward the center and around the center unitedly, he would have understood that it could happen that the falling *stone* could come grazing the *Tower* whether it was moving or standing still, and consequently he would have realized that from this *grazing* nothing could be inferred regarding the *motion* or the *rest of the Earth*. But this does not otherwise excuse *Aristotle*, not only because he ought to have said so if he had held such a *concept*, it being such a *principal point* in his *argument*, but even more so because one cannot say either that such an *effect* is *impossible*, nor that *Aristotle* *judged it impossible*. The *first* cannot be said, because shortly I will show that it is not only *possible*, but *necessary*; nor can the *second* be said, because *Aristotle* himself grants to *fire* the ability to go upward *naturally* in a *straight line*, and to move in a circle with the *diurnal motion* <note>The daily rotation of the heavens.</note> shared by the *Heaven* with the entire *element of fire*, and with the greater part of the *air*; if, therefore, he does not consider it *impossible* to mix the *straight* upward motion with the *circular* communicated to the *fire* and the *air* by the *lunar concave* <note>In Aristotelian cosmology, the sphere of the moon was the boundary between the changing Earthly realm and the unchanging heavens.</note>, he should much less repute as *impossible* the *straight* downward motion of the *stone* combined with the *circular* motion, which would be *natural* to the entire *terrestrial globe*, of which the *stone* is a part.

<margin>Aristotle admits that fire moves straight upward by its nature, and in a circle by participation.</margin>SIMP. That does not seem the same to me, because if the *element* of *fire* goes in a circle together with the *highly fluid air*, it is a very easy, indeed a necessary thing, that a *particle* of *fire* rising up from the *earth*, in passing through the *mobile air*, should receive that *same movement*, being a *body* so *thin*, *light*, and *very easy* to be moved; but that a *very heavy stone*, or a *cannonball*, coming from on high to the bottom and being left to its own devices, should let itself be transported either by *air* or *anything else*, is entirely *unthinkable*. # On Galileo

<page-num>135</page-num>

Then there is the experiment so characteristic of the stone dropped from the top of a ship's mast; which, while the ship stands still, falls at the foot of the mast, but when the ship moves, it falls as far away from that same point as the ship has traveled forward during the time of the stone's fall; which is not a few cubits <note>original: "braccia" — a historical unit of length, literally "arms," roughly 23 inches</note> when the ship's course is fast.

<margin>Disparity between the falling of the stone from the top of a ship's mast and from the summit of a Tower.</margin>

SALVIATI: There is a great disparity between the case of the ship and that of the Earth, assuming the terrestrial globe had a diurnal motion. For it is a most manifest thing that the motion of the ship, just as it is not its natural motion, is likewise accidental to all the things that are in it; hence it is no wonder that the stone, which was held at the top of the mast, once released into liberty, descends to the bottom without any obligation to follow the motion of the ship. But the diurnal revolution is given as a proper and natural motion to the terrestrial globe, and consequently to all its parts; and as it is impressed by nature indelibly upon them, therefore that stone which is at the top of the Tower has as its primary instinct the going around the center of its whole in twenty-four hours, and it exercises this natural talent eternally, in whatever state it may be placed.

And to be persuaded of this, you will have to do nothing else but change an antiquated impression made in your mind; and say: just as I have estimated until now that it is a property of the terrestrial globe to stay immobile around its center, and I have never had any difficulty or repugnance in learning that any of its particles likewise remains naturally in that same rest; so it is quite right that if the natural instinct of the terrestrial globe were to go around in twenty-four hours, it would also be the intrinsic and natural inclination of every one of its parts, not to stand still, but to follow the same course. And thus, without running into any inconvenience, one may conclude that because the motion conferred upon the ship by the force of the oars—and through it to all things found within it—is not natural but foreign, it is quite right that the stone, once separated from the ship, reduces itself to its natural state and returns to exercising its pure and simple natural talent.

<margin>The part of the air lower than the highest mountains follows the motion of the Earth.</margin>

It is added that it is necessary that at least that part of the air which is lower than the greatest heights of the mountains is snatched up and carried in a circle by the roughness of the terrestrial surface; or perhaps that, being mixed with many terrestrial vapors and exhalations, it naturally follows the diurnal motion, which does not happen with the air <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

I remain unconvinced that the air can imprint into a very large stone, or into a large ball of iron or lead that might weigh, for example, two hundred pounds, the motion with which the air itself moves, and which it perhaps communicates to feathers, snow, and other very light things; on the contrary, I see that a weight of that sort, exposed to whatever most impetuous wind, is not moved from its place even a single finger's breadth; now consider if the air will carry it along.

SALVIATI. There is a great disparity between your experiment and our case. You have the wind overtake that stone while it is at rest, and we expose to the air—which is already moving—the stone, which is also already moving with the same velocity, such that the air does not have to confer a new motion upon it, but only maintain it, or to put it better, not hinder the motion already conceived: you want to drive the stone with a foreign motion outside of its nature, and we want to preserve it in its natural one. If you wanted to produce a more accurate experiment, you should say that one should observe—if not with the eye of the forehead, at least with that of the mind—what would happen when an Eagle, carried by the impetus of the wind, lets a stone fall from its talons; which, because it was already flying at the same rate as the wind upon leaving the claws, and after departing enters into a medium moving with equal velocity, I am of the strong opinion that it would not be seen to fall straight down perpendicularly, but that following the course of the wind, and adding to it that of its own gravity <term>gravity: here used in the classical sense of "heaviness" or the natural tendency to fall</term>, it would move with a transverse motion.

SIMPLICIO. It would be necessary to be able to perform such an experiment; and then judge according to the outcome; meanwhile, the effect of the ship has until now seemed to applaud our opinion.

SALVIATI. You said well "until now"; because perhaps in a little while it might change appearance. And so as not to keep you, as they say, any longer on the rack <note>original: "su le bacchette" - an idiom meaning to keep someone in suspense or under pressure</note>; tell me, Mr. Simplicio, does it seem to you internally that the experiment...

# On Galileo

->On Galileo<-

If upon this surface you placed a ball that was perfectly spherical and made of a heavy, very hard material—for example, bronze—and left it to its own devices, what do you believe it would do? Do you not believe (as I do) that it would remain still?
SIMP. *What if that surface were inclined?*
SALV. *Yes; for I have already supposed it to be so.*

SIMP. *I do not believe that it would stay still at all; on the contrary, I am certain that it would move toward the decline spontaneously.*
SALV. *Pay close attention to what you are saying, Mr. Simplicio, because I am certain that it would stop in whatever place you set it.*

SIMP. *Since you, Mr. Salviati, make use of these kinds of suppositions, I shall begin to not wonder at all that you reach entirely false conclusions.*
SALV. *You hold it as most certain, then, that it would move toward the decline spontaneously?*
SIMP. *What doubt is there?*

SALV. *And you hold this as firm, not because I have taught it to you (for I was trying to persuade you of the contrary), but by yourself and by your own natural judgment.*
SIMP. *Now I understand your trickery; you spoke that way to test me, and (as the common folk say) to "pump me for information," but not because you truly believed it to be that way.*

SALV. *So it is. And how long would that ball continue to move, and with what speed? And take note that I have specified a perfectly round ball and an exquisitely polished plane, in order to remove all external and accidental impediments. And likewise, I want you to abstract from the impediment of the Air, by means of its resistance to being parted, and all other accidental obstacles, if any others there might be.*

SIMP. *I have understood it all very well, and as to your question, I reply that it would continue to move infinitely, if the inclination of the plane lasted that long, and with a continually accelerated motion; for such is the nature of heavy moving bodies, that <term>they acquire strength as they go</term> <note>original: "vires acquirunt eundo" — a classical Latin phrase often used to describe how falling objects gain momentum</note>: and the greater the declivity, the greater the speed would be.*

SALV. *But if one wanted that ball to move upward upon that same surface, do you believe that it would go there?*

<summary>Salviati uses a Socratic method to lead Simplicio into defining the laws of motion on an inclined plane, establishing that a heavy sphere will accelerate infinitely in a vacuum if the slope continues. This passage is a foundational moment in the development of the concept of acceleration and the removal of "accidental" forces like friction and air resistance.</summary>

SALV. Now tell me what *would happen to the same moving body upon a surface* that was neither *upward-sloping* nor *downward-sloping*.
SIMP. Here I must think a little about the *answer*. There *being no downward slope*, there can be no *natural inclination toward motion*; and there being no *upward slope*, there can be no *resistance to being moved*, so that it would come to be *indifferent between the propensity for and the resistance to motion*; it seems to me, then, that it *ought naturally to remain there still*. But I am *forgetful*, *because it was not long ago that Mr. Sagredo made me understand* that *this is what would follow*.
SALV. So I believe, if someone were to place it there *still*; but if it were *given an impetus toward some direction*, what *would follow*?
SIMP. *It would follow that it would move toward that direction*.
SALV. But what kind of *movement*? One *continually accelerated*, as on *downward-sloping planes*, or *successively retarded*, as *on upward ones*?
SIMP. I cannot *discern any cause for acceleration* nor for *retardation* there, as there is neither *downward* nor *upward slope*.
SALV. Yes: but if there were no *cause for retardation*, much less should there be—

# Second Dialogue

SIMPLICIO: *You wish to state as your final conclusion that, since that stone moves with a motion indelibly impressed upon it, it will not leave the ship, but rather will follow it, and ultimately fall in the same spot where it falls when the ship stands still. And so I say as well, that this would follow if there were no external impediments to disturb the movement of the stone after it is set free. These impediments are two: one is the projectile's inability to break through the air with its own impetus alone, having lost the power of the oars in which it shared as part of the ship while it was on the mast; the other is the new downward motion of falling, which must surely be an impediment to the other progressive motion.*

SALVIATI: *As for the impediment of the air, I do not deny it to you; if the falling body were of light material, such as a feather or a tuft of wool, the delay would be very great, but in a heavy stone it is very small. You yourself said a little while ago that the force of the most impetuous wind is not enough to move a large stone from its place; now consider what the quiet air will do when encountered by a rock moving no faster than the ship itself. However, as I have said, I grant you this small effect which may depend on such an impediment; just as I know you will grant me that if the air moved with the same speed as the ship and the rock, the impediment would be absolutely null. As for the other matter of the supervening downward motion: first, it is manifest that these two—I mean the circular motion around the center <note>The center of the Earth</note> and the straight motion toward the center—are neither contrary, nor destructive to one another, nor incompatible. Because as for the moving body, it has no resistance at all to such motion; for you yourself have already granted that resistance exists against motion that moves away from the center, and inclination exists toward motion that approaches the center. Whence it necessarily follows that for a motion that neither approaches nor departs from the center, the moving body has neither resistance nor propensity, nor consequently any reason for the faculty impressed upon it to diminish. And because the motivating cause is not a single one that must weaken due to a new operation, but rather two distinct causes—of which gravity <term>gravity: the natural tendency of heavy bodies to move toward the center</term> attends only to drawing the body to the center, and the impressed virtue <term>impressed virtue: an early concept of momentum or inertia</term> to leading it around the center—no occasion for impediment remains.*

SIMPLICIO: *The discourse truly is, in appearance, quite probable,*

# Second Dialogue

If two arrows were shot from the same bow—one point-first in the usual manner, and the other sideways, that is, by placing its length along the string and shooting it while stretched out—I would like to know which of them would travel further. Please favor me with a response, even though the question may perhaps seem more ridiculous to you than otherwise; and excuse me, because I, who am (as you see) rather thick-headed <note>original: "groffetto" - literally "a bit coarse" or "dim-witted," used here as a self-deprecating joke by Sagredo</note>, cannot reach any higher with my speculation.

SIMPLICIO. I have never seen arrows shot sideways; nevertheless, I believe that, turned crosswise, it would not travel even a twentieth part of the distance it goes when shot point-first.

SAGREDO. And because I have believed the same, an occasion has arisen for me to doubt the conflict between Aristotle’s word and experience. For as far as experience goes, if I place two arrows on that table at a time when a brisk wind is blowing—one placed in line with the wind and the other crosswise—the wind will swiftly carry away the latter and leave the former alone. And the same, it seems, ought to happen if Aristotle’s doctrine were true regarding the two arrows shot with the bow: because the crosswise one is pushed by a great quantity of air moved by the string—that is, by as much as its length—whereas the other arrow receives an impulse from no more air than the tiny circle of its thickness. I cannot imagine the cause of such a difference, and I would desire to know it.

SIMPLICIO. The cause seems quite manifest to me; it is because the arrow shot point-first has to penetrate a small quantity of air, and the other has to cleave as much as its entire length.

<margin>The medium hinders the motion of projectiles, and does not confer it.</margin>SAGREDO. So, then, must the shot arrows penetrate the air? Oh, if the air goes with them—or rather, is that which carries them—what penetration can there be? Do you not see that, in this way, it would be necessary for the arrow to move with greater velocity than the air? And who confers this greater velocity upon the arrow? Would you say that the air gives it a velocity greater than its own? Understand then, Mr. Simplicio, that the business proceeds exactly the reverse of what Aristotle says; and it is as false that the medium confers motion to the projectile as it is true that the medium alone is what brings it hindrance. Once this is understood, you will understand without difficulty that when the air...

And if what has been said so far were not enough for him, there is the evidence of experience to settle it, which can fully reassure him. In that experiment, the most one could see would be the falling object lagging behind, provided it were made of a very light material and the air did not follow the motion of the ship; but when the air moves with equal velocity, no imaginable difference would be found, neither in this nor in any other experiment, as I am about to tell you. *Now, if in this case no difference appears, what should one expect to see in the stone falling from the top of the Tower, where the circular motion is not accidental or external to the stone, but natural and eternal, and where the air punctually follows the motion of the Tower, and the Tower that of the terrestrial globe? Do you have anything else to reply, Mr. Simplicio, on this particular point?*

SIMP. Nothing else, except that I do not see the mobility of the Earth proven so far.

SALV. Nor have I intended to prove it yet, but only to show how nothing can be gathered from the experiment brought forth by the adversaries as an argument for the Earth's stability; just as I believe I shall show regarding the others.

SAGR. Please, Mr. Salviati, before moving on to something else, allow me to bring up a certain difficulty that has been revolving in my imagination while you were so phlegmatically <note>Meaning calmly or with great patience.</note> breaking down this ship experiment for Mr. Simplicio?

SALV. We are here to discuss, and it is good that everyone raises the difficulties that occur to them, for this is the path to arrive...

<margin>A marvelous occurrence in the motion of projectiles.</margin>
**SAGREDO**: If it be true that the impetus with which the ship moves remains indelibly impressed upon the stone after it has separated from the mast, and if it be further true that this motion brings no impediment or delay to the straight downward motion natural to the stone, a marvelous effect in nature must necessarily follow. Let the ship be still, and let the time of a stone's fall from the top of the mast be two pulse-beats; then let the ship move, and let the same stone be dropped from the same place. According to what has been said, it will still take the time of two beats to reach the bottom, during which time the ship will have traveled, for example, twenty <term>braccia</term> <note>A "braccio" (plural "braccia") was a historical Italian unit of measurement, roughly an arm's length or about 23 inches.</note>. Thus, the true motion of the stone will have been a transverse line, much longer than the first straight and perpendicular one (which is merely the length of the mast), yet the ball will have traversed it in the same amount of time. Suppose again the motion of the ship is much more accelerated, so that the stone in falling must traverse a transverse line even longer than the other; and in short, however much the speed of the ship is increased, the falling stone will describe ever longer and longer transverse lines, and yet it will traverse them all in the same two pulse-beats. 

By this same similarity, if there were a <term>culverin</term> <note>A type of long-range cannon used from the 15th to 17th centuries.</note> leveled at the top of a tower, and from it shots were fired at <term>point-blank</term> <note>original: "punto bianco" - referring to a shot fired horizontally, parallel to the horizon.</note>—that is, parallel to the horizon—regardless of whether the charge given to the piece was small or large, so that the ball fell now a thousand braccia away, now four thousand, now six thousand, now ten thousand, etc., all these shots would be completed in times equal to one another. Each would be equal to the time the ball would consume in coming from the mouth of the gun to the ground if it were simply let fall straight down perpendicularly without any other impulse. Now, it seems a marvelous thing that in the same brief time of a plumb-line fall to the ground from a height of, say, one hundred braccia, the same ball, driven by fire, can traverse now four hundred, now a thousand, now four thousand, and now ten thousand braccia; so that in all point-blank shots, the ball always remains in the air for equal times.

**SALVIATI**: The consideration is most beautiful for its novelty, and if the effect be true, it is marvelous. Of its truth, I have no doubt; and were it not for the accidental impediment of the air, I hold it for certain that if, at the moment the ball leaves the piece, another were let fall from the same height straight down...

Salviati confirms this theoretical independence of motions, noting that only air resistance interferes with this perfect mathematical symmetry.</summary>

# Second Dialogue

SAGREDO: Slowly, Mr. Simplicio. Do you know that in the parts of a moving body that turns around its center, one finds movements toward every side? So that some parts ascend, others descend, some go forward, and others backward?
SIMPLICIO: I know it, and Aristotle has taught it to me.
SAGREDO: And by what demonstration? Tell me, please.
SIMPLICIO: By that of the senses.
SAGREDO: *Therefore* Aristotle has made you see what you would not have seen without him? Could he have ever lent you his eyes? You mean to say that Aristotle had told you, alerted you, and reminded you of it, but not taught it. When, therefore, a <term>hoop</term> <note>original: "ruzzola" - a wooden disk or hoop used in a popular Italian game</note> turns upon itself without changing location—not parallel, but upright to the horizon—some of its parts ascend, the opposite parts descend, the upper parts go one way, and the lower parts the opposite way. Imagine now a hoop that, without changing location, turns rapidly upon itself and stays suspended in the air; and while turning in such a manner, it is let fall perpendicularly to the ground. Do you believe that once it has reached the ground, it will continue to turn upon itself without changing location, as before?
SIMPLICIO: No, sir.
SAGREDO: But what will it do?
SIMPLICIO: It will run along the ground rapidly.
SAGREDO: And toward which side?
SIMPLICIO: Toward that side where its <term>rotation</term> <note>original: "vertigine" - used here in the classical sense of whirling or circular motion</note> carries it.
SAGREDO: In its rotation there are parts—that is, the upper ones—that move contrary to the lower ones; therefore, one must say which ones it will obey. As for the ascending and descending parts, some will not yield to the others; nor will the whole go down, being impeded by the earth, nor up, because it is heavy.
SIMPLICIO: The hoop will go turning along the ground toward that side where its upper parts tend.
SAGREDO: And why not where the contrary parts tend—that is, those that touch the ground?
SIMPLICIO: Because those on the ground are impeded by the roughness of the contact—that is, by the very <term>ruggedness</term> <note>original: "scabrosità" - referring to friction or surface texture</note> of the earth; but the upper parts, which are in the thin and yielding air, are impeded very little or not at all, and therefore the hoop will go in their direction.
SAGREDO: So that the "sticking," so to speak, of the bottom parts to the earth causes them to stay back, and only the upper parts are pushed forward.
SALVIATI: And therefore, if the hoop were to fall on ice or another surface...

SAGR. And this too you know by your own experience. Therefore tell me: when you let a <term>hoop</term><note>original: "ruzzola" - a wooden disk or hoop used in a popular Italian tossing game</note> fall from your hand without it spinning on its own, what would happen when it hits the ground?

SAGR. Could it not happen that, upon hitting the ground, it might acquire motion? Think on it more carefully.
SIMP. Unless we let it fall upon some stone that had a slope—as children do with <term>marbles</term><note>original: "chioſe" - likely referring to small stones or tokens used in games</note>—and by hitting the slanting stone at an angle, it acquired a circular motion within itself, by which it then continued to move forward along the ground, I do not see how else it could do anything but stop where it struck.
SAGR. There you have it; in some way it can acquire a new <term>spin</term><note>original: "vertigine" - Galileo uses this term to describe rotational motion or "dizziness" of the object</note>. When, therefore, the hoop is tossed high and falls back down, why can it not happen to strike the slant of some rock fixed in the earth that slopes toward the direction of the motion? And by acquiring a new spin from such a blow, in addition to the first spin given by the string, might it not double its motion and make it faster than it was at its first impact on the ground?
SIMP. Now I understand that this could easily follow. And I am considering that if the hoop were made to spin in the opposite direction, upon reaching the ground there would be the opposite effect: that is, the motion of the spin would retard the forward motion of the projectile.
SAGR. It would retard it, and sometimes impede it altogether, if the spin were fast enough. And from this arises the explanation of that effect which the most expert players of <term>tennis</term><note>original: "palla a corda" - an early form of tennis played in a court with a rope or net</note> perform to their advantage; that is, to deceive the opponent by <term>cutting</term><note>original: "trinciar" - to slice or cut the ball to give it backspin</note> the ball. This means returning it with the racket held obliquely, so that the ball acquires a spin within itself contrary to its forward motion. From this it follows that upon hitting the ground, the bounce—which, if the ball were not spinning, would go toward the opponent, giving him the usual time to return it—remains as if dead, and the ball flattens against the ground, or bounces much less than usual, and breaks the timing of the return. For this reason also, one sees those who play with wooden balls to see who can get closest to a fixed mark; when playing on a treacherous street full of obstacles that would make the ball deviate in a thousand ways and not go toward the mark at all, to avoid them all, they throw the ball not by rolling it along the ground, but through the air, as if they had to throw...

But to return to the principal problem, which was the cause of these others arising: I say that it is possible for someone moving very rapidly to let a ball drop from their hand, which, once it has reached the ground, not only follows the motion of the person but even anticipates it by moving with greater speed. And to see such an effect, I want the course to be that of a **carriage**, to which a sloping board is fixed on the outside, so that the lower part faces toward the horses and the upper part toward the rear wheels. 

Now, if during the fastest run of the carriage, someone inside lets a ball fall down the slope of that board, as it comes rolling down it will acquire a spin within itself. This spin, added to the motion impressed by the carriage, will carry the ball along the ground much faster than the carriage itself. And if another sloping board were arranged in the opposite direction, one could temper the motion of the carriage in such a way that the ball, sliding down the board, would remain immobile upon reaching the ground, and sometimes even run in the opposite direction of the carriage. 

But we have departed too long from the subject matter; if Mr. Simplicio <note>A character in the dialogue representing the traditional Aristotelian view</note> remains satisfied with the solution to the first argument against the mobility of the earth—taken from objects falling perpendicularly—we may proceed to the others.

**SALVIATI** <note>The character representing Galileo's own views</note>: The digressions made thus far are not so alien to the matter being treated that they can be called totally separate from it; besides, these reasonings depend on those things that are awakened in the imagination, not just of one person, but of three of us, who moreover discourse for our own pleasure. Nor are we bound to that strictness that would be required of one who professionally <note>original: "ex professo"</note> treats a subject methodically with the intention of publishing it. I do not want our **Poem** <note>Galileo refers to the dialogue as a "Poem" to emphasize its literary and philosophical freedom</note> to be so constrained to that unity that it leaves us no open field for episodes.

*episodes, for the introduction of which any small connection should suffice; and as if we had gathered to tell stories, let it be permitted for me to tell mine, which the hearing of yours will bring to my mind.*
