SALVIATI: *I have sometimes thought of it, and I have no doubt at all that if one were certain of the nature of the motion with which the heavy body descends to reach the center of the terrestrial globe, by then mixing it with the common circular motion of the diurnal conversion <note>The daily rotation of the Earth on its axis</note>, one would find precisely what sort of line it is that is described by the center of gravity of the moving body in the composition of these two motions.*

SAGREDO: *Of the simple motion toward the center depending on gravity, I believe that one can absolutely believe without error that it is along a straight line, exactly as it would be if the Earth were immobile.*

SALVIATI: *As for this part, not only can we believe it, but experience renders us certain of it.*

SAGREDO: *But how does experience assure us of it, if we never see any motion other than the one composed of the two—the circular and the downward?*

SALVIATI: *On the contrary, Mr. Sagredo, we see nothing but the simple downward motion; for the other circular motion, common to the Earth, the Tower, and ourselves, remains imperceptible and as if it were nothing. Only that of the stone, which is not shared by us, remains observable; and of this, the senses demonstrate that it is along a straight line, as it always comes parallel to the same Tower, which is built straight and perpendicular upon the terrestrial surface.*

SAGREDO: *You are right, and I have shown myself all too simple-minded in not remembering something so easy. But since this is well known, what else do you say you desire in order to understand the nature of this downward motion?*

SALVIATI: *It is not enough to understand that it is straight; one must know if it is uniform, or rather non-uniform; that is, if it always maintains the same...*

*...with the same speed, or whether it goes on slowing down or accelerating:*

SALVIATI. *Even this is not enough; it would be necessary to know according to what proportion such acceleration occurs: a problem that, until now, has not been treated by any philosopher or mathematician that I know of; even though entire volumes and very large writings have been produced by philosophers, and particularly the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note>, regarding motion.*
SIMPLICIO. *Philosophers occupy themselves principally with universals; they find definitions and the most common symptoms, leaving then certain subtleties and certain minutiae—which are more like curiosities—to the mathematicians. And Aristotle was content to excellently define what motion is in the universal; and of local motion <term>local motion: movement from one place to another</term> to show the principal attributes: namely, that one is natural, another violent; one is simple, another composite; one is uniform, another accelerated. Regarding the accelerated, he was content to provide the reason for the acceleration, leaving then the investigation of the proportion of such acceleration, and of other more particular accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" refers to non-essential properties or characteristics</note>, to the mechanic or other inferior artist.*
SAGREDO. *All well and good, my Mr. Simplicio. But you, Mr. Salviati, descending sometimes from the throne of Peripatetic majesty, have you ever played around with the investigation of this proportion of the acceleration of falling heavy bodies?*
SALVIATI. *I have had no need to think about it, because our common friend, the Academician <note>A reference to Galileo himself</note>, already showed me a treatise of his on motion, where this was demonstrated along with many other accidents; but it would be too great a digression if, for this, we wanted to interrupt the present discourse (which is itself already a digression) and perform, as they say, a play within a play.*
SAGREDO. *I am content to release you from such a narration for the present, on the condition, however, that this be one of the propositions reserved to be examined among the others in another particular session, because such knowledge is greatly desired by me. <margin>The line described by a <term>naturally falling body</term>, assuming the <term>motion of the earth</term> about its own <term>center</term>, would probably form the <term>circumference of a circle</term>.</margin>
around one of its fixed extreme points, as the <term>center</term> of its revolution. But because the <term>straight motion</term> of the <term>falling heavy body</term> is continually <term>accelerated</term>, it is necessary that the line resulting from the combination of the two movements goes on successively departing with greater and greater proportion from the <term>circumference</term> of that circle which the <term>center of gravity</term> of the stone would have traced had it remained always atop the Tower. And it is necessary that this departure be small at the beginning—indeed minimal, or rather, the most minimal possible—since the falling body, departing from rest (that is, from the privation of downward motion) and entering into <term>straight motion</term> downwards, must necessarily pass through all the degrees of slowness that exist between rest and any given velocity, which degrees are infinite; just as has already been discussed and concluded at length. <note>Galileo refers here to his law of acceleration, arguing that objects do not jump to a speed but pass through every infinitesimal stage of velocity.</note>

Given, then, that such is the progress of <term>acceleration</term>, and it being furthermore true that the falling body goes to end at the <term>center of the earth</term>, the line of its <term>composite motion</term> must be such that it goes on always departing with greater proportion from the top of the Tower—or to put it better, from the <term>circumference</term> of the circle described by the top of the Tower by the revolution of the earth—but that such distances are infinitely smaller and smaller the less the moving body is found to have moved from the first point where it rested. Besides this, it is necessary that this line of <term>composite motion</term> goes to terminate at the <term>center of the earth</term>. Now, having made these two presuppositions, I previously went about describing around the <term>center</term> A, with the <term>semidiameter</term> <note>radius</note> AB, the circle BI representing the <term>terrestrial globe</term>; and extending the <term>semidiameter</term> AB to G, I described the height of the Tower BC. Then, having divided the line CA in the middle at E, with center E and interval EC, I describe the semicircle CIA. Regarding this, I now say that it can be believed with great probability that a stone falling from the summit of the Tower C moves with a <term>composite motion</term> of the common <term>circular</term> one and its own <term>straight</term> one. For, marking on the <term>circumference</term> CD some equal parts CF, FG, GH, HL, and drawing straight lines from the points F, G, H, L toward the <term>center</term> A, the parts of these intercepted between the two <term>circumferences</term> CD and BI will always represent the same Tower CB, transported by the <term>terrestrial globe</term>

# On Galileo

-> [Salviati speaking] <-
I do not claim that it has been proven, but rather that we have proceeded thus far—and will continue to proceed—by considering the strength of the reasons assigned by philosophers as proof of the Earth's immobility. Of these, the first argument, taken from bodies falling perpendicularly, suffers from the difficulties you have heard. I do not know how significant these have seemed to Signor Simplicio, and therefore, before passing to the test of the other arguments, it would be well for him to produce whatever he has to say in reply.

**Simplicio:** As for this first point, I truly confess to having heard various subtleties to which I had not previously given thought; and since they come to me as new, I cannot have the answers so ready at hand. However, I do not consider this argument of falling bodies to be among the strongest for the Earth's immobility; that will not be the case with the firing of artillery, and especially those shots fired against the diurnal <note>The daily rotation of the Earth on its axis.</note> motion.

**Sagredo:** The flight of birds troubles me just as much as the artillery and all the other experiments cited above cause me difficulty. But these birds, which fly forward and backward at their own will, and turn in a thousand ways—and what matters more, stay suspended in the air for entire hours—these, I say, unsettle my imagination. I cannot understand how, amidst so many whirls, they do not lose the motion of the Earth, or how they can keep up with such a great velocity, which ultimately exceeds their own flight by many, many multiples.

**Salviati:** Truly, your doubt is not without reason, and perhaps Copernicus himself did not find a solution to it that was to his entire satisfaction; and for that reason, perhaps, he remained silent on it, even though he was quite concise in examining the other contrary reasons. I believe this was due to his loftiness of mind, being founded upon greater and higher contemplations; in the same way that lions are little moved by the annoying barking of small dogs. We shall therefore save the instance of the birds for last, and in the meantime, we will seek to satisfy Signor Simplicio regarding the others, by showing him in the usual manner that he himself holds the solutions in his hand, even if he does not realize it. And beginning with "shots of elevation" <note>term: *tiri di volata* — long-range artillery shots fired at an upward angle rather than point-blank.</note> made with the same piece, powder, and ball—one toward the East and the other toward the West—tell me what it is that moves you to believe that the shot toward the West (if the diurnal revolution were that of the terrestrial globe) ought to result in a much longer distance than the one toward the East?

<margin>L</margin> I am moved...

<margin>Reason why it seems that an artillery shot toward the west should result in a longer distance than one toward the east.</margin>
SIMPLICIO. I am moved to believe so because, in a shot toward the East, while the ball is outside the cannon, it is followed by the cannon itself, which—carried by the Earth—likewise runs swiftly toward that same direction; hence the fall of the ball to the ground occurs a short distance from the piece. On the contrary, in a westward shot, before the ball strikes the ground, the cannon has retreated a great deal toward the East; thus the space between the ball and the cannon—that is, the range of the shot—will appear longer than the other by as much as the travel of the artillery (that is, of the Earth) during the time both balls were in the air.

SALVIATI. I wish that we could find some way to perform an experiment corresponding to the motion of these projectiles, just as we did with the ship for the motion of objects falling from top to bottom, and I am thinking of a way.

<margin>Experiment of a moving carriage to see the difference in shots.</margin>
SAGREDO. I believe a very suitable test would be to take a small open carriage and fit it with a large crossbow <note>original: "balestrone da bolzoni," a heavy crossbow for firing square-headed bolts</note> at a forty-five degree elevation, so that the shot would reach its maximum possible distance. Then, while the horses are running, fire once toward the direction of travel, and then again toward the opposite direction, taking very careful note of where the carriage is at the exact moment the bolt sticks into the ground in both the one and the other shot. In this way, one could see exactly how much larger one shot results than the other.

SIMPLICIO. It seems to me that such an experiment is very well suited; and I have no doubt that the shot—that is, the space between the arrow and where the carriage is at the moment the arrow hits the ground—will be much smaller when one fires in the direction of the carriage's travel than when one fires in the opposite direction. For example, let the shot itself be three hundred cubits <note>original: "braccia," a historical unit of length roughly equal to an arm's length</note>, and let the travel of the carriage, during the time the bolt is in the air, be one hundred cubits. Therefore, firing in the direction of travel, out of the three hundred cubits of the shot, the carriage covers one hundred of them; thus, when the bolt strikes the ground, the space between it and the carriage will be only two hundred cubits. But on the contrary, in the other shot, with the carriage running opposite to the bolt, when the bolt has covered its three hundred cubits and the carriage its other hundred in the opposite direction, the distance placed between them will be found to be four hundred cubits.

SALVIATI. Would there be any way to make these shots come out equal?

SIMPLICIO. I would know of no other way than by making the carriage stand still.

## On Galileo.

SALV. This is known; but I am asking what happens when the carriage is driven at full speed.
SIMP. One would have to strengthen the bow when shooting in the direction of the travel, and then weaken it when shooting against the direction of travel.
SALV. Here then, we see there is indeed another remedy. But how much would it be necessary to strengthen it, and how much then to weaken it?
SIMP. In our example where we have supposed that the bow could shoot three hundred <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement, literally "arms," roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</note>, it would be necessary for the shot toward the direction of travel to strengthen it so that it would shoot four hundred braccia; and for the other, to weaken it so much that it would not shoot more than two hundred. In this way, both shots would result in three hundred braccia in relation to the carriage; for the carriage, with its own travel of one hundred braccia, would subtract from the shot of four hundred and add to the shot of two hundred, thus reducing both to three hundred.
SALV. But what effect does the greater or lesser strength of the bow have upon the arrow?
SIMP. The strong bow drives it with greater velocity, and the weaker one with less; and the same arrow goes further one time than the other in proportion to how much greater the velocity is with which it leaves the <term>nock</term> <note>original: "cocca" — the notched end of the arrow where it fits the bowstring</note> one time compared to the other.
SALV. So that to make the arrow, when shot in either direction, move an equal distance away from the moving carriage, it is necessary that if in the first shot of the proposed example it departs with, for instance, four degrees of velocity, in the other shot it departs with only two. But if the same bow is used, it always receives three degrees from it.
SIMP. That is so; and for this reason, when shooting with the same bow while the carriage is in motion, the shots cannot result in being equal.
SALV. I had forgotten to ask: at what velocity is it supposed, in this particular experiment, that the carriage is traveling?
SIMP. The velocity of the carriage must be supposed as one degree in comparison to that of the bow, which is three.
SALV. Yes, yes, that makes the account come out right. But tell me, when the carriage travels, do not all the things that are in the carriage also move with that same velocity?
SIMP. Without a doubt.
SALV. Therefore the <term>bolt</term> <note>original: "bolzone" — a heavy-headed arrow or crossbow bolt</note> also moves, and the bow, and the string upon which it is stretched.

SIMPLICIO: That is so.
SALVATI: Therefore, in discharging the <term>bolt</term><note>original: "bolzone" - a type of heavy arrow or projectile for a crossbow</note> in the direction of the carriage's travel, the bow imparts its three degrees of velocity into a bolt that already possesses one degree, thanks to the carriage which carries it in that direction with such speed; so that upon leaving the <term>nock</term><note>the notch at the end of the arrow that fits onto the bowstring</note> it finds itself with four degrees of velocity. Conversely, shooting in the other direction, the same bow confers its same three degrees to a bolt that is moving in the opposite direction with one degree; so that in separating from the string, it is left with only two degrees of velocity. But you have already admitted that to make the shots equal, the bolt must depart once with four degrees and the other time with two; therefore, without changing the bow, the very travel of the carriage is what balances the accounts. Experience then seals this for those who would not or could not be capable of understanding the reason. Now apply this discourse to the <margin>The argument taken from artillery fire toward the east and toward the west is resolved.</margin> artillery, and you will find that whether the earth moves or stands still, shots made with the same force must always turn out equal, regardless of which direction they are aimed. The error of <term>Aristotle</term><note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose geocentric views Galileo is challenging</note> is that fixed and deep-seated impression that the earth stands still, which you cannot or do not know how to strip away, even when you wish to philosophize about what would follow, assuming the earth moved. And so, in the other argument, you fail to consider that while the stone is atop the <term>Tower</term>, it does—regarding its movement or lack thereof—exactly what the terrestrial globe does, because you have it fixed in your mind that the earth stands still. You always reason about the fall of the stone as if it departed from rest; whereas you ought to say: if the earth stands still, the stone departs from rest and descends perpendicularly; but if the earth moves, the stone likewise moves with equal velocity. It does not depart from rest, but from a motion equal to that of the earth, with which it mixes the subsequent downward motion, composing a transverse path.
SIMPLICIO: But good God, if it moves transversely, why do I see it moving straight and perpendicularly? This is surely to deny manifest sense; and if we must not believe the senses, by what other door must we enter to philosophize?
SALVATI: In relation to the earth, the Tower, and us—who all move together in conservation with the <term>diurnal motion</term><note>The daily rotation of the Earth on its axis</note> along with the stone—the diurnal motion is as if it were not there; it remains insensible, it remains imperceptible.

<summary>Salviati explains that the Earth's rotation is imperceptible to its inhabitants because everything moves together, resolving the paradox of why falling objects appear to drop straight down even if the Earth is rotating.</summary>

Regarding the specific work of the painter, he would have sketched exactly the same thing even if the ship had been stationary. But the tiny motions, forward and backward, to the right and to the left, communicated by the painter's fingers to the pen and not to the sheet, being unique to the pen, were able to leave a trace upon the paper, which remained immobile relative to those specific movements. In the same way, it is true that as the Earth moves, the motion of a stone coming downward has actually been a long stretch of many hundreds, and even many thousands of cubits <term>braccia: an Italian measure of length, literally "arms"</term>; and if it could have marked its course in stable air or another surface, it would have left a very long transverse line. And because it is equal, the ball always stays perpendicularly above the mouth of the artillery and finally falls back into it. Maintaining itself always directly above the piece, it also appears continually above the head of whoever is near the piece; thus, it seems to us that it rises exactly perpendicularly toward our zenith <note>original: "vertice"</note>.

...if the technique were such, he replied to me no, but that the method was much easier and more certain; and that they operate in the same way for a hit as when they shoot at a stationary bird. That is, they adjust their aim to the flying bird, and by moving the <term>arquebus</term><note>An early type of portable long gun or musket.</note> they follow it, always keeping the sight upon it until they fire, and thus they hit them just like the others that are still. Thus, the ball receives from the fire a straight motion upward, and from the barrel a declining motion following the flight of the bird, exactly as was just said regarding the firing of artillery. In that case, the ball receives from the fire the motion to go high toward the zenith, and from the motion of the Earth the inclination toward the East; from both it makes a composite motion that follows the course of the Earth. To one who watches it, it appears only to go straight up, returning afterward down along the same line.

Therefore, keeping the aim continually directed toward the target ensures that the shot strikes true. To keep the aim on the mark, if the target stays still, the barrel must also be held still; and if the target moves, the barrel will be kept on the mark by moving it. From this depends the proper answer to the other argument about firing artillery at a target placed toward the South or toward the North. In that case, it was insisted that if the Earth moved, the shots would all end up wide toward the West, because in the time that the ball, having left the piece, travels through the air to the mark, the mark—carried toward the East—would leave the ball behind toward the West.

<margin>The objection taken from artillery shots toward the South and North is resolved.</margin>

I respond, therefore, by asking: once the artillery is adjusted to the mark and left that way, does it continue to always look at the same mark, whether the Earth moves or stays still? One must answer that the aim does not change at all, because if the target stays still, the artillery likewise stays still; and if the target, carried by the Earth, moves, the artillery also moves with the same tenor. By maintaining the aim, the shot always succeeds correctly, as is manifest from the things said above.

*But here it seems to me a timely occasion to note a certain latitude that is perhaps granted with excessive liberality by the followers of Copernicus to the opposing side. I mean granting them, as secure and certain, some experiments that the adversaries truly have never performed; such as, for example, that of objects falling from the mast of a ship while it is in motion, and many others. Among these, I hold for certain that one is this: making a trial of whether Eastern artillery shots turn out high and Western ones low. One second, therefore, is more than the time of the ball's flight. And because the diurnal revolution takes twenty-four hours, the Western horizon rises fifteen degrees per hour; that is, fifteen minutes of a degree per minute of an hour; that is, fifteen seconds of a degree per second of an hour. SALVIATI. A subtlety worthy of Mr. Sagredo. But whether this variation is to be seen in the motion or the stillness of the Earth, <margin>It is necessary to be very cautious in granting the truth of experiments to those who have never performed them.</margin> since it can only be extremely small, it cannot help but remain submerged among the very large variations that continually occur due to many accidental factors. And let all this be said and granted as a "good measure" to Mr. Simplicio, and only as a warning of how cautious one must be in accepting as true many experiments cited by those who have never performed them, but who boldly produce them as they would need to be in order to serve their cause. I say that this is given as an extra point to the Gentleman...

*Signor Simplicio, the plain truth is that regarding the effects of these shots <note>referring to projectile motions discussed previously</note>, the exact same thing must happen whether the terrestrial globe is in motion or at rest. <margin>Experiments and reasons against the motion of the Earth appear conclusive only insofar as they keep us trapped in fallacies.</margin>

*SAGREDO. For my part, I remain fully satisfied thus far, and I understand very well that whoever impresses upon their imagination this general sharing of the diurnal rotation <note>the 24-hour rotation of the Earth</note> among all terrestrial things—to all of which it naturally belongs, just as in the old concept they believed rest around the center belonged to them—will discern without any obstacle the fallacy and the equivocation that made the produced arguments seem conclusive. There remains only some small doubt in my mind, as I mentioned above, regarding the flight of birds. Since they are living creatures, they have the faculty to move at their pleasure in a hundred thousand ways, and to keep themselves separated from the Earth for a long time in the air, wandering there with very disordered turnings. I do not quite grasp how, amidst such a great mixture of movements, that primary common motion <note>the Earth's rotation</note> does not become confused and lost; and how, if they were to be stripped of it, they could compensate for it and match it with their flight to keep up with the towers and the trees, which flee toward the East with such headlong speed—I say so headlong that at the great circle of the globe <note>the Equator</note> it is little less than a thousand miles per hour, of which I do not believe the flight of swallows makes even fifty.*

*SALVIATI. If the birds had to keep up with the course of the trees by the help of their wings, they would be in a bad way; and if they were deprived of the universal rotation, they would be left so far behind, and their course toward the West would appear so furious to anyone who could see them, that it would far surpass that of an arrow. Indeed, I believe we would not be able to perceive them, just as one does not see artillery balls while they scud through the air driven by the fury of the fire. But the truth is that the proper motion of the birds—I mean their flying—has nothing to do with the universal motion, to which it brings neither help nor hindrance. And that which keeps such motion unaltered in the birds is the air itself through which they go wandering, which...*

## Second Dialogue

Following the natural rotation <note>original: "vertigine della terra"; referring here to the circular motion or revolution of the globe</note> of the earth, just as it carries the clouds along with it, so too does it carry the birds and every other thing that might be found suspended within it. Thus, as far as following the earth is concerned, the birds do not have to think about it; for this purpose, they could sleep forever.

**SAGREDO**: That the air can carry the clouds with it—being materials that are very easy to move due to their lightness, and being stripped of any other contrary inclination; or rather, being materials that themselves participate in earthly conditions and properties—this I understand without any difficulty. But that birds, which as living beings can move with a motion even contrary to the diurnal <note>daily</note> rotation, could have that motion restored to them by the air once they have interrupted it, seems to me somewhat difficult to accept. This is especially so because they are solid and heavy bodies; and we, as was said above, see stones and other heavy bodies remain resistant <note>original: "contumaci"; literally stubborn or defiant</note> against the impetus of the air. Even when they do allow themselves to be overcome, they never acquire as much velocity as the wind that carries them.

**SALVIATI**: Let us not, Mr. Sagredo, grant so little force to the air in motion. It is powerful enough to move and carry well-laden ships, to uproot forests, and to ruin towers when it moves rapidly. Yet, in these violent operations, it cannot be said that its motion is anywhere near as fast as that of the diurnal revolution.

**SIMPLICIO**: Here then, the air in motion will also be able to continue the motion of projectiles, according to the doctrine of Aristotle <note>Aristotle argued that projectiles were pushed along by the air behind them</note>; it indeed seemed a strange thing to me that he should have erred in this particular.

**SALVIATI**: It could do so, without doubt, if the air could continue the motion within itself. But just as when the wind ceases, the ships no longer travel and the trees are no longer uprooted, so too—if the motion is not continued in the air after the stone has left the hand and the arm has stopped—it must be that something other than the air makes the projectile move.

**SIMPLICIO**: And how can you say that when the wind ceases, the motion of the ship ceases? On the contrary, one sees that when the wind has stopped, and even with the sails lowered, the vessel continues to run for entire miles.

**SALVIATI**: But this is against you, Mr. Simplicio; for once the air that was striking the sails and conducting the ship has stopped, the ship nonetheless continues its course without the help of the medium.

**SIMPLICIO**: One could say that it was the water that was the medium, which conducted the ship and maintained its motion.

It could—

SALV. SALV. Your discourse has much probability in appearance, and to doubt appropriately is not the mark of ordinary minds; *nevertheless, once the appearance is shaken off, I believe that in reality it has not a hair more strength than the others already considered and resolved.*

SALVIATI: That you have greater difficulty with this instance than with the others seems to me to depend on the birds being animate, and thus able to use force at their pleasure against the primary motion innate in earthly things. In the same way, we see them while they are alive flying even upwards—a motion impossible for them as heavy bodies—whereas when dead they can do nothing but fall downwards. Therefore, you believe that the reasons which apply to all the types of <term>projectiles</term><note>Latin: *proietti*. In this context, objects thrown or set in motion by an external force.</note> mentioned above cannot apply to birds. This is very true; and because it is true, we do not see those projectiles do what birds do. For if you let a dead bird and a living one fall from the top of a Tower, the dead one will do exactly what a stone does: that is, it will first follow the general diurnal <note>Daily rotation of the Earth.</note> motion, and then the downward motion as a heavy body. But if the bird released is alive, what prevents it—while the diurnal motion always remains within it—from throwing itself by the beating of its wings toward whichever part of the Horizon it most pleases? This new motion, being its own particular movement and not shared by us, must be perceptible to us. If it has moved toward the West with its flight, who is to prevent it from returning to the Tower with an equal beating of its feathers? For ultimately, taking flight toward the West was nothing other than subtracting one single degree from the diurnal motion (which has, for example, ten degrees of velocity), leaving it with nine while it flew; and when it alighted on the ground, the common ten returned to it. To these, by flying toward the East, it could add one, and with the eleven return to the Tower. In short, if we consider well and more intimately contemplate the effects of the flight of birds, they do not differ in any way from projectiles sent toward all parts of the world, except that the latter are moved by an external projector and the former

# On Galileo

-> [From] Galileo <-

...a bowl of water with small fish inside; also hang a small bucket up high that pours water drop by drop into another narrow-mouthed vessel placed below. While the ship stands still, observe carefully how those small winged creatures fly with equal speed toward all parts of the room; the fish will be seen swimming indifferently in every direction; the falling drops will all enter the vessel placed beneath them. And if you throw something to a friend, you will not need to throw it with more force toward one side than the other, provided the distances are equal; and jumping with your feet together, as they say, you will cross equal spaces in every direction. Once you have observed all these things carefully—though there is no doubt they must happen this way while the vessel stands still—have the ship move with whatever speed you wish. Provided that the motion is uniform <note>original: "moto uniforme"; meaning motion at a constant speed in a straight line</note> and not fluctuating this way and that, you will not recognize the slightest change in any of the aforementioned effects, nor will you be able to determine from any of them whether the ship is moving or standing still. 

When jumping, you will cross the same spaces on the floorboards <note>original: "tavolato"; the wooden decking of the ship</note> as before; nor, because the ship moves very swiftly, will you make larger jumps toward the stern than toward the prow, even though while you are in the air, the floorboards beneath you slide in the direction opposite to your jump. And when throwing something to a companion, you will not need to throw it with more force to reach them if they are toward the prow and you are toward the stern than if you were situated in the opposite positions. The drops will fall, just as before, into the lower vessel, without a single one falling toward the stern, even though while the drop is in the air, the ship travels many spans <term>span: a unit of length based on the width of a human hand</term>. The fish in their water will swim toward the front of the bowl with no more effort than toward the back, but will come to food placed anywhere on the rim of the bowl with equal ease. Finally, the butterflies and flies will continue their flights indifferently toward all sides; it will never happen that they are driven toward the wall facing the stern, as if they were exhausted from keeping up with the swift course of the ship, from which they would have been separated by remaining in the air for a long time. And if you burn a few grains of incense to make a little smoke, it will be seen ascending on high and hovering like a little cloud, moving indifferently toward one side or the other...

# On Galileo

<margin>The stupidity of some who imagine the Earth began to move only when Pythagoras first said that it moved.</margin>

...they have never doubted, but firmly believed, that all other men along with them have esteemed the Earth to have been created immobile, and maintained as such throughout all past centuries. Perhaps matured in this concept, they are then astonished to hear that someone grants it motion—as if, after having held it immobile, they foolishly think it only then, and not before, set itself in motion when Pythagoras (or whoever else was first) said that it moved. Now, that such a most foolish thought—I mean, believing that those who admit the motion of the Earth held it to be stable from its creation until the time of Pythagoras, and only made it mobile after Pythagoras judged it so—should find a place in the minds of common men and those of shallow wit, I do not marvel. But that the likes of Aristotle and Ptolemy should themselves have fallen into this childishness seems to me truly a much more strange and inexcusable simplicity.

SAGREDO: So, Mr. Salviati, do you believe that Ptolemy thought he had to maintain the stability of the Earth in his disputes against men who, while granting that it had been immobile until the time of Pythagoras, only then affirmed it had become mobile when Pythagoras attributed motion to it?

<margin>Aristotle and Ptolemy seem to refute the mobility of the Earth against those who might claim that, after being still for a long time, it began to move in the time of Pythagoras.</margin>

SALVIATI: One cannot believe otherwise, if we well consider the manner he employs in refuting their saying; the refutation of which consists in the demolition of buildings and the hurling of stones, animals, and men themselves toward the Sky. And because such ruin and flinging cannot happen to buildings and animals that are not first upon the Earth, nor can men be placed or buildings constructed upon the Earth unless it is itself still, it is therefore manifest from this that Ptolemy proceeds against those who, having for some time granted rest to the Earth—that is, at the time when animals, stones, and masons could dwell and build Palaces and Cities upon it—then make it precipitously mobile to the ruin and destruction of those buildings and animals, etc. For if they had attributed such a <term>vertigo</term> <note>original: "vertigine"; here meaning a rapid whirling or rotatory motion</note> to the Earth from its first creation, he would have refuted it by saying that if the Earth had always moved, it would never have been possible to establish upon it either men or stones, and much less to construct buildings and found Cities, etc.

### Second Dialogue

SIMP. I am still not quite convinced of this <term>Aristotelian</term> <note>Referring to the followers of Aristotle, who believed the Earth was the unmoving center of the universe</note> and <term>Ptolemaic</term> <note>Referring to Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose geocentric model dominated Middle Ages thought</note> impropriety.

But if, in his argument, he says the Earth does not move because the spheres, men, and buildings already placed on Earth would be thrown off, he assumes the Earth was once in such a state that it allowed the spheres and men to dwell and build upon it; which consequently implies it had been stationary for some time—that is, fit for the habitation of animals and the construction of buildings. Do you now understand what I meant to say?

SIMP. I do, and I don't; but this matters little to the merits of the case. A small error by <term>Ptolemy</term>, committed through inadvertence, cannot be enough to move the Earth if it is indeed immobile. But jokes aside, let us come to the nerve of the argument, which seems to me insoluble.

<margin>Fast rotation has the power to extrude and scatter.</margin>
SALV. And I, Mr. <term>Simplicio</term> <note>The character representing the traditional Aristotelian view</note>, wish to tie it even tighter and strengthen it further by showing even more sensibly how it is true that heavy bodies, rotated with speed around a stable center, acquire an impetus to move away from that center—even when they are in a state of having a natural propensity to go toward it. Let a small bucket with water inside be tied to the end of a rope; holding the other end firmly in the hand, with the rope and arm forming the radius and the <term>shoulder joint</term> acting as the center, let the vessel be whirled around rapidly so that it describes the circumference of a circle. Whether this circle is parallel to the horizon, or vertical to it, or inclined in any way, it will follow in all cases that the water will not fall out of the vessel; rather, the person spinning it will always feel the rope pull and exert force to move further away from the shoulder. And if a hole is made in the bottom of the bucket, the water will be seen to spurt out no less toward the Sky than laterally or toward the Earth. If small stones are put in place of water, spinning them in the same way will make them exert the same force against the rope; and finally, we see children

**SIMPLICIO.** The motion of the stone, as long as it is in the notch, is circular; that is, it goes through an arc of a circle, whose stable center is the joint of the shoulder, and the radius is the cane together with the arm.

**SALVIATI.** And when the stone escapes from the cane, what is its motion? Does it continue its previous circular path, or does it go along another line?

# Second Dialogue

SIMP. It would not continue to move in a circle at all, because in that case it would not distance itself from the shoulder of the thrower, whereas we see it travel very far away.

SALV. By what motion, then, does it move?

SIMP. Let me think about it for a moment, for I have not given it much thought before.

SALV. Master Sagredo, listen closely: here is the *a certain remembering* <note>original: "quoddam reminisci"; a Platonic concept suggesting that learning is actually the soul recalling innate knowledge</note> well-applied in the field. You are thinking hard on it, Master Simplicio.

<margin>Motion impressed by the thrower is only in a straight line.</margin>
SIMP. In my opinion, the motion conceived upon leaving the notch <note>The "cocca" or notch of a throwing stick or bow</note> can only be along a straight line; indeed, it is necessarily along a straight line, if we understand the pure external impetus. It troubled me slightly to see it describe an arc, but because such an arc always bends downwards and not toward any other side, I understand that this decline comes from the gravity of the stone, which naturally pulls it toward the bottom. The impressed impetus, I say without hesitation, is along a straight line.

SALV. But along which straight line? For infinite lines can be produced in all directions from the notch of the rod, and from the point where the stone separates from the rod.

SIMP. It moves along that line which is in the direction of the motion the stone made while with the rod.

SALV. You have already said that the motion of the stone, while it was in the notch, was circular; now, being circular and being straight are contradictory, as there is no straight part within a circular line.

SIMP. I do not mean that the projected motion is in the direction of the entire circle, but of that last point where the circular motion ended. I understand it within myself, but I do not know well how to explain it.

SALV. And I also perceive that you understand the matter, but you do not have the proper terms to express it; now, these I can certainly teach you—that is, I can teach you the words, but not the truths, which are things. And to make you see firsthand that you know the thing, and only lack the terms to express it: tell me, when you fire a ball with an arquebus <note>term: arquebus; an early type of portable long gun</note>, in which direction does it acquire the impetus to go?

SIMP. It acquires the impetus to go along that straight line which follows the direction of the barrel—that is, which declines neither to the right nor the left, neither up nor down.

SALV. Which, in short, is the same as saying that it makes no angle at all with the line of the straight motion made through the barrel.

SALVIATI. *Of a straight line that touches a circle, which of its points is the closest of all to the center of that circle?*

SIMPLICIO. *That is certainly so.*

## Second Dialogue

*This new knowledge increases rather than diminishes my disbelief that the earth could move in a circle with such speed without throwing stones, animals, etc., toward the sky.*

Continuing along this line, the motion always moves further away from the thrower; and you have said that the projectile would continue to move along such a straight line if an inclination downward were not added to it by its own weight, from which the curving of the line of motion derives. Now I will go a little further, and I ask you: if the moving body, after separation, in continuing its straight motion, always moves away equally from the center—or, if you prefer, from the circumference of that circle of which the preceding motion was a part? *SIMP.* No, sir; because the tangent near the point of contact deviates very little from the circumference, with which it forms an extremely narrow angle; but in moving further and further away, the distance increases always with greater proportion. So that in a circle that had, for example, a diameter of ten cubits <term>braccia: an Italian unit of measurement, literally "arms," roughly 23 inches</term>, a point on the tangent that was [a certain distance] from the contact would be three or four times further from the circumference than a point only one span <term>palmo: a hand-breadth or "span" measurement</term> away from the contact. And the point that was half a span away, likewise, I believe would hardly deviate a fourth part of the distance of the second; so that near the contact, for an inch or two, one hardly perceives that the tangent is separated from the circumference.

*SALV.* So the departure of the projectile from the circumference of the preceding circular motion is, at the beginning, extremely small?

*SIMP.* Almost imperceptible.

## Second Dialogue

*SIMPLICIO:* I would say, for example, that if that [the rotational speed] were a million times faster than this [the speed of falling], the feather, and even the stone, would be extruded <note>original: "estruse"; meaning flung off or ejected by centrifugal force</note>.

*SALVIATI:* You say so, and you speak falsely, solely due to a deficiency—not of Logic, or of Physics, or of Metaphysics—but of Geometry. For if you understood even the first elements, you would know that from the center of a circle one can draw a straight line to the tangent that cuts it in such a way that the part of the tangent between the point of contact and the secant is one, two, or three million times greater than that part of the secant which remains between the tangent and the circumference. As the secant moves closer to the point of contact, this proportion increases infinitely. Therefore, there is no need to fear that, however fast the whirling <note>original: "vertigine"; referring to the Earth's rotation</note> may be and however slow the downward motion, the feather or anything lighter could begin to lift itself; for the downward inclination always overcomes the speed of the projection.

->Horizontal line AB<- <note>Referring to the diagram</note> above which the motion of projection would occur, and the projectile would continue to travel along it with **uniform motion**, if gravity did not incline it downward. Now, imagine a straight line produced from point A, which forms any angle with AB; let this be AE. Let us mark several equal spaces on AB: *Af*, *fb*, *bk*, and from these, let us draw the perpendiculars *fg*, *hi*, *kl* down to the line AE. 

And because, as has been said at another time, a falling heavy body—starting from rest—continually acquires a greater degree of velocity from time to time, according as that same time increases; we can imagine the spaces *Af*, *fb*, *hk* <note>The text likely intends *Af*, *fh*, *hk* to match the diagram's equal time intervals</note> representing equal times; and the perpendiculars *fg*, *hi*, *kl* representing the degrees of velocity acquired in said times. Thus, the degree of velocity acquired in the total time *Ak* is as the line *kl* compared to the degree *hi* acquired in time *Ah*, and the degree *fg* in time *Af*. These degrees *kl*, *hi*, *fg* have (as is manifest) the same proportion as the times *kA*, *hA*, *fA*. 

If other perpendiculars are drawn from points noted at will on the line *fA*, one will always find smaller and smaller degrees [of velocity] unto infinity, proceeding toward point A, which represents the first instant of time and the first state of rest. This retreat toward A represents for us the first propensity for downward motion, diminished unto infinity by the approach of the moving body to the first state of rest—an approach that can be increased infinitely. 

We shall now find the other diminution of velocity, which can also be made unto infinity, through the diminution of the **gravity** <note>In this context, "gravity" refers to the specific weight or the downward "heaviness" of the object</note> of the moving body. This will be represented by producing other lines from point A which contain smaller angles than the angle BAE, such as this line AD. By intersecting the parallels *kl*, *hi*, *fg* at points *m*, *n*, *o*, it illustrates for us the degrees *fo*, *hn*, *km* acquired in the times *Af*, *Ah*, *Ak*. These are smaller than the other degrees *fg*, *hi*, *kl* acquired in the same times; the latter being from a heavier moving body, and the former from a lighter one. And it is manifest that by pulling the line EA toward AB, narrowing the angle EAB (which can be done unto infinity, just as gravity can be diminished unto infinity), one likewise...

tends to infinitely diminish the velocity of the falling body, and consequently the cause that prevented the projection; and therefore it seems that from the union of these two reasons against the projection, both diminished to infinity, the projection cannot be hindered. And reducing the entire argument into brief words, we shall say: by narrowing the angle EAB, the degrees of velocity <term>lk, ih, gf</term> <note>referring to points on a geometric diagram in the original text</note> are diminished. Furthermore, by pulling the parallel lines <term>kl, hi, fg</term> toward the angle A, those same degrees are also diminished, and both types of diminution extend to infinity. Therefore, the velocity of the downward motion can indeed be diminished so much (being able to be doubly diminished to infinity) that it is not sufficient to restore the moving body onto the circumference of the wheel, and consequently, to cause the projection to be hindered and removed.

On the other hand, to ensure that the projection does not occur, it is necessary that the spaces through which the projectile must descend to reunite with the wheel are made so short and narrow that, however slow—or rather, infinitely diminished—the descent of the moving body may be, it still suffices to lead it back there. And therefore, it would be necessary to find a diminution of these spaces that is not only made to infinity, but of such an infinity that it surpasses the double infinity occurring in the diminution of the velocity of the downward-falling body. 

But how shall one magnitude be diminished more than another which is already doubly diminished to infinity? Now, let Mr. Simplicio <note>Simplicio is the character representing the Aristotelian traditionalist in Galileo's dialogues</note> note how well one can philosophize about nature without Geometry! The degrees of velocity diminished to infinity—both by the diminution of the gravity of the moving body and by the approach to the first term of motion, that is, to the state of rest—are always determined, and they proportionately correspond to the parallels comprised between two straight lines meeting in an angle conforming to angle BAE or BAD, or another infinitely more acute, but nonetheless always <term>rectilinear</term> <note>consisting of straight lines</note>. 

But the diminution of the spaces through which the moving body must be led back onto the circumference of the wheel is proportionate to another kind of diminution, contained within lines that comprise an angle infinitely narrower and more acute than any rectilinear acute angle whatsoever, such as this one: Let any point C be taken on the perpendicular AC, and making it the center, let an arc AmP be described with the interval CA. This arc will cut the parallel lines that determine the degrees of velocity, however minimal they may be and even if contained within the narrowest rectilinear angle...

<summary>Galileo argues that the geometric rate at which a projectile's required return-path shrinks is "more infinite" than the rate at which its falling velocity decreases, proving that centrifugal projection is mathematically inevitable. He uses this to mock those who attempt to study physics (natural philosophy) without the aid of geometry.</summary>

## Second Dialogue

*...of Galileo; of which parallel lines, the parts remaining between the arc and the tangent AB are the quantities of the spaces and the returns upon the wheel. These are always smaller, and smaller in a greater proportion, the closer they approach the point of contact—smaller, I say, than those parallels of which they are parts. The parallels contained between the straight lines, as they retreat toward the angle, always decrease in the same proportion; for example, if AB is divided in the middle at point F, the parallel HI will be double that of FG. By subdividing FA in the middle, the parallel produced from the point of division will be half of FG; and continuing the subdivision infinitely, the subsequent parallels will always be half of the ones immediately preceding them. But this does not happen with the lines intercepted between the tangent and the circumference of the circle; because, having made the same subdivision in FA, and assuming for example that the parallel coming from point B were double that which comes from F, this latter will then be more than double the following one. Continually, as we come toward the point of contact A, we will find the preceding lines contain the next following ones three, four, ten, hundred, thousand, hundred thousand, and a hundred million times, and more unto infinity. The shortness of such lines, therefore, is reduced to such an extent that it far exceeds what is necessary to ensure that the projectile, however light it may be, returns—or rather, always maintains itself upon the circumference.* <note>Galileo is using a geometric proof to show that the gap between a circle and a tangent line closes much faster than the gap between two straight lines, explaining why centrifugal force cannot overcome gravity at the start of motion.</note>

SAGREDO. *I remain very well convinced of the whole discourse and the force with which it compels; nevertheless, it seems to me that anyone wishing to challenge it could still raise some difficulty. They might say that of the two causes which make the descent of the moving body slower and slower unto infinity, it is manifest that the one depending on the proximity to the starting point of the descent always increases in the same proportion, just as the parallels always maintain the same proportion among themselves, etc. But that the diminution of that same speed, depending on the diminution of the gravity of the moving body (which was the second cause), also occurs in that same proportion, does not seem so manifest. And who assures us that it does not occur according to the proportion of the lines intercepted between the secant and the circumference, or perhaps even with a greater proportion?* <note>Sagredo is playing the "devil's advocate," questioning if the loss of effective weight as an object moves toward the top of a circle follows the same mathematical rules as the geometric gaps discussed.</note>

# On Galileo

<margin>N 3</margin>

In several places he affirms this as a manifest proposition; you, for the sake of the adversary, cast this into doubt and assert that it could be that the velocity increases with a greater proportion—even infinitely greater—than that of the gravity <note>In this context, "gravity" refers to the weight or the downward tendency of the object.</note>. Thus, the entire preceding discourse would fall to the ground. It remains for me, in order to sustain it, to say that the proportion of the velocities is much smaller than that of the gravities; and in this way, I not only support but fortify what has been said. Of this, I bring experience as proof, which will show us that a heavy body, even thirty or forty times heavier than another—such as, for example, a ball of lead and one of cork—will not move even remotely twice as fast. Now, if the projection <note>The "projection" refers to the object being flung off the Earth by its rotation.</note> would not occur even if the velocity of the falling body decreased according to the proportion of the gravity, much less will it occur whenever the velocity decreases only slightly, even if much of the weight is taken away.

But even assuming that the velocity decreased with a proportion much greater than that by which the gravity was diminished—even if it were the same proportion by which those parallel lines decrease between the tangent and the circumference—I do not perceive any necessity that persuades me that the projection of materials, however light they may be, must occur. On the contrary, I still affirm that it will not happen; meaning, however, materials that are not "lightest" in the sense of being deprived of all gravity and which by their nature go upwards, but those that descend very slowly and have very little gravity.

And what moves me to believe this is that the diminution of gravity, made according to the proportion of the parallels between the tangent and the circumference, has as its ultimate and highest limit the nullity of weight, just as those parallels have as the ultimate limit of their diminution the contact point itself, which is an indivisible point. Now, gravity is never diminished to the ultimate limit, because then the moving body would not be heavy; but the space for the return of the projectile to the circumference is indeed reduced to the ultimate smallness, which is when the moving body rests upon the circumference at the very point of contact. Thus, to return there, it has no need of any space; and therefore, let the propensity for downward motion be as minimal as you wish, it is always more than enough to lead the moving body back to the circumference, from which it is distant by the minimum space—that is, by nothing.

<summary>The author argues that objects will not be flung off a rotating Earth because the downward tendency (gravity) always overcomes the infinitesimal distance created by a tangent line at the point of contact. He uses the comparison of lead and cork balls to show that speed does not decrease as rapidly as weight does.</summary>

<keywords>Galileo, velocity, gravity, projection, centrifugal force, lead ball, cork, tangent, circumference, falling bodies</keywords>

SAGREDO. *Truly the reasoning is very subtle, yet equally conclusive; and one is forced to confess that attempting to treat natural questions without Geometry is an attempt to do that which is impossible to be done.*

SIMPLICIO. *I would not do such a wrong to Plato, but I would certainly say with Aristotle that he immersed himself too much in, and became too enamored of, his Geometry; because ultimately these mathematical subtleties, Mr. Salviati, are true in the abstract, but when applied to sensible and physical matter, they do not correspond. SALVIATI. *So, you do not believe, then, that the tangent touches the surface of the terrestrial globe at a single point?*

SIMPLICIO. *Not only do I not believe it is a single point, but I believe that for many, many dozens, and perhaps hundreds of cubits <note>term: "braccia" (arms/cubits), a common Renaissance unit of measurement</note>, a straight line goes along touching the surface even of water, let alone the earth, before separating from it.*

## Second Dialogue

*...at a single point, you make use of a sphere that is not a sphere, and a plane that is not a plane; for by your own account, either these things are not found in the world, or if they are found, they are ruined when applied to the task. SIMPLICIO. *I believe that the proposition of the philosophers <note>Simplicio refers to the Aristotelian tradition which often separated mathematical ideals from physical reality</note> should be understood in that sense; because there is no doubt that the imperfection of matter means that things taken in the concrete do not correspond to those considered in the abstract.*

SALVIATI. *How do they not correspond? On the contrary, what you yourself are saying right now proves that they correspond exactly.*

SIMPLICIO. *In what way?*

SALVIATI. *Do you not say that because of the imperfection of matter, that body which ought to be a perfect sphere, and that plane which ought to be a perfect plane, do not turn out in the concrete as one imagines them in the abstract?*

SIMPLICIO. *That is what I say.*

<margin>
Things in the abstract turn out precisely as they do in the concrete.
</margin>
SALVIATI. *Therefore, whenever you apply a material sphere to a material plane in the concrete, you are applying an imperfect sphere to an imperfect plane; and these, you say, do not touch at a single point. But I tell you that even in the abstract, an immaterial sphere that is not a perfect sphere can touch an immaterial plane that is not a perfect plane, not at a point, but with part of its surface; so that, thus far, what happens in the concrete happens in the same way in the abstract. But if their surfaces were well polished, and if both were placed upon a table so that one did not weigh down upon the other, and they were pushed very slowly toward one another, I have no doubt that they could be brought to simple contact at a single point.*

# Second Dialogue

*...shore, that possesses a perfectly spherical shape; and seeing Mr. Salviati <note>Salviati is the spokesperson for Galileo's own views in the dialogue</note> lend him his assent in a certain way by not contradicting him; I would therefore like to know if the same difficulty is found in shaping a solid of some other figure—that is, to explain myself better, if greater difficulty is found in wanting to reduce a piece of marble into the shape of a perfect sphere, than into a perfect pyramid, or a perfect horse, or a perfect locust.*

<margin>The spherical figure is more easily imprinted than any other.</margin>
<margin>The circular figure is the only one placed among the postulates.</margin>
<margin>Spherical figures of different sizes can be formed with a single instrument.</margin>

And responding to your first question, I say that if any figure can be given to a solid, the spherical is the easiest of all others, just as it is also the simplest, and holds among solid figures that place which the circle holds among surface figures. The description of the circle, being easier than all others, is the only one judged by mathematicians worthy of being placed among the postulates <term>postulates: fundamental assumptions or starting points in geometry</term> pertaining to the descriptions of all other figures. And the formation of the sphere is so easy that if a circular void is carved into a flat plate of hard metal, inside of which any solid—roughly rounded—is randomly revolved, it will by itself, without any other artifice, reduce itself into a spherical figure as perfect as possible; provided that such a solid is not smaller than the sphere that would pass through that circle. And what is even more worthy of consideration is that within that same hollow, spheres of different sizes will be formed. As for what is required to form a horse, or (as you say) a locust, I leave that to your judgment, for you know that very few sculptors will be found in the world capable of doing it. And I believe that Mr. Simplicio will not disagree with me on this particular point.*

**SIMP.** *I do not know if I disagree with you at all. My opinion is that none of the named figures can be perfectly obtained; but to approach as closely as possible to the most perfect degree, I believe it is incomparably easier to reduce a solid to a spherical figure than to the form of a horse or a locust.*

# On Galileo.

<margin>Irregular forms are difficult to introduce.</margin>

**SIMPLICIO.** *Just as the great ease in forming a sphere derives from its absolute simplicity and uniformity, so too does extreme irregularity make it most difficult to introduce other figures.*

**SAGREDO.** *Therefore, since irregularity is a cause of difficulty, would even the shape of a stone broken at random with a hammer be among those difficult to introduce, it being perhaps even more irregular than that of a horse?*

**SIMPLICIO.** *So it must be.*

**SAGREDO.** *But tell me: whatever shape that stone has, does it possess it most perfectly, or not?*

**SIMPLICIO.** *The shape it has, it possesses so perfectly that no other fits it quite so precisely.*

**SAGREDO.** *Therefore, if among irregular figures—which are supposedly difficult to achieve—one finds infinite examples perfectly obtained, by what reason can it be said that the simplest figure, and therefore the easiest of all, is impossible to find?*

**SALV.** *We have until now passed over and granted to Ptolemy, as an indubitable effect, that since the flinging of the stone proceeds from the velocity of the wheel moved around its center, the cause of that flinging increases as much as the velocity of the whirling <term>vertigine</term> <note>The Latinate term for rotation or circular motion.</note> increases; from which it was inferred that, the velocity of the terrestrial whirling being supremely greater than that of any machine we can artificially make turn, the resulting extrusion <note>The act of being thrust or thrown out.</note> of stones, animals, etc., ought to be most violent. Now I note that in this discourse there is a very great fallacy, while we indifferently and absolutely compare the velocities among themselves. It is true that if I make a comparison of the velocities of the same wheel, or of two equal wheels, the one that is turned more quickly will fling stones with greater impetus, and as the velocity increases, the cause of the projection will also increase in the same proportion; but when the velocity is made greater, not by increasing the speed in the same wheel (which would be done by making it complete a greater number of revolutions in equal times), but by increasing the diameter and making the wheel larger, so that while maintaining the same time for one revolution in the small wheel as in the large, and only in the large wheel the velocity is greater because its circumference is larger, let no one believe that the cause of the fling—*

SIMPLICIO. *Mr. Sagredo, this time you have shown yourself unlike your usual self, you who are accustomed to penetrating all things in a moment; and now you overlook a fallacy placed in the experiment of the rods, which I have been able to penetrate. And this is the different manner of operating when making the projection now with the short rod, and now with the long one; because to want the stone to escape from the notch, one must not continue its motion uniformly, but when it is at its fastest, it is necessary to hold back the arm and repress the velocity of the rod. Because of this, the stone, which is already in very fast motion, escapes and moves with impetus; but such restraint cannot be made in the larger rod, which by its length and flexibility does not entirely obey the brake of the arm, but continuing to accompany the stone for some space by gently braking it, keeps it joined to itself, and does not let it flee as if it had struck a hard obstacle. If both rods struck a restraint that stopped them, I believe that the stone would likewise escape from both, even if their movements were equally fast.*

SAGREDO. *With Mr. Salviati's permission, I will respond somewhat to Mr. Simplicio, since he has turned to me; and I say that in his discourse there is some good and some bad: good, because almost all of it is true; bad, because it is not entirely to our purpose,*

**SIMPLICIO.** I shall begin, then, with the instances contained in the booklet of conclusions, and then I will come to the others. First, then, the author goes about calculating with great sharpness how many miles per hour a point on the terrestrial surface located under the Equinoctial <note>The Equator.</note> travels, and how many are traveled by other points located on other parallels; and not content with investigating such movements in hourly times, he finds them even in a minute of an hour; nor content with the minute, he tracks it down to a second scruple <note>A "scruple" refers to a small unit of time or measurement; here, a second.</note>. But he goes further, to show most clearly how many miles a cannonball would travel in such times if placed in the concave of the Lunar Orb—supposing it even as large as Copernicus himself imagines it, to remove all subterfuges from the adversary. And having made this most ingenious and exquisite computation, he demonstrates that a heavy body <term>heavy body: "un grave," referring to an object with mass that naturally falls toward the center of the Earth</term> falling from up there would consume much more than six days to arrive at the center of the Earth, where all heavy things naturally tend. Now, if by absolute divine power, or by some Angel, a very large cannonball were miraculously transferred up there and placed at our vertical point, and from there left to its own freedom, it is indeed—in his and my opinion—a most incredible thing that in descending downward it would always maintain itself on our vertical line, continuing to revolve with the Earth around its center for so many days, describing a spiral line <note>The path resulting from the combination of falling straight down and rotating with the Earth.</note> under the Equinoctial in the plane of that great circle; and under other parallels, spiral lines around Cones; and under the Poles, falling in a simple straight line. # On Galileo

<note>This page is from Galileo's "Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems" (1632), featuring the characters Salviati (Galileo's spokesman), Sagredo (the intelligent layman), and Simplicio (the defender of Aristotelian tradition).</note>

...falling from the concave of the Moon, it would arrive at the center of the Earth; and I seem to recall that the time would not be so long; it would be well for you to tell us by what rule this author has made his calculation.

**SIMPLICIO.** He has done it to prove his point *a fortiori* <note>Latin: "with even stronger reason"</note>—granting a great advantage to the opposing side—by supposing that the speed of the falling body along the vertical line toward the center of the Earth were equal to the speed of its circular motion, performed in the great circle of the concave of the Lunar Orb. By this comparison, it would travel twelve thousand six hundred German miles in one hour; a thing which truly borders on the impossible. Nevertheless, to be overly cautious and give every advantage to the [other] side, he supposes it to be true, and concludes that the time of the fall must in any case be more than six days.

**SALVIATI.** And is this his entire progression? And with this demonstration does he prove the time of such a fall must be more than six days?

**SAGREDO.** It seems to me that he has behaved quite discreetly; since it was within his power to assign whatever speed he pleased to such a falling body—and consequently make it reach the Earth in six months, or even six years—he contented himself with six days. But please, Mr. Salviati, refresh my palate by telling me in what manner your calculation proceeded, since you say you have performed it once before; for I am quite sure that if the question did not require some ingenious operation, you would not have applied your mind to it.

**SALVIATI.** It is not enough, Mr. Sagredo, that the conclusion be noble and great, but the point lies in treating it nobly. And who does not know that in dissecting the limbs of an animal, one can discover infinite wonders of provident and most wise Nature? Yet for every one that the anatomist cuts, the butcher quarters a thousand. And I, in seeking now to satisfy your request, do not know with which of these two habits I shall appear on stage; yet taking heart from the appearance of Mr. Simplicio’s author, I will not fail to recite for you (if I can remember it) the method I held. But before I set my hand to anything else, I cannot help but say that I strongly doubt that Mr. Simplicio has faithfully reported the method by which this author of his finds that the cannonball, in coming from the concave of the Moon to the center of the Earth, would consume more than six days; because, if he had supposed that its speed in descending were...

# Concerning Galileo.

<margin>
Calculation and fact of the time of the fall of an artillery ball from the concave of the Moon to the center of the Earth.
</margin>

<margin>
Acceleration of the natural motion of heavy bodies occurs according to the odd numbers starting from unity.
The spaces passed by the falling heavy body are as the squares of the times.
</margin>

starting from rest, they go on continually accelerating; an effect known and observed by everyone, except for the aforementioned modern author, who, by not speaking of acceleration, makes it uniform <note>original: "equabile" — meaning constant speed</note>. But this general knowledge is of no profit if one does not know according to what proportion this increase in speed is made: a conclusion that remained unknown to all Philosophers until our own times; and first discovered and demonstrated by our Academician <note>A reference to Galileo himself, a member of the Accademia dei Lincei</note> and common friend, who, in some of his writings not yet published but shown in confidence to me and some of his other friends, demonstrates how the acceleration of the straight motion of heavy bodies occurs according to the odd numbers starting from unity <note>original: "ab unitate"</note>; that is, having marked whatever and however many equal times one wishes, if in the first time the moving body, starting from rest, has passed a certain space, such as for example one rod <note>term: "canna" — a traditional Italian unit of length</note>, in the second time it will pass three rods, in the third five, in the fourth seven, and so on consequently, according to the succeeding numbers; which in short is the same as saying that the spaces passed by the moving body, starting from rest, have between them a duplicate proportion of that which the times have, in which such spaces are measured; or we might say, that the spaces passed are between them as the squares of the times.

**SAGREDO.** I hear a marvelous thing being said; and of this, you say there is a Mathematical demonstration?

<margin>
Entire and new science of the Academician regarding local motion.
</margin>

**SALVIATI.** Purest Mathematics; and not only of this, but of many other most beautiful properties <note>original: "passioni" — used here in the classical sense of "attributes" or "properties" of a physical body</note> pertaining to natural motions and to projectiles as well, all discovered and demonstrated by our friend. I have seen and studied them all with my greatest pleasure and wonder, seeing a whole new knowledge raised up concerning a subject about which hundreds of volumes have been written; and yet not even one of the infinite admirable conclusions contained therein was observed or understood by anyone before our friend.

**SAGREDO.** You make me lose the desire to hear any more of our started discourses, and only wish to hear some of the demonstrations you hint at; therefore, either tell them to me now, or at least give me your firm word to hold a particular session with me on them, also with Mr. Simplicio present, if he should have a taste for hearing the properties and accidents of the primary effect of Nature.

**SIMPLICIO.** I shall undoubtedly have it; although, as far as pertains to the natural philosopher, I do not believe that descending to cer-

# On Galileo.

To avoid having further occasion to interrupt the flow, let us suppose we
wish to perform the calculation based on an iron ball of one hundred pounds,
which, through repeated experiments, descends from a height of
one hundred <term>braccia (arms)</term> <note>A Florentine unit of measure, approximately 58 centimeters or 23 inches.</note> in five seconds of an hour. And because, as
I have told you, the spaces measured by the falling body increase in
duplicate proportion—that is, according to the squares of the times—
since the time of one minute is twelve times the time
of five seconds, if we multiply the one hundred braccia by
the square of 12 (which is 144), we will have 14,400, which will be the
number of braccia that the same moving body will cover in one
minute of an hour. Following the same rule, because
one hour is 60 minutes, by multiplying 14,400 (the number of
braccia covered in one minute) by the square of 60 (which is 3,600),
the result will be 51,840,000: the number of braccia to be covered
in one hour, which is 17,280 miles. And wishing to know the space
that would be covered in 4 hours, we will multiply 17,280 by
16 (which is the square of 4), and we will get 276,480 miles.
This number is much greater than the distance from the lunar concave
to the center of the earth, which is 196,000 miles—taking
the distance of the concave to be 56 terrestrial semi-diameters, as
the modern author does, and the semi-diameter of the earth to be 3,500 miles
of 3,000 braccia each, which are our Italian miles.
Therefore, Master Simplicio, that space from the concave of the Moon
to the center of the earth, which your calculator said could not
be crossed except in much more than six days; you see how, by
making the calculation based on experience, and not on one's fingers, it
would be crossed in much less than 4 hours; and making the exact
calculation, it is crossed in 3 hours, 22 minutes, and 4 seconds.
**SAGR.** Please, dear Sir, do not deprive me of this exact
calculation, because it must be a most beautiful thing.
**SALV.** It truly is; however, having (as I said) observed with
diligent experience how such a moving body covers in falling
the height of 100 braccia in 5 seconds of an hour, we shall say: if
100 braccia are covered in 5 seconds, in how many seconds will
588,000,000 braccia (which is the total of 56 semi-diameters of the earth)
be covered? The rule for this operation is that one
multiplies the third number by the square of the second, resulting in
14,700,000,000, which must be divided by the first, that is, by
100; and the square root of the quotient, which is 12,124, is the
number sought—that is, 12,124 seconds of an hour, which are 3 hours,
22 minutes, and 4 seconds.

## Second Dialogue

**SAGREDO.** *I have seen the operation, but I do not understand anything of the reason for working it this way, nor does it seem the right time now to ask for it.*
**SALVIATI.** *On the contrary, I want to tell it to you, even though you do not ask for it, because it is quite easy. Let us mark these three numbers with the letters A first, B second, C third. A and C are the numbers of the spaces <note>The distances traveled</note>. B is the number of the time; we seek the fourth number, also of time. And because we know that whatever proportion space A has to space C, the square of time B must have to the square of the time being sought; therefore, by the golden rule <note>The "Rule of Three," a mathematical method to find a fourth value from three known ones</note> one shall multiply the number C by the square of number B, and the product shall be divided by number A. The quotient will be the square of the number being sought, and its square root will be the sought number itself. Now you see how easy it is to understand.*

Behold, then, how the motion in the concave is not as the modern author says—that is, of a speed impossible to be shared by the falling ball, etc.
