comprehension, you have explained the whole matter much more lucidly than I, and you have even made me think of adding something more. Since the increase in accelerated motion is continuous, one cannot divide the degrees of velocity—which is always increasing—into any specific number; because they change from moment to moment, they are always infinite. Therefore, we can better illustrate our intention by imagining a triangle, such as this one, ABC. Let us take as many equal parts as we like on the side AC, namely AD, DE, EF, and FG, and draw straight lines through the points D, E, F, and G parallel to the base BC. Here, I want us to imagine the parts marked on the line AC to be equal intervals of time, and the parallels drawn through the points D, E, F, and G to represent the degrees of accelerated velocity, increasing equally in equal times. Let point A be the state of rest <note>original: "quiete"</note>, from which the moving body <note>term: "mobile" - a generic term used in early physics for any object in motion</note> departs. For example, in the time AD, it has acquired the degree of velocity DH; in the following time, the velocity has increased beyond the degree DH up to the degree EI, and consequently made even greater in the succeeding times, according to the growth of the lines FK, GL, and so on. But because acceleration occurs continuously from moment to moment, and not discretely from one measurable part of time to another—point A being set as the minimum moment of velocity (that is, the state of rest and the first instant of the subsequent time AD)—it is clear that before acquiring the degree of velocity DH in the time AD, the body has passed through infinite other lesser and lesser degrees gained in the infinite instants that exist within the time DA, corresponding to the infinite points on the line DA. Therefore, to represent the infinity of degrees of velocity that precede the degree DH, one must conceive of infinite lines, always smaller and smaller, imagined to be drawn from the infinite points of the line DA parallel to DH. This infinity of lines ultimately represents for us the surface of the triangle AHD. In this way, we shall understand any space passed over by the moving body with a motion that, beginning from rest, proceeds uniformly

# Of Galileo

*...accelerating, having consumed and made use of infinite degrees of increasing velocity, corresponding to the infinite lines which, starting from point A, are understood to be drawn parallel to the line HD, and to IE, KF, LG, BC, continuing the motion as long as we please.*

*Now let us complete the entire parallelogram AMBC, and let us extend to its side BM not only the parallels marked in the triangle, but the infinity of those which are understood to be produced from all the points of the side AC. And just as BC was the greatest of the infinite lines of the triangle, representing to us the maximum degree of velocity acquired by the moving body in accelerated motion, and the entire surface of that triangle was the mass and the sum of all the velocity with which, in time AC, it passed through such a space; so the parallelogram becomes a mass and aggregate of just as many degrees of velocity, but each one equal to the maximum BC. This mass of velocity comes to be double the mass of the increasing velocities of the triangle, just as the parallelogram is double the triangle. Therefore, if the moving body, which in falling has made use of the degrees of accelerated velocity according to the triangle ABC, has passed through such a space in a certain time, it is quite reasonable and probable that, making use of uniform velocities corresponding to the parallelogram, it would pass with equable <note>uniform or constant</note> motion in the same time through a space double that passed by the accelerated motion.*

**SIMPLICIO** *In natural science, one must not seek exquisite mathematical evidence.*

# Concerning Galileo

SAGREDO: The books have just arrived; take them, Mr. Simplicio, and find the passage that is in question.

## Second Dialogue

<margin>
We have no greater knowledge of what moves heavy bodies downward than of what moves the Stars in a circle; nor do we know anything of these causes beyond the names we have assigned to them.
</margin>

**SALV.** *You are mistaken, Mr. Simplicio; you should have said that everyone knows it is called "gravity." But I am not asking you for the name; I am asking for the essence of the thing. Of this essence, you know no more than you know of the essence of whatever moves the Stars in a circle—except for the name, which has been applied to the former and made familiar and domestic through the frequent experience we see a thousand times a day. It is not that we actually understand what principle or what <term>virtue</term> <note>In this context, "virtue" (virtù) refers to an inherent power or capacity to produce an effect.</note> it is that moves a stone downward any more than we know what moves it upward once it has left the thrower, or what moves the Moon in a circle; except, as I said, for the name "gravity," which we have assigned to it as a more specific and proper term. Meanwhile, we assign the more generic term "impressed virtue" to the other, and to the celestial motion we attribute an "intelligence"—either assisting or informing—and to infinite other motions, we give "nature" as the cause.*

**SIMP.** *It seems to me that this author asks for much less than the answer you are denying him. He does not ask you what specifically and by name is the principle that moves heavy and light bodies in a circle; rather, whatever it may be, he only seeks to know if you consider it intrinsic or extrinsic. For even if I do not know, for example, what gravity is by which the earth descends, I do know that it is an internal principle, since it moves spontaneously when not hindered. On the other hand, I know that the principle moving it upward is external, even if I do not know what the virtue is that was impressed upon it by the thrower.*

**SALV.** *How many questions we would have to divert into if we wanted to decide all the difficulties that come attached one after the other! You call the principle that moves a heavy projectile upward "external," and you would even call it "preternatural" and "violent." But perhaps it is no less internal and natural than that which moves it downward. It might perhaps be called external and violent while the mobile body is joined to the thrower; but once separated, what external thing remains as the mover of the arrow or the ball?* <margin>The virtue that carries heavy projectiles upward is no less natural to them than the gravity that moves them downward.</margin> *One must necessarily say that the virtue carrying it upward is no less internal than that which moves it downward; and I consider the upward motion of heavy bodies, due to the conceived <term>impetus</term> <note>Impetus: the force or energy with which a body moves.</note>, to be just as natural as the downward motion depending on gravity.*

**SIMP.** *This I will never admit, because the latter has an internal, natural, and perpetual principle, while the former is external, violent, and finite.*

# Of Galileo

*SALVIATI:* If you withdraw from granting me that the principles of motion for heavy bodies—both downward and upward—are equally internal and natural, what would you do if I told you they could even be one and the same in number?

*SIMPLICIO:* I leave that for you to judge.

<margin>Contrary principles cannot naturally reside in the same subject.</margin>

*SALVIATI:* On the contrary, I want you yourself to be the judge. Tell me then: do you believe that within the same natural body there can reside internal principles that are contrary to one another?

*SIMPLICIO:* I believe absolutely not.

*SALVIATI:* Of the earth, of lead, of gold, and in short, of the heaviest materials, what do you estimate to be their natural intrinsic inclination? That is, toward which motion do you believe their internal principle pulls them?

*SIMPLICIO:* Toward the motion toward the center of heavy things—that is, to the center of the universe and of the Earth—where, if unimpeded, they would be led.

*SALVIATI:* So that, if the terrestrial globe were perforated by a well passing through its center, an artillery ball dropped through it, moved by a natural and intrinsic principle, would be led to the center; and it would perform this entire motion spontaneously and by an intrinsic principle. Is it not so?

*SIMPLICIO:* I hold that as certain.

*SALVIATI:* But having reached the center, do you believe it would pass further on, or rather, that it would immediately cease its motion there?

*SIMPLICIO:* I believe that it would continue to move for a very long space.

*SALVIATI:* But this motion beyond the center—would it not be upward and, by your own definition, <term>preternatural</term> <note>meaning "outside of nature" or forced</note> and violent? And upon what other principle would you make it depend, except for that very same one which led the ball to the center, and which you have called intrinsic and natural? Can you find an external <term>proponent</term> <note>original: "proiciente," an external force or thrower</note> that newly arrives to drive it upward? And this which is said of motion through the center is also seen by us up here: for the internal <term>impetus</term> <note>the force or energy with which a body moves</note> of a heavy body falling down a sloping surface, if that same surface bends upward at the bottom, will carry it upward without interrupting the motion at all. A lead ball hanging from a string, moved from the perpendicular, descends spontaneously pulled by its internal inclination, and without any pause passes the lowest point; and without any other motor arriving, it moves upward. I know that

## Second Dialogue

*You will not deny that the principle which moves heavy bodies downward is just as natural and internal as that which moves light bodies upward. Therefore, I put to your consideration a wooden ball which, descending through the air from a great height—and thus moving by an internal principle—reaches a depth of water and continues its descent. Without any other external mover, it submerges for a long stretch; and yet, downward motion through water is preternatural <note>Against its natural tendency to float</note> for it, and all this depends on a principle that is internal, and not external, to the ball. **SIMP.** *I believe there are answers to all these examples, even if they do not occur to me at the moment; but however that may be, the author continues by asking upon what principle this circular motion of heavy and light bodies depends; that is, whether from an internal or external principle. Following this, he demonstrates that it can be neither one nor the other, saying: "If from an external source: does God excite it by a continuous miracle? Or truly an Angel, or the air?" <note>original: "Si ab externo; Deus ne illum excitat per continuum miraculum? an verò Angelus, an aer?"</note> And indeed, many assign it to the latter. But against this...*

**SALV.** *Do not weary yourself in reading the objections, because I am not one of those who attribute such a principle to the surrounding air. As for the miracle or the Angel, I would rather incline toward that side; because that which begins by divine miracle or angelic operation—such as the transportation of a cannonball into the concave of the Moon—it is not improbable that by virtue of the same principle it should also do the rest. But as for the air, it is enough for me that it does not impede the circular motion of the mobile bodies said to move through it; and to do this, it is sufficient (nor is more required) that the air itself moves with the same motion, and that it completes its revolutions with the same speed as the terrestrial globe.*

**SIMP.** *And he will likewise rise up against this, asking: who carries the air around, nature or violence? And he refutes nature by saying that this is against the truth, against experience, and against Copernicus himself.*

**SALV.** *It is not against Copernicus at all, who does not write such a thing, and this author attributes it to him with an excess of courtesy; rather, he says—and in my opinion says well—that the part of the air near the earth, being more like terrestrial evaporation, can have the same nature, and naturally follow the...*

**SALVIATI.** Copernicus will say that this natural propensity of elementary bodies to follow the terrestrial motion has a limited sphere, beyond which such natural inclination would cease; furthermore, as I have said, it is not the air that carries with it the moving bodies which, being separated from the Earth, follow its motion; so all the instances that this author produces to prove that the air cannot cause such effects fall away.

**SIMPLICIO.** Since that is not the case, it must be said that such effects depend on an internal principle, against which position *the second most difficult, indeed inextricable questions arise* <note>original: "oboriuntur difficillimæ, immò inextricabiles quæstiones secundæ"</note>, which are the following: *Is that internal principle an accident or a substance? If the first, what kind is it? For until now, no quality capable of circular motion seems to have been recognized.* <note>original: "Principium illud internum vel est accidens, vel substantia, si primum, quale nam illud? nam qualitas loco motiua circū hactenus nulla videtur esse agnita."</note>

**SALVIATI.** How is it that there is no knowledge of any? Are there not these very principles that move all these elementary matters around together with the Earth? You see how this author assumes as true the very thing that is in question.

**SIMPLICIO.** He says that this is not seen, and it seems to me that he is right in this.

**SALVIATI.** It is not seen by us because we are revolving together with them.

**SIMPLICIO.** Hear the other instance: *Even if it existed, how could it be found in things so contrary? In fire as in water? In air as in earth? In living things as in those lacking a soul?* <note>original: "Quæ etiam si esset, quomodo tamen inueniretur in rebus tam contrarijs? in igne, vt in aqua? in aere, vt in terra? in viuentibus, vt in anima carentibus?"</note>

**SALVIATI.** Assuming for now that water and fire are contraries, as are air and earth (though there would be much to say about that), the most that could follow from this is that motions which are contrary to each other cannot be common to them; so that, for example, the motion—

# Second Dialogue

...upward, which naturally belongs to fire, cannot belong to water; but just as water is by nature contrary to fire, so too should the motion contrary to that of fire—which is downward motion—suit it. But as for circular motion, which is contrary neither to upward nor downward motion—and indeed can be mixed with both, as Aristotle <note>original: "Aristot."</note> himself affirms—why should it not equally belong to both heavy and light bodies? Furthermore, the motions that cannot be common to both living and non-living things are those that depend on the soul; but as for those belonging to the body insofar as it is elemental, and consequently participating in the qualities of the elements, why should they not be common to both the corpse and the living being? Therefore, if circular motion is proper to the elements, it must also be common to mixed bodies.

**SAGREDO:** This author must believe that if a dead cat falls from a window, it would be impossible for a living one to fall in the same way, since he thinks it improper for a corpse to share the qualities that belong to a living thing.

**SALVIATI:** This author's discourse, then, does not conclude against someone who might say that the principle of circular motion for heavy and light bodies is an internal accident; I do not know how well he will demonstrate that it cannot be a substance.

**SIMPLICIO:** He rises up against this with many oppositions. The first of which is this: *If according to the second point (namely, if you say such a principle is a substance), it is either matter, or form, or a composite; but again, so many diverse natures of things are repugnant to this, such as birds, snails, rocks, arrows, snow, smoke, hail, fish, etc., all of which, though differing in species and genus, would be moved by their own nature circularly, despite being most diverse in their natures, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Si secundum... naturis diuersissima, &c."</note>

**SALVIATI:** If these named things are of diverse natures, and things of diverse natures cannot have a common motion, then if we are to satisfy them all, we must think of something other than just two motions, upward and downward. **SIMPLICIO:** It seems you are making fun of these arguments.

**SALVIATI:** Not at all, Signor Simplicio; but the answer has already been given above, namely,

# On Galileo.

*...that is to say, if a downward or upward motion can be attributed to the things mentioned, a circular motion could no less be attributed to them; and staying within the Peripatetic doctrine <note>The philosophy of Aristotle and his followers</note>, would you not place a greater diversity between an elementary comet and a celestial star than between a fish and a bird? And yet both of those move circularly. Now continue with the second argument.*

**SIMP.** If the Earth were to stand still by the will of God, would the rest rotate or not? If the latter is false—that it is natural to gyrate—if the former, the previous questions return; and truly it would be a marvel that a gull could not hover over a little fish, a lark over its little nest, and a crow over a snail or a stone, even if it wished to. <note>original Latin: "Si terra staret per voluntatem Dei..." Simplicio is quoting an opponent of Copernicus who argues that if the Earth stopped, birds would be swept away by the continuing rotation of the atmosphere.</note>

**SALV.** *For my part, I would give a general answer: that granted it were by the will of God that the Earth ceased its diurnal vertigo <note>The daily rotation of the Earth on its axis</note>, those birds would do whatever that same will of God pleased. But if this author should desire a more particular answer, I would tell him that they would do the exact opposite of what they would do if, while they were suspended in the air separated from the Earth, the terrestrial globe were suddenly set into a most precipitous motion by Divine will. It is now up to this author to assure us of what would happen in such a case.*

**SAGR.** *Pray, Mr. Salviati, grant to this author at my request that if the Earth stopped by God's will, the other things separated from it would continue to revolve in their natural motion, and let us hear what impossibilities or inconveniences would follow. For I, for my part, cannot see any greater disorders than those the author himself produces: namely, that larks, even if they wanted to, could not stay over their nests, nor crows over snails or stones. From this it would follow that crows would have to endure a longing for snails, and the little larks would die of hunger and cold, being unable to be either fed or brooded by their mothers. This is all the ruin I can see following from the author's statement. See, Mr. Simplicio, if any greater inconveniences ought to follow.*

**SIMP.** *I cannot discern any greater ones, but it is quite believable that the author discerns other natural disorders beyond these, which perhaps for his own worthy reasons he did not wish to bring forward. I shall follow, then, with the third instance.* Furthermore, how does it happen that these things, so varied, move only from the West to the East [along] paralle- <note>original Latin: "Insuper qui fit vt istæ res tā variæ..." # Second Dialogue

<margin>Why do they move toward the Equator? So that they are always moving and never at rest?</margin>
**SALVIATI:** They move from West to East parallel to the Equinoctial <note>The celestial equator</note> without stopping, in exactly the same manner that you believe the fixed stars move from East to West parallel to the Equinoctial without stopping.

**SIMPLICIO:** <note>original: "Quare quò ſunt altiores celerius, quò humiliores tardius?"</note> Why is it that the higher they are, the faster they move, and the lower they are, the slower?

**SALVIATI:** Because in a sphere, or in a circle that turns around its center, the parts furthest away describe larger circles, and those closer describe smaller ones in the same amount of time.

**SIMPLICIO:** <note>original: "Quare quæ Æquinoctiali propiores in maiori, quæ remotiores in minori circulo feruntur?"</note> Why are those closer to the Equinoctial carried in a larger circle, and those further away in a smaller circle?

**SALVIATI:** To imitate the starry sphere, in which those stars closest to the Equinoctial move in larger circles than those further away.

**SIMPLICIO:** <note>original: "Quare Pila eadē ſub Æquinoctiali tota circa centrū terræ ambitu maximo, celeritate incredibili; ſub polo vero circa centrum proprium gyro nullo, tarditate ſuprema volueretur?"</note> Why would the same ball, when under the Equinoctial, travel around the center of the earth in the greatest circuit with incredible speed; yet under the pole, it would turn around its own center with no rotation at all and with the greatest slowness?

**SALVIATI:** To imitate the stars of the firmament, which would do the same thing if the <term>diurnal motion</term> <note>The daily rotation of the heavens or the Earth</note> belonged to them.

**SIMPLICIO:** <note>original: "Quare eadem res, pila vgr. plumbea..."</note> Why would the same object—for example, a lead ball—if it once circled the earth by describing a great circle, not continue to travel everywhere according to a great circle, but instead, when moved away from the Equinoctial, be driven in smaller circles?

**SALVIATI:** Because they would do exactly that—or rather, they have already done so according to the doctrine of Ptolemy <note>The ancient Greek astronomer who proposed a geocentric model</note>—namely, certain fixed stars which were once very close to the Equinoctial and described the largest circles, and now that they are far from it, they describe smaller ones.

**SAGREDO:** Oh, if only I could keep all these fine points in mind, I would feel I had made a great acquisition! Mr. Simplicio, you must lend me that little book, for there must surely be a sea of strange and most exquisite things within it.

**SIMPLICIO:** I shall make you a gift of it.

**SAGREDO:** Oh no, I would never deprive you of it; but are the questions finished yet?

**SIMPLICIO:** No, sir; listen further. <note>original: "Si latio circularis grauibus, & leuibus"</note> If circular motion is natural to heavy and light bodies...

# From Galileo:

Is the motion of light bodies natural, such as that which occurs along a straight line? For if it is natural, how can circular motion also be natural, since it differs in kind from the straight? If it is violent <note>original: "violentus"; in Aristotelian physics, "violent" motion is forced and contrary to an object's nature</note>, how is it that an ignited missile flying upward—its sparkling head moving away from the earth—does not instead revolve in a circle, etc.?

<margin>Regarding mixed motion: we do not see the circular part because we participate in it.</margin>
**SALV.** *It has already been said a thousand times that circular motion is natural for the whole and for the parts while they are in their best arrangement; straight motion is for restoring disordered parts to order. Though it is better to say that parts, whether ordered or disordered, never move in a purely straight motion, but in a mixed motion, which could even be purely circular. However, only one part of this mixed motion remains visible and observable to us—namely, the straight part—while the other circular part remains imperceptible because we also participate in it. This applies to rockets <note>original: "razzi"</note>, which move upward and in a circle; but we cannot distinguish the circular motion because we are moving with it ourselves. But I do not believe this author has ever understood this mixture, since one sees how he resolutely claims that rockets go straight up and do not go around at all.*

**SIMP.** Why does the center of a sphere falling under the Equator describe a spiral in its plane, while under other parallels it describes a spiral on a cone? And under the pole, does it descend along the axis in a helical line, tracing a path marked upon a cylindrical surface? <note>Simplicio is quoting a Latin objection regarding the complex geometric paths a falling object would take if the Earth were rotating.</note>

**SALV.** *Because of the lines drawn from the center to the circumference of the sphere—which are those along which heavy bodies descend—the one that ends at the Equator traces a circle, and those that end at other parallels describe conical surfaces; and the axis describes nothing else but remains as it is. And if I must tell you my opinion freely, I will say that I cannot draw any useful conclusion from all these questions that weighs against the motion of the Earth. For if I were to ask this author (granting him for a moment that the Earth does not move) what would happen in all these particulars if it **did** move as Copernicus wishes, I am quite sure he would say that all these effects would follow—the very ones he now opposes as "inconveniences" to disprove mobility. Thus, in this man's mind, necessary consequences are instead reputed to be absurdities. But please, if there is anything else, let us dispatch with this tedium.*

**SIMP.** *In what follows, there is more against Copernicus and his followers,*

He dismisses geometric objections about spiral paths as being the necessary, logical consequences of a rotating Earth rather than proofs against it.</summary>

# Second Dialogue

*...those who claim that the motion of parts separated from their whole exists only for the purpose of reuniting with that whole; but that it is absolutely natural to move circularly according to the diurnal rotation <note>original: "vertigine diurna"; the daily rotation of the Earth</note>. ## Second Dialogue

<margin>
Heavy things exist before the center of gravity.
</margin>
<margin>
If the great aggregate of heavy bodies were moved, the particles separated from it would follow it.
</margin>

I have seen it myself; and I will say that I believe heavy things exist before the common center of gravity; so that it is not a center—which is nothing more than an indivisible point, and therefore of no efficacy—that attracts heavy materials to itself. Rather, these materials, naturally conspiring toward union, form for themselves a common center, which is that point around which parts of equal moments <note>In this context, "moments" refers to the tendency of a weight to cause motion or maintain equilibrium.</note> consist. Therefore, I estimate that if the great aggregate of heavy bodies were transferred to any place whatsoever, the particles that were separated from the whole would follow it; and if unimpeded, they would penetrate it until they found parts less heavy than themselves. But having arrived where they encountered heavier materials, they would descend no further. And so I estimate that in a cavern filled with air, the entire vault would exert pressure, and would only be violently sustained above that air if its hardness could not be overcome and broken by gravity; but I believe that detached stones would descend to the center and would not float upon the air. Nor could it be said for that reason that they were not moving toward their "whole," since they move to the place where all parts of the whole would move if they were not impeded.

**SIMPLICIO:** What remains is a certain error that he <note>Referring to the author of the booklet Simplicio is reading.</note> notes in a follower of Copernicus. This follower, by making the earth move with both annual and diurnal motion in the same manner that a carriage wheel moves upon the circle of the earth and upon itself, ended up making either the terrestrial globe too large or the great orbit <note>term: "orbe magno" (Great Orbit) - the path of the Earth's annual revolution around the Sun.</note> too small; seeing as 365 revolutions of the Equinoctial <note>The Earth's equator.</note> are much less than the circumference of the great orbit.

**SALVIATI:** Take care, for you are mistaken and are saying the opposite of what must be written in the booklet; for one must say that such an author ended up making the terrestrial globe too small or the great orbit too large, and not the terrestrial too large and the annual too small.

**SIMPLICIO:** The mistake is not mine at all: here are the words of the booklet:

> He does not see that he constructs either the annual circle smaller than is right, or the terrestrial globe much larger than is just. <note>original: "Non videt, quod vel circulum annuum æquo minorem, vel orbem terreum iuſto multò fabricet maiorem."</note>

**SALVIATI:** Whether the first author erred, I cannot know, since the author of the booklet does not name him; but the error of the booklet is manifest and inexcusable, whether that first follower of Copernicus erred or not, since the author of the booklet passes over such a material error without noticing it, and does not remark upon it,

# On Galileo

<margin>It is not contradictory to be able to measure and describe a line greater than any large circle imaginable using the circumference of a small circle, even with only a few rotations.</margin>

*...and he does not correct it. But let this be forgiven, as an error of inadvertence rather than anything else. And it did not occur to me to tell you how he had later found a way to remove them from the Heavens; because, as he proceeded in this refutation by way of computations and Parallaxes—matters little or not at all understood by me—I had not read them. I had only studied these instances against the motion of the Earth, which are, after all, natural arguments.*

# Second Dialogue

SALVIATI: *I understand perfectly. <margin>In the Copernican opinion, the criterion of philosophy is ruined.</margin>

**And first, if the opinion of Copernicus is accepted, the Criterion of natural Philosophy seems to be, if not utterly destroyed, at least violently shaken.** <note>original Latin: "Et primo si opinio Copernici recipiatur Criterium naturalis Philosophiæ ni prorsus tollatur, vehementer saltem labefactari videtur."</note>

*This "Criterion" requires, according to the opinion of all schools of Philosophers, that sense and experience be our guides in philosophizing. But in the Copernican position, the senses are greatly deceived; for they visibly perceive, at close range and through the purest media, very heavy bodies descending in a perfectly straight perpendicular line, never deviating a single hair's breadth from that path. Despite this, according to Copernicus, our sight is deceived in such a clear matter: that motion is not straight at all, but a mixture of straight and circular.*

SALVIATI: *This is the first argument that Aristotle, Ptolemy, and all their followers produce. It has already been abundantly answered, and the fallacy <term>paralogism: a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning</term> has been shown. It has been quite clearly declared how motion that is common to us and to other moving bodies is as if it did not exist.*

SIMPLICIO. *On the contrary, no; here are the words that immediately follow:* "Furthermore, we also are rotated by the circling of the earth, etc." <note>original Latin: "Præterea nos quoq; rotamur ex circunductione terræ, &c."</note>

<margin>
In the way of Copernicus, one must deny the senses.
</margin>

SIMPLICIO. *The same argument continues, showing that in the way of Copernicus one must deny one's own sensations; because this principle by which we go around with the earth is either intrinsic to us or external to us—that is, a carrying away by the earth itself. And if it is this second case, since we do not feel such a carrying, it must be said that the sense of touch does not feel its own joined object, nor its impression on the sensory organ. But if the principle is intrinsic, we would not feel a local motion <term>local motion: movement from one place to another</term> deriving from ourselves, and we would never notice a propensity perpetually attached to us.*

SALVIATI. *So that the argument of this philosopher hits here: whether that principle by which we move with the earth is external or internal, we should feel it in every way; and not feeling it, it is neither one nor the other, and therefore we do not move.*

And the occurrence is the appearance to those who walk along a street at night of being followed by the Moon at a pace equal to their own, while they see it skimming the eaves of the roofs above which it appears to them, in exactly the same manner as a cat would do, which, actually walking upon the tiles, kept behind them. An appearance which, if reasoning did not intervene, would all too clearly deceive the sight.*

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and physical debate regarding the motion of the Earth, specifically addressing arguments raised against the Copernican system based on Aristotelian principles of causality.</meta>

# Concerning Galileo

<margin>Three axioms that are assumed to be self-evident.</margin>
...many self-evident axioms. The first of these is that every effect depends on some cause. The second is that *nothing produces itself*: from which it follows that *it is not possible for the mover and that which is moved to be entirely the same thing*. This is manifest not only in things moved by an external motor, but it is also gathered from the proposed principles that the same occurs in natural motion depending on an internal principle; otherwise, since the mover, as mover, is the cause, and the moved, as moved, is the effect, the exact same thing would be both cause and effect. Therefore, *a body does not move its whole self—that is, that the whole moves and the whole is moved*; rather, it is necessary to distinguish in some way within the moved thing the <term>efficient principle</term> <note>The primary source of change or rest; the "agent" of the motion.</note> of the motion from that part which is moved by said motion. The third axiom is that *in things subject to the senses, one thing, insofar as it is one, produces only one thing*; that is, the soul in the animal certainly produces diverse operations, but with diverse instruments—namely sight, hearing, smell, and generation—but always with diverse instruments. In short, one perceives in sensible things that diverse operations derive from a diversity existing within the cause.

<margin>A simple body, such as the Earth, cannot move with three diverse motions.</margin>
Now, if these axioms are joined together, it will be a most clear thing that a simple body, such as the Earth, cannot by its nature move simultaneously with three greatly diverse motions; because, by the suppositions made, the whole does not move its whole self; it is therefore necessary to distinguish within it three principles for three motions; otherwise, a single principle would produce multiple motions. But if it contained within itself three principles of natural motions in addition to the part being moved, it would not be a simple body, but a composite of three moving principles and the moved part.

<margin>The Earth cannot move with any of the motions attributed to it by Copernicus.</margin>
If, therefore, the Earth is a simple body, it will not move with three motions; indeed, it will not move with any of those attributed to it by Copernicus, as it must move with only one. This is manifest by the arguments of Aristotle: that it moves toward its own center, as shown by its parts, which descend at right angles to the spherical surface of the Earth.

<margin>Responses to the arguments against the motion of the Earth taken from the nature of things.</margin>
**SALV.** <note>Salviati, the character representing Galileo's own views in the Dialogue.</note> Many things could be said and considered regarding the texture of this argument; but since we can resolve it in few words, I do not wish for now to expand unnecessarily; all the more so because the response is supplied to me by the author himself, where he says that in an animal, diverse operations are produced by a single principle: whence I...

<meta>The text cuts off with the catchword "per" (for/by), indicating the start of the next page's argument.</meta>

Now see how shrewdly he goes to meet your response, as if he had almost foreseen it.*

## Second Dialogue

<margin>The elements sharing a common motion is of no more or less consequence than their sharing a suitable rest.</margin>
...to derive such knowledge from other uncommon qualities; and therefore, whoever should take away from the elements only this common rest, and leave them all their other operations, would not at all block the path that leads us to the knowledge of their essences. But Copernicus takes nothing else from them but this common rest, and transforms it for them into a most universal motion, leaving them their gravity <note>weight</note>, lightness, their upward and downward motions, slower or faster, their rarity, density, the qualities of heat, cold, dryness, moisture, and in short, all other things. Therefore, such an absurdity as this author imagines does not exist in the Copernican position; nor does agreeing in an identity of motion matter more or less than agreeing in an identity of rest, regarding the diversifying or not diversifying of natures. Now tell me if there is any other argument to the contrary.

<margin>Bodies of the same genus have motions that agree in genus.</margin>
SIMPLICIO. There follows a fourth instance, also taken from natural observation, which is that bodies of the same genus have motions that agree in genus, or rather, they agree in rest. But in the Copernican position, bodies that agree in genus, and are most similar among themselves, would have a supreme disagreement regarding motion—indeed, a diametrical repugnance; because stars so similar to one another would nonetheless be so dissimilar in motion, since six planets would go around perpetually, but the Sun and all the fixed stars would remain perpetually motionless.

<margin>Another argument also against Copernicus.</margin>
<margin>It is argued from the Earth being dark by nature, and the Sun and fixed stars being lucid, that the former is mobile and the latter are immobile.</margin>
SALVIATI. The form of the argument seems conclusive to me; but I truly believe that the application or the subject matter is defective; and as long as the author wishes to persist in his assumption, the consequence will without doubt come directly against him. The progress of the argument is this: among the worldly bodies, there are six that perpetually move, and these are the six planets; of the others—namely the Earth, the Sun, and the fixed stars—it is doubted which of them moves and which stands still. It being necessary that if the Earth stands still, the Sun and the fixed stars move, and it also being possible that the Sun and the fixed stars remain immobile if the Earth were to move: the question is, in doubt of the fact, to whom motion can more suitably be attributed, and to whom rest. Natural discourse dictates that motion should be estimated to belong to those who most agree in genus and essence with those bodies that undoubtedly move, and rest to those who most differ from them. And since eternal rest and perpetual motion are accidents... <note>The text cuts off here as it reaches the end of the page.</note>

# On Galileo

It is manifest that the nature of a body that is always mobile must be vastly different from the nature of one that is always stable. Let us seek, therefore, while we remain uncertain between motion and rest, whether by way of some other significant condition we might investigate which more closely resembles the bodies that are certainly mobile: the Earth, or rather the Sun and the fixed stars. But behold, nature, favorable to our need and desire, provides us with two distinguished conditions, no less different than motion and rest; these are light and darkness—that is, being by nature most splendid, and being dark and deprived of all light. Therefore, bodies adorned with an internal and eternal splendor are vastly different in essence from bodies deprived of all light. The Earth is deprived of light; the Sun is most splendid in itself, and no less so are the fixed stars. The six mobile planets <note>The six planets known at the time: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and the Earth itself in the Copernican model.</note> totally lack light, just like the Earth; therefore, their essence agrees with the Earth and differs from the Sun and the fixed stars. Thus, the Earth is mobile, while the Sun and the stellar sphere are immobile.

SIMPLICIO: But the author will not concede that the six planets are dark, and he will stand firm on that negation; or rather, he will argue for a great conformity of nature between the six planets, the Sun, and the fixed stars, and a deformity between these and the Earth based on conditions other than darkness and light. Indeed, now that I notice it, in the fifth instance that follows, there is placed the supreme disparity between the 
<margin>Another difference between the Earth and the celestial bodies taken from purity and impurity.</margin>
Earth and the celestial bodies. In this, he writes that there would be great confusion and disturbance in the System of the Universe and among its parts according to the Hypothesis of Copernicus; because among celestial bodies that are immutable and incorruptible—according to Aristotle, Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe, the Danish astronomer.</note>, and others—among bodies, I say, of such nobility (by the confession of everyone, including Copernicus himself, who affirms that they are ordered and disposed in an excellent constitution, and who removes from them all inconstancy of power); among bodies, I say, so pure—that is, between Venus and Mars—to place the sink <note>original: "sentina" - a term for the lowest part of a ship where filth collects, used here metaphorically for the Earth as a place of decay.</note> of all corruptible matters: namely the Earth, water, air, and all mixtures.

But how much more excellent a distribution, and more convenient to nature—indeed, to God the Architect himself—to sequester the pure from the impure, the mortal from the immortal, as the other schools teach us. They teach us how these impure and fleeting matters are contained within the narrow concave of the Lunar Orb, above which the Celestial things then rise in an uninterrupted series.

<margin>
Copernicus causes a disturbance in Aristotle's Universe.

<margin>
Fallacy of the author of the *Anti-Tycho*. <note>Refers to Scipione Chiaramonti’s book defending the Aristotelian view against Tycho Brahe and Copernicus.</note>

<margin>
It is foolishly said that the Earth is outside of Heaven.

SALVIATI. *It is true that the Copernican system causes a disturbance in Aristotle's universe; but we are dealing with our own true and real universe. Furthermore, when this author wishes to infer the disparity of essence between the Earth and the celestial bodies—based on the incorruptibility of the latter and the corruptibility of the former according to Aristotle—and from this disparity concludes that motion must belong to the Sun and the fixed stars while the Earth remains immobile, he wanders into a fallacy <term>Paralogism: a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning</term> by assuming the very thing at issue. This is because Aristotle infers the incorruptibility of celestial bodies from their motion, and it is that very motion which is in dispute: whether it belongs to them or to the Earth. As for the vanity of these rhetorical inferences, enough has already been said. And what could be more foolish than to say that the Earth and the elements are banished and separated from the celestial spheres, and confined within the Lunar Orb? Is the Lunar Orb not one of the celestial spheres itself, and by their own consensus, held in the very midst of all the others? This would be a strange way to separate the pure from the impure and the diseased from the healthy: giving the infected a residence in the heart of the City! I should have thought the pest-house <note>original: "lazzeretto" — a hospital for those with contagious diseases</note> ought to be removed as far away as possible. Copernicus admires the arrangement of the parts of the universe because God placed the great lamp, which was to provide the highest splendor to His entire Temple, in the center of it and not off to one side. As for the terrestrial globe being situated between Venus and Mars, we shall treat that shortly; and you yourself, for the sake of this author, shall attempt to remove it from there. But please, let us not entwine these rhetorical flourishes with the solidity of demonstrations; let us leave them to the orators, or rather to the poets, who with their pleasantries have known how to praise the most vile and sometimes even pernicious things. If anything else remains, let us dispatch it as soon as possible.*

<margin>
Argument taken from animals who need rest, even though their motion is natural.
</margin>

But what does such a movement have to do with that of the Earth, which is immense in comparison to theirs? And what is more: to make it move with three different motions <note>Copernicus proposed three motions for Earth: daily rotation, annual revolution, and a third "tilting" motion to explain the seasons</note> pulling in different directions? Who could ever assert such things, except those who have sworn themselves to be their defenders? Nor is that which Copernicus produces of any value in this case: that because this motion is natural to the Earth and not*

# On Galileo

*...violent [motion] produces effects contrary to those of violent motions; and that things subjected to force dissolve easily and cannot long endure, whereas those made by nature are preserved in their optimal state; this response, I say, is invalid, as it is overturned by our own. For an animal is indeed a natural body, not one fabricated by art, and its movement is natural, deriving from the soul—that is, from an intrinsic principle; whereas violent motion is that whose principle is external, and to which the moved thing contributes nothing. Nevertheless, if the animal continues its motion for a long time, it grows weary, and even dies if it tries to force itself obstinately. You see, therefore, how in nature one encounters on all sides traces that contradict the position of* **Copernicus**, *and never any that favor it. And so as not to have to take up the part of this opponent again, hear what he produces against* **Kepler** *(with whom he disputes) regarding what* **Kepler** *himself maintained against those to whom it seems inconvenient, or rather impossible, to increase the stellar sphere to an immense size, as the position of* **Copernicus** *requires.*

<margin>Argument from Kepler in favor of Copernicus. The author of the *Antitycho* <note>The *Antitycho* was a work by Scipione Chiaramonti (1621) defending the Aristotelian view against Tycho Brahe and Kepler.</note> insists against Kepler.</margin>

*Thus* **Kepler** *insists, saying:* It is more difficult to extend an accident beyond the measure of its subject than to increase the subject without the accident. <note>original: "Difficilius est accidens præter modulum subiecti intendere, quam subiectum sine accidente augere." Kepler argues it is more "natural" to have a massive, still universe than a smaller one moving at impossible speeds.</note> Copernicus, therefore, acts with greater probability, for he increases the Sphere of the fixed Stars without motion, rather than Ptolemy, who increases the motion of the fixed stars with immense velocity.

<margin>Velocity in circular motion increases as the diameter of the circle increases.</margin>

*The author resolves this objection, marveling at how much* **Kepler** *is deceived in saying that in the* **Hypothesis** *of* **Ptolemy** *the motion is increased beyond the measure of the subject: for it seems to him that it is not increased except in accordance with the measure, and that according to its growth, the velocity of the motion increases. This he proves by imagining a millstone that completes one revolution in 24 hours, which motion would be called very slow; then, imagining its radius extended as far as the distance of the Sun, its extremity would equal the speed of the Sun; extending it to the stellar sphere, it would equal the speed of the fixed stars, even though at the circumference of the millstone it is very slow. Applying now this consideration of the millstone to the stellar sphere, let us imagine a point on its radius as near to the center as the radius of the millstone: the same motion which in the stellar sphere is very fast, at that point will be very slow. But it is the size of the body that makes it become, from very slow,*

Explanation of the true sense of Kepler's saying, and his defense.

<margin>
The order of nature is to make smaller orbits circulate in shorter times, and larger ones in longer times.
</margin>

of Saturn's revolution is longer than all the times of the other smaller spheres, being thirty years. Here, too, the author is in the wrong, nor can he deny having artfully disguised his understanding of the words in order to charge Kepler with too crass an ignorance; but the deception was so coarse that, even with such a great deduction, it could not diminish the concept of his doctrine that Kepler has impressed upon the minds of the learned—

# Concerning Galileo.

learned men. As for the objection against the perpetual motion of the earth, based on the idea that it would be impossible for it to continue without tiring out—given that even animals, which move naturally and from an internal principle, grow weary and have need of rest to relax their limbs . .

<margin>
A feigned response from Kepler with a certain hidden wit.
</margin>

**SAGREDO.** I seem to hear Kepler <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), the German astronomer who proved planets move in elliptical orbits.</note> answering him that there are indeed animals that refresh themselves from fatigue by rolling on the ground; and therefore one should not fear that the terrestrial globe will grow weary; rather, one can reasonably say that it enjoys a perpetual and most tranquil rest, maintaining itself in an eternal revolution.

**SALVIATI.** You, Mr. Sagredo, are too witty and satirical: but let us set jokes aside while we treat serious matters.

<margin>
Animals would not tire if their motion proceeded like that attributed to the terrestrial globe.

The cause of animals becoming tired.

The motion of an animal is more rightly called violent than natural.
</margin>

**SAGREDO.** Forgive me, Mr. Salviati, but what I am saying is not at all as irrelevant as you perhaps make it out to be, because a movement that serves as rest and to remove fatigue from a body exhausted by travel can much more easily serve to prevent it from coming at all; just as preventative remedies are easier than curative ones. And I hold for certain that if the motion of animals proceeded like this one attributed to the earth, they would not tire at all; for the tiring of an animal's body derives, in my belief, from employing only one part to move itself and all the rest of the body: as, for example, in walking, the thighs and legs are employed solely to carry themselves and all the remainder. On the other hand, you will see the movement of the heart to be, as it were, indefatigable, because it moves only itself. Furthermore, I do not know how true it is that the movement of an animal is natural and not rather <term>violent</term> <note>In Aristotelian physics, "natural" motion is toward a body's rightful place (like a stone falling), while "violent" motion is forced against that nature.</note>; indeed, I believe it can be said with truth that the soul moves the limbs of the animal naturally with a <term>preternatural</term> <note>Beyond or outside the normal course of nature.</note> motion. Because if upward motion is preternatural for heavy bodies, raising the legs and thighs (which are heavy bodies) to walk cannot be done without violence, and therefore not without effort from the mover. Climbing up a ladder carries the heavy body upward against its natural inclination, from which exhaustion follows due to the natural resistance of gravity to such motion. But to move a mobile body with a movement to which it has no resistance at all, what weariness or diminution of strength <note>original: "diminuzion di virtù"</note>...

<summary>In this excerpt from Galileo's Dialogue, the characters Sagredo and Salviati debate whether the Earth would "tire out" from constant rotation, concluding that exhaustion only occurs when a force acts against a body's natural inclination.</summary>

*Should one fear for the virtue and strength of the mover? And why should its form be diminished where none is exerted at all?*

*SIMPLICIO: The contrary motions, by which the terrestrial globe is imagined to move, are those upon which the author <note>Referring to Scipione Chiaramonti, a critic of Galileo</note> founds his objection.*

*SAGREDO: It has already been said that they are not contrary at all, and that in this the author has greatly deceived himself; so much so that the force of the entire objection turns against the challenger himself, insofar as he wishes for the "prime mover" <term>Primum Mobile: in Ptolemaic astronomy, the outermost sphere that carries all others</term> to snatch away all the lower spheres against the motion which they, at the same time and continually, exert. It is the prime mover, then, that ought to grow weary, since besides moving itself it must carry so many other spheres which, moreover, resist it with a contrary motion. Thus, that final conclusion which the author inferred—saying that in examining the effects of nature one always encounters things favorable to the opinion of Aristotle and Ptolemy, and never any that do not oppose Copernicus—requires great consideration. It is better to say that since one of these*
<margin>For true propositions, one finds conclusive arguments, but not for false ones.</margin>
*two positions is true and the other necessarily false, it is impossible that for the false one there should ever be found a reason, experience, or right discourse favorable to it, just as none of these things can be repugnant to the truth. A great diversity, therefore, must be found between the discourses and arguments produced by one side and the other for and against these two opinions; the strength of which I shall leave for you to judge yourself, Signor Simplicio.*

*SALVIATI: You, Signor Sagredo, carried away by the speed of your wit, just now cut off my reasoning while I wished to say something in response to this last argument of the author; and although you have more than sufficiently answered him, I wish in any case to add something that I had in mind then. He posits it as a very improbable thing that a dissipatable and corruptible body, such as the Earth, could perpetually move with a regular motion, especially as we see animals finally grow weary and have need of rest; and the improbability increases for him because such motion must be of incomparable and immense velocity compared to that of animals. Now, I cannot understand why the velocity of the Earth should disturb him now, while that of the stellar sphere—so very much greater—brings him no more considerable disturbance than if it were the velocity of a millstone, which...*

# On Galileo

<margin>Fatigue is more to be feared in the starry sphere than in the terrestrial globe.</margin>

*...which in 24 hours completes a single revolution. If, because the speed of the Earth's rotation is modeled on that of a millstone, one does not draw consequences of greater efficacy than that, let the author cease to fear the Earth becoming tired; because not even the most weak and sluggish animal—I say not even a chameleon—would tire itself by moving no more than five or six cubits <note>original: "braccia," a historical unit of measurement roughly equal to an arm's length</note> in 24 hours. But if he wishes to consider the speed no longer on the model of the millstone, but absolutely, and insofar as in 24 hours the moving body must traverse a vast space, he should show himself much more reluctant to grant it to the starry sphere, which, with a speed incomparably greater than that of the Earth, must carry with it thousands of bodies, each one vastly larger than the terrestrial globe...*

*It remains now for us to see the proofs by which the author concludes that the new stars of '72 and '604 <note>Refers to the supernovae observed in 1572 (Tycho's Nova) and 1604 (Kepler's Nova)</note> were sublunary <note>term: sublunary (located below the moon, in the changing atmosphere, rather than the "unchanging" heavens)</note> and not celestial, as the astronomers of those times were commonly persuaded. A truly great undertaking; but I have thought—since this writing is new to me and long due to the many calculations—that it will be more expedient for me to look over as much of it as I can between tonight and tomorrow morning. Then tomorrow, returning to our usual discussions, I will report to you what I have gathered; and if time remains, we shall come to discuss the annual motion attributed to the Earth. Meanwhile, if you have anything to say, and in particular Mr. Simplicio, regarding matters pertaining to the diurnal <note>term: diurnal (daily rotation)</note> motion which I have examined at great length, we still have a little time left to talk...*

**SIMPLICIO:** *Nothing remains for me to say, except that the discourses held this day have indeed seemed to me full of very acute and ingenious thoughts produced on Copernicus's behalf in confirmation of the Earth's motion. However, I do not yet feel persuaded to believe it; because, in the end, the things said conclude nothing more than that the reasons for the Earth's stability are not necessary; but no demonstration has yet been produced for the contrary side which necessarily convinces and concludes its mobility...*

**SALVIATI:** *I have never undertaken, Mr. Simplicio, to remove you from your opinion, nor would I dare to definitively pass judgment on such a great dispute; but it has only been, and will also be in the following disputes, my intention to make manifest to you that...*

# Second Dialogue

*Those who have believed that this extremely rapid twenty-four-hour motion belongs to the Earth alone, and not to the universe (with the sole exception of the Earth), were not convinced that it could or should be so blindly, as they say. Rather, they had very clearly seen, heard, and examined the reasons for the opposing opinion, and had also responded to them with no small effort. **SIMPLICIO.** *The question is so great and so noble that I shall listen to the discussion with great curiosity, assuming that I am to hear everything that can be said on such a subject. I shall then, at my own convenience, reflect more deeply upon what has been heard and what is yet to be heard; and if I gain nothing else, it will be no small thing to be able to discuss these matters with a firmer foundation.*

**SAGREDO.** *Therefore, so as not to tire Mr. Salviati any further, we shall put an end to today’s reasoning, and tomorrow we shall resume our discourses as usual, with the hope of hearing great novelties.*

**SIMPLICIO.** *I am leaving the book on the new stars <note>A reference to the astronomical debates regarding the supernovae of 1572 and 1604.</note> behind, but I am taking back this one on the conclusions, to review what is written there against the annual motion, which must be the subject of tomorrow’s arguments.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap for the letter 'I', featuring elaborate floral and foliate motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

**SAGREDO.** *The great desire with which I have been awaiting your Lordship's arrival, to hear your new thoughts regarding the annual revolution <note>original: "conuersionne annua"</note> of this globe of ours, has made the past night hours seem very long to me, as well as those of this morning. These were not spent idly, however; indeed, I stayed awake for a good part of them retracing in my mind yesterday's arguments, weighing the reasons brought forward by both sides in favor of the two contrary positions: that of Aristotle and Ptolemy, and this one of Aristarchus and Copernicus. Truly, it seems to me that whichever of these men was mistaken deserves to be excused, such are the apparent reasons that may have persuaded them—at least as long as we limit ourselves to those produced by these first, most venerable authors. But since the Peripatetic opinion <note>The "Peripatetics" were followers of Aristotle, who believed the Earth remained stationary at the center of the universe.</note> has had many followers and cultivators due to its antiquity, while the other has had very few—first because of its obscurity and then because of its novelty—I seem to perceive among those many followers, and particularly among the modern ones, some who have introduced other quite childish, if not ridiculous, reasons to support the opinion they deem true.*

<margin>Some, in their reasoning, first fix themselves upon the conclusion they believe, and then adapt their arguments to it.</margin>
**SALVIATI.** *The same has occurred to me, and even more so than to your Lordship, as I have heard some reasons produced that I would be ashamed to repeat—I will not say to avoid blackening the reputation of their authors, whose names can always be kept silent, but so as not to debase the honor of the human race. In my observations, I have finally become certain that there are some men who, reasoning preposterously, first establish the conclusion in their brains; and because it is either their own or belongs to a person of great credit to them, they impress it so firmly that it is entirely impossible to ever eradicate it. Then, regarding those reasons that occur to them or that they hear others bring forward in confirmation of their established concept—however simple and foolish <note>original: "infulse," meaning tasteless or insipid</note> they may be—*

### Third Dialogue

*whatever they may be, they immediately grant their assent and applause; and on the contrary, those ideas which are presented to them in opposition—however ingenious and conclusive they may be—they receive not only with nausea, but with disdain and the bitterest anger. Some of these men, driven by fury, would not be far from attempting any scheme to suppress and silence their adversary; and I myself have seen some experience of this.*

**SAGREDO** *These men, therefore, do not deduce their conclusions from premises, nor do they establish them through reasons; rather, they accommodate—or to put it better, they distort and twist—the premises and reasons to fit their already established and "nailed-down" conclusions. It is not wise, then, to engage with such people; all the less so because dealing with them is not only unpleasant, but even dangerous. Therefore, we shall continue with our Mr. Simplicio, whom I have known for a long time as a man of the highest integrity, and entirely stripped of any malice. Furthermore, he is very well-versed in the Peripatetic doctrine <note>The philosophy of Aristotle and his followers, who were known for walking while teaching.</note>; so I can rest assured that whatever does not occur to him in support of Aristotle's opinion will not easily occur to anyone else. But here he is now, quite out of breath, having made us wait for him a long while today; we were just now speaking ill of you.*

<margin>The movement of the water between the ebb and the flow is not interrupted by rest.</margin>

**SIMPLICIO** *You must not accuse me, but rather blame Neptune <note>The Roman god of the sea, used here as a poetic personification of the tides.</note> for this long delay of mine; for in this morning's ebb, he withdrew the waters in such a manner that the gondola carrying me—having entered a certain canal not far from here where there are no stone embankments—ran aground. I was forced to wait there for more than a full hour for the return of the sea. While staying there, unable to get out of the boat which had run aground almost suddenly, I observed a particular detail that seemed quite marvelous to me: it was that as the waters were falling, they could be seen fleeing away very swiftly through various small rivulets, the mud already being uncovered in many places; and while I was watching this effect, I saw this motion cease all at once, and without any interval of time, the same water began to turn back. The sea changed from retreating to advancing without remaining stationary for even a moment; an effect which, in all the time I have frequented Venice, I have never happened to see before.*

**SAGREDO** *It probably has not happened to you many times to be stranded like that among tiny rivulets; because they have so very little*

### Third Dialogue

*...that I thought I had read the evening before, whether it was truly written there, or if it had been my own ghosts and fantastic imaginings of the night: and in short, I find to my great sorrow that what is written and printed there is indeed true—something I would not have wished for the sake of this philosopher's reputation. That he does not recognize the vanity of his undertaking seems impossible to me; both because it is too obvious, and because I remember hearing him named with praise by our Academic friend <note>The "Academic friend" refers to Galileo himself, the author, who was a member of the Accademia dei Lincei</note>. It also seems too improbable to me that, to please others, he could have been induced to hold his reputation in such low esteem as to publish a work from which he could expect nothing but blame among the intelligent.*

**SAGREDO.** *Add to this, that those [intelligent ones] will be far fewer than one percent compared to those who will celebrate him and exalt him above all the greatest minds that are or ever have been. Here is one who knew how to uphold the Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> unalterability of the Heavens against a host of astronomers, and who, to their greater shame, struck them down with their own weapons! What do you expect four or six people per province—who might spot his shallow arguments—can do against the innumerable many who, being unable to discover or comprehend them, are carried away by the outcry? They applaud him all the more, the less they understand him. Add also, that even those few who do understand will refrain from answering such lowly and inconclusive writings; and this with good reason, because for those who understand there is no need, and for those who do not understand, it is wasted effort.*

**SALVIATI.** *The most fitting punishment for their demerit would truly be silence, were there not other reasons for which it is perhaps almost necessary to speak up. One of these is that we Italians are all being branded as ignorant, giving those from beyond the mountains <note>The "Oltramontani" or "Ultramontanes," referring to scholars in Northern Europe (Protestant lands)</note> cause for laughter—especially those who are separated from our religion. I could show you many famous examples of such men who mock our Academician and all the mathematicians in Italy for having allowed the nonsense of a certain Lorenzini <note>Antonio Lorenzini, who wrote a critique of the astronomical findings regarding the New Star of 1572</note> against the astronomers to be published and maintained without contradiction. But even this could be overlooked compared to another greater occasion for laughter that might be offered to them, stemming from the silence of the learned regarding the follies of such opponents to doctrines they do not understand.*

*SAGREDO. I desire no greater example of the petulance of these men, and of the misfortune of a man like Copernicus <note>Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), who proposed the heliocentric model where the Earth revolves around the Sun.</note>, subjected to being attacked by those who do not even understand his primary position—the very reason they have declared war against him.*

*SALVIATI. You will be no less amazed by the manner in which he refutes the Astronomers who assert that the new stars were higher than the orbits of the planets, and perhaps even in the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the sphere of the fixed stars, the outermost shell of the universe in traditional cosmology.</note> itself.*

*SAGREDO. But how could you have examined this entire book in such a short time? It is a large volume, and the demonstrations must be numerous.*

*SALVIATI. I have focused on these first refutations of his. In these, using twelve demonstrations based on the observations of twelve Astronomers—all of whom judged that the new star of '72 <note>The supernova of 1572, often called Tycho's Nova, which appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia.</note> appearing in Cassiopeia was in the firmament—he attempts to prove the opposite: that it was sublunary <note>term: sublunary (below the moon). In Aristotelian physics, the region below the moon was subject to change and decay, while the heavens above were eternal and unchanging.</note>. He does this by comparing, in pairs, the meridian altitudes taken by different observers in places of different latitudes, proceeding in the manner you will soon hear. And because, in examining this first progression of his, I seem to have discovered that this author is a great distance away from being able to conclude anything against the Astronomers in favor of the Peripatetic philosophers <note>Followers of Aristotle, who maintained that the heavens were immutable and that no "new" stars could be created there.</note>—and that their own opinion is confirmed much more conclusively—I did not wish to apply myself with similar patience to examining his other methods. Instead, I have given them a very superficial glance, certain that the same ineffectiveness found in these first attacks exists in the others. As you will see in practice, very few words are enough to refute this entire work, even though it is constructed with so many laborious calculations, as you see. However, listen to my process. This author, to pierce his adversaries with their own weapons (as I say), takes a great number of observations made by those very men—some 12 or 13 authors in number—and performs his calculations on a portion of them, concluding that such stars were lower than the Moon. Now, because proceeding by interrogation pleases me greatly, and since the author himself is not here, let Mr. Simplicio answer the questions I shall ask as he believes the author would have answered. And assuming we are discussing the aforementioned star of '72 that appeared in Cassiopeia, tell me, Mr. Simplicio, if you believe that it could be located in different places at the same time—that is, to be between...*

# Concerning Galileo.

<margin>
*The minimum and maximum elevations of the new star do not differ from each other more than the Polar altitudes do, if the new star is located in the Firmament.*
</margin>

*And to ensure that even Mr. Simplicio <note>The character in Galileo's dialogue representing the traditional Aristotelian view.</note>, though unskilled in calculations and demonstrations, remains capable of understanding at least the inconclusiveness of this author's proofs, I first put into consideration how both he and all the astronomers with whom he is in controversy agree that the new star was devoid of its own motion, and only circled according to the diurnal motion of the "prime mover" <note>The outermost sphere in the Ptolemaic system that carries the stars.</note>. However, they disagree regarding its location: the latter placing it in the Celestial region—that is, above the Moon, and perhaps among the fixed stars—and the former judging it to be near the Earth, that is, beneath the concavity of the Lunar orb.*

*And because the position of the new star in question was toward the North, and not at a great distance from the Pole—such that for us Northerners it never set—it was an easy thing to be able to take its meridian altitudes with astronomical instruments, both the minimum below the Pole and the maximum above it. From the comparison of these altitudes, taken from different places on Earth located at various distances from the North (that is, differing from each other in their Polar altitudes), one could argue the distance of the star. For if it had been in the firmament among the other fixed stars, its meridian altitudes taken at different Polar elevations would necessarily differ from each other by the same differences found between those elevations. For example, if the elevation of the star above the horizon was 30 degrees when taken in a place where the Polar altitude was, for instance, 45 degrees, it was necessary that the elevation of the same star would have increased by 4 or 5 degrees in those more Northern countries where the Pole was higher by those same 4 or 5 degrees.*

*But if the distance of the star from the Earth were quite small in comparison to that of the Firmament, its meridian altitudes must necessarily increase notably more than the Polar altitudes as we approach the North. And from that greater increase—that is, from the excess of the increase in the star's elevation over the increase in the Polar altitude (which is called the difference of parallax <term>Parallax: the apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different lines of sight</term>)—one promptly calculates, with a clear and certain method, the distance of the star from the center of the Earth. Now, this author takes the observations made by thirteen astronomers at different Polar elevations, and by comparing a small portion of them at his own choosing, he calculates through twelve pairings that the height of the new star was always below the Moon; but he achieves this by...*

### Third Dialogue

**SAGREDO.** *But what does the author say about these? Perhaps he has not considered them?*

**SALVIATI.** *He has considered them only too well; but he says that the observations upon which the calculations render the star infinitely distant are erroneous, and that they cannot be reconciled with one another.*

**SIMPLICIO.** *Oh, this seems to me a weak retreat; because the opposing party could say with equal reason that those observations are erroneous from which he concludes the star to have been in the elementary region.* <note>The "elementary region" refers to the area below the moon, where Aristotle believed all change and decay occurred.</note>

**SALVIATI.** *Oh, Mr. Simplicio, if I should succeed in making you understand the artifice—though it is not a very sophisticated artifice—of this author, I would wish to rouse your wonder, and even your indignation, when you perceive how he, cloaking his cunning with the veil of your simplicity and that of other pure philosophers, wishes to insinuate himself into your grace by scratching your ears and inflating your ambition, showing that he has convinced and silenced these "little astronomers" <note>original: "Astronometti"</note> who wanted to assault the impregnable unalterability of the Peripatetic Heaven <note>The "Peripatetic Heaven" refers to the Aristotelian view that the heavens are perfect and unchanging.</note>, and what is more, silenced and convinced them with their own weapons. I will make every effort to do so; and meanwhile, let Mr. Sagredo pardon Mr. Simplicio and me for perhaps boring him a bit too much, while with an excessive circuit of words (excessive, I say, for his very rapid apprehension) I go about trying to make clear a thing that it is well should not remain hidden or unknown to him.*

**SAGREDO.** *I shall listen to your discourse not only without boredom, but with pleasure; and I wish all the Peripatetic philosophers could be present, so that they might understand how much they ought to remain obliged to this protector of theirs.*

**SALVIATI.** *Tell me, Mr. Simplicio, if you have fully understood how—the new star being placed on the meridian circle there toward the North—to one who traveled from the south toward the North, that same new star would rise above the horizon just as much as the Pole does, provided that it were truly placed among the fixed stars; but, if it were notably lower, that is, closer to the earth, it would appear to rise more than the said Pole; and always more so, the greater the proximity?*

**SIMPLICIO.** *I believe I understand it perfectly, in sign of which I will try to make a mathematical figure of it; and in this large circle I will mark the Pole P, and in these two lower circles I will mark two stars seen from a point on the earth, which shall be A, and let the two stars be—*

...not these *B* and *C* seen along the same line *ABC* in front of a fixed star *D*. Then, traveling on the earth as far as the point *E*, the two stars will appear to me separated from the fixed star *D* and moved closer to the Pole *P*. The lower one, *B*, will appear to have moved more, appearing to me at *G*, and the one at *C* less, appearing at *F*; but the fixed star *D* will have maintained the same distance from the Pole.

*SALV.* I see that you understand very well. I believe you also comprehend how, because star *B* is lower than *C*, the angle formed by the rays of sight which, starting from the two places *A* and *E*, join at *C*—that is, this angle *ACE*—is narrower, or we might say more acute, than the angle formed at *B* by the rays *AB* and *EB*.

*SIMP.* It is very clearly seen by the senses.

*SALV.* And also, because the earth is very small and almost imperceptible <note>original: "insensibile"</note> compared to the firmament, and consequently because the space *AE* that one can travel on earth is very short in comparison to the immense length of the lines *EG* and *EF* from the earth to the firmament, you come to understand that the star *C* could be raised and distanced so very far from the earth that the angle formed in it by the rays starting from the same points *A* and *E* would become extremely acute, and as if absolutely imperceptible and null.

*SIMP.* This too I understand perfectly.

*SALV.* Now know, Mr. Simplicio, that astronomers and mathematicians have found infallible rules by way of Geometry and Arithmetic to be able—by means of the size of these angles *B* and *C* and their differences, adding to this the knowledge of the distance between the two places *A* and *E*—to find to within a span <note>A "palmo" or span was a traditional unit of measurement; here it implies great precision.</note> the distance of sublime things; provided, however, that the said distance and said angles are taken accurately.
