### Third Dialogue

**SIMPLICIUS.** *So, if the rules derived from Geometry and Arithmetic are correct, then all the fallacies and errors encountered when trying to investigate the heights of new stars <note>The "new star" refers to the Supernova of 1572 or 1604, which challenged the Aristotelian idea of an unchanging heaven.</note>, or comets, or other things, must depend on the distance A. E. and on the angles B. C. not being well measured. Thus, all those discrepancies seen in these twelve investigations depend not on defects in the calculation rules, but on errors committed in investigating those angles and distances through instrumental observations.*

**SALVIATI.** *That is so, and there is no difficulty at all in this. Now it is necessary that you note carefully how, in moving the star further away from B to C, whereby the angle becomes ever more acute, the ray EBG continuously moves away from the ray ABD on the side below the angle; as shown by the line EGF, whose lower part EC is more remote from the part AC than EB is. But it can never happen that, by any immense distance, the lines AD and EF totally disconnect, as they must finally go to join at the star: one could only say they separated and were reduced to being parallel if the distance were infinite, a case which cannot occur. But because (note well) the distance of the Firmament <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note>, in relation to the smallness of the earth, as has already been said, is considered as infinite; therefore the angle contained by the rays which, drawn from points A and E, terminate in a fixed star, is estimated as null, and those rays as two parallel lines. Therefore, one concludes that it can only be affirmed that the new star was in the Firmament when, from the collation of observations made in different places, one gathers by calculation that the said angle is imperceptible and the lines are as if parallel. But when the angle is of a notable quantity, the new star must necessarily be lower than the fixed stars—and even lower than the Moon, provided that the angle ABE were greater than that which would be formed at the center of the Moon.*

**SIMPLICIUS.** *Then the distance of the Moon is not so great that such an angle remains imperceptible in her case?*

**SALVIATI.** *No, sir; on the contrary, it is perceptible not only in the Moon, but in the Sun as well.*

**SIMPLICIUS.** *But if this is so, it could also be that such an angle is observable in the new star without it being lower than the Sun, let alone the Moon.*

<summary>Salviati explains the concept of parallax, arguing that while fixed stars are so distant their light rays appear parallel, the distance of a "new star" or comet can be determined by measuring the angle of observation from different points on Earth.</summary>

From the things declared so far, I believe you are quite capable of understanding how the distance of the new star can never be made so immense that the oft-mentioned angle entirely vanishes, and that the two rays from the observers at locations **A** and **E** become parallel lines: and consequently, to understand perfectly that if the calculation should show from the observations that such an angle is totally null, or the lines are truly parallel, we would be certain the observations were, at the very least, slightly erroneous. But, when the calculation shows us those same lines have separated not only to the point of equidistance—that is, to being parallel—but have passed beyond that limit and have widened more at the top than at the bottom, then one must resolutely conclude the observations were made with less accuracy, and in short, are mistaken; as they lead us to a manifest impossibility. You must then believe me, and know as a most certain truth, that two straight lines departing from two points marked upon another straight line are wider at the top than at the bottom when the angles contained within them above that line are greater than two right angles: and when these are equal to two right angles, those lines would be parallel; but if they were less than two right angles, the lines would be converging, and if extended, would undoubtedly form a triangle.

SIMP. Wherefore, by widening the lines **A.B.** and **E.B.** (while keeping them fixed at the points...

# On Galileo.

*...this other note, where I record many other combinations. I believe this to be absolutely necessary; because there being four observations in number that serve for a single investigation—namely, two different altitudes of the Pole <note>The celestial pole, used to determine latitude</note>, and two different elevations of the star, made by different observers, in different places, and with different instruments—anyone who has any knowledge of such practice will say it is impossible that among all four some error has not occurred. <margin>Astronomical instruments are easily subject to error.</margin>

**SIMPLICIO.** *It cannot be that he regards them as anything but very cautious and intelligent; because if he esteemed them inept at such exercise, he might as well banish his own book as concluding nothing, being founded upon suppositions full of errors; and he would be selling us for too simple-minded if he believed he could persuade us of a false proposition of his through their inexperience.*

**SALVIATI.** *Therefore, since these observers are such as they are, and yet for all that they have erred, and it is thus necessary to amend their errors in order to extract from their observations as much knowledge as possible, it is fitting that we apply to them the smallest and closest amendments and corrections possible; provided they suffice to bring the observations from impossibility to possibility. So that, for example, if one can temper a manifest error and a patent impossibility in one of their observations by adding or subtracting 2 or 3 minutes, and with such an amendment reduce it to the possible, one should not wish to adjust it with the addition or subtraction of 15, 20, or 50.*

**SIMPLICIO.** *I do not believe the author would contradict this; because, granted that they are judicious and expert men, one must believe rather that they have erred by a little than by a lot.*

### Third Dialogue

SALV. *Now note what follows. Of the locations where the new star might be placed, some are manifestly impossible, and others are possible. It is absolutely impossible that it was at an infinite distance above the fixed stars, because such a place does not exist in the world; and had the star been placed there, it would have been invisible to us. It is also impossible that it went creeping along the surface of the earth, and even more so that it was inside the terrestrial globe itself. Possible locations are those which are currently under controversy, as it does not repugn our intellect that a visible object, appearing as a star, could be above the Moon no less than below it. Now, while one seeks to determine through observations and calculations—made with that certainty to which human diligence can arrive—what its true place was, one finds that the majority of these calculations render it more than an infinitely high interval above the Firmament <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note>; others render it close to the surface of the earth, and some even below said surface. Of the others, which place it in locations that are not impossible, none agree among themselves. Thus, it must be said that all the observations are necessarily fallacious; so that, if we wish to gather any fruit from so many labors, we must resort to corrections, amending all the observations.*

SIMP. *But the author will say that of the observations which place the star in impossible locations, no account should be taken, as they are infinitely erroneous and fallacious; and one should only accept those that place it in possible locations. Among these alone, one should search—by way of the most probable and numerous coincidences—to discover, if not the particular and exact site (that is, its true distance from the center of the earth), at least the knowledge of whether it was among the elements <note>The sublunary sphere: earth, water, air, fire</note> or indeed among the Celestial bodies.*

SALV. *The argument you make now is the very same that the author has made in favor of his cause, but with too unreasonable a disadvantage to the opposing side. I shall speak for them, and you shall answer for the author. ### Third Dialogue

*that the star is infinite, it would be necessary for the error in observation to have been infinite, and therefore uncorrectable, and as such, rejectable; but the business,* my Mr. Simplicio, *does not work that way. Regarding your failure to understand how this matter stands, I excuse you as one inexperienced in such dealings; but I cannot, under such a cloak, palliate the error of the author. He, by concealing the understanding of this—persuading himself that we truly would not understand it—hoped to make use of our ignorance to further credit his doctrine among the multitude of the little-informed. However, as a warning to those who are more credulous than understanding, and to lead you out of error, know that it can happen (and most often will happen) that an observation which places the star, for example, at the distance of Saturn, might—by adding or subtracting a single minute <note>A minute is 1/60th of a degree of arc.</note> from the elevation taken with the instrument—make it become infinitely distant, and therefore turn the possible into the impossible. Conversely, those calculations built upon such observations that yield an infinitely distant star can often, by adding or subtracting a single minute, pull it back into a possible location. And what I say of a minute can also happen with a correction of a half, or a sixth, or even less.*

*Now, fix this well in your mind: that at very high distances, such as, for example, the height of Saturn or that of the fixed stars, the smallest errors made by the observer upon the instrument render a determined and possible location infinite and impossible. This does not happen with sublunary <note>Below the moon; the region of the universe traditionally thought to be subject to change.</note> distances close to the Earth, where it may happen that an observation from which it was gathered that the star was distant, for example, 4 terrestrial semidiameters <note>The radius of the Earth.</note>, could be increased or decreased not just by one minute, but by ten, or a hundred, or many more, without the calculation rendering it even infinitely remote, nor even higher than the Moon. Understand from this that the magnitude of the (so to speak) instrumental errors is not to be judged by the outcome of the calculation, but by the actual quantity of degrees and minutes numbered upon the instrument. Those observations ought to be called more accurate, or less erroneous, which—with the addition or subtraction of fewer minutes—restore the star to a possible place; and among the possible places, one must believe the true location was that around which the greatest number of distances, calculated from the most accurate observations, coincide.*

I resolve the matter in this way. ### On Galileo.

*...the angle BCD, the difference in parallax <note>Parallax is the apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different points; here used to calculate celestial distance.</note>. And because the angle BAD, contained between the vertical lines, is equal to the distance between the polar altitudes <note>The difference in latitude between two observation points.</note>, it will be 4 degrees and 40 first minutes; and I note it here to the side. From this, I find the chord from the table of arcs and chords; and I note it next, which is 8,142 parts, of which the semidiameter <term>semidiameter: the radius of the Earth</term> AB is 100,000. I then easily find the angle BDC, because half of the angle BAD, which is 2 degrees and 20 first minutes, added to a right angle <note>90 degrees</note>, gives the angle BDF as 92 degrees and 20 first minutes. By adding to this the angle CDF, which is the distance from the zenith <note>The point directly overhead</note> of the star's greatest altitude, which here is 62 degrees and 25 first minutes, it gives us the quantity of the angle BDC as 154 degrees and 45 first minutes. I note this along with its sine, taken from the table, which is 42,657; and below this, I note the angle of the parallax BCD as 0 degrees and 2 first minutes, with its sine being 58.*

*And because in the triangle BCD, the side DB is to the side BC as the sine of the opposite angle BCD is to the sine of the opposite angle BDC; therefore, if the line BD were 58, BC would be 42,657. And because the chord DB is 8,142 (of which the semidiameter BA is 100,000) and we seek to know how many of those same parts BC is, we shall say by the golden rule <term>golden rule: the rule of three, a method to find a fourth value from three known ratios</term>: if when BD is 58, BC is 42,657, then when the same DB were 8,142, what would BC be? Therefore, I multiply the second term by the third, which gives me 347,313,294; this must be divided by the first, that is, by 58. The quotient would be the number of parts of the line BC, of which the semidiameter AB is 100,000. To know how many semidiameters BA the same line BC contains, it would be necessary to divide the same found quotient again by 100,000; and we would have the number of semidiameters contained in BC. Now, the number 347,313,294 divided by 58 gives 5,988,160 1/4, as seen here:*

These, as you see, are five investigations which place the star far above the Moon; here I want you to reflect upon that particular point I mentioned to you a moment ago: namely, that at great distances, the alteration—or let us say the correction—of a very few minutes moves the star across <term>vast spaces</term> <note>original: "gradiss.mi spazij"</note>. For example, in the first of these investigations, where the calculation rendered the star 60 semi-diameters distant from the center with a <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different points; used here to calculate distance.</note> of 2 minutes; if one wished to maintain that it was in the Firmament <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note>, one has only to correct the observations by 2 minutes, or even less, because then the parallax ceases, or becomes so small that it renders the star at an immense distance, such as the Firmament is accepted by everyone to be. In the second investigation, an amendment of less than 4 prime minutes does the same. In the third and fourth, just as in the first, a mere two minutes replaces the star even above the fixed stars. In the preceding one, a quarter of a minute—that is, 15 seconds—gives us the same result. But this will not happen in the sublunary heights <note>The region below the Moon, traditionally considered the realm of change and decay.</note>; for, imagine whatever distance you please, and try to correct the investigations made by the author and adjust them so that they all correspond to the same determined distance, and you will see how much larger the amendments you must make will need to be.

**SAGREDO:** It would be nothing but good for our full understanding to see some example of what you say.

**SALVIATI:** Establish at your own pleasure whatever determined sublunary distance you wish to place the Star, and with little trouble we can see for ourselves if corrections—similar to those we have seen suffice to return it to the fixed stars—will bring it to the place you have established.

### Third Dialogue

**SAGR.** To take the most favorable distance for the author, let us assume it is the greatest of all those investigated by him in his twelve inquiries; for while there is a controversy between the astronomers and him—the former saying the star was above the Moon and the latter below—any small distance that he proves it to have been below gives him the victory.

**SALV.** Let us take, then, the seventh inquiry made based on the observations of Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe, the famous Danish astronomer</note> and Thaddaeus Hagecius, through which the author finds the star to have been 32 semidiameters <note>A semidiameter is the radius of the Earth, used here as a unit of astronomical distance</note> away from the center [of the Earth]. This location is the most favorable for his side. And to give him every advantage, I want us to place it at the most unfavorable distance for the astronomers, which is to locate it even above the Firmament <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note>. This being established, let us go searching for what corrections would be necessary to apply to his other eleven inquiries so that they might elevate the star to the distance of 32 semidiameters. And let us begin with the first, calculated based on the observations of Hainzel and Maurolico: in which the author finds the distance from the center to be about 3 semidiameters, with a parallax of 4 degrees, 42 minutes, and 30 seconds. Let us see now if, by reducing it to only 20 minutes, it rises up to 32 semidiameters. Here is the very brief and exact operation: I multiply the sine of the Angle BDC by the sine of the chord.

BD. and I divide the result, having removed the last 5 figures, by the sine of the Parallax <note>The "last 5 figures" refers to the decimal shift used in early modern trigonometric calculations</note>; the result is 28 and a half semidiameters <note>A semidiameter is a terrestrial radius, the standard unit for measuring celestial distances at the time</note>. *That which the author then adds in amendment of the observations—namely, that it is not enough to withdraw the difference of the Parallax, neither by a single minute, nor even by the eighth part of 1 minute—is true. But I say that not even the tenth part of 1 minute will reduce the height of the star to 32 semi-diameters, because the sine of the tenth part of 1 minute (that is, of 6 seconds) is 3, by which, if in our rule we divide 90, or let us say, if we divide 9,058,672 by 300,000, the result will be 30 and 58672/100000, which is to say a little more than 30 and a half semi-diameters.*

### Third Dialogue

*From this, it can be seen (as I have noted previously) that if the author were to establish the distance of 32 Earth radii <note>The author uses "semidiameters," a standard Renaissance unit for measuring celestial distances relative to Earth's size.</note> as the true location of the New Star, the correction required for his other 10 investigations would be immense. I say 10, because the second investigation, being quite high, can be reduced to the height of 32 radii with a correction of only 2 minutes of a degree. However, to make all of them place the star at that distance, one would require a reduction of Parallaxes <term>Parallax: the apparent displacement of an object when viewed from different positions; used here to calculate distance.</term> such that the total subtractions would amount to more than 756 minutes. In contrast, for the 5 investigations calculated by me—which place the Star above the Moon—to correct them so that they place it in the Firmament <note>The "Firmament" refers to the sphere of the fixed stars, the most distant part of the Aristotelian universe.</note>, a correction of only 10 and a quarter minutes is sufficient.*

Now add to these another 5 investigations which place the star precisely in the Firmament without the need for any correction at all; thus, we will have 10 investigations in agreement that place it in the Firmament, requiring a correction for only 5 of them (as has been seen) of 10 and a quarter minutes. Whereas, for the correction of the author's other 10 investigations to reduce them to a height of 32 radii, you would need amendments of 756 minutes out of 836. That is, one must subtract 756 from a total of 836 to make the star rise to the height of 32 radii—and even that correction is not enough.

The investigations which immediately, without further correction, place the star without Parallax—and therefore in the Firmament, and even in the most remote parts of it, and in short as high as the Pole itself—are these 5 noted here.

Regarding the rest of the pairings that can be made from the observations of all these astronomers, those that place the star at an infinitely high distance are many more in number—specifically about 30 more—than the others which, through calculation, place the star below the Moon. And because (as we have agreed) it is to be believed that the observers likely erred by a small amount rather than a large one, it is a manifest thing that the corrections to be applied to the observations—which place the star at an infinite height—in order to bring it back down, will lead it into the Firmament <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note> sooner and with less amendment than they would lead it below the Moon. Thus, all of these support the opinion of those who place it among the fixed stars. Add to this that the corrections required for such amendments are much smaller than those by which the star could be reduced from an improbable proximity to the height most favorable for this author, as has been seen in the past examples. Among these impossible proximities, there are three that seem to remove the star from the center of the earth by a distance less than a semi-diameter <note>The Earth's radius</note>, making it in a certain way revolve underground; and these are those combinations in which, the Polar altitude of one of the observers being greater than the Polar altitude of the other, the elevation of the star taken by the former is less than the elevation of the star taken by the latter. And such combinations are those noted here below.

This first one is of the Landgrave <note>Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel</note> with Gemma <note>Cornelius Gemma</note>; where the Polar altitude of the Landgrave, 51 degrees 18 minutes, is greater than the Polar altitude of Gemma, which is 50 degrees 50 minutes; but the altitude of the star for the Landgrave, 79 degrees 30 minutes, is less than that of the star for Gemma, 79 degrees 45 minutes.

<meta>Catchword: The others</meta>

*The observation of Munofio <note>Original: "Munofio," likely referring to the astronomer Michael Maestlin</note> gives no Parallax <term>Parallax: the apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different lines of sight; used here to determine distance from Earth</term>, and therefore places the new star among the highest fixed stars: that of Ainzelio <note>Original: "Ainzelio," referring to Paul Hainzel</note> places it at an infinite distance, but with a correction of half a minute, it is restored among the fixed stars: and the same is drawn from Ursino <note>Original: "Ursino," referring to Nicolaus Reimers Ursus</note>, with a correction of 12 minutes. **SAGREDO.** *But what defense does he find against such obvious contradictions?*

**SALVIATI.** *One of those weakest threads: saying that the Parallaxes are diminished thanks to refractions <term>Refraction: the bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere, which can make celestial objects appear higher than they actually are</term>, which, acting in opposition, elevate the phenomenon where the Parallaxes lower it. Now, judge for yourself how much this miserable refuge is worth, given that even if this effect of refractions were as effective as some Astronomers have recently introduced, the most it could do regarding raising a phenomenon above the Horizon more than is true—while it is already 23 or 24 degrees high—would be to diminish it by about 3 minutes of Parallax. This adjustment is far too small to pull the star below the Moon, and in some cases, it is less than the advantage we granted in admitting that the excess of the lower distance from the Pole over the upper distance is entirely Parallax. This advantage is something much clearer and more palpable than the effect of refraction, the magnitude of which I doubt, and not without reason. But furthermore, I ask this author if he believes that those Astronomers, whose observations he uses, had knowledge of these effects of refractions and took them into consideration or not: if they knew and considered them, it is reasonable to believe that they took them into account when assigning the true elevations of the star, making those deductions from the degrees of height seen on the instruments that were appropriate due to the alterations.*

calculations of refractions; so that the distances pronounced by them would then be the corrected and true ones, and not the apparent and false ones. But if he believes that such authors did not reflect upon the said refractions, it must be confessed that they have likewise erred in determining all those things which cannot be perfectly adjusted without the modification of refractions; among which things is the precise investigation of the polar altitudes <note>The latitude of the observer, determined by the height of the celestial pole above the horizon.</note>, which are commonly taken from the two Meridian altitudes of any of the fixed stars that are always visible <note>Circumpolar stars that do not set below the horizon.</note>. These altitudes will be altered by refraction in exactly the same way as those of the new star; such that the polar altitude deduced from them will be defective, and share in the same lack that this author ascribes to the altitudes assigned to the new star; that is, both the former and the latter being placed, with equal error, higher than the truth. 

But such an error, as far as it pertains to our present business, does not prejudice it at all: because we have no need to know anything else but the difference between the two distances of the new star from the Pole, while it was below it and then above it. It is a clear thing that such distances will be the same, whether the alteration of refraction is applied commonly to the star and to the Pole, or commonly amended for both. The author's argument would have some weight, though very weak, if he had assured us that the altitude of the Pole had been assigned precisely and amended from the error depending on refraction, from which the same Astronomers <note>Referring to observers like Tycho Brahe.</note> had then not guarded themselves in assigning us the altitudes of the new star; but he has not made us sure of this, nor perhaps could he, nor perhaps (and this is more credible) was such caution neglected by the observers.

Since the observation cannot place the center of the pupil of the eye exactly at the center of the <term>sextant</term><note>An astronomical instrument used to measure the angular distance between two objects.</note> (the instrument used in observing the intervals between two stars), but keeps it elevated above said center by the distance of that pupil from some bone in the cheek where the head of the instrument rests, an angle is formed in the eye more acute than that formed by the sides of the sextant. This angle of the rays also differs from itself when looking at stars slightly elevated above the <term>Horizon</term> compared to those same stars placed at a great height. This angle becomes different as the instrument is raised while keeping the head still; but if, in raising the sextant, one were to bend the neck back and raise the head along with the instrument, the angle would then remain the same. ...through which the ray of the eye is made to pass; this eye is also held at a distance from the instrument of a palm, or two, or even more. With these excuses, he persuades himself to make us believe he has compensated for that difference which amounts to more than a hundred minutes. I speak of the fact that no notable diversity was observed in the distances between a fixed star and the New Star <note>The supernova of 1572</note> throughout their entire circulation. If that star had been as close as the Moon, the variation should have been greatly conspicuous even to the naked eye, without any instrument at all—especially when comparing it with the eleventh star of Cassiopeia, its neighbor at one and a half degrees; the distance should have varied by more than two diameters of the Moon, as the most intelligent astronomers of those times well noted.

**SAGREDO:** I seem to see that unhappy farmer who, after all his expected harvests have been beaten down and destroyed by the storm, goes about with a languid and bowed face, gleaning relics so meager that they would not suffice to feed even a chick for a single day.

**SALVIATI:** Truly, this author has risen against the challengers of the Inalterability of the Heavens <note>The Aristotelian doctrine that the heavens are perfect and unchanging</note> with too meager a provision of arms; and with too fragile a chain has he attempted to pull the New Star of Cassiopeia down from the highest regions into these low, elementary ones. And because it seems to me that the great difference between the motives of those astronomers and this, their opponent, has been clearly demonstrated, it will be well for us to leave this part aside and return to our principal matter. In this follows the consideration of the annual motion commonly attributed to the Sun, but then—first by Aristarchus of Samos <note>An ancient Greek astronomer who first proposed a heliocentric model</note> and later by Copernicus—taken from the Sun and transferred to the Earth. I hear Mr. Simplicio coming vigorously provided against this position, particularly with the rapier and shield of the booklet of "Mathematical Conclusions or Disquisitions" <note>Referring to a work by Locher/Scheiner attacking Copernicanism</note>, the objections of which it would be well to begin proposing.

**SIMPLICIO:** I wish, if it pleases you, to reserve them for last, as they are the most recently discovered.

# Third Dialogue

**SALVIATI.** It will therefore be necessary, following the method we have held until now, that you proceed in an orderly fashion by proposing the contrary arguments, both those of Aristotle and of other ancients; I shall do the same, so that nothing remains behind without being carefully considered and examined. Likewise, Mr. Sagredo, with the vivacity of his wit, will bring forth his thoughts as he feels them awakened.

**SAGREDO.** I shall do so with my usual freedom; and because you so command it, you will also be obliged to excuse it.

**SALVIATI.** The favor will oblige me to thank you, not to excuse you. But let Mr. Simplicio now begin to raise those difficulties which prevent him from being able to believe that the Earth, like the other planets, can move in a circle around a stable center.

**SIMPLICIO.** The first and greatest difficulty is the repugnance and incompatibility between being in the center and being far from it. For, if the terrestrial globe must move in one year along the circumference of a circle—that is, beneath the Zodiac—it is impossible that at the same time it could be in the center of the Zodiac. Yet, that the Earth is in such a center is proved in many ways by Aristotle, by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer who formalized the geocentric (Earth-centered) model.</note>, and by others.

**SALVIATI.** You argue very well; there is no doubt that whoever wishes to make the Earth move along the circumference of a circle must first prove that it is not in the center of that same circle. It follows, then, that we should see whether the Earth is or is not in that center around which I say it revolves, and where you say it is placed. But before this, it is also necessary that we clarify whether you and I have the same concept of this center. Therefore, tell me what and where this intended center of yours is.

**SIMPLICIO.** I understand the center to be that of the universe, that of the world, that of the starry sphere, that of the Heavens.

<margin>It has not yet been proven by anyone whether the World is finite or infinite.</margin>
**SALVIATI.** Although I could quite reasonably dispute with you whether such a center exists in nature—seeing as neither you nor anyone else has ever proven whether the world is finite and shaped, or rather infinite and boundless—nevertheless, granting you for now that it is finite, terminated in a spherical figure, and therefore possesses its center, it will be necessary to see how credible it is that the Earth, rather than some other body, is found in that very center.

**SIMPLICIO.** That the world is finite, terminated, and spherical is proven by Aristotle with a hundred demonstrations.

# Of Galileo.
### 317

<margin>Aristotle's demonstrations to prove that the universe is finite all fail if one denies that it is mobile.</margin>
SALVIATI. *Which are then all reduced to a single one, and that single one to nothing; because if I deny him his assumption—namely, that the universe is mobile—all his demonstrations fail, because he only proves that to be finite and bounded which belongs to the universe that is mobile. But in order not to multiply disputes, let it be granted for now that the world is finite, spherical, and has its center. And since such a shape and center have been argued from its mobility, it will be nothing but very reasonable if, from the same circular movements of the worldly bodies, we proceed to the particular investigation of the proper location of such a center. Indeed, Aristotle himself reasoned and determined in the same manner, making the center of the universe that very point around which all the Celestial spheres revolve, and in which he believed the terrestrial globe to be placed. Now tell me, Mr. Simplicio, if Aristotle found himself constrained by the most evident experiences to partially change this arrangement and order of the universe, and to confess to having been mistaken in one of these two propositions—that is, either in placing the earth in the center, or in saying that the Celestial spheres moved around such a center—which of the two confessions do you believe he would choose?*

<margin>Aristotle makes the center of the universe that point around which all the celestial spheres revolve.</margin>
SIMPLICIO. *I believe that if the case should happen, the Peripatetics* <note>The followers of Aristotle's philosophy, often criticized by Galileo for their rigid adherence to his texts over observation.</note>

SALVIATI. *I am not asking about the Peripatetics; I am asking about Aristotle himself. As for the former, I know very well what they would answer; they, as most reverent and humble slaves of Aristotle, would deny all the experiences and all the observations in the world, and would even refuse to see them so as not to have to confess them, and would say that the world stands as Aristotle wrote, and not as nature wills; for having taken away the support of that authority, with what would you have them appear in the field? And therefore, tell me instead what you estimate Aristotle himself would do.*

SIMPLICIO. *Truly, I would not know how to decide which of the two inconveniences he would repute to be the lesser.*

SALVIATI. *Please do not use this term "inconvenience" for what might necessarily be so. It was an inconvenience to want to place the earth in the center of the celestial revolutions; but since you do not know which way he would be inclined, and I esteeming him a man of great genius, let us go on examining which of the two choices is the more reasonable, and let us repute that one to be the one received by Aristotle. Resuming then our reasoning from the beginning, and granted for the sake of Aristotle...*

### Third Dialogue

*...of Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE), the Greek philosopher whose geocentric views Salviati is challenging.</note> that the world (of whose size we have no sensory knowledge beyond the fixed stars), being of spherical shape and moving circularly, must necessarily have a center, both in respect to its shape and its motion. Being certain, moreover, that within the starry sphere there are many orbs, one inside the other with their stars, which also move circularly, we seek to find what is more reasonable to believe and to say: that these contained orbs move around the same center of the world, or rather around another center quite far from it? <margin>It is more fitting that the container and the contained move around the same center rather than different ones.</margin>
**SIMPLICIO:** *If we could stop at this single presupposition, and were sure of not encountering something else that might disturb us, I would say that it would be much more reasonable to say that the container and the contained parts all moved about a common center rather than different ones.*

<margin>If the center of the world is the same as that around which the planets move, the Sun, and not the Earth, is located in it.</margin>
**SALVIATI:** *Now, if it be true that the center of the world is the same as that around which the orbs of the worldly bodies—that is, the planets—move, it is a most certain thing that not the Earth, but rather the Sun is found located in the center of the world. So that, as far as this first simple and general apprehension is concerned, the middle place belongs to the Sun, and the Earth is found as remote from the center as it is from the Sun itself.*

**SIMPLICIO:** *But by what do you argue that not the Earth, but the Sun, is at the center of the revolutions of the planets?*

<margin>Observations from which it is gathered that the Sun, and not the Earth, is at the center of the celestial revolutions.</margin>
**SALVIATI:** *This is concluded from most evident and therefore necessarily conclusive observations. The most palpable of these, for excluding the Earth from such a center and placing the Sun there, is finding all the planets now closer and now farther from the Earth, with differences so great that, for example, Venus at its farthest is found six times more remote from us than when it is at its closest, and Mars rises almost eight times higher in one state than in another. See, meanwhile, if Aristotle was mistaken by just a little in believing that they were always equally remote from us.*

**SIMPLICIO:** *What then are the indications that their movements are around the Sun?*

**SALVIATI:** *One argues this in the three superior planets—Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—from their being always closest to the Earth when they are in opposition <note>term: opposition; when a planet is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun.</note> to the Sun, and farthest when they are toward conjunction <note>term: conjunction; when a planet is in the same direction as the Sun from the Earth's perspective.</note>, and this approaching and drawing away...*

### Third Dialogue

<margin>If the annual motion is given to the earth, it is necessary to assign the diurnal motion to it as well.</margin>
the movement of one year, leaving the Sun at rest. And if this were the case, it follows by necessary consequence that the diurnal <note>daily</note> motion also belongs to the earth; because if the Sun stood still and the earth did not revolve upon itself, but only had the annual movement around the Sun, our year would be nothing more than one day and one night—that is, six months of day and six months of night, as has been said elsewhere. See then how gracefully that most headlong motion of 24 hours is removed from the universe, and how the fixed stars, which are so many Suns conforming to our own Sun, enjoy a perpetual rest. See, furthermore, what ease is found in this first sketch for giving the reasons for such great appearances in the celestial bodies.

**SAGREDO:** I perceive it very well; but just as you gather great probability for the truth of such a system from this simplicity, others perhaps, on the contrary, might make opposite deductions. They might doubt, not without reason, how such a constitution—being most ancient among the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras who proposed a non-geocentric universe</note> and so well-suited to the appearances—has had so few followers over the progress of thousands of years, and was rejected by **Aristotle** himself, and even after **Copernicus**, continues to meet the same fortune.

<margin>Arguments more than childish, yet sufficient to keep the simple-minded in the opinion of the earth's stability.</margin>
**SALVIATI:** If you, Mr. Sagredo, had occasionally stumbled—as I have many, many times—upon hearing what sort of follies are sufficient to make the common people stubborn and unpersuadable in even lending an ear, let alone their assent, to these novelties, I believe your wonder at finding so few followers of this opinion would greatly diminish. In my view, little esteem should be given to brains for whom a "most conclusive" demonstration to keep them fixed in the immobility of the earth is seeing that they will not be at dinner in **Constantinople** this morning, nor at supper in **Japan** tonight; and who are certain that the earth, being so very heavy, cannot climb up above the Sun and then headlong drop down below. Of such people, whose number is infinite, we need not take account, nor record their nonsense, nor seek to gain the company of men in whose definition only the *genus* <note>the general category of "animal"</note> enters and the *difference* <note>the specific trait of "rationality"</note> is missing, to have them as companions in most subtle and delicate opinions. Furthermore, what gain would you ever expect to make with all the demonstrations in the world upon brains so stolid that they are not sufficient by themselves to recognize their own extreme follies? # Of the Galileos.

<margin>It is shown how improbable the opinion of Copernicus is.</margin>
<margin>Reason and discourse in Aristarchus and Copernicus prevail over manifest sense.</margin>
From your wonder, you marvel that there are so few followers of the opinion of the <term>Pythagoreans</term><note>Followers of Pythagoras, who some believed held the view that the Earth moves.</note>; and I am astonished how anyone has ever been found until now who has embraced and followed it. We have already seen that the reasons against the diurnal rotation of the Earth, which you have already examined, have a very great appearance of truth; and the fact that the <term>Ptolemaics</term><note>Followers of Ptolemy, who placed the Earth at the center of the universe.</note>, the <term>Aristotelians</term>, and all their followers received them as most conclusive is a very great argument for their efficacy. **SAGREDO:** Are we then to have other vigorous conflicts against this annual movement as well?

**SALVIATI:** We are; and so evident and sensible that if a superior and more excellent sense than the common and natural ones had not accompanied reason, I greatly doubt that I too would have been much more reluctant toward the Copernican system than I have been since a clearer lamp than the usual one has given me light.

# On Galileo

<margin>Response to the first three objections against the Copernican system.</margin>
*...of others, which appear contrary to this position. Now, coming to the explanations and responses to the three very serious objections mentioned, I say that the first two not only do not oppose the Copernican system <note>The heliocentric model where the Earth revolves around the Sun</note>, but greatly and absolutely favor it; because both Mars and Venus show themselves to be unequal to themselves <note>meaning they change in apparent size</note> according to the assigned proportions; and Venus, when below the Sun, appears crescent-shaped, and changes its phases punctually in the same manner as the Moon.*

**SAGREDO:** *But how was this hidden from Copernicus, yet manifest to you?*

**SALVIATI:** *These things cannot be understood except through the sense of sight, which by nature was not granted to men so perfect that it could arrive at discerning such differences; indeed, the very instrument of seeing brings impediment to itself. But after it pleased God in our age to grant to human ingenuity such a marvelous invention as to be able to perfect our vision by multiplying it 4, 6, 10, 20, 30, and 40 times, infinite objects—which either because of their distance or their extreme smallness were invisible to us—have been made highly visible by means of the Telescope <term>Telescopio: Galileo's "spyglass" which revolutionized 17th-century astronomy</term>.*

**SAGREDO:** *But Venus and Mars are not among the objects invisible due to their distance or smallness; rather, we perceive them with simple natural sight. Why, then, do we not distinguish the differences in their sizes and shapes?*

<margin>Reason why it happens that Venus and Mars do not appear to us to vary in size as much as they should.</margin>
**SALVIATI:** *In this, the impediment of our own eye plays a large part, as I have just hinted to you. By the eye, shining and distant objects are not represented to us simple and pure; rather, it presents them to us garlanded with adventitious <note>accidental or external</note> and foreign rays, so long and thick that their naked little body shows itself to us enlarged 10, 20, 100, and a thousand times more than it would represent itself if that radiant head of hair, which is not its own, were removed.*

**SAGREDO:** *Now I remember having read something on this matter—I do not know if it was in the "Letters on Sunspots" <note>original: "lettere solari"</note> or in "The Assayer" <note>original: "Saggiatore"</note> by our common friend <note>A reference to Galileo himself</note>—but it will be nothing but good, both to refresh my memory and for the understanding of Signor Simplicio, who perhaps has not seen such writings, to declare to us more distinctly how this business stands; the knowledge of which I think is very necessary to remain fully capable of understanding what is now being discussed.*

<margin>Shining objects appear surrounded by adventitious rays. The reason why luminous bodies appear enlarged more so as they are smaller.</margin>
**SALV.** The confidence that such men have in their own discernment is no less unreasonable than the low esteem they have for the judgment of others; and it is a great thing that they consider themselves fit to judge such an instrument better without ever having tested it, than those who have made, and continue to make every day, thousands upon thousands of experiments with it. But let us please leave aside this sort of stubborn person, whom one cannot even approach without honoring them more than they deserve. Returning to our subject, I say that shining objects—whether because their light is refracted in the moisture that is upon the pupils, or reflected in the edges of the eyelids, spreading its reflected rays over those same pupils, or perhaps for some other cause—show themselves to our eye surrounded by new rays, and therefore much larger than their bodies would appear to us if stripped of such irradiation. This enlargement occurs in greater and greater proportion as these lucid objects are smaller and smaller; in exactly that manner, if we supposed that the fringe of shining hair <note>Galileo uses the metaphor of "hair" to describe the blurry halo or diffraction spikes seen around stars with the naked eye.</note> was, for example, four inches, which, when added around a circle that had a diameter of four inches, would increase its apparent size nine times; but—

**SIMP.** I suspect you meant to say three times; because adding four inches on this side and four on that to the diameter of a circle that is itself four inches, one comes to triple its quantity, and not to increase it nine times.

<margin>Surface figures increase in the duplicate proportion of their lines.</margin>
**SALV.** A little Geometry, Mr. Simplicio! It is true that the diameter increases three times, but the surface area—which is what we are talking about—increases nine times. Because, Mr. Simplicio, the areas of circles are to each other as the squares of their diameters; and a circle that has a diameter of four inches, compared to another that has twelve, has that proportion which the square of four has to the square of twelve—that is, the proportion of 16 to 144. <margin>It is shown through clear experience that more brilliant bodies irradiate much more than those that are less bright.</margin>

I have many times seen Jupiter and Venus together, 25 or 30 degrees distant from the Sun; when the air was quite dark, Venus appeared a good 8 or even 10 times larger than Jupiter when viewed with the naked eye. But when viewed through the Telescope, the disk of Jupiter was truly perceived to be four times larger—and more—than that of Venus. However, the vividness of Venus's splendor was incomparably greater than the very languid light of Jupiter; this proceeded from nothing other than Jupiter being very far from the Sun and from us, while Venus is near to us and to the Sun. Having declared these things, it will not be difficult to understand how it can be that Mars—when it is at opposition to the Sun, and therefore seven times closer to Earth than when it is near conjunction—hardly appears 4 or 5 times larger in the former state than in the latter, whereas we ought to see it more than 50 times as large. Irradiation alone is the cause of this; for if we strip it of its adventitious rays, we will find it enlarged precisely according to the proper proportion.

<margin>The Telescope is the best means for removing the "hair" from the stars.</margin>

<margin>Another second cause for the small apparent increase of Venus.</margin>

Thus, because the light is small and weak, its irradiation is less ample and vivid than when it shows us its entire shining hemisphere. # Concerning Galileo

*...according to those calculations, they correspond to the same appearances, caring little about admitting some irregularities that in fact*
<margin>Copernicus restored Astronomy based on the suppositions of Ptolemy.</margin>
*presented difficulties in other respects. And Copernicus himself writes that in his early studies he restored the science of Astronomy upon the same suppositions of Ptolemy, and corrected the movements of the planets in such a way that the computations responded very accurately to the appearances, and the appearances to the calculations, provided however that one took each planet separately. But he adds that when he then wanted to assemble the entire structure of these individual constructions, the result was a monster and a chimera composed of members most disproportionate to one another and entirely incompatible; so that while the "pure calculator" astronomer might be satisfied, there was no satisfaction or peace for the "philosophical" astronomer. And because he understood very well that if celestial appearances could be saved with assumptions*
<margin>What moved Copernicus to establish his system.</margin>
*that were false in nature, this could be achieved much better from true suppositions, he began to search diligently to see if any among the distinguished men of antiquity had attributed to the world another structure than the commonly received one of Ptolemy. Finding that certain Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who proposed the Earth moved around a "Central Fire."</note> had specifically attributed the diurnal <term>diurnal: daily</term> rotation to the earth, and others the annual motion as well, he began to compare the appearances and the particulars of the planetary motions against these two new suppositions, all of which things he had readily at hand. Seeing that everything corresponded to its parts with wonderful ease, he embraced this new constitution and found peace within it.*

SIMPLICIO: *But what irregularities are in the Ptolemaic constitution that are not even greater in this Copernican one?*

<margin>Improprieties that are in the system of Ptolemy.</margin>
*movable in a circle should move irregularly around its own center, and regularly around another point? <note>This refers to the "equant," a mathematical device used by Ptolemy that Galileo found physically absurd.</note> And yet such deformed movements are in the fabric of Ptolemy, whereas in Copernicus all are uniform around their own centers. In Ptolemy, it is necessary to assign contrary movements to the celestial bodies, making them all move from East to West, and at the very same time from West toward East; whereas in Copernicus, all celestial revolutions are in a single direction, from West to East. ### Third Dialogue

*What shall we say of the apparent motion of the planets, which is so irregular that they not only move fast at times and slower at others, but sometimes stop entirely, and even after a long interval return backward? To save these appearances, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer who championed the geocentric model</note> introduced massive Epicycles <note>term: Epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to explain retrograde motion in a geocentric system</note>, adapting one for each planet with certain rules of inconsistent motions—all of which are swept away by a single, very simple motion of the Earth. And would you not call it a most great absurdity, Mr. Simplicio, if in Ptolemy’s construction—where each planet is assigned its own spheres, one above the other—it were often necessary to say that Mars, positioned above the sphere of the Sun, descended so far that, breaking through the solar sphere, it fell below it and approached the Earth more closely than the solar body itself, and shortly thereafter rose immeasurably above it? And yet this, and other irregularities, are cured by the single and most simple annual motion of the Earth.*

**SAGREDO** *These stations, retrogressions, and directions, which have always seemed to me great improbabilities—I would like to better understand how they proceed in the Copernican system.*

<margin>
A most great argument in favor of Copernicus is the removal of stations and retrogressions from the motions of the planets.
</margin>
<margin>
The annual motion of the Earth alone causes the great inequalities of motion in the five planets.
</margin>
<margin>
Demonstration of the inequalities of the 3 superior planets depending on the annual motion of the Earth.
</margin>

**SALVIATI** *You shall see them proceed in such a way, Mr. Sagredo, that this single conjecture should be sufficient for anyone who is not more than stubborn or unteachable to make him lend his assent to all the rest of this doctrine. I tell you, therefore, that without changing anything in the 30-year motion of Saturn, the 12-year motion of Jupiter, the 2-year motion of Mars, the 9-month motion of Venus, and the approximately 80-day motion of Mercury, the annual motion of the Earth alone, between Mars and Venus, causes the apparent inequalities in the motions of all five named stars. And for an easy and full understanding of the whole, I wish to draw its figure. Therefore, suppose the Sun to be placed in the center O, around which we will mark the orbit described by the Earth in its annual motion BGM; and let the circle described by Jupiter around the Sun in 12 years be this bgm; and in the starry sphere, let us understand the Zodiac yus. Furthermore, in the annual orbit of the Earth, we will take several equal arcs BC, CD, DE, EF, FG, GH, HI, IK, KL, LM; and in the circle of Jupiter, we will mark other arcs passed in the same times in which the Earth passes its own, which shall be bc, cd, de, ef, fg, gh, hi, ik, kl, lm—each of which will be proportionally smaller than those marked in the Earth's orbit, just as the motion of Jupiter under the Zodiac is slower than the annual motion.*

# Of Galileo.

<margin>The annual motion of the earth is most fit to explain the irregularities of the five planets. The Sun itself testifies that the annual motion belongs to the earth.</margin>

*You see, Gentlemen, with what ease and simplicity the annual motion—if it were attributed to the earth—is adapted to explain the apparent irregularities observed in the movements of the five planets: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury; removing them all and reducing them to uniform and regular motions. Of this marvelous effect, Nicolaus Copernicus was the first to make the cause manifest to us. But of another effect, no less admirable than this, and which binds the human intellect with a knot perhaps even more difficult to untie to admit this annual revolution and assign it to our terrestrial globe, the Sun itself brings us a new and unexpected conjecture. The Sun seems to have been unwilling to escape alone the attestation of such a distinguished conclusion; rather, as a witness beyond all exception, it has chosen to take part. Hear, then, this profound and new marvel.*

<margin>The Lincean Academician <note>Galileo Galilei, a member of the Accademia dei Lincei (Academy of the Lynxes).</note> was the first discoverer of the Sunspots and all other celestial novelties. History of the Academician's long progress regarding the observations of Sunspots.</margin>

*The first discoverer and observer of the Sunspots, as well as all other celestial novelties, was our Lincean Academician; he discovered these in the year 1610 while still holding the chair of Mathematics at the University of Padua. There, and in Venice, he spoke of them with several people, some of whom are still living; and a year later, he showed them in Rome to many Gentlemen, as he asserts in the first of his letters to Mr. Mark Welser, Duumvir of Augsburg <note>A high-ranking magistrate in the city of Augsburg.</note>. He was the first who, against the opinions of those too timid and too jealous of the unalterability of the Heavens <note>Referring to the Aristotelian belief that the heavens were perfect and unchanging.</note>, affirmed that such spots were matter that was produced and dissolved in short periods of time. Regarding their location, he held they were contiguous to the body of the Sun and revolved around it; or rather, carried by the solar globe itself, which turned upon its own center in the space of about a month, they completed their rotations. In the beginning, he judged this motion of the Sun to occur around an axis perpendicular to the plane of the Ecliptic <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note>, seeing as the arcs described by these spots across the disk of the Sun appeared to our eyes as straight lines parallel to the plane of the Ecliptic. These, however, were partially altered by certain accidental, wandering, and irregular movements to which the spots are subject, and by which they change their positions among themselves in a tumultuous manner without any order—sometimes many huddling together, sometimes separating, some dividing into several, and greatly changing their shapes, which are for the most part very extravagant. And although such inconstan—*

<margin>A concept suddenly occurring to the Lincean Academic <note>Galileo</note> regarding the great consequence following the motion of the Sunspots.</margin>
"Filippo, it seems to me that a path is opening toward a great consequence. For if the Axis around which the Sun revolves is not erected perpendicularly to the plane of the Ecliptic <note>the apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note>, but is inclined upon it—as the curved passage just observed suggests to me—we shall have such a conjecture regarding the states of the Sun and the Earth as has never been provided by any other encounter, neither so firm nor so conclusive." Awakened by such a high promise, I urged him to openly reveal his concept to me. And he said:

<margin>Strange mutations to be observed in the movements of the Spots, foreseen by the Academic, if the annual motion belonged to the Earth.</margin>
*"If the annual motion belongs to the Earth through the Ecliptic around the Sun; and if the Sun is situated in the center of said Ecliptic, and there turns upon itself, not around the Axis of said Ecliptic (which would be the Axis of the Earth's annual motion) but upon an inclined one, it must follow that strange mutations will represent themselves to us in the apparent movements of the Sunspots, even assuming that such an Axis of the Sun persists perpetually and immutably in the same inclination and in the same direction toward the same point in the universe. Because as the terrestrial globe travels around it in its annual motion, it must first follow that to us, carried by the Earth, the passages of the Spots will sometimes appear to be made in straight lines, but this only twice a year; and at all other times they will show themselves as sensibly curved arcs. Secondly, the curvature of such arcs for one half of the year will appear to us inclined in the opposite way to what is discerned in the other half; that is, for six months the convex side of the arcs will be toward the upper part of the solar disc, and for the other six months toward the lower. Thirdly, as the Spots begin to appear and, so to speak, be born to our eye on the left side of the solar disc, and go on to hide and set on the right side, the Eastern boundaries—that is, of the first appearances—will for six months be lower than the opposite boundaries of the disappearances; and for the other six months the opposite will happen, namely, that the Spots, being born from higher points and descending from them, will come to hide themselves in lower points during their courses. And for only two days of the entire year will such points of rising and setting be balanced; after which equilibrium, the inclination of the Spots' journeys beginning slowly, and becoming greater day by day, in three months..."*

### Third Dialogue

<margin>
If the Earth were immobile in the center of the Zodiac, it would be necessary to attribute four different movements to the Sun, as is explained at length.

no, the causes of these movements reside in motions within the solar body itself. First, it would be necessary for the Sun to revolve upon itself, carrying with it the Spots; which it has been supposed, or rather demonstrated, are adherent to the solar surface. Secondly, it would be necessary to say that the Axis of this solar conversion is not parallel to the Axis of the Ecliptic <note>The Ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun across the sky; its axis is the line perpendicular to this plane.</note>, which is to say, that it is not erected perpendicularly above the plane of the Ecliptic. Because, if it were so, the passages of these Spots would appear to us as straight lines, parallel to the Ecliptic. Therefore, this Axis is inclined, since the passages for the most part appear to be made in curved lines. In the third place, it would be necessary to say that the inclination of this Axis is not fixed, nor continually facing the same point in the Universe, but rather that from moment to moment it goes on changing direction. Because, if the tilt continually faced the same point, the passages of the Spots would never change appearance; whether straight or curved, tilted up or down, ascending or descending, however they appeared once, they would always appear so. It is therefore necessary to say that this Axis is convertible; and at times is found in the plane of the extreme circle bounding the visible Hemisphere—at which time, I say, the passages of the Spots appear as straight lines and more tilted than ever, which happens twice a year. At other times, it is found in the plane of the observer's meridian, in such a way that one of its Poles falls in the visible solar Hemisphere and the other in the hidden one; and both distant from the extreme points, or let us say from the Poles of another Axis of the Sun, which is parallel to the Axis of the Ecliptic (which second Axis it will be necessary to assign to the Globe of the Sun). Distant, I say, by as much as the inclination of the Axis of the revolution of the Spots requires; and furthermore, that the pole falling in the visible Hemisphere is at one time in the upper part, and at another in the lower. For a necessary argument for this happening is given by the passages when they are balanced and at their maximum curvature, now with their convex side toward the lower part, and at another time toward the upper part of the solar disc. And because such states are continually changing, with the inclinations and the curvatures becoming now greater and now lesser; and sometimes reducing the former to perfect equilibrium and the latter to perfect straightness, it is necessarily required to place the same Axis of the revolution mon- <note>original: "mestrua" - referring to a monthly cycle.</note>

# Of Galileo. 347

<note>Galileo is discussing the apparent paths of sunspots across the solar disc, which change throughout the year.</note>

...monthly <term>rotation</term> <note>original: "conuersione"</note> of the Sunspots to have its own specific revolution, by which its Poles describe two circles around the Poles of another Axis. This second axis must therefore be assigned (as I have said) to the Sun; the semi-diameter of these circles corresponds to the amount of inclination of that same Axis. And it is necessary that the time of its period be one year, since such is the time in which all the appearances and variations in the passage of the Spots return to their original state. And that the revolution of this Axis occurs over the Poles of the other Axis parallel to that of the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note>, and not around other points, is clearly indicated by the maximum inclinations and the maximum curvatures [of the sunspot paths], which are always of the same magnitude.

So that, finally, to keep the Earth stable in the center, it would be necessary to attribute to the Sun two movements around its own center, upon two different Axes: one of which completes its revolution in a year, and the other in less than a month. This assumption, to my mind, appears very difficult and almost impossible. And this depends on having to attribute to the same solar body two other movements around the Earth upon different Axes: describing the Ecliptic with one in a year, and with the other forming spirals or circles parallel to the <term>Equinoctial</term> <note>The celestial equator</note> once per day. 

Therefore, regarding that third movement which must be assigned to the globe of the Sun in itself (I am not speaking of that nearly monthly one which carries the Spots, but I mean the other, which must shift the Axis and the Poles of this monthly one), no reason is seen why it should finish its period in a year (as if depending on the annual motion through the Ecliptic) rather than in twenty-four hours (as if depending on the diurnal motion over the Poles of the Equinoctial). I know that what I am saying at present is quite obscure, but it will become clear to you when we speak of the <term>third annual motion</term> <note>Copernicus proposed a "third motion" to explain why the Earth's axis remains pointed in the same direction as it orbits the Sun</note> assigned by Copernicus to the Earth. 

Now, when these four movements—so incongruent with one another (all of which would necessarily have to be attributed to the same body of the Sun)—can be reduced to a single and most simple one assigned to the Sun upon an Axis that never changes; and when, without introducing any innovation in the movements assigned to the terrestrial globe for so many other reasons, one can so easily explain so many extravagant appearances in the movements of the solar Spots, it truly seems that this choice is not to be rejected.

**SAGR.** *The counsel which Mr.* Simplicio *adheres to is excellent and holy, and worthy of being received and followed by everyone, as that which, deriving from the highest wisdom and supreme authority, can alone be embraced with certainty. # On Galileo.

<margin>Tycho’s argument is founded upon false hypotheses. Litigants who are in the wrong will seize upon a single word spoken accidentally by the opposing party.</margin>
...against Copernicus; and it was only recently that I discovered the fallacy—or rather, the fallacies—of this discourse, which is built upon entirely false hypotheses and upon a specific pronouncement made by Copernicus himself. This statement has been seized upon by his detractors with a most punctual narrowness, much like those litigants who, having the wrong side of the main merit of a case, latch onto a single little word uttered incidentally by the other party, and upon that they make a clamor without ceasing. For your clearer understanding: after Copernicus had explained those wonderful consequences that derive from the annual motion of the Earth in relation to the other planets—namely, the direct and retrograde motions of the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> in particular—he added that this apparent change remained imperceptible in the fixed stars. He noted that this variation is more visible in Mars than in Jupiter (because Jupiter is further away), and even less so in Saturn (being further than Jupiter), and thus it was imperceptible in the fixed stars due to their immense distance from us compared to the distance of Jupiter or Saturn.

<margin>The apparent diversity of motion in the planets remains imperceptible in the fixed stars.</margin>
At this point, the adversaries of this opinion rise up. Taking that aforementioned "imperceptibility" mentioned by Copernicus as if he meant it were something that is really and absolutely nothing, and adding that even one of the smallest fixed stars is indeed perceptible (since it falls under the sense of sight), they proceed to calculate—with the intervention of other false assumptions—and conclude that according to the doctrine of Copernicus, one must admit that a fixed star is much larger than the entire <term>Great Orb</term> <note>The "Orbe Magno" refers to the diameter of the Earth's annual orbit around the Sun.</note>.

<margin>Assuming that a fixed star of the sixth magnitude is no larger than the Sun, the diversity which is great in the planets remains as if imperceptible in the fixed stars.</margin>
Now, in order to uncover the vanity of this entire progression, I shall show that by assuming a fixed star of the <term>sixth magnitude</term> <note>The traditional classification of the faintest stars visible to the naked eye.</note> is no larger than the Sun, it is concluded with true demonstration that the distance of these fixed stars from us is so great that it suffices to ensure the annual motion of the Earth (which causes such large and observable variations in the planets) does not appear notable in them. At the same time, I will show in detail the great fallacies in the assumptions made by the adversaries of Copernicus.

<margin>The distance of the Sun contains 1,208 semidiameters of the Earth. The diameter of the Sun is half a degree.</margin>
And first, I suppose with Copernicus himself, and in agreement with his adversaries, that the semidiameter of the Great Orb—which is the distance from the Earth to the Sun—contains 1,208 semidiameters of the Earth. Secondly, I state, with the assent of the same parties and in accordance with the truth, that the apparent diameter of the Sun at its average distance is about half a degree, which is 30 first minutes, which are 1,800 seconds, or 108,000 thirds. And because...

### Third Dialogue

<margin>
The diameter of a fixed star of the first magnitude, and of one of the sixth. How much larger the apparent diameter of the Sun is than that of a fixed star.
</margin>
<margin>
The distance of a fixed star of the sixth magnitude, assuming the star to be equal in size to the Sun.
</margin>
<margin>
In the fixed stars, the parallax <note>original: "diversità d'aspetto" - the apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from different locations</note> caused by the great orbit is only slightly larger than that caused by the Earth in relation to the Sun.
</margin>

The apparent diameter of a fixed star of the first magnitude is no more than 5 seconds, that is, 300 thirds; and the diameter of a fixed star of the sixth magnitude is 50 thirds (and here lies the greatest error of Copernicus's adversaries). Therefore, the diameter of the Sun contains the diameter of a fixed star of the sixth magnitude 2,160 times. And thus, if one were to assume a fixed star of the sixth magnitude to be truly equal to the Sun, and no larger—which is the same as saying that if the Sun were moved so far away that its diameter appeared to be one of the 2,160 parts of what it shows us now—its distance would have to be 2,160 times greater than it actually is now. This is to say that the distance of the fixed stars of the sixth magnitude is 2,160 semidiameters of the <term>great orbit</term> <note>The "orbe magno" refers to the Earth's annual orbit around the Sun in the Copernican model.</note>. And because the distance of the Sun from the Earth contains, by common consent, 1,208 semidiameters of the Earth itself, and the distance of the fixed stars (as has been said) is 2,160 semidiameters of the great orbit, it follows that the semidiameter of the Earth in comparison to the great orbit is much larger (nearly double) than the semidiameter of the great orbit in relation to the distance of the starry sphere. Therefore, the parallax in the fixed stars caused by the diameter of the great orbit can be little more observable than that which is observed in the Sun resulting from the semidiameter of the Earth.

**SAGREDO:** This, as a first step, is a great reduction.

<margin>
A star of the sixth magnitude is made 106 million times larger than necessary by the author of the booklet.
</margin>

**SALVIATI:** It is indeed, since a fixed star of the sixth magnitude—which, according to the calculation of this author, needed to be as large as the entire great orbit to maintain Copernicus's assertion—by simply placing it as equal to the Sun (which Sun is much less than the 106-millionth part of that same great orbit), renders the starry sphere so large and high that it suffices to remove the objection raised against Copernicus.

**SAGREDO:** Please, do this calculation for me.

<margin>
Calculation of the size of the fixed star relative to the great orbit.
</margin>

**SALVIATI:** The calculation is easy and very brief. The diameter of the Sun is eleven semidiameters of the Earth, and the diameter of the great orbit contains 2,416 of the same, according to the common consensus of the parties; so that the diameter of the orbit contains that of the Sun approximately 220 times. And because spheres are to each other as the cubes of their diameters, let us take the cube of 220, which is 10,648,000, and we will have the great orbit larger than the Sun 106 million and 480 thousand times. It was to this great orbit that this author claimed a star of the sixth magnitude must be equal.

<meta>The error...</meta>

**SAGREDO.** The error of these men, then, consists in being greatly deceived when taking the apparent diameter of the fixed stars.

Common deception of all astronomers regarding the sizes of the stars.

<margin>
Venus renders the error of astronomers inexcusable in determining the sizes of the stars.

**SALVIATI.** That is the error, but it is not the only one; and truly I remain greatly amazed how so many astronomers, and even those of great name—such as Alfraganus, Albategnius, Thabit ibn Qurra <note>original: "Alfragano, Albategno, Tebizio"</note>, and more recently the followers of Tycho and Clavius <note>original: "i Ticoni, i Clauij"</note>, and in short all the predecessors to our Academician <note>Galileo</note>—have been so deeply deceived in determining the sizes of all the stars, both fixed and wandering <note>planets</note>, except for the two luminaries <note>the Sun and Moon</note>. Nor did they pay attention to the adventitious irradiation <term>adventitious irradiation: a visual effect where bright objects appear larger against a dark background due to light scattering in the eye</term>, which deceptively shows them a hundred or more times larger than when they are seen without their "hair" <note>the blurry fringe or rays of light surrounding a star</note>. This inadvertence of theirs cannot be excused, because it was in their power to see them at their pleasure without the hair; it is enough to look at them at their first appearance in the evening, or their last concealment at dawn. If nothing else, Venus—which is often seen at midday so small that one must sharpen the sight, and yet on the following night appears as a very large torch—should have made them aware of their fallacy. I will not believe that they estimated the true disk to be that which shows itself in deep darkness, and not that which is discerned in a luminous environment; for our own lights <note>lamps or candles</note>, which seen at night from afar appear large, yet from nearby show their true, small, and defined flame, could have sufficiently made them cautious. Indeed, if I must freely state my opinion, I believe absolutely that none of these men—not even Tycho himself, so accurate in handling astronomical instruments, and who built such large and exact ones without sparing great expense—ever set themselves to actually take and measure the apparent diameter of any star, except for the Sun and the Moon. Rather, I think that arbitrarily, and as they say "by eye," one of the most ancient among them pronounced the matter to be so, and the followers then, without any other check, stood by the first statement; for if any of them had applied themselves to making some test of it, they would have undoubtedly become aware of the deception.

**SAGREDO.** But if they lacked the Telescope, and you have already said that our friend <note>Galileo</note> came to the knowledge of the truth with such an instrument, they should be excused, and not accused of negligence.
