### Third Dialogue

<margin>Method for measuring the apparent diameter of a star.</margin>
*...to achieve the goal. It is true that such an instrument <note>referring to the telescope</note>, by showing the star's disk bare and magnified a hundred or a thousand times, makes the operation much easier; however, one can also achieve the same result without the instrument, though not as exactly. I have done this many times, and the method I followed is this: I hung a thin cord toward a certain star—I used the Lyre <note>the star Vega in the constellation Lyra</note>, which rises between the North and the Northeast—and then, by moving closer to or further away from this cord placed between me and the star, I found the spot from which the thickness of the cord precisely hides the star from me. Once this was done, I measured the distance from my eye to the cord. This distance becomes one of the sides forming the angle at the eye which rests upon the thickness of the cord; this angle is similar to—or rather, the same as—the angle which, in the starry sphere, rests upon the diameter of the star. From the proportion of the cord's thickness to its distance from the eye, using a table of arcs and chords <note>a trigonometric table</note>, I immediately found the size of the angle. I used, however, the usual caution observed when taking such acute angles: not to assume the intersection of the visual rays occurs at the center of the eye—where they only arrive after being refracted—but rather beyond the eye, where the size of the pupil actually directs them to converge.*

**SAGR.** *I understand this caution, though I have a slight doubt about it; but what bothers me more is that in this operation, when performed in the darkness of night, it seems to me that one measures the diameter of the irradiated disk <note>the "glare" or "halo" seen around stars</note> and not the true, bare body of the star.*

**SALV.** *Not at all, sir; because the cord, in covering the bare little body of the star, strips away those "hairs" <note>Galileo uses "capelli" (hairs) to describe the radiating fringes of light</note> which are not the star's own, but belong to our eye. The star is deprived of these as soon as its true disk is hidden. In making the observation, you will see how unexpectedly that great torch—which seemed as though it could only be hidden by a much larger obstacle—is covered by a very thin cord. To then measure most exactly and find how many such cord-thicknesses fit into the distance from the eye, I do not take just a single diameter of the cord; instead, by lining up many pieces of the same cord on a board so that they touch, I use a compass to take the entire space occupied by 15 or 20 of them. With that measurement, I then measure the distance (already taken with another thinner thread) from the cord to the convergence of...*

And to make the white strip remain hidden by the black one, it will be necessary to bring the eye closer. Having approached it, then, so much that the middle strip occupies <insert>covers</insert> the remote one, and having noted how much it was necessary to approach, the quantity of such an approach will be a certain measure of how far the true convergence of the visual rays is distant from the eye in such an operation; and we shall have, moreover, the diameter of the pupil, or rather of that hole from which the visual rays emerge. For that part will be to the width of the black paper as the distance from the convergence of the lines (which were produced through the edges of the papers) to the place where the eye stood when it first saw the remote paper hidden by the intermediate one, is to the distance between the two papers. # On Galileo.

<note>This page is from Galileo's "Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems" (1632), featuring the characters Salviati, representing Galileo's views, and Simplicio, the Aristotelian philosopher.</note>

...that, having the stellar sphere so high, they constitute for it a superior sphere—and therefore a larger one—as the slowest of all, and make it move in twenty-four hours, while the one below it moves in 36,000 years? But of these disproportionalities, enough was said yesterday.

<margin>Immense sizes and numbers are incomprehensible to our intellect.</margin>

SALV. I would wish, Mr. Simplicio, that you would suspend for a moment the affection you bear for the followers of your opinion, and tell me sincerely whether you believe that they comprehend in their minds that magnitude which they later judge cannot be attributed to the universe because of its immensity. For my part, I believe they do not; and it seems to me that just as in the apprehension of numbers, once one begins to pass those thousands of millions, the imagination becomes confused and can no longer form a concept, so it also happens in apprehending immense sizes and distances. The result for our reasoning is similar to what happens to our senses: while on a clear night I look toward the stars, I judge by sense their distance to be only a few miles, and that the fixed stars are not at all more remote than Jupiter or Saturn, or even the Moon. But look no further than the past controversies between the <term>Astronomers</term><note>Those using mathematical observation, like Tycho Brahe</note> and the <term>Peripatetic philosophers</term><note>Followers of Aristotle</note> regarding the distance of the new stars <insert>supernovae</insert> of Cassiopeia and Sagittarius; the former placed them among the fixed stars, while the latter believed them to be lower than the Moon. So impotent is our sense to distinguish great distances from very great ones, even though the latter are in fact many thousands of times greater than the former. And finally, I ask you, oh foolish man: Do you comprehend with your imagination that magnitude of the universe which you then judge to be too vast? If you do comprehend it, would you presume that your apprehension extends further than <term>Divine power</term><note>The infinite capacity of God to create</note>? Would you say that you imagine things greater than those God can bring forth? But if you do not comprehend it, why do you wish to pass judgment on things you do not understand?

SIMP. These arguments all proceed very well, and it is not denied that the Heavens may surpass our imagination in size, just as God could have created it a thousand times larger than it is. ### Third Dialogue

*...to what end then is there interposed between the highest orb of Saturn and the stellar sphere a vast space without any stars, superfluous and vain? To what end? For whose convenience and utility?*

<margin>
Nature and God occupy themselves in the care of men as if they cared for nothing else.
Example of God's care over the human race taken from the Sun.
</margin>

SALVIATI: *It seems to me, Mr. Simplicius, that we arrogate too much to ourselves when we insist that the sole care of us is the adequate work and the limit beyond which Divine wisdom and power does or disposes nothing else. I would not wish for us to shorten His hand so much, but rather that we be content in the certainty that God and Nature are so occupied with the government of human affairs that they could not apply themselves more even if they had no other care than that of the human race alone. This, I believe, can be explained with a most fitting and noble example taken from the operation of the Sun's light. While the Sun attracts those vapors or warms that plant, it attracts and warms them in such a way as if it had nothing else to do; indeed, in ripening that cluster of grapes—or even just that single grain—it applies itself so effectively that it could not apply itself more if the end of all its business were the ripening of that single grain alone. Now, if this grain receives from the Sun everything that can be received, and not the slightest bit is usurped from it by the Sun producing a thousand thousand other effects at the same time, it would be a matter of envy or folly to blame that grain if it believed or demanded that the action of the solar rays be employed for its benefit alone. I am certain that nothing is left behind by Divine Providence of that which pertains to the government of human affairs; but that there cannot be other things in the universe depending upon His infinite wisdom, I could not, for my part, according to what my reason dictates, bring myself to believe. Nevertheless, if the facts were otherwise, there would be no reluctance in me to believe the reasons brought to me by a higher intelligence. In the meantime, when I am told that an immense space interposed between the orbs of the planets and the stellar sphere—devoid of stars and idle—would be useless and vain, as also that such immensity for the reception of the fixed stars (which exceeds our every apprehension) would be superfluous, I say that it is temerity <note>rashness or excessive boldness</note> to wish to make our weakest discourse the judge of the works of God, and to call vain or superfluous everything in the universe that does not serve us.*

# Concerning Galileo.

<margin>

</margin>

# Third Dialogue

<margin>
The vanity of the argument of those who judge the starry sphere to be too vast in the Copernican position.
</margin>

*...vast, compared to that of the Moon, every other magnitude that exceeds another of the same kind by a similar or greater proportion would have to be called "too vast," and for this reason denied to exist in the world. Thus, elephants and whales would undoubtedly be chimeras and poetic imaginings; because the former, being too vast in relation to ants (which are land animals), and the latter in respect to minnows <note>original: "spillancole," a small Mediterranean fish</note> (which are fish and are certainly seen to exist in the nature of things <note>original: "in rerum natura"</note>), would be too immense. This is because the elephant and the whale absolutely surpass the ant and the minnow by a much greater proportion than the starry sphere surpasses that of the Moon, even imagining said sphere to be as large as is necessary to accommodate the Copernican system.*

<margin>
The space assigned for a fixed star is much smaller than that of a planet.
</margin>

*Furthermore, how large is the sphere of Jupiter, or that of Saturn, assigned as the receptacle for a single star, and a very small one at that, in comparison to a fixed star? Certainly, if one had to assign to each fixed star such a part of the mundane space <note>the physical universe</note> for its dwelling, it would be necessary to make the orb where the innumerable multitude of them resides many, many thousands of times larger than what is sufficient for the needs of Copernicus.*

<margin>
A star is called small in respect to the magnitude of the space that surrounds it.
</margin>

*Besides, do you not call a fixed star "very small"—I mean even the most visible ones, let alone those that escape our sight—and we call them so in comparison to the surrounding space?*

<margin>
The entire starry sphere, from a great distance, could appear as small as a single star.
</margin>

*Now, if the entire starry sphere were a single shining body, who is there who does not understand that in infinite space one can designate a distance so great that such a lucid sphere would appear as small as, or even smaller than, a fixed star appears to us now from the Earth? From there, we would then judge as "small" that very same thing which we here call immeasurably large.*

**SAGREDO.** It seems to me the greatest silliness <note>original: "inezzia"</note> of those who would wish that God had made the universe more proportioned to the small capacity of their discourse than to His immense, or rather infinite, power.

**SIMPLICIO.** All this that you say is well and good; but that which the opposing party insists upon is having to concede that a fixed star must be not merely equal to, but so much larger than the Sun, even though both are particular bodies situated within the starry orb. And it seems to me that this author asks very much to the point when he demands: To what end, and for whose benefit, are these machines...

# Third Dialogue

...deny now their influence on the earth; or rather, that (contradicting yourself) you grant that appearing so tiny does not detract from their operation; or truly (and this would be a more sincere and modest concession) you grant and freely confess that our judgment regarding their sizes and distances is a vanity, if not to say a presumption or temerity.

<margin>
That distant objects appear small is a defect of the eye, as is demonstrated.
</margin>

**SALVIATI.** But I come to another point: upon what foundation does he say that the stars appear so small? Perhaps because we see them as such? And does he not know that this comes from the instrument we use in looking at them—that is, from our eye? And that this is true is shown by changing the instrument; we shall see them larger and larger, as much as we please. And who knows but that to the earth, which beholds them without eyes, they may show themselves as very great, and as they really are? But it is time that, leaving these trivialities, we come to matters of more moment. Having already demonstrated two things: first, how far it is sufficient to place the Firmament <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note> so that the diameter of the Great Orb <note>The Earth's annual orbit around the Sun</note> makes no greater difference there than the terrestrial globe does at the distance of the Sun; and then having likewise demonstrated how, to make a star of the Firmament appear to us of the size we see it, it is not necessary to make it larger than the Sun; I would now like to know if Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe, the Danish astronomer</note> or any of his followers has ever attempted to investigate in any way whether there can be perceived in the starry sphere any appearance by which one might more resolutely deny or admit the annual motion of the earth.

<margin>
Tycho or his followers have not attempted to see if there is any appearance in the Firmament against or in favor of the annual motion.
</margin>

**SAGREDO.** I would answer "no" for them; nor have they had any need to do so, since Copernicus himself says that such a difference <note>Stellar parallax</note> does not exist there. And they, arguing *ad hominem* <note>original: "ad hominem"; arguing against the person's own premises</note>, grant it to him; and upon this assumption they show the improbability that follows: namely, that it would be necessary to make the sphere so immense that a fixed star, to appear as large as it does to us, would in reality have to be a mass so immense that it would exceed the size of the entire Great Orb—a thing which is then, as they say, altogether incredible.

->SALVIATI<-

SALV. I am of the same opinion, and I believe precisely that they argue against the man <note>referring to Copernicus</note> more in defense of another man <note>likely Aristotle or Ptolemy</note> than out of a desire to come to the knowledge of the truth. And not only

but not sought; or because of its smallness, or for lack of exact instruments, it was not grasped by *Copernicus*. # On Galileo

<margin>
Motion, where it is shared, is as if it did not exist.
</margin>

*You also will remain in the same place on Earth; transport the Earth wherever you please, and you will never change your position relative to the Poles, the circles, or any other earthly thing. This is because such transport is common to you and to all terrestrial things; and motion, where it is shared, is as if it did not exist. Just as you will not change your position relative to the terrestrial Poles (position, I say, in the sense of them rising or falling for you), so likewise you will not change it relative to the Poles imagined in the Heavens, provided that by Celestial Poles we understand (as has already been defined) those two points marked by the Earth's axis extended out to that sphere. It is true that such points in the Heavens change when the transport of the Earth is done in such a way that its Axis goes to strike other and different points of the immobile celestial sphere, but our position relative to them does not change such that the second point rises higher for us than the first. Whoever wishes for one of the points of the Firmament <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note> corresponding to the Earth's poles to rise and the other to fall must walk upon the Earth toward one while moving away from the other; for transporting the Earth, and ourselves with it (as I have already said), achieves nothing.*

<margin>
An appropriate example to explain how the height of the pole should not vary by means of the Earth's annual motion.
</margin>

**SAGREDO.** *Grant me the favor, Mr. Salviati, that I might explain this matter very clearly with an example—one that is quite coarse, yet equally suited to this purpose. There is no doubt that if you walked along the gangway toward the mast for 25 or 30 paces, and aimed the same instrument again at the same masthead, you would find its elevation to be greater, having increased by, say, 10 degrees. But if, instead of walking those 25 or 30 paces toward the mast, you remained still at the stern and had the entire galley move toward that direction, do you believe that by means of the journey of 25 or 30 paces the elevation of the foremast would appear to have increased by 10 degrees?*

**SIMPLICIO.** *I believe, and I understand, that it would not increase by even a single hair's breadth for a journey of a thousand, nor of a hundred thousand miles, let alone 30 paces. Having found it written only in general terms that the annual movement of the earth in the great orb <note>original: "orbe magno," referring to the Earth's orbital path around the Sun</note> should not be admitted because it is not likely that no apparent change would be seen in the fixed stars because of it, and then not hearing it said specifically what such apparent changes ought to be, and in which stars, makes me very reasonably estimate that those who stop at that generic pronouncement have not understood, nor perhaps even sought to understand, how the business of these changes proceeds, nor what things they are saying ought to be seen. I am moved to judge thus by knowing that the annual movement attributed by Copernicus to the earth, when it must become sensible in the starry sphere, does not have to produce an apparent change equally with respect to all stars; rather, such appearance must be greater in some, smaller in others, still smaller in others, and finally in others absolutely nothing, however large the circle of this annual motion were assumed to be. The changes, then, that ought to be seen are of two kinds: one is the stars changing their apparent size, and the other is the varying of their heights on the* Meridian *; which consequently brings about the changing of their rising and setting points, and their distances from the zenith, etc.*

**SAGREDO.** *I seem to see a tangled skein of these revolutions being prepared for me, which God grant I may ever be able to untangle; for to confess my defect to Mr. Salviati, I have sometimes thought about it, and have never been able to find the thread—and I do not speak so much of this which pertains to the fixed stars, as of another more terrible matter which you have brought before me...*

<margin>The greatest difficulty against Copernicus regarding what appears in the Sun and the fixed stars.</margin>
...brought back to mind by remembering these Meridian altitudes, rising latitudes <note>The "rising latitude" or "ortive amplitude" refers to the distance along the horizon between due east and the point where a celestial body rises.</note>, and distances from the zenith, etc. My brain-reeling arises from what I will tell you now. Copernicus posits the stellar sphere as immobile, and the Sun in the center of it likewise immobile. Therefore, every change that appears to us to occur in the Sun or in the fixed stars must necessarily belong to the Earth—that is, to us. But the Sun rises and falls in our Meridian through a very great arc of almost 47 degrees, and varies its rising and setting widths on oblique horizons by even greater and greater arcs. Now, how can the Earth ever incline and raise itself so notably toward the Sun, and not at all toward the fixed stars, or by so little that it is an imperceptible thing? This is the knot that has never been able to pass through my comb <note>An Italian idiom meaning a problem that is difficult to untangle or resolve.</note>; and if you untie it for me, I will esteem you more than an Alexander <note>A reference to Alexander the Great cutting the Gordian Knot.</note>.

SALVIATI. These are difficulties worthy of Mr. Sagredo's intellect, and the doubt is such that even Copernicus himself almost despaired of being able to explain it in a way that would make it intelligible. This is seen both from his own confession of its obscurity and from his returning to it twice in two different ways to declare it. And I ingenuously confess not to have understood his explanation until after I made it intelligible by another quite plain and clear method; but not, however, without a long and laborious application of the mind.

<margin>Aristotle's argument against the ancients who held that the Earth was a planet.</margin>
SIMPLICIO. Aristotle saw the same difficulty and used it to refute certain ancients who held that the Earth was a planet. Against them, he argues that if this were so, it would be necessary for the Earth, like the other planets, to have more than one motion, from which there would follow this variation in the risings and settings of the fixed stars, and likewise in their Meridian altitudes. And since he proposed the difficulty and did not resolve it, it must be that it is, if not of impossible, at least of difficult solution.

SALVIATI. The greatness and force of the knotting makes the untying more beautiful and admirable, but I do not promise it to you for today; I beg you to excuse me until tomorrow. For now, we will go on considering and explaining those changes and diversities which, because of the annual motion, ought to be perceived in the fixed stars, just as we were saying just now. # On Galileo.

Let the angle of diversity—or what we might call the parallax <note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different points.</note>—of the star placed at the Pole *F.* be *AFB.* Let that of the star placed at *H.* be the angle *AHB*, and of the star at *E.* be the angle *AEB.* I say that the angle of diversity of the polar star *F.* is the **maximum**, and among the others, the one **closest to the maximum** is greater than the **more remote**: that is, angle *F.* is greater than angle *H.*, and this is greater than angle *E.* Let a circle be understood as described around the triangle *FAB.* And because angle *F.* is acute (since its base *AB.* is smaller than the diameter *DC.* of the semicircle *DFC.*), it will be placed in the larger portion of the circumscribed circle cut by the base *AB.* And because this *AB.* is divided in the middle and at right angles by *FG.*, the center of the circumscribed circle will be on the line *FG.* Let it be point *I.* And because of the lines drawn from point *G.* (which is not the center) to the circumference of the circumscribed circle, the **maximum** is that which passes through the center, *GF.* will be greater than any other line drawn from point *G.* to the circumference of the same circle; therefore, such a circumference will cut the line *GH.* (which is equal to the line *GF.*), and in cutting *GH.* it will also cut *AH.* Let it be cut at *L.*, and let the line *LB.* be joined. Thus, the two angles *AFB.* and *ALB.* will be equal, as they are in the same portion of the circumscribed circle: but the exterior angle *ALB.* is greater than the interior angle *H.* Therefore, angle *F.* is greater than angle *H.* And by the same method, we shall demonstrate that angle *H.* is greater than angle *E.*, because the center of the circle described around triangle *AHB.* is on the perpendicular *GF.*, to which the line *GH.* is closer than *GE.*, and therefore its circumference cuts *GE.* and also *AE.*, whence the proposition is manifest.

We conclude, therefore, that the diversity of appearance (which, using the proper <term>technical term of the art</term>, we may call the **parallax of the fixed stars**) is greater or lesser according to whether the observed stars are more or less close to the Pole of the Ecliptic <note>The point on the celestial sphere exactly 90 degrees from the Ecliptic plane.</note>, so that finally, for the stars that are on the Ecliptic itself, such diversity is reduced to nothing. <margin>The Earth approaches and moves away from the fixed stars of the Ecliptic by as much as the diameter of the <term>Great Orb</term> <note>The Earth's annual orbit around the Sun.</note>.</margin> As for the Earth approaching or moving away from the stars by such motion: it approaches and moves away from those on the Ecliptic by the full diameter of the Great Orb, as we have just seen; but for the stars around the Pole of the Ecliptic, such approaching or moving away is almost nothing, and for the others, this diversity becomes greater as they are closer to the Ecliptic. We can, in the th—

# Concerning Galileo

The distance and separation, by which the same star ought to appear now larger and now smaller, is imperceptible and almost null in stars near the Pole of the Ecliptic <note>The point in the sky directly above the plane of Earth's orbit</note>, but it is greatest in stars located on the Ecliptic itself, and moderate in those in between. The opposite occurs with the other variation—that is, there is no rising or lowering <note>referring to vertical parallax</note> in stars located on the Ecliptic, while it is greatest in those surrounding the Pole of the Ecliptic, and moderate in the intermediate ones. Furthermore, both of these variations are more perceptible in stars that are closer; in those further away they are less perceptible, and finally, in those extremely distant, they would vanish. This is as much as concerns my part; it remains now, as I see it, to satisfy Mr. Simplicio, who I do not believe will easily agree to dismiss as imperceptible such variations deriving from a movement of the Earth so vast, and from a change that transports the Earth to places distant from each other by twice as much as the distance from us to the Sun.

**SIMPLICIO:** To speak freely, I feel a great reluctance in having to concede that the distance of the fixed stars must be so great that these declared variations must be entirely imperceptible in them.

<margin>In objects that are very distant and luminous, a small approach or departure is imperceptible.</margin>
**SALVIATI:** Do not give yourself over entirely to despair, Mr. Simplicio, for perhaps there is still some moderation for your difficulties. And first, that the apparent size of the stars is not seen to alter sensibly should not seem at all improbable to you, seeing as you witness human judgment in such matters being so profoundly deceived, especially when looking at shining objects. For example, if you yourself were looking at a lit torch from a distance of 200 paces, and it moved 3 or 4 cubits <term>braccia: an old Italian unit of measurement, roughly the length of an arm</term> closer to you, would you believe you could notice it because it appeared larger? For my part, I certainly would not notice it even if it approached me by 20 or 30; indeed, I have sometimes happened to see such a light at such a distance and not be able to decide whether it was coming toward me or moving away, while it was actually approaching me. But what of it? If the same approach and departure (I mean double the distance from the Sun to us) is almost totally imperceptible in the star of Saturn, and little observable in Jupiter, what must it be in the fixed stars, which I do not believe you would be reluctant to place twice as far away as Saturn? In Mars, which by approaching us...

# Third Dialogue

SIMPLICIO. *Your Lordship need not labor any further on this particular point, as I am already convinced that what has been said regarding the lack of change in the apparent size of the fixed stars could very well happen; but what shall we say of the other difficulty, which arises from not perceiving any variation in their change of aspect?* <note>Simplicio refers to "stellar parallax"—the shift in a star's position that should be visible if the Earth moves around the Sun.</note>

SALVIATI. *We shall say something that may perhaps satisfy you even in this regard. To be brief, would you not be satisfied if those mutations were actually perceived in the stars which you think must necessarily be seen if the annual motion belonged to the Earth?*

SIMPLICIO. *I would be, without a doubt, as far as this particular is concerned.*

<margin>
If any annual mutation were perceived in the fixed stars, the motion of the Earth would suffer no contradiction.
</margin>

SALVIATI. *I would wish you to say that, if such a diversity were perceived, nothing more would remain that could cast doubt upon the mobility of the Earth, given that no other explanation could be assigned to such an appearance. But even if this were not sensibly apparent, mobility is not thereby removed, nor is immobility necessarily concluded. For it may be (as Copernicus affirms) that the immense distance of the starry sphere renders such minimal appearances unobservable. These, as has been said, may perhaps not have been sought after until now, or if sought, not sought in the proper manner—that is, with the exactness necessary for such minute details. Such precision is difficult to achieve, both due to the defects of astronomical instruments, which are subject to many alterations, and also through the fault of those who handle them with less diligence than is required.*

<margin>
It is proved how little astronomical instruments are to be trusted in minute observations.
</margin>

*A necessarily conclusive argument for how little such observations are to be trusted is the diversity we find among astronomers in assigning locations—I will not say of new stars <note>Supernovae</note> and comets, but of the fixed stars themselves, and even of polar altitudes, in which they are most often found to disagree with one another by many minutes. **SALV.** <note>Salviati, the character representing the Copernican view in Galileo's dialogue.</note> One must not, nor can one, deny anything requested by Mr. Sagredo; and the delay I asked for was for no other purpose than to have time to reorganize in my imagination those premises which serve for a broad and clear explanation of the manner in which the aforementioned occurrences follow, as much in the Copernican position as in the Ptolemaic; indeed, with much greater ease and simplicity in the former than in the latter. From this, it may be clearly understood that the [Copernican] hypothesis is as easy for nature to put into effect as it is difficult for the intellect to comprehend. Nevertheless, by making use of an explanation other than that used by Copernicus, I hope to make its understanding much less obscure; to do this, I will propose some suppositions that are self-evident and manifest, and they shall be the following:

<margin>The Copernican system is difficult to understand but easy to effect. Necessary propositions to properly understand the consequences of the earth's movements.</margin>

**First.** *Given that the earth, a spherical body, turns about its own axis and poles, every point marked on its surface describes the circumference of a circle, larger or smaller according to whether the marked point is more or less distant from the poles. And of these circles, the greatest is that which is drawn by a point equally distant from said poles; and all these circles are parallel to each other, and we shall call them parallels.*

**Second.** *The earth being of a spherical shape and of opaque substance, it is continually illuminated by the Sun across half of its surface, while the other half remains in darkness. And since the boundary that distinguishes the illuminated part from the dark part is a great circle <note>original: "cerchio massimo"</note>, we shall call it the circle terminator of light.*

**Third.** *When the circle terminator of light passes through the poles of the Earth, it would cut (being a great circle) all the parallels into equal parts; but not passing through the poles, it will cut them all into unequal parts, except for the middle circle alone, which, being a great circle, is likewise cut into equal parts.*

**Fourth.** *As the earth turns around its own poles, the lengths of the days and nights are determined by the arcs of the parallels cut by the circle terminator of light; and the arc which*

# Of Galileo

<margin>
The annual motion of the Sun, as it follows according to the way of Copernicus.
</margin>

Eastward, that is, according to the order of the signs <note>The signs of the Zodiac</note>. It is already manifest that while the Earth is in Capricorn (♑), the Sun will appear in Cancer (♋); and as the Earth moves through the arc of Capricorn (♑) and Aries (♈), the Sun will appear to move through the arc of Cancer (♋) and Libra (♎). In short, it runs through the Zodiac according to the order of the signs in the space of a year, and with this first assumption, the apparent annual movement of the Sun under the Ecliptic <note>The Sun's apparent path across the sky</note> is satisfied without controversy. Now, coming to the other movement—that is, the diurnal <note>daily</note> rotation of the Earth upon itself—it is necessary to establish its Poles and its Axis. This Axis must be understood not to stand perpendicularly above the plane of the Ecliptic (that is, not parallel to the Axis of the great orbit), but tilted from a right angle by about 23 and a half degrees, with its North Pole toward the Axis of the great orbit, while the center of the Earth is at the solstitial point of Capricorn (♑). Understanding, then, the terrestrial globe to have its center at point ♑, we shall mark the Poles and its Axis AB, inclined above the diameter of ♑ and ♋ by 23 and a half degrees, so that the angle A-♑-♋ becomes the complement of a quadrant, namely 66 and a half degrees. This inclination must be understood to be immutable, and we shall understand the upper Pole A to be the North <note>original: "Boreale"</note> and the other B to be the South <note>original: "Auſtrale"</note>.

Imagining now the Earth revolving upon itself around the Axis AB in twenty-four hours, also from West toward East, circles parallel to each other will be described by all the points noted on its surface. We shall mark in this first position of the Earth the greatest circle CD <note>The Equator</note>, and the two distant from it by 23 and a half degrees, EF above <note>Tropic of Cancer</note> and GH below <note>Tropic of Capricorn</note>, and the other two extremes IK and LM, distant by a similar interval from the Poles AB <note>The Arctic and Antarctic circles</note>. And just as we have noted these five, so we can understand innumerable others parallel to these, described by the innumerable points of the terrestrial surface. Let us now understand the Earth, with the annual motion of its center, transferring itself to the other places already noted, but passing there by such a law that its own Axis AB not only does not change its inclination above the plane of the Ecliptic, but also never varies its direction. Thus, maintaining itself always parallel to itself, it continually looks toward the same parts of the universe, or let us say of the Firmament; where, if we understood it to be prolonged, its highest point would describe a circle parallel and equal to the great orbit of Libra (♎), Capricorn (♑), Aries (♈), and Cancer (♋), as the upper base of a Cylinder described by itself in its annual motion over the lower...

# Third Dialogue

...lower base <note>The text refers to the zodiacal signs Capricorn, Aries, and Libra</note> Capricorn, Aries, and Cancer. And therefore, given this immutability of inclination, we shall mark these other three figures around the centers of Aries, Cancer, and Libra, similar in every respect to the first one described around the center of Capricorn. Let us now consider the first figure of the earth, in which—because the axis AB declines from the perpendicular above the diameter Capricorn-Cancer by 23 and a half degrees toward the Sun O, and the arc AI is also 23 and a half degrees—the illumination of the Sun will light up the hemisphere of the terrestrial globe exposed toward the Sun (of which half is seen here). This is divided from the dark part by the <term>terminator of light</term> <note>The line dividing day from night</note> IM, by which the parallel CD, being a great circle <note>The Equator</note>, will be divided into equal parts; but all the others will be divided into unequal parts, since the terminator of light IM does not pass through the Poles AB.

Furthermore, the parallel IK, together with all the others described within it and closer to Pole A <note>The North Pole</note>, will remain entirely within the illuminated part; conversely, the opposite ones toward Pole B <note>The South Pole</note> contained within the parallel LM will remain in darkness. Besides this, because the arc AI is equal to the arc FD, and the arc AF is common to both, the two arcs IKF and AFD will be equal, and each will be a quadrant <note>A quarter of a circle, or 90 degrees</note>; and because the entire arc IFM is a semicircle, the arc MF will be a quadrant, and equal to the other FKI. Therefore, the Sun O, in this state of the earth, will be vertical to whoever is at point F. 

But due to the diurnal <note>daily</note> revolution around the stable Axis AB, all points of the parallel EF pass through the same point F; and therefore, on such a day, the Sun at midday will be vertical to all the inhabitants of the parallel EF, and it will appear to them to describe in its apparent motion the circle that we call the **Tropic of Cancer**. 

But for the inhabitants of all the parallels that are above the parallel EF toward the Boreal <note>North</note> Pole A, the Sun declines from their vertex <note>The zenith, or point directly overhead</note> toward the South; and conversely, for all the inhabitants of the parallels that are below EF toward the Equinoctial <note>Equator</note> CD and the Austral <note>South</note> Pole B, the Meridian Sun is elevated beyond their vertex toward the Boreal Pole A. 

It is seen next how, of all the parallels, only the greatest one, CD, is cut into equal parts by the terminator of light IM. But the others, which are below and above the said greatest circle, are all cut into unequal parts; and of the upper ones, the <term>semidiurnal</term> <note>half-day</note> arcs—which are those on the part of the terrestrial surface illuminated by the Sun—are greater than the <term>seminocturnal</term> <note>half-night</note> ones, which remain in darkness; and the opposite happens for the remaining ones that are below the greatest circle CD.

Now it is clearly seen how, because the Axis A.B. has not changed its inclination, but has remained parallel to itself, the aspect and situation of the Earth is exactly the same as that of the first figure; except that the hemisphere which in the first was illuminated by the Sun, in this one remains in darkness, and that which in the first position was dark is now illuminated. Thus, what happened before regarding the differences of days and nights—concerning them being longer or shorter than each other—now happens in reverse.*

*And first, it is seen that where in the first figure the circle I.K. was entirely in the light, it is now entirely in the dark; and the opposite circle L.M. is now entirely in the light, which before was entirely dark. Of the parallels between the great circle C.D. <note>The Equator</note> and Pole A, the semi-diurnal arches are now smaller than the semi-nocturnal ones, which was the opposite before. Likewise, toward Pole B, the semi-diurnal arches are now larger than the semi-nocturnal ones, the opposite of what occurred in the other state of the Earth.*

<margin>A marvelous occurrence depending on the fact that the Earth's axis does not tilt.</margin>

*The Sun is now seen to be vertical to the inhabitants of the Tropic G.N. <note>Tropic of Capricorn</note> and to have lowered toward the South for those of the parallel E.F. by the entire arc E.C.G., that is, 47 degrees. In short, it has passed from one Tropic to the other, crossing the Equinoctial <note>The Equator</note> by rising and falling in the Meridians by the said space of 47 degrees. And all this change derives not from the Earth tilting or elevating itself, but on the contrary, from it never tilting or elevating at all; and in short, from it always maintaining itself in the same constitution with respect to the universe, solely by surrounding the Sun situated in the middle of the same plane, in which it moves circularly around it with its annual motion.*

*And here a marvelous occurrence is to be noted: that just as the axis of the Earth maintains the same direction toward the universe, or let us say toward the highest sphere of the fixed stars...*

### Third Dialogue

*if it causes the Sun to appear to us to rise and decline by such a distance—that is, by 47 degrees—and the fixed stars not to decline or rise at all; so, on the other hand, if the same axis of the Earth were maintained continually with the same inclination toward the Sun, or let us say toward the axis of the Zodiac <note>The "axis of the Zodiac" refers to a line perpendicular to the Ecliptic plane.</note>, no change would appear to occur in the Sun regarding its rising and lowering. Instead, it reclines from its first state by 47 degrees and inclines toward the opposite side, so that to restore the same inclination of the same Pole A toward the Sun, it would be necessary, by turning the terrestrial globe according to the circumference ACBD, to move it toward E by the same 47 degrees; and by that many degrees, any fixed star observed on the Meridian would appear to have risen or declined. # Concerning Galileo.

side, tell me, I pray you, what extravagances or overly forced subtleties make this Copernican system seem less plausible to you?

**SIMPLICIO.** In truth, I have not entirely understood it, perhaps because I do not even have ready at hand the reasons given by *Ptolemy* <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Roman astronomer whose Earth-centered model dominated science for 1,400 years.</note> for these same effects—I mean those stations, retrogradations, approaches, and withdrawals of the planets; the lengthening and shortening of days, the changing of the seasons, etc. But leaving aside the consequences that depend on the primary suppositions, I sense no small difficulties in the suppositions themselves. When these suppositions are knocked down, they pull down the ruin of the entire building. Now, because the whole machine of *Copernicus* seems to me to be founded upon unstable foundations, since it rests on the mobility of the earth, if this is removed, there is no need to move on to other disputes. And to remove this, it seems to me that the axiom of *Aristotle* is more than sufficient: that for a simple body, only one single simple motion can be natural. But here, to the earth—a simple body—are assigned three, if not four, movements, and very different from one another; for besides the straight motion, as a heavy body toward the center <note>The traditional Aristotelian view that heavy objects naturally move in a straight line toward the center of the universe.</note>, which cannot be denied it, there is attributed to it a circular motion in a great circle around the Sun in a year, and a rotation upon itself in twenty-four hours. And then, what is most exorbitant—and perhaps for this reason you remain silent about it—is another rotation around its own center, contrary to the first one of twenty-four hours, which is completed in a year. To this, my intellect feels the greatest repugnance.

<margin>
Four diverse motions attributed to the earth.
</margin>

<margin>
Downward motion belongs not to the terrestrial globe, but to its parts.
Annual motion and diurnal motion are compatible in the earth.
</margin>

**SALVIATI.** As for the downward motion, it has already been concluded that it does not belong to the terrestrial globe at all, which has never moved with such a movement, nor is it ever to move; but it is (if it exists at all) the tendency of the parts to reunite with their whole. As for the annual and diurnal movements, these being made in the same direction, they are perfectly compatible—in the same way that if we let a ball go down a sloping surface, it will spontaneously turn upon itself while descending. As for the third motion attributed to it by *Copernicus*, occurring upon its own axis in exactly one year to preserve its axis inclined and directed toward the same part of the Firmament <note>This "third motion" was Copernicus's way of explaining why the Earth's axis always points toward the North Star as it orbits the sun; Galileo later showed this wasn't a "motion" at all, but simply the axis maintaining its orientation.</note>, I will tell you something worthy of the greatest consideration: that is, so far is it <note>original: "tantum abest"</note> from there being any repugnance in it (even though it is made contrary to the other annual motion),

Salviati begins to refute this by explaining how different motions can naturally coexist in a single body.</summary>

### Third Dialogue

<margin>
Every suspended and balanced body, when carried around the circumference of a circle, naturally acquires a motion within itself contrary to the first. This is an experiment which sensibly demonstrates two contrary motions naturally occurring in the same moving body.
</margin>

*...indigence <note>original: "indigenza"; likely referring to a lack of difficulty or resistance</note>, or any difficulty, for it most naturally and without any driving cause belongs to any suspended and balanced body. If such a body is carried around the circumference of a circle, it immediately and by itself acquires a rotation around its own center, contrary to the motion that carries it around. This rotation is of such speed that both complete one revolution in precisely the same amount of time. You can see this wonderful experiment, so suited to our purpose, by placing a floating ball in a basin of water. Holding the vessel in your hand, if you turn yourself around on the soles of your feet, you will immediately see the ball begin to turn within itself with a motion contrary to that of the basin, and finish its revolution exactly when the vessel finishes its own. Now, what else is the Earth but a globe suspended and balanced in thin and yielding air? When carried around in a year through the circumference of a great circle <note>the "orbe magno" or Earth's annual orbit around the Sun</note>, must it not acquire, without any other mover, a yearly rotation <note>original: "vertigine"</note> around its own center, contrary to that other annual movement?*

<margin>
The third motion attributed to the Earth is rather a remaining immutable.
</margin>

*You will see this effect, but if you then consider it more accurately, you will realize that this is not a real thing, but a simple appearance. What seems to you to be a revolution within itself is actually a lack of movement and a total preservation of immutability relative to everything outside of you and the vessel that remains immobile. For if you mark a spot on that ball and observe which part of the wall of the room, or the countryside, or the Heavens it faces, you will see that during the revolution of the vessel and yourself, that mark always faces the same direction. But comparing it to the vessel and to yourself, who are moving, it will indeed appear to be changing direction, and with a motion contrary to yours and the vessel's, it will seem to travel through every point of the rim. Thus, it can be said with greater truth that you and the vessel are rotating around the immobile ball, rather than the ball turning inside the vessel. In this manner, the Earth—suspended and balanced in the circumference of the great orbit and situated so that one of its marks, such as its North Pole <note>original: "Polo Boreale"</note>, faces a certain star or other part of the Firmament <note>the sphere of fixed stars</note>—remains always directed toward that same point, even though it is carried by the annual motion through the circumference of that great orbit. This alone is sufficient to cease the wonder and remove every difficulty. But what will Mr. Simplicio <note>the character representing the traditional Aristotelian view in Galileo's dialogue</note> say if to this...*

<summary>Galileo explains the Earth's "third motion" (axial constancy) using the analogy of a floating ball in a basin, arguing that what appears to be a rotation is actually the Earth maintaining a fixed orientation in space as it orbits the Sun.</summary>

<margin>Axioms commonly accepted by all philosophers.</margin>

**On Galileo.**

**SIMPLICIO.** *I believe that stones, marbles, metals, gems, and so many other diverse materials are exactly like jewels and external, superficial ornaments of the primary globe, which I think, in its mass, immeasurably exceeds all these other things.*

**SALVIATI.** *And this principal and vast mass, of which the things you named are almost like excrescences and ornaments; of what material do you believe it is composed?*

**SIMPLICIO.** *I think it is the simple, or less impure, element of earth.*

**SALVIATI.** *But by "earth," what do you mean? Perhaps this which is scattered through the fields, which is broken with spades and plows, where grains are sown and fruits are planted, and where great forests grow spontaneously, and which, in short, is the habitation of all animals and the womb of all vegetables?*

**SIMPLICIO.** *That is what I would say was the primary substance of this globe of ours.*

**SALVIATI.** *Oh, this does not seem to me to be well said; because this earth, which is broken, sown, and which is fruitful, is a part—and a very thin one—of the surface of the globe, which does not go deep except for a short distance in comparison to the distance to the center. Experience shows us that one does not dig very far down before finding materials quite different from this exterior crust, firmer, and not good for the production of vegetables. Besides, it is credible that the innermost parts, being pressed by the very heavy weights that lie above them, are as packed and hard as any hardest rock. Add to this that fertility would have been granted in vain to those materials which were never to produce fruit, but to remain eternally buried in the deep and dark abysses of the earth.*

**SIMPLICIO.** *And who assures us that the innermost parts, near the center, are infertile? Perhaps they too have their productions of things unknown to us.*

**SALVIATI.** *You, as much as anyone else, could be certain of this, as one who can well understand that if the integral bodies of the universe are produced only for the benefit of the human race <note>Salviati is here using Simplicio's own Aristotelian/anthropocentric logic against him to argue that the deep interior of the Earth must be different from the surface.</note>, this one above all others must be destined solely for the conveniences of us, its inhabitants. But what benefit could we derive from materials so hidden and remote from us that they never—*

### Third Dialogue

<margin>
The internal parts of the terrestrial globe must be extremely solid.
</margin>

*...are we never to make them manageable for ourselves? Therefore, the internal substance of this globe of ours cannot be a fragile, dissipable matter, lacking coherence like this superficial layer we call earth; rather, it must be a body that is very dense and solid, and in short, a very hard stone. And if it truly must be such, what reason is there to be more reluctant to believe that it is a Loadstone <note>original: "Calamita"; the natural magnet</note> than a porphyry, a jasper, or some other hard marble? Perhaps if Gilbert <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603), author of De Magnete</note> had written that this globe is internally made of sandstone <note>original: "pietra serena"; a grey sandstone typical of Florentine architecture</note> or of chalcedony, would the paradox have seemed less exorbitant to you?*

SIMPLICIO: *That the innermost parts of this globe are more compressed, and therefore more packed and solid—and increasingly so the deeper they go—I concede, and Aristotle also concedes it; but that they should degenerate and be anything other than earth of the same sort as this on the superficial parts, I hear nothing that necessitates my conceding it.*

<margin>
Our globe would be called stone instead of earth if such a name had been given to it from the beginning.
</margin>

SALVIATI: *I have not undertaken this reasoning for the purpose of concluding demonstratively to you that the primary and real substance of this globe of ours is Loadstone; but only to show you that no reason is found why one should be more reluctant to concede that it is of Loadstone than of some other material. And you, if you consider it well, will find it not improbable that a single pure and arbitrary name has moved men to believe that it is made of earth; and this is because they have commonly used this name "earth" from the beginning to signify both that matter which one plows and sows, as well as to name this globe of ours. If the denomination of the globe had been taken from stone—as it could no less have been taken from that than from earth—saying that its primary substance was stone would surely have found no reluctance or contradiction in anyone. And this is all the more probable as I hold for certain that if one could peel this great globe, removing a layer a thousand or two thousand cubits <note>original: "braccia"; a traditional Italian unit of length</note> thick, and then separate the stones from the earth, the pile of rocks would be much, much larger than that of the fertile soil.* <margin>Gilbert's progress in his philosophizing.</margin> *As for the reasons that conclusively prove, in fact, that this globe of ours is made of Loadstone, I have produced none for you, nor is this the time to produce them—especially since you can see them at your convenience in Gilbert's work. Only to encourage you to read it, I want to explain to you with a certain simi—*

# Concerning Galileo.

<margin>The wonderful internal power of the terrestrial globe to always face the same part of the Heaven. The terrestrial globe made of Lodestone.</margin>
*...lack of a cooperating cause, we shall add a wonderful intrinsic power of the terrestrial globe to face with its specific parts toward specific parts of the Firmament. I speak of the magnetic power shared most constantly by almost any piece of Lodestone <note>original: "Calamita"; the naturally magnetized mineral magnetite</note>. And if every tiny particle of such stone has this power within itself, who would doubt that the same resides more deeply in this entire earthly globe, which abounds in such material, and that perhaps the globe itself, as to its internal and primary substance, is nothing other than an immense mass of Lodestone?*

SIMPLICIO. *So, you are one of those who adhere to the magnetic philosophy of William Gilbert?*

<margin>Magnetic Philosophy of William Gilbert.</margin>
SALVIATI. *I certainly am, and I believe I have as companions all those who have attentively read his book and verified his experiments; nor would I be without hope that what happened to me in this case could happen to you as well, provided that a curiosity similar to mine—and a recognition that infinite things in nature remain unknown to human intellects—might free you from slavery to this or that particular writer on natural things, loosen the reins on your reasoning, and soften the stubbornness and resistance of your senses, so that they might not refuse at times to give ear to voices never heard before. But (permit me to use this term)* <margin>Pusillanimity of common minds.</margin> *the pusillanimity <note>timidity or lack of courage</note> of common minds has reached such a point that they not only blindly grant the gift, or rather the tribute, of their own assent to everything they find written by those authors who were credited to them by their teachers in the first infancy of their studies, but they refuse even to listen to, let alone examine, any new proposition or problem. This is true even though the idea has not only never been refuted, but not even examined or considered by their preferred authors. One such problem is investigating what the true, proper, primary, internal, and general matter and substance of this earthly globe of ours might be. Although it never entered the mind of Aristotle, nor anyone else before Gilbert, to think whether it might be Lodestone—and thus neither Aristotle nor others have refuted such an opinion—nevertheless, I have encountered many who, at the first mention of this, like a horse that takes fright at a shadow, have recoiled and fled from discussing it, dismissing such a concept as a vain chimera, or rather as a solemn madness. And perhaps Gilbert's book would not have come into my hands, if a Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle's philosophy</note> philosopher...*

# On Galileo

<margin>
Multiple properties of the Loadstone <note>original: "Calamita" - a naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite.</note>.

*...the progression he maintains in his philosophizing. I know that you understand very well how much the knowledge of accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential properties of a thing, like color or weight, as opposed to its "essence."</note> contributes to the investigation of the substance and essence of things; therefore, I want you to use diligence in informing yourself well of many accidents and properties that are found singularly in the Loadstone, and in no other stone nor in any other body. Such would be, for example, the attracting of iron; the conferring upon it, solely by its presence, the same power; the communicating to it likewise the property of looking toward the Poles, just as it retains such a property within itself. And beyond this, make sure to see by proof how there resides in it the power to confer upon the magnetic needle not only the ability to straighten itself under a Meridian toward the Poles with horizontal motion (a property already known for some time), but a newly observed accident: that of declining (while staying balanced under the Meridian already marked upon a small sphere of Loadstone)—declining, I say, up to determined marks, more or less, according as such a needle is held closer or further from the Pole, until directly over the Pole itself it stands upright perpendicularly, whereas over the middle parts it stays parallel to the Axis. Furthermore, endeavor to test how, while the power to attract iron resides much more vigorously toward the Poles than near the middle parts, such force is notably stronger in one Pole than in the other, and this in all pieces of Loadstone; the stronger Pole of which is the one that looks toward the South <note>original: "Austro" - the South wind or direction.</note>. Note next that in a small Loadstone, this Southern Pole, though more powerful than the other, becomes weaker whenever it must support iron in the presence of the Northern <note>original: "Boreale"</note> Pole of another much larger Loadstone. And so as not to make a long discourse, assure yourself through experience of these and many other properties described by Gilbert <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603), whose work "De Magnete" laid the foundation for the study of magnetism.</note>; all of which are so uniquely characteristic of the Loadstone that none of them belong to any other material.*

<margin>
An argument concluding that the terrestrial globe is a Loadstone.
</margin>

*Tell me now, Mr. Simplicio, if you were presented with a thousand pieces of different materials, but each one covered and wrapped in a cloth under which it was hidden, and you were asked that, without uncovering them, you should try to guess from exterior signs the material of each one; and if in your testing you encountered one which openly showed all the properties you already knew to reside in the Loadstone alone, and in no other material, what judgment would you make of the essence of such a body? ### Third Dialogue

*...of Ebony, or of Alabaster, or of Tin?*

SIMPLICIO. *I would say, without a moment's doubt, that it was a piece of Loadstone <note>original: "Calamita"; a naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite</note>.*

SALVIATI. *If that is the case, then say resolutely that beneath this cover and rind of earth, stones, metals, water, etc., there is hidden a great Loadstone. This is because anyone who takes the care to observe them will recognize around the Earth all those same phenomena that are seen to belong to a true and exposed globe of Loadstone. Even if one saw nothing else but the behavior of the declinatory needle <note>a magnetic compass needle that tips up or down to show the dip of the Earth's magnetic field</note>, which, when carried around the earth, inclines more and more as it approaches the North Pole <note>original: "Polo Boreale"</note> and declines less toward the Equator <note>original: "Equinoziale"</note>—under which it finally returns to equilibrium—this alone should be enough to persuade even the most reluctant judgment.*

*I will remain silent regarding that other wonderful effect which is perceptibly seen in all pieces of Loadstone: for us inhabitants of the Northern Hemisphere, the South Pole <note>original: "Polo Meridionale"</note> of said Loadstone is stronger than the other. This difference is perceived to be greater the further one moves from the Equator; directly under the Equator, both parts are of equal strength, but notably weaker. However, in the Southern regions, far from the Equator, the nature changes, and that part which was weaker for us acquires vigor over the other. All of this matches what we see happen to a small piece of Loadstone in the presence of a large one; the power of the larger one, prevailing over the smaller, makes it obedient. Depending on whether it is held on this side or that side of the large stone's equator, it undergoes the same changes that I have said are made by every Loadstone carried to this side or that side of the Earth's equator.*

<margin>An armed Loadstone <note>a magnet fitted with iron caps or "armor" to concentrate its strength</note> supports much more iron than an unarmed one.</margin>

SAGREDO. *I was persuaded at the first reading of Gilbert's book <note>William Gilbert’s "De Magnete" (1600), the foundational text on magnetism</note>; and having encountered an excellent piece of Loadstone, I made many observations over a long time, all worthy of extreme wonder. But above all, it seems stupendous to me how much its faculty for supporting iron is increased by "arming" it in the manner that the same author teaches. By arming my piece, I multiplied its strength eightfold; where unarmed it barely supported nine ounces of iron, armed it supported more than six pounds. Perhaps you have seen this very piece in the Gallery of your Most Serene Grand Duke <note>referring to the Medici rulers of Tuscany</note> (to whom I yielded it), supporting two small iron anchors.*

# Of Galileo.

**SALV.** *I saw it many times, and with great wonder, until a much greater amazement was caused in me by a small piece found in the hands of our Academician <note>Galileo himself, a member of the Accademia dei Lincei</note>. This piece, weighing no more than six ounces and supporting barely two ounces when unarmed <note>without a metal casing or "armor"</note>, supports 160 ounces when armed. Thus, it comes to hold 80 times more when armed than unarmed, and supports a weight 26 times greater than its own. This is a much greater marvel than anything Gilbert could have encountered, who writes that he was never able to find a Magnet <note>original: "Calamita"</note> that could manage to support four times its own weight.*

**SAGR.** *It seems to me that this stone offers a vast field for human intellects to philosophize upon. I have speculated a thousand times within myself how it can be that it grants to that iron which arms it a force so superior to its own, and finally, I find nothing that satisfies me; nor do I derive much substance from what Gilbert writes regarding this particular. I do not know if the same happens to you.*

**SALV.** *I highly praise, admire, and envy this author for having conceived such a stupendous concept regarding a matter handled by infinite sublime minds yet noticed by none of them. He also seems to me worthy of the greatest praise for the many new and true observations made by him, to the shame of so many lying and vain authors who write not only what they know, but everything they hear from the foolish common folk, without seeking to ensure its truth through experience—perhaps so as not to diminish the size of their books. What I would have desired in Gilbert is that he had been a slightly greater Mathematician, and in particular well-grounded in Geometry <note>original: "Geometria"</note>. The practice of this would have made him less resolute in accepting as conclusive demonstrations those reasons which he produces as the true causes of the true conclusions observed by him. These reasons (speaking freely) do not bind and tighten with that force which must indubitably be possessed by those reasons adduced for natural, necessary, and eternal conclusions. # On Galileo

*...so to speak) that connect the two pieces of iron are many more than those which connect a lodestone <note>original: "Calamita"; the natural magnetic mineral magnetite</note> with iron. This is because the substance of the lodestone is more porous and less pure, which means that not all the points and filaments on the surface of the iron find matching points on the surface of the lodestone with which to unite. That the substance of iron (and especially well-purified iron, such as the finest steel) consists of parts significantly more dense, subtle, and pure than the material of the lodestone is evident from the fact that its edge can be reduced to an extreme thinness, such as the edge of a razor, to which a piece of lodestone could never be brought by a long shot.*

<margin>The impurity of the lodestone is shown to the senses.</margin>
*Furthermore, the impurity of the lodestone and its being mixed with other types of stone is first perceived by the senses: from the color of certain small spots, mostly whitish; and then by presenting to it a needle hanging from a thread, which cannot rest upon such small stones, but, being attracted by the surrounding parts, seems to flee from those spots and jump onto the lodestone contiguous to them. And just as some of these heterogeneous parts are very visible due to their size, so we can believe that others, inconspicuous due to their smallness, are disseminated in great abundance throughout the entire mass. What I am saying is confirmed (that is, that the multitude of contact points made between iron and iron is the cause of such a firm union) by an experiment: if we present the sharp tip of a needle to the armature <note>The iron casing or "cap" added to a magnet to increase its lifting power</note> of the lodestone, it will not attach itself more strongly than it would to the bare stone itself. This can derive from nothing else than the two contacts being equal—that is, both consisting of a single point. But what is more? Take a needle and place it on the lodestone so that one of its ends protrudes somewhat, and present a nail to it. The needle will immediately attach itself to the nail in such a way that, by pulling the nail back, the needle will remain suspended, attached at its ends to both the lodestone and the iron; and by pulling the nail even further, it will detach the needle from the lodestone—provided, however, that the eye of the needle is joined to the nail and the point to the lodestone. But if the eye is toward the lodestone, upon removing the nail, the needle will remain attached to the lodestone. This happens (in my judgment) for no other reason than that the needle, being thicker toward the eye, touches in many more points than the very sharp tip does.*

# Concerning Galileo.

*...the tiny particles of iron, although perhaps more continuous than those of any other body (as shown by its ability to take a higher polish than any other material), do not all—indeed, only a few—actually meet the pure Lodestone; and since the points of contact are few, the attachment is weak. But, because the "armor" <note>The metal casing or "capping" used to enhance a magnet's strength.</note> of the Lodestone, in addition to touching a large part of its surface, also clothes itself in the power of the neighboring parts, even those not touched; and since that face to which the other is applied is exactly flattened, and the iron to be supported is similarly well-flattened, the contact is made of innumerable tiny particles, if not perhaps of the infinite points of both surfaces, whereby the attachment becomes extremely strong. This observation of flattening the surfaces of the irons that must touch was not noticed by Gilbert <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603), author of 'De Magnete'.</note>; indeed, he makes the irons rounded, so that their contact is small; hence it happens that the tenacity with which these irons attach is much less.*

**SAGREDO.** *I remain, as I just said, little less satisfied by the reason assigned than if it were a pure Geometric demonstration; and because we are dealing with a physical problem, I believe that Mr. Simplicio will also find himself satisfied as far as natural science allows, in which we know that one must not seek Geometric evidence.*

<margin>Sympathy and antipathy: terms used by philosophers to easily give reasons for many natural effects.</margin>
**SIMPLICIO.** *It truly seems to me that Mr. Salviati, with a fine circuit of words, has so clearly explained the cause of this effect that any mediocre mind, even if not learned, could remain capable of understanding it; but we, keeping ourselves within the terms of the art, reduce the cause of these and other similar natural effects to "sympathy," which is a certain suitability and mutual appetite that arises between things that are similar to each other in quality; just as, on the contrary, that hatred and enmity by which other things naturally flee and hold each other in horror, we call "antipathy."*

<margin>A pleasant example to declare the little efficacy of certain philosophical discourses.</margin>

### Third Dialogue

<margin>The fallacy of those who call the Magnet a mixed body, and the terrestrial globe a simple body.</margin>
*...true, primary, and integral substance of our globe, retains the same nature. And notice this fallacy: you call the Magnet a mixed body <note>In Aristotelian physics, a "mixed body" is a compound of the four elements, whereas a "simple body" is a pure element.</note>, and the terrestrial globe a simple body, even though the globe is visibly a hundred thousand times more composite. For, besides containing thousands upon thousands of diverse materials, it contains a great abundance of that which you call mixed—I mean the Magnet. This seems to me the same as if someone were to call bread a mixed body, and a simple body an "Ogliopotrida" <note>original: "Ogliopotrida"; a Spanish-style stew (Olla Podrida) containing many different ingredients.</note>, into which a significant quantity of bread enters, along with a hundred different side dishes.*

<margin>Peripatetic discourse full of fallacies and contradictions.</margin>
*It truly seems a wonderful thing to me, among others, regarding the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching.</note>, who concede (nor can they deny it) that our terrestrial globe is in fact a composite of infinite diverse materials; they further concede that for composite bodies, the motion must be composite; the motions that can be composed are the straight and the circular, given that two straight motions, being contrary, are incompatible with each other. They affirm that the pure element of Earth is not to be found; they confess that it has never moved with any local motion; and then they wish to posit in nature that body which is not found, and make it movable by that motion which it has never exercised, nor is ever to exercise; and to that body which exists, and has always existed, they deny that motion which they first conceded ought naturally to belong to it.*

SALVIATI: *Pray, Mr. Sagredo, let us not weary ourselves further with these particulars, especially since you know that our goal has not been to resolutely determine or accept this or that opinion as true, but only to propose for our pleasure those reasons and responses that can be brought forward for one side and the other. Mr. Simplicio responds thus in defense of his Peripatetics; therefore, let us leave the judgment pending and the determination in the hands of those who know more than we do. And because it seems to me that we have discussed the system of the universe at great length over these three days, it will now be time for us to come to the greatest phenomenon <term>accidente massimo: a major physical occurrence or property</term> from which our reasonings originated: I speak of the ebb and flow of the sea <note>The tides.</note>, the cause of which it seems can quite probably be referred to the motions of the Earth. # On Galileo.

If a small sphere of Lodestone <note>original: "Calamita"; a naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite</note> could be exactly balanced, it would not turn upon itself, because there is no reason why it should do so. For if the entire terrestrial globe has by nature the property of turning around its own center in twenty-four hours, and all its parts must also have this—I mean, to turn together with their *whole* around its center in twenty-four hours—they already effectively possess this motion while remaining on the Earth and revolving along with it. To assign them a revolution around their own private center would be to attribute to them a second movement very different from the first; they would thus have two: namely, revolving in twenty-four hours around the center of the whole, and turning around their own. Now, this second motion is arbitrary, and there is no reason to introduce it. If, in detaching a piece of Lodestone from the entire natural mass, its ability to follow the mass were taken away (as it did while joined), so that it remained deprived of the revolution around the universal center of the terrestrial globe, then perhaps someone might believe with greater probability that it would adopt a new rotation <note>original: "vertigine"</note> around its particular center. But if, no less separated than joined, it continues nonetheless its first, eternal, and natural course, why wish to burden it with another new one?

<margin>
Vain discourse of some to prove the element of water has a spherical surface.
</margin>

# DAY
## FOURTH.

**SAGREDO.** I do not know if your return to our usual discussions has truly been later than customary, or if perhaps the desire to hear the thoughts of Mr. Salviati regarding such a curious matter has made it seem so to me. I have spent a full hour lingering at the window, waiting from moment to moment to see the gondola appear which I had sent to fetch you.

<margin>
Nature, as if in a jest, allows the ebb and flow of the sea to applaud the mobility of the Earth. The ebb and flow and the terrestrial mobility mutually confirm one another.

# Fourth Dialogue

<margin>
First general conclusion: the impossibility of the flow and ebb of the sea occurring if the terrestrial globe remains immobile.
</margin>
...having examined the effects and occurrences, partly seen and partly heard from *others, which are observed in the movements of the waters; and having read and heard the great vanities produced by many as causes for such occurrences, I have felt myself drawn, in no small way, to admit these two conclusions (provided the necessary assumptions are made): that if the terrestrial globe is immobile, the flow and ebb of the sea <note>original: "flusso, e reflusso"; the tides</note> cannot naturally occur; and that, when the previously assigned movements are granted to the same globe, it is necessary that the sea be subject to flow and ebb, in accordance with everything that is observed within it.*

SAGR. *The proposition is a grand one, both in itself and for what it draws in its wake; therefore, I shall listen all the more attentively to its explanation and confirmation.*

<margin>
Knowledge of effects leads to the investigation of causes.
</margin>
SALV. *Because in natural questions—of which this one we have at hand is one—the knowledge of effects is that which leads us to the investigation and discovery of causes, and without that, our path would be a walking in the dark; indeed, it would be more uncertain, since we would not know where we wished to emerge, whereas the blind at least know where they wish to arrive. Therefore, before all other things, it is necessary to have knowledge of the effects for which we seek the causes. Of these effects, you, Mr. Sagredo, must be more abundantly and more surely informed than I am; as one who, besides being born and having lived for a long time in Venice <note>Venice is famous for its "Acqua Alta" and noticeable tidal shifts, unlike much of the Mediterranean</note>, where the flow and ebb are very notable for their size, you have also sailed to Syria, and as a sharp and curious mind, you must have made many observations. These reports, being for the most part not well-aligned and consequently quite uncertain, can bring confusion rather than confirmation to our speculations.
