# Of Galileo. 411

...a path never before trodden by others, with firm hope that minds more speculative than mine will expand upon it and penetrate much further than I have done in this, my first discovery. And even though in other seas remote from us there may occur phenomena that do not happen in our Mediterranean, the reason and cause that I shall produce will not, for that reason, cease to be true, provided that it is verified and fully satisfies the phenomena that occur in our sea; because, ultimately, there must be only one true and primary cause for effects that are of the same kind. I shall therefore relate the history of the effects that I know to be true, and I will assign to them the cause I believe to be true; and you, Gentlemen, will produce others known to you in addition to mine, and then we shall test whether the cause adduced by me can satisfy those as well.

<margin>Three periods of the ebbs and flows: daily, monthly, and annual.</margin> I say, then, that there are three periods observed in the ebbs and flows <note>original: "flussi, e reflussi" — the tides</note> of the sea waters. The first and principal one is this great and most well-known one, namely the **daily** period, according to which, at intervals of several hours, the waters rise and fall; and these intervals in the Mediterranean are mostly about 6 hours each—that is, they rise for 6 hours and fall for another 6. *The second period is **monthly**, and it seems to take its origin from the motion of the Moon; not that it introduces other movements, but it only alters the magnitude of those already mentioned, with a notable difference depending on whether the Moon is full, waning, or in quadrature with the Sun. The third period is **annual**, and it appears to depend on the Sun, also altering only the daily movements by making them different in magnitude at the times of the Solstices compared to what they are at the Equinoxes.*

We shall speak first of the daily period, as it is the principal one, and the one upon which it seems the Moon and the Sun secondarily exert their action with their monthly and annual alterations. *Three diversities are observed in these hourly changes;* <margin>Diversities that occur in the daily period.</margin> *for in some places the waters rise and fall without making a progressive motion; in others, without rising or falling, they move now toward the East <note>original: "Leuante"</note> and then run back toward the West <note>original: "Ponente"</note>; and in others, they vary in height and also vary in their course, as happens here in Venice, where the waters rise upon entering and fall upon exiting. This occurs at the extremities of the lengths of gulfs that extend from West to East and end in shores, upon which the water, in rising...*

<summary>Galileo identifies three distinct tidal periods—daily, monthly, and annual—proposing that while the daily cycle is primary, the Sun and Moon act as secondary modifiers of its intensity. He notes regional variations in how tides manifest, specifically citing the unique behavior of the waters in Venice and the Mediterranean.</summary>

<margin>Truth does not have so little light that it cannot be discerned amidst the darkness of falsehoods.</margin>

## Of Galileo. 415

**SALVIATI.** *Therefore, Mr. Simplicio, since we must introduce a miracle to produce the ebb and flow of the sea, let us miraculously make the Earth move; by its motion, the sea will then move naturally. This operation will be much simpler—and I would even say more "natural" among miracles—insofar as making a globe rotate (of which we see so many others moving) is less difficult than making an immense mass of water go forward and backward, faster here and slower there, rising and falling more in one place and less in another, and in some places not at all, and performing all these diverse movements within the same vessel that contains it. Furthermore, these would be many different miracles, whereas the other is but one. Add to this that the miracle of making the water move would necessarily draw another in its wake: the miracle of keeping the Earth steady against the impulses of the water, which would be powerful enough to make it wobble now toward this side and now toward that, if it were not miraculously held still.*

**SAGREDO.** *Please, Mr. Simplicio, let us suspend our judgment for a while before sentencing this new opinion—which Mr. Salviati wishes to explain to us—as vain. Let us not group it so quickly with the old, ridiculous ones. As for the miracle, let us likewise resort to it only after we have heard the arguments contained within natural limits; although, to speak my mind, all the works of Nature and of God appear miraculous to me.*

**SALVIATI.** *And I hold the same view; nor does saying that the natural cause of the tides is the movement of the Earth preclude this from being a miraculous operation. Now, resuming our reasoning, I repeat and affirm that it has been unknown until now how the waters contained within our Mediterranean basin <note>The "Mediterranean basin" here refers generally to the enclosed seas known to the speakers, including the Adriatic.</note> can make those movements we see them make, so long as the basin and containing vessel itself remains immobile. What creates the difficulty and renders this matter inextricable are the things I shall say next, which are observed daily. Therefore, take note:*

Furthermore, if this water comes through the Strait, there remains the other difficulty: how is it led to rise so much here in such remote parts, without first rising to a similar or greater height in the closer parts? In short, I do not believe that either obstinacy or subtlety of wit can ever find a remedy for these difficulties, nor consequently sustain against them the stability of the Earth while remaining within natural limits.

# Of Galileo.

... is waiting to hear in what manner these wonders can follow without hindrance from the motions already assigned to the earth.

<margin>
Natural and true effects follow without difficulty.
</margin>

**SALV.** Since these effects must come as a consequence of the movements that naturally belong to the earth, it is necessary not only that they find no resistance or hindrance, but that they follow easily—and not only follow with ease, but with necessity. Indeed, it must be impossible for them to happen in any other way, for such is the property and condition of natural and true things. Having established, then, the impossibility of being able to give a reason for the movements perceived in the waters while simultaneously maintaining the immobility of the vessel that contains them, let us proceed to see if the mobility of the container can itself produce the effect conditioned in the manner that is observed to follow.

<margin>
Two sorts of movements of the containing vessel can make the waters contained therein rise and fall.
</margin>

Two sorts of movements can be conferred upon a vessel by which the water contained in it would acquire the faculty to flow within it, now toward one end, now toward the other, and there now to rise and now to fall. The first would be when now one, now the other of these ends is lowered; for then the water, flowing toward the inclined part, would alternately rise and fall in this end and that. But because this rising and falling is nothing other than moving away from and approaching the center of the earth, such a sort of movement cannot be attributed to the concavities <note>The basins of the seas and oceans.</note> of the earth itself, which are the vessels containing the water; the parts of these vessels, by whatever motion might be attributed to the terrestrial globe, can neither approach nor move away from its center.

<margin>
Concavities of the earth cannot approach or move away from its center.
</margin>

The other sort of movement is when the vessel moves (without tilting at all) with a progressive motion that is not uniform, but changes speed, sometimes accelerating and other times slowing down. From this irregularity, it would follow that the water—contained in the vessel but not fixedly attached like its other solid parts, but rather, due to its fluidity, almost separate and free, and not obliged to follow all the changes of its container—would, upon the slowing of the vessel, retain part of the impetus <term>impetus: the force or energy with which a body moves</term> already conceived and flow toward the forward part, where it would necessarily rise. Conversely, when new speed is added to the vessel, the water, by retaining part of its slowness and staying somewhat behind before becoming accustomed to the new impetus, would remain toward the rear part, where it would rise somewhat. Which

<margin>
Progressive and unequal motion can make the water contained in a vessel flow.
</margin>

# Fourth Dialogue

We can more clearly declare and manifest these effects to the senses with the example of one of those barges <note>original: "Barche"</note> which continually come from Lizzafusina <note>A landing point on the Venetian mainland near the mouth of the Brenta canal.</note> full of fresh water for the use of the City. Let us imagine, then, such a barge coming with moderate speed through the Lagoon, placidly carrying the water with which it is filled; but then, either by running aground or by some other impediment placed against it, it is notably slowed down. The contained water will not, however, lose the impetus it has already acquired in the same way as the barge; instead, preserving it, the water will run forward toward the prow, where it will notably rise, while sinking at the stern. But if, on the contrary, a new speed is added with a notable increase to the same barge in the middle of its placid course, the contained water—before becoming accustomed to it—will retain its slowness and remain behind, that is, toward the stern, where it will consequently rise, while sinking at the prow. This effect is indubitable and clear, and can be experimented with at any hour; in which I want us to note for now three particulars. The first is that to make the water rise in one of the extremities of the vessel <note>original: "vafo" (vaso); here referring to the container or barge.</note>, there is no need for new water, nor for it to run there from outside the other extremity. The second is that the water in the middle does not rise or sink notably, unless the course of the barge were extremely fast and the impact or other restraint that held it back were very forceful and sudden; in which case all the water might not only run forward, but for the most part jump out of the barge. The same would also happen if, while it was walking slowly, a most violent impetus suddenly overtook it; but when a moderate retardation or incitement overtakes its quiet motion, the parts in the middle (as I have said) rise and sink unobservably; and the other parts, according as they are nearer to the middle, rise less, and the more distant ones rise more. The third is that while the parts around the middle undergo little change in rising and sinking compared to the waters at the extreme ends, they conversely run much further forward and backward in comparison to the extremes. Now, my Lords, what the barge does in respect to the water contained by it, and what the contained water does in respect to the barge its container, is exactly the same as what the Mediterranean basin <note>original: "vafo Mediterraneo"</note> does in respect to the waters contained by it, and what the contained waters do in respect to the Mediterranean basin, their container. It follows now that we demonstrate—

<meta>catchword: demonstrate,</meta>

# On Galileo. 419

<margin>
The parts of the terrestrial globe accelerate and decelerate in their motion.
</margin>
...let us show how, and in what manner, it is true that the Mediterranean, and all other gulfs, and in short all parts of the Earth move with a notably irregular motion, even though no movement other than a regular and uniform one is assigned to the globe as a whole.

*SIMPLICIO:* At first glance, to me—who am neither a mathematician nor an astronomer—this has the appearance of a great paradox. If it were true that while the movement of the whole is regular, that of the parts (remaining always joined to their whole) could be irregular, the paradox would destroy the axiom which affirms that *the nature of the whole and of the parts is the same* <note>original: "eandem esse rationem totius, & partium"</note>.

*SALVIATI:* I shall demonstrate my paradox, and to you, Master Simplicio, I shall leave the task of either defending the axiom from it or bringing them into agreement. My demonstration will be brief and very easy, depending on the matters discussed at length in our past arguments, without introducing even a single syllable for the sake of the ebb and flow <note>The "ebb and flow" refers to the tides.</note>.

<margin>
Demonstration of how the parts of the terrestrial globe accelerate and decelerate.
</margin>
We have said there are two motions attributed to the terrestrial globe. The first is the annual motion made by its center along the circumference of the great orbit <term>Great Orbit: the Earth's path around the Sun</term> under the Ecliptic according to the order of the signs—that is, from West toward East. The other is made by the same globe revolving around its own center in twenty-four hours, and this likewise from West toward East, though around an axis somewhat inclined and not equidistant to that of the annual conversion. From the composition of these two movements, each uniform in itself, I say there results an irregular motion in the parts of the Earth. So that this may be more easily understood, I shall explain it by drawing a figure. First, around center A, I shall describe the circumference of the great orbit B.C. Within this, having taken any point B, we shall describe around it as a center this smaller circle DEFG, representing the terrestrial globe. We shall understand this globe to travel through the entire circumference of the great orbit with its center B from West toward East <note>original: "da Ponente verso Leuante"</note>—that is, from part B toward C. Furthermore, we shall understand the terrestrial globe to turn around its own center B, also from West toward East, following the succession of points DEFG in the space of twenty-four hours.

The parts of a circle moved regularly around its own center move at different times with contrary motions.

### Fourth Dialogue

*...under Equilibrium, but propelled by its own impetus <note>original: "impeto"; the momentum or force of a moving body</note> it will overshoot it, rising in the part where it was previously lower; nor will it stop here, but returning back again with more repeated reciprocations of flow, it will give us a sign that it does not wish to be suddenly reduced from a conceived velocity of motion to the deprivation of it and to a state of rest, but wishes to be reduced to it successively, failing little by little, slowly; in exactly that way that we see any weight hanging from a cord, after having been once removed from its state of rest—that is, from the perpendicular—return to it and settle there by itself, but not before it has overshot it many times this way and that with its alternating runs and returns.*

<margin>In shorter vessels the reciprocations are more frequent.</margin>

*The second accident to be noted is that the reciprocations of movement just now declared are made and replicated with greater or lesser frequency—that is, in shorter or longer times—according to the different lengths of the vessels containing the waters; so that in shorter spaces the reciprocations are more frequent, and more rare in longer ones; just as in the same example of pendulous bodies <note>Galileo is drawing a direct analogy between the sloshing of water and the physics of a pendulum</note> we see the reciprocations of those hanging from longer cords are less frequent than those hanging from shorter threads.*

<margin>Greater depth makes the reciprocations of the water more frequent.</margin>

*And here for the third notable point, it should be known that not only the greater or lesser length of the vessel is the cause of making the water perform its reciprocations in different times; but the greater or lesser depth works the same way. And it happens that of waters contained in receptacles of equal lengths but unequal depths, that which is deeper makes its vibrations in shorter times, and the reciprocations of shallower waters are less frequent.*

<margin>The water rises and falls at the ends of the vessel, and runs in the middle parts.</margin>

*Fourth, two effects that the water produces in such oscillations <note>original: "libramenti"; the balancing or swinging motion</note> are worthy of being noted and diligently observed; one is the alternating rising and falling toward this and that extremity; the other is the moving and running, so to speak, horizontally forward and backward. Therefore, the six-hour period is no more proper or natural than those of other time intervals, but is perhaps the most observed because it is the one that applies to our Mediterranean, which for many centuries was the only navigable sea; even though such a period is not observed in all its parts. This is because in some narrower places, such as the Hellespont <note>the Dardanelles</note> and the Aegean, the periods are much shorter and also very different from one another. Because of this variety and its causes, which were incomprehensible to Aristotle, some say that after he had long observed it from certain rocks of Negroponte <note>the island of Euboea</note>, driven by despair, he threw himself into the sea and deliberately drowned himself.

<margin>The reason why some seas, although very long, do not experience ebb and flow.</margin>
In the third place, we shall have a very clear reason why it happens that some seas, although very long, such as the Red Sea, are nonetheless almost entirely exempt from ebbs and flows. This occurs because its length does not extend from East to West, but rather traverses from the Southeast <term>Sirocco: a Mediterranean wind from the southeast</term> toward the Northwest <term>Maestro: the Master wind or Mistral, from the northwest</term>. Since the movements of the Earth are from West to East, the impulses of the waters always strike against the meridians and do not move from parallel to parallel. Therefore, in seas that extend transversely toward the poles and are narrow in the other direction, there remains no cause for ebbs and flows, except by participation with another sea with which they might communicate and which is subject to great movements.

<margin>Why ebbs and flows are greatest at the ends of gulfs and minimal in the middle parts.</margin>
In the fourth place, we will very easily understand the reason why the ebbs and flows are greatest regarding the rising and falling of the waters at the extremities of Gulfs, and minimal in the middle parts; as daily experience shows us here in Venice, located at the extremity of the Adriatic, where commonly such a difference amounts to 5 or 6 feet. But in places of the Mediterranean distant from the extremities, such change is very small, such as at the islands of Corsica and Sardinia, and on the shores of Rome and Livorno, where it does not exceed half a foot. We shall also understand how, conversely, where the rises and falls are small, the currents and returns are great. It is an easy thing, I say, to understand the cause of these accidents, since we have manifest examples of them in every sort of artificially [made] vessel...

# Fourth Dialogue

<margin>Why the flow of water is faster in narrow places than in spacious ones.</margin>
Furthermore, considering in the fifth place how the same quantity of moved water—though moving slowly through a spacious channel—must by necessity flow with great impetus when passing through a narrow place, we shall have no difficulty understanding the cause of the great currents found in the narrow channel that separates Calabria from Sicily. For all the water supported in the eastern part of the sea by the expanse of the Island and the Ionian Gulf, although it descends slowly toward the West due to its vastness, it nevertheless drops rapidly and creates the greatest agitation when constricted in the Bosporus <note>original: "Bosforo"; here referring generally to a narrow strait</note> between Scylla and Charybdis <note>Famous whirlpools and rock hazards in the Strait of Messina, often personified in classical mythology.</note>. The currents must also be very great in the Strait of Magellan, which connects the vast Ethiopic and Southern <note>The Pacific Ocean.</note> Oceans.

<margin>A discussion of some more hidden occurrences observed in the ebbs and flows.</margin>
It follows now in the sixth place that, to account for some of the more hidden and unexpected occurrences observed in this matter, we should make another important consideration regarding the two primary causes of the ebbs and flows <term>flussi e reflussi: the tides</term>, subsequently composing and mixing them together. The first and simplest of these is (as has been said many times) the specific acceleration and retardation of the parts of the earth, from which the waters would have a fixed period of flowing toward the East and returning toward the West within the space of twenty-four hours. The other cause is that which depends on the water's own gravity; once set in motion by the primary cause, the water then seeks to return to equilibrium with repeated oscillations. These are not determined by a single, fixed time, but have as many variations in timing as there are different lengths and depths of the basins and gulfs of the seas. Depending on this second principle, some waters would flow and return in one hour, others in two, four, six, eight, ten, and so on. Now, if we begin to join the primary cause—which has its stable period of twelve hours—with any of the secondary ones which might have a period of, for example, five hours...

<margin>Section 5.</margin>
*it will happen that at certain times the primary cause and the secondary cause <note>Galileo refers to the primary cause as the Earth's dual motion (rotation and revolution) and the secondary causes as the specific local conditions like the length and depth of the sea basins.</note> will agree to make both impulses toward the same direction; and in this conjunction, and so to speak, unanimous conspiracy, the flows will be great. At other times it happens that the primary impulse comes in a certain way to oppose that which the secondary period would bring; and in such a comparison, one of the principles taking away what the other would give, the motions of the waters will be weakened, and the sea will be reduced to a very quiet and almost immobile state. And at other times, according as the same two principles neither entirely oppose each other nor go entirely uniformly, other changes will occur regarding the increase and decrease of the ebbs and flows. It can also happen that two very large seas, communicating through some narrow channel, happen to have—through the mixture of the two principles of motion—one cause of flow at the same time that the other has a cause of contrary movement. In this case, in the channel where these seas communicate, extraordinary agitations occur with opposite movements, and vortices, and most dangerous boilings, of which there are continuous reports and practical experiences. From such discordant movements, depending not only on the diverse positions and lengths, but greatly also on the diverse depths of the communicating seas, there will arise at certain times various commotions in the waters, irregular and unobservable, the reasons for which have greatly disturbed, and still disturb, mariners when they encounter them, without seeing that neither the force of winds nor any other grave alteration of the air could be the cause. Of which perturbation of the air we must, in other accidents, take great account, and take it as a third and accidental cause, powerful enough to greatly alter the observation of the effects depending on the secondary and more essential causes. And there is no doubt that if impetuous winds continue to blow, for example from the East <note>original: "Levante"</note>, they will hold up the waters, prohibiting their ebb: whence, the second and then the third repetition of the flow arriving at the determined hours, they will swell greatly; and thus sustained for some days by the force of the wind, they rise more than usual, causing extraordinary floods.*

We must also ->(and it will be like the seventh problem)<- have awareness of another cause of movement, depending on the great abundance of water from the rivers that go to discharge themselves into seas that are not

# Fourth Dialogue

<margin>The reason why in some narrow channels the sea water is seen to flow always in the same direction.</margin>
...very vast, where in the channels, or straits, that communicate with such seas, the water is seen to flow always in the same direction: as happens in the Thracian Bosphorus <note>The Strait of Istanbul</note> below Constantinople, where the water flows always from the Black Sea toward the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>; because in that Black Sea, due to its shortness, the primary causes of the *ebb and flow* <note>The tides</note> have little efficacy. But on the contrary, as very great rivers discharge into it, and such a great flood of water must pass and pour out through the strait, the current there is quite notable, and always toward the south. Where we must further observe that such a strait and channel, although quite narrow, is not subject to perturbations like the Strait of Scylla and Charybdis <note>The Strait of Messina</note>; because the former has the Black Sea above toward the North, and the Propontis, the Aegean, and the Mediterranean placed below it, though over a long distance toward the South. But as we have already noted, seas, however long they may be from North to South, are not subject to the *ebb and flow*; but because the Strait of Sicily is placed between parts of the Mediterranean that extend for great distances from West to East—that is, according to the current of the *ebb and flow*—the agitations there are very great. They would be even greater between the Pillars <note>The Pillars of Hercules, or Strait of Gibraltar</note> if the Strait of Gibraltar were narrower; and they report those of the Strait of Magellan to be the greatest of all.

This is as much as occurs to me for now to tell you concerning the causes of this first diurnal period of the *ebb and flow*, and its various accidents; if you have anything to propose, you may do so, before we pass to the other two periods, the monthly and the annual.

<margin>An objection is raised against the hypothesis of the Earth's mobility, assumed for the sake of the ebb and flow of the sea.</margin>
SIMPLICIO: It does not seem to me that it can be denied that the discourse you have made proceeds very probably by arguing, as we say, *from supposition* <note>original: "ex suppositione"</note>—that is, assuming that the Earth moves with the two movements attributed to it by Copernicus. But if such movements are excluded, the whole thing remains vain and invalid; and the exclusion of such a hypothesis is quite manifestly pointed out to us by your own discourse. You, with the supposition of the two terrestrial movements, give a reason for the *ebb and flow*; and conversely, reasoning in a circle, from the *ebb and flow* you draw the evidence and confirmation of those same movements. Passing to a more specific discourse, you say that water, being a fluid body and not tenaciously attached to the Earth, is not constrained to obey punctually every one of its movements, from...

Therefore, the air should be much less likely to follow the movements of the Earth. And so, if the Earth moved in that manner, we who inhabit it, being carried by it with such speed, should perpetually feel a wind from the East <note>original: "da Leuante"</note> striking us with intolerable force. Experience daily warns us that this should follow: for if, when riding the post-horse at a speed of only 8 or 10 miles per hour through still air, the meeting of it with our faces feels like a wind striking us with no small force, what should our rapid course of 800 or 1000 miles per hour do against air free from such motion? Yet, we feel nothing of such an occurrence.

<margin>Response to the objection made against the rotation <term>vertigine</term> <note>Literally "vertigo" or "whirling," referring here to the axial rotation of the terrestrial globe.</note> of the terrestrial globe.</margin>
**SALV.** To this objection, which has much apparent merit, I respond that it is true that the air is thinner and lighter, and by its lightness less adherent to the Earth than water, which is so much heavier and more corporeal. However, the conclusion you deduce from these conditions is false—namely, that because of its lightness, thinness, and lesser adherence to the Earth, it should be more exempt than water from following the terrestrial movements, such that its "disobedience" would become sensible and manifest to us who fully participate in those movements. On the contrary, the opposite happens. For, if you remember well, the cause of the ebb and flow of the water assigned by us consists in the water *not* following the inequality of the movement of its vessel, but retaining the impetus previously conceived, without diminishing or increasing it with that precise measure by which it increases or diminishes in its vessel. Because, therefore,

<margin>Water is more suited to preserving a conceived impetus than air is.</margin>
the "disobedience" to a new increase or decrease of motion consists in the conservation and maintenance of the impetus first conceived, that moving body which is more suited to such conservation will also be more adapted to demonstrating the effect that follows as a consequence of such conservation. Now, how much water is disposed to maintain a conceived agitation, even though the cause that impressed it has ceased, is shown to us by the experience of seas highly disturbed by impetuous winds; their waves, even though the air has calmed and the wind ceased, remain in motion for a long time, as the sacred Poet gracefully sang:

### Fourth Dialogue

<margin>
Light bodies are easier to move than heavy ones, but are less capable of preserving motion.

*As the deep Aegean, etc.* <note>A reference to a poetic description of the sea's momentum, likely from Tasso's "Gerusalemme Liberata."</note> *And continuing in such a manner in its commotion depends on the gravity of the water; because, as has been said at another time, light bodies are indeed much easier to be moved than heavier ones, but they are also much less capable of preserving the motion impressed upon them once the moving cause ceases. Thus the air, being in itself extremely thin and light, is most easily movable by any minimal force, but is also most inept at preserving motion once the mover ceases; therefore, as for the air that surrounds the terrestrial globe, I would say that due to its adherence it is carried around no less than the water, and especially that part which is contained by the "vessels," which vessels are the plains surrounded by mountains; and we can much more reasonably affirm that this portion is carried in rotation, snatched up by the roughness of the earth, than that the upper part is snatched up by the celestial motion, as you Peripatetics* <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> *assert.*

<margin>
It is more reasonable that the air is snatched up by the rough surface of the earth than by celestial motion.
</margin>

<margin>
The rotation of the earth is confirmed with a new argument taken from the air.
</margin>

*What I have said so far seems to me a quite competent response to the instance raised by Mr. Simplicio; nevertheless, with a new objection and a new response founded upon a wonderful experiment, I wish to give him superabundant satisfaction and confirm to Mr. Sagredo the mobility of the terrestrial globe. I have said that the air, and in particular that part of it which does not rise above the summits of the highest mountains, is carried around by the roughness of the terrestrial surface; from which it seems to follow as a consequence that if the surface of the earth were not unequal, but smooth and polished, there would remain no reason for it to pull the air along in its company, or at least to lead it with such uniformity. Now, the surface of this globe of ours is not entirely scabby and rough, but there are very large areas that are quite smooth, namely the surfaces of the vast seas, which, being also very far from the ridges of the mountains that might surround them, do not seem to have the power to lead the overlying air with them; and not leading it, one ought to feel in those places that which follows as a consequence.*

SIMPLICIO. *I also wanted to promote this same difficulty, which seems to me to be of great efficacy.*

SALVIATI. *You speak very well, so that Mr. Simplicio, from not feeling in the air that which would consequently happen if this globe of ours went in rotation, you argue for its immobility. But if that which seems to you a necessary consequence should be felt, in fact and by experien—*

# Of Galileo.

...if it were felt, would you accept it as an indication and a sufficiently strong argument for the mobility of the same globe?

**SIMP.** *In this case, you must not speak with me alone, because if that were to happen, and the cause were hidden from me, perhaps it might be known to others.*

**SALV.** *So that with you, one can never win, but is always on the losing side; and therefore it would be better not to play; nevertheless, so as not to abandon the third [participant], I will continue forward. We were saying just now, and I repeat with some addition, that the air, as a thin and fluid body, and not firmly joined to the earth, seemed to have no necessity to obey its motion, except insofar as the roughness of the terrestrial surface snatches it and carries with it a part contiguous to it, which exceeds the greatest heights of the mountains by no great distance; which portion of air should be all the less resistant to the terrestrial rotation <note>original: "conversione terrestre"</note>, as it is filled with vapors, fumes, and exhalations—materials all participating in earthly qualities, and consequently naturally suited for the same movements.*

<margin>The vaporous part near the earth participates in its movements.</margin>

*But where the causes of motion were lacking—that is, where the surface of the globe had large flat spaces, and there was less of the mixture of earthly vapors—there the cause by which the ambient air should totally obey the snatching of the terrestrial rotation would partly cease; so that in such places, while the earth turns toward the East, one should continually feel a wind striking us, blowing from the East toward the West. And such a breeze should be made more sensible where the whirling of the globe is fastest: which would be in the places furthest from the Poles, and near the greatest circle of the diurnal rotation <note>The Equator</note>. But indeed, in fact, experience greatly applauds this philosophical discourse, since in the vast seas, and in those parts far from land and situated under the Torrid Zone <note>The tropics</note>—that is, comprised between the Tropics, where earthly evaporations are also lacking—a perpetual breeze is felt moving from the East, with such constant tenor that ships, thanks to it, travel prosperously to the West Indies; and from the same, setting sail from the Mexican shores, they plow with the same favor through the Pacific Sea toward the East Indies to us, but West to them.*

<margin>A perpetual breeze within the Tropics blows toward the west. Navigations.</margin>

*Whereas, on the contrary, navigations from there toward the East are difficult and uncertain, nor can they be made in any way by the same routes, but one must coast closer to land, to find—*

<margin>Motion of the water depending on the motion of the Heavens.</margin>

# Concerning Galileo.

<margin>It is more probable that the continuous motion of the air and water is explained by making the earth mobile than by making it stable.</margin>

SALVIATI. *It cannot be denied that your argument is ingenious and possesses a good deal of probability; I say probable, however, in appearance, but not in existence and reality. It has two parts: in the first, it accounts for the continuous motion of the Eastern breeze <note>original: "aura Orientale"; referring to the trade winds</note> and also for a similar motion in the water; in the second, it wishes to draw the cause of the ebb and flow <note>The tides</note> from the same source. The first part has (as I have said) some semblance of probability, but it is nonetheless far less than that which we derive from the terrestrial motion; the second is entirely not only improbable, but absolutely impossible and false. And coming*

<margin>It is improbable that the element of fire is carried along by the concave sphere of the Moon.</margin>

*to the first part, where it is said that the lunar concave <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the sphere of the moon was thought to be the boundary of the sublunary world</note> carries away the element of Fire, and all the air down to the summits of the highest mountains, I say first, that it is doubtful whether the element of Fire even exists; but granted that it does, there is great doubt concerning the sphere of the Moon, as well as all the others—that is, whether such solid and vast bodies exist, or whether instead, beyond the air, there extends a continuous expansion of a substance much thinner and purer than our air, through which the Planets go wandering, as is now beginning to be held even by a good portion of the same philosophers. But whether it be in this way or that, there is no reason why Fire, by a simple contact with a surface which you estimate to be most polished and smooth, could be carried around throughout its entire depth by a motion foreign to its natural inclination; as has been extensively proven and demonstrated with sensible experiments by the Assayer <note>original: "il saggiatore"; a reference to Galileo's 1823 work on the scientific method</note>; besides the other improbability of such motion being transferred from the very thin Fire through the much denser air, and from this then into the water. But that a body with a rough and mountainous surface, in turning upon itself, should lead with it the air contiguous to it, and into which its prominences go striking, is not only probable but necessary; and one can always see the experiment of it, though even without seeing it, I do not believe there is an intellect that would doubt it. As for the other part, granted that*

<margin>The ebb and flow cannot depend on the motion of the Heavens.</margin>

*the air and even the water were led by the motion of the Heavens, such motion would nonetheless have nothing to do with the ebb and flow. Because, since from a single and uniform cause nothing can follow but a single and uniform effect, that which one ought to perceive in the water would be a continuous and uniform course from East toward West, and only in that sea which, returning into itself, surrounds the entire globe; but in the seas*

# Concerning Galileo.

*...parts of the lunar month, and at different times of the Solar Year: as if both the Moon and the Sun took part in the work and in the production of such effects. This is something totally repugnant to my intellect, which—seeing that this movement of the seas is a local and sensible <note>Meaning "perceivable by the senses."</note> motion made in an immense mass of water—cannot bring itself to subscribe to "lights," to "temperate heats," to "predominance by occult qualities," and similar vain imaginings. These are so far from being, or being able to be, the causes of the tide, that on the contrary, the tide is the cause of them—that is, the cause of bringing them into brains more suited to loquacity and ostentation than to the speculation and investigation of nature's most secret works. Such people, rather than reducing themselves to uttering that wise, ingenious, and modest phrase,* "I do not know," *rush to let any great extravagance escape from their mouths, and even from their pens. And merely seeing that the same Moon and the same Sun do not operate with their light, their motion, or their great or temperate heat upon smaller vessels of water—indeed, that to make water rise by heat one must bring it almost to a boil—and in short, that we cannot artificially imitate the movements of the tide in any way except by the motion of the vessel: should this not assure everyone that all other things produced as causes of such an effect are vain fantasies, and entirely alien to the truth?*

<margin>
Alterations in effects argue for alterations in the causes.
</margin>

*I say, therefore, that if it is true that for one effect there is only one primary cause, and that between the cause and the effect there is a firm and constant connection, it is a necessary thing that whenever a firm and constant alteration is seen in the effect, there must be a firm and constant alteration in the cause. And because the alterations that happen to the ebbs and flows <note>The tides.</note> in different parts of the year and the month have their firm and constant periods, it is necessary to say that a regulated alteration occurs at those same times in the primary cause of the ebbs and flows.*

<margin>
The causes of the monthly and annual periods of the tides are assigned at length.
</margin>

*The alteration then, which is found at said times in the ebbs and flows, consists in nothing other than their magnitude; that is, in the waters rising and falling more or less, and in flowing with greater or lesser impetus. Therefore, it is necessary that whatever is the primary cause of the ebb and flow increases or diminishes its force at those specific times. But it has already been concluded that the inequality and deformity <note>Irregularity or non-uniformity.</note> of the motion of the vessels containing the water is the primary cause of the tides; therefore, it must be that such deformity, from time to time, correspondingly—*

Of these, the diurnal rotation <note>original: "vertigine diurna"</note>, by sometimes adding to and sometimes subtracting from the annual motion, is what produces the deformity in the composite motion. It follows that if these additions and subtractions were always made in the same proportion relative to the annual motion, the cause of the ebb and flow would certainly continue, but it would occur perpetually in the same manner. However, we need to find the cause for these same ebbs and flows becoming greater or lesser at different times. Therefore, we must (if we wish to retain the identity of the cause) find an alteration in these additions and subtractions that makes them more or less powerful in producing those effects that depend on them. But I do not see how such power or lack of power can be introduced, except by making these same additions and subtractions sometimes greater and sometimes lesser, so that the acceleration and retardation of the composite motion occurs sometimes with a greater and sometimes with a lesser proportion.

*SALVIATI.* I am here to satisfy you. We were reduced to finding in what manner the additions and subtractions of the terrestrial rotation <term>vertigine: the spinning or rotation of the Earth</term> upon the annual motion could be made now with greater and now with lesser proportion; which diversity, and nothing else, could be assigned as the cause of the monthly and annual alterations seen in the magnitude of the ebbs and flows <note>The tides.</note>.

<margin>The proportion of the additions of the rotation over the annual motion can be altered in three ways.</margin>
I consider now how this proportion of the additions and subtractions of the diurnal rotation and the annual motion can be made greater or lesser in three ways. The first is by increasing and decreasing the speed of the annual motion while keeping the additions and subtractions made by the diurnal rotation at the same magnitude; because the annual motion is about three times greater—that is, faster—than the diurnal motion (even considering the great circle), if we increase it further, the additions or subtractions of the diurnal motion will cause less alteration to it. But on the contrary, by making it slower, it will be altered with a greater proportion by that same diurnal motion; in the same way that adding or subtracting four degrees of speed to that which moves at twenty degrees alters its course less than those same four degrees added or subtracted to one moving at only ten degrees. The second way would be by making the additions and subtractions larger or smaller while keeping the annual motion at the same speed; which is as easy to understand as it is manifest that a speed of, for example, 20 degrees is altered more by the addition or subtraction of 10 degrees than by the addition or subtraction of 4. The third way would be when these two are joined together, decreasing the annual motion and increasing...

# On Galileo

delay, deliver us both from this labor.

SALV. I will do my best to overcome my harsh powers of expression, whose dullness will be supplemented by the sharpness of your wit. There are two phenomena whose causes we must investigate: the first concerns the diversities that occur in the ebbs and flows during the monthly period <note>original: "periodo mestruo," referring to the lunar month</note>; and the other pertains to the annual period. First, we shall speak of the monthly, then we shall treat the annual; and it is necessary that everything be resolved according to the foundations and hypotheses already established, without introducing any novelty either in Astronomy or in the Universe for the sake of the tides. Instead, let us demonstrate that for all the diverse phenomena seen in them, the causes reside in things already known and accepted as true and indubitable.

<margin>A most true hypothesis: that revolutions are completed in shorter time in smaller circles than in larger ones; which is explained with two examples.</margin>
I say, therefore, that it is a true, natural, and indeed necessary thing that the same moving body, set in circular motion by the same moving force <term>moving force: "virtù mouente," the internal or external power causing motion</term>, completes its course in a longer time through a larger circle than through a smaller one. This is a truth accepted by all and confirmed by all experiences, of which we shall produce some.

<margin>First example.</margin>
In wheeled clocks, and particularly in large ones, to regulate the time, the craftsmen fit a certain horizontal swinging bar, and at its ends they attach two lead weights. When the timing goes too slowly, by merely bringing said weights somewhat closer to the center of the bar, they make its vibrations more frequent; and conversely, to delay it, it is enough to pull the same weights further toward the ends; because in this way the vibrations become less frequent, and consequently the intervals of the hours are lengthened.

<margin>Second example.</margin>
Here the moving force is the same—namely, the counterweight—the moving bodies are the same lead weights, and their vibrations are more frequent when they are closer to the center, that is, when they move through smaller circles. Let equal weights be suspended from unequal cords, and having been moved from the perpendicular, let them be set free; we will see those attached to shorter cords make their vibrations in shorter times, as those which move through smaller circles. But furthermore: let such a weight be attached to a cord which passes over a nail fixed in the ceiling, and you hold the other end of the cord in your hand; and having given the hanging weight its start, while it is making its vibrations, pull the end of the cord you have in hand so that the weight is gradually raised. You will see, in its rising, the frequency of its vibrations increase, as those which

# Fourth Dialogue

<margin>
Two notable specific phenomena regarding pendulums and their vibrations.

...they continue to move through smaller circles. And here I want you to note two particulars worthy of being known. One is that the vibrations of such a pendulum occur by such necessity under specific determined times, that it is entirely impossible to make them occur under other times, except by lengthening or shortening the cord. You can verify this presently through experience <note>Galileo uses "experience" (esperienza) here in the sense of a controlled experiment.</note> by tying a stone to a string and holding the other end in your hand; try, if by any artifice used, you can succeed in making it go back and forth under any but a determined time, except by lengthening or shortening the string, which you will see is absolutely impossible. The other truly marvelous particular is that the same pendulum makes its vibrations with the same frequency—or with a very small and almost imperceptible difference—whether they are made through very large arcs or through very small ones of the same circumference. I say that if we remove the pendulum from the perpendicular by only one, two, or three degrees, or even if we remove it by 70, 80, or even up to an entire quadrant <note>A "fourth" or "quadrant" refers to 90 degrees.</note>, once left to its own liberty, it will make its vibrations with the same frequency in either case; as much in the first, where it has to move through an arc of 4 or 6 degrees, as in the second, where it has to pass through arcs of 160 or more degrees. This will be seen more clearly by suspending two equal weights from two equally long threads, then removing one from the perpendicular by a small distance and the other by a very large one; once released, they will go and return in the same amount of time, the one through very small arcs and the other through very large ones.

</margin>

And the same phenomena are to be understood for all the other smaller arcs taken from the lowest terminus B upwards.

# Fourth Dialogue

local motion, both of natural moving bodies and of projectiles: a subject treated extensively by our <term>Lyncean Academician<note>A reference to Galileo Galilei himself, who was a member of the Accademia dei Lincei (Academy of the Lynxes).</note></term>. We have a most prompt observation of this from the <term>Medicean Planets<note>The four largest moons of Jupiter (Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto), discovered by Galileo and named in honor of the Medici family.</note></term>, which complete their revolutions around Jupiter in short times. # On Galileo

It is necessarily required to say that when the Moon is at a smaller distance from the Sun—that is, at the time of conjunction <note>The New Moon, when the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun</note>—it must travel through greater arcs of the "great orb" <note>The *orbe magno* refers to the Earth's annual orbit around the Sun in the Copernican system</note> than when it is at a greater distance, namely at opposition and the full moon. This lunar inequality must also be shared by the Earth; for if we imagine a straight line drawn from the center of the Sun through the center of the terrestrial globe and extended to the lunar orbit, this would be the radius of the great orb, in which the Earth, if it were alone, would move uniformly. 

But if we place another body on that same radius to be carried along—positioning it once between the Earth and the Sun, and another time beyond the Earth at a greater distance from the Sun—it is inevitable that in this second case, the common motion of both along the circumference of the great orb (due to the distance of the Moon) will turn out somewhat slower than in the other case, when the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun at a smaller distance. 

So, in this event, exactly what happens in a clock <note>original: *horiuolo*; Galileo is comparing the Earth-Moon system to a pendulum clock</note> occurs: the Moon represents for us that lead weight which is attached sometimes further from the center to make the vibrations of the rod less frequent, and sometimes closer to make them more frequent. From this, it can be made manifest how the annual movement of the Earth in the great orb and under the Ecliptic is not uniform, and how its irregularity derives from the Moon and has its monthly periods and restorations. 

And because it had been concluded that the periodic monthly and annual alterations of the ebbs and flows <note>The tides</note> could not derive from any other cause than from the altered proportion between the annual motion and the additions and subtractions of the diurnal rotation <note>The "diurnal vertigo" or the Earth's daily spinning on its axis</note>, and since such an alteration could happen in two ways—either by altering the annual motion while keeping the quantity of additions fixed, or by changing the size of these additions while maintaining the uniformity of the annual motion—we have already found the first of these two ways. It is founded upon the irregularity of the annual motion, which depends on the Moon and has its monthly periods. It is therefore necessary that, for this reason, the ebbs and flows have a monthly period within which they become greater and smaller. Now you see how the cause of the monthly period resides in the annual motion; and at the same time, you see what the Moon has to do with this business, and how she plays her part without having anything to do with the seas or the waters.

<meta>catchword: Sagr.</meta>

<summary>Galileo explains that the Earth's annual orbit is not perfectly uniform because the Moon acts like a shifting weight on a pendulum, speeding up or slowing down the Earth's progress. This irregularity in the Earth's speed is proposed as the true cause of the monthly tidal cycles, rather than any direct "attraction" from the Moon on the water.</summary>

# Fourth Dialogue

**SAGR.** *If someone who had no knowledge of any kind of stairs were shown a very high tower and asked if they had the heart to reach its supreme height, I believe absolutely that they would say no, not understanding that there was any way to get there other than by flying. But if one showed them a stone no higher than half a cubit* <note>A "braccio" or cubit was a common Renaissance measure of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertips.</note> *and asked if they believed they could step up onto it, I am certain they would answer yes; and they would not deny that they could easily climb it not just once, but 10, 20, or 100 times. Therefore, when the stairs were shown to them—by means of which, with the ease they had already granted, they could reach the place they had just claimed was impossible to arrive at—I believe that, laughing at themselves, they would confess their lack of foresight. You, Mr. Salviati, have guided me so gently from step to step that, not without wonder, I find myself reached with minimal effort at that height where I believed one could not arrive. It is quite true that because the staircase was dark, I did not realize I was approaching or had reached the top until, coming out into the luminous air, I discovered a great sea and a great countryside. And just as in climbing one step there is no fatigue at all, so each one of your propositions seemed so clear to me that, as they added little or nothing new, the gain seemed small or nothing to me; thus the wonder increases in me all the more for the unexpected success of this discourse, which has led me to the understanding of something I considered inexplicable. One difficulty alone remains for me from which I desire to be freed: and this is that if the movement of the Earth together with that of the Moon under the Zodiac* <note>The "Zodiac" refers to the path of the planets against the background of the stars.</note> *are irregular, such irregularity should have been observed and noted by astronomers, which I do not know to have happened. Therefore you, who are better informed than I on these matters, free me from the doubt and tell me how the matter stands.*

<margin>Many things may still remain unobserved in Astronomy.</margin>

It is to be believed that the first observers of the Heavens knew nothing other than a common motion...*

But among all the great men who have philosophized upon such a marvelous effect of nature, I marvel more at Kepler <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), the German astronomer who correctly identified that the moon caused the tides, though Galileo here rejects his "occult" explanation in favor of a mechanical one.</note> than at others; he, being of a free and acute genius, and having at hand the motions attributed to the earth, nevertheless gave ear and assent to the Moon's dominion over the water, and to occult properties, and similar puerilities.*

**SAGREDO** *I am of the opinion that what has happened to these more speculative thinkers is exactly what is happening to me right now: namely, the inability to understand the entanglement of the three periods—annual, monthly, and daily—and how their causes appear to depend on the Sun and the Moon, without either the Sun or the Moon having anything to do with the water itself. To fully understand this business, I require a more fixed and lengthy application of mind, which until now remains quite clouded by the novelty and difficulty of the subject. But I do not despair that by returning to solitude and silence to ruminate on what remains undigested in my imagination, I shall come to possess it. We have, therefore, from the discourses of these four days, great attestations in favor of the Copernican system. Among these, three in particular—the first taken from the stations and retrogradations of the planets and their approaches to and retreats from the earth; the second from the revolution of the Sun upon itself and what is observed in its spots; the third from the ebbing and flowing of the sea—show themselves to be quite conclusive.*

# On Galileo.

**SAGR.** This is not the first time I have heard mention of the **exquisite learning of this Gentleman <note>Referring to the unnamed author, Galileo himself</note>, and how much he shows himself to be an anxious protector of all men of letters; and if this, or any other of his works, shall come to light, we can already be certain that it will be a distinguished thing.**

**SALV.** **Now, because it is time to put an end to our discourses, it remains for me to pray you that if, in reviewing more leisurely the things I have brought forward, you should encounter difficulties or doubts not well resolved, you might excuse my defect—partly for the novelty of the thought, partly for the weakness of my wit, partly for the grandeur of the subject, and finally because I do not pretend, nor have I pretended from others, that assent which I myself do not lend to this fantasy. I could very easily admit this to be a most vain chimera and a most solemn paradox. And you, Mr. Sagredo, although in the discourses we have had you have many times shown with great applause that you remained satisfied with some of my thoughts, I estimate that this has proceeded in part more from their novelty than from their certainty, but much more from your courtesy, which believed and desired, by its assent, to bring me that pleasure which we naturally take from the approval and praise of our own things. And just as your kindness has obliged me to you, so has the ingenuity <note>In this context, "ingenuità" implies a candid or straightforward nature</note> of Mr. Simplicio pleased me. Indeed, his constancy in sustaining with such force and so intrepidly the doctrine of his master <note>Aristotle</note> has made me most affectionate toward him. And as I render thanks to your lordship, Mr. Sagredo, for your most courteous affection, so I ask pardon of Mr. Simplicio if sometimes I have upset him with my too bold and resolute speech; and be certain that I have not done this moved by any sinister affection, but only to give him greater occasion to bring forth lofty thoughts, so that I might make myself more learned.**

**SIMP.** **There is no need for you to offer these excuses, which are superfluous, especially to me, who, being accustomed to finding myself in circles and public disputes, have a hundred times heard the disputants not only grow heated and upset with one another, but even break out into injurious words, and sometimes come very close to blows. As for the discourses we have had, and in particular this last one concerning the reason for the ebbing and flowing of the sea <term>tides: the "flusso e reflusso"</term>, I truly do not remain entirely capable of grasping it; but from whatever very tenuous idea I have formed of it, I confess your thought seems to me well in-**

<meta>catchword: -genious (gegnoſo)</meta>

<summary>The dialogue concludes with Salviati offering a humble defense of his theories as mere "fantasies" and "paradoxes," while the characters exchange formal apologies and thanks for the intellectual debate. Simplicio admits he does not fully understand the theory of the tides but acknowledges its ingenuity.</summary>

<keywords>Galileo, Sagredo, Salviati, Simplicio, tides, scientific method, academic courtesy, Aristotelianism, paradox</keywords>

# Fourth Dialogue of Galileo

*...ingenious than any others I have ever heard, but I do not for that reason consider it true and conclusive; rather, keeping always before my mind's eye a most solid doctrine, which I once learned from a most learned and eminent person <note>A reference to Pope Urban VIII, who insisted that God's omnipotence could produce the tides in ways beyond human logic.</note>, and to which one must necessarily submit, I know that if both of you were asked whether God, in His infinite power and wisdom, could have granted to the element of water that reciprocal motion which we perceive in it in some way other than by making the containing vessel move, I know, I say, that you will reply that He could have, and would have known how to do this in many ways, even ways unthinkable to our intellect. From this I immediately conclude that, this being the case, it would be excessive boldness if anyone should wish to limit and compel the divine power and wisdom to one of his own particular fantasies.*

**SALV.** *An admirable and truly angelic doctrine! To which that other divine precept corresponds most harmoniously, which, while it grants us permission to dispute concerning the constitution of the World, adds to us (perhaps so that the exercise of human minds may not be cut short or grow idle) that we are not to find out the work created by His hands. <note>A paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 3:11, suggesting that man cannot fully fathom God's creation.</note> Let, then, the exercise permitted and ordained to us by God serve to recognize and all the more admire His greatness, the less we find ourselves fit to penetrate the profound abysses of His infinite wisdom.*

**SAGR.** *And this may be the final conclusion of our four-day discussions; after which, if it pleases Signor Salviati to take some interval of rest, it is only right that it be granted to him by our curiosity—on the condition, however, that when it is less inconvenient for him, he returns to satisfy the desire, mine in particular, regarding the problems left behind and recorded by me, to be proposed in one or two other sessions, as agreed. And above all, I shall be waiting with extreme eagerness to hear the elements of the new science of our Academician <note>Referring to Galileo himself, as a member of the Accademia dei Lincei.</note> concerning local motions, both natural and violent. <note>A reference to Galileo's next major work, "Two New Sciences," which would focus on physics and mechanics.</note> And in the meantime, we may, according to our custom, go for an hour to enjoy the breeze in the gondola that awaits us.*

---

->THE END.<-

<summary>The dialogue concludes with Simplicio offering a cautionary theological argument on God's omnipotence, followed by the characters' agreement to meet again to discuss the physics of motion.</summary>
<keywords>Divine wisdom, human intellect, local motion, Venice, gondola, Urban VIII, limits of science</keywords>

# Digitization Reference Page

->**[Technical Image for Digitization]**<-

This page contains technical tools used by the archivist to ensure that the digital copy perfectly matches the physical book in both size and color. 

<image-desc>
A technical setup image used in the digitization process. The background is a dark, textured protective mat. The image contains:
1. A vertical white ruler on the left side (Oregon Rule Co., U.S.A.) with markings for measuring the height of the volume.
2. A horizontal ruler at the top and another partial ruler at the bottom to provide scale for the width.
3. A color calibration target <note>term: "color checker"; a standardized grid of colors used by photographers to ensure the digital image shows colors exactly as they appear in real life</note> featuring a 24-patch grid.
4. A small portion of the green book binding is visible on the far right edge, showing the physical condition of the volume's cover.
</image-desc>

**Technical Vocabulary used in this process:**
*   **Calibration:** The act of adjusting the camera and lighting so that the digital image is a true representation of the original.
*   **Color Checker:** A tool used to calibrate the "white balance" and color accuracy of the digital file.
*   **Digitization Equipment:** The specialized scanners and cameras used to preserve historical manuscripts.

<summary>This page shows the technical calibration tools, including rulers and a color checker, used during the digitization of the 1632 edition to ensure scientific accuracy in the digital reproduction.</summary>
<keywords>calibration, digitization, color checker, preservation, archiving equipment, color accuracy</keywords>
